notes:
19 year-old Michael Donald was chosen at random by two members (Henry Hays, 25, and James L. “Tiger” Knowles, 17) of the United Klans of America in order to make a statement about white supremacy. He was taken into the county side beaten with a tree limb, strangled, and had his throat cut, and then hanged his body from a tree on Herndon St. in a black-white neighborhood of Mobile, across from a house owned by Bennie Jack Hays, Henry Hays’ father. In 1983 Hays and Knowles were arrested and tried: Hays was sentenced to death (electrocuted in 1997) and Knowles to life in prison but paroled in 2010. In 1989, Benjamin Frank Cox, 28, was convicted for being an accomplice to the homicide and sentenced to life in prison. Bennie Jack Hays was indicted for inciting the murder and his first trial ended in a mistrial and before he could be retried, he died of an heart attack. Beulah Mae Donald and the Southern Poverty Law Center sued the UKA in 1984 for “wrongful death” and in 1987 she was awarded seven million dollars, which they didn’t have; it did bankrupt the UKA and she received $51,875 from the sales of the UKA’s headquarters building.

According to the 3/6 Dispatch & News, the body of 21 year-old Willie Joe Sanford, black, a sawmill worker, was found in Limestone Creek; he had been missing since 2 February; “The Negro’s hands and feet had been bound with wire and the body wired to underbrush in the creek bed. ... The mutilated body bore numerous knife wounds and two head injuries that apparently and been inflicted by some sharp instrument.” The 3/13 Dispatch & News notes that no progress had been made in the Sanford case and prints a long statement made by Judge J. K. Whaley to the Grand Jury condemning the killing in very strong language. From the Panama City News, “Hawkinsville, Ga. (UP)—A Pulaski County grand jury today investigated a Negro’s death which a judge described as ‘plainly and simply mob violence.’ Judge John K. Whaley of McRae, in charging the jury Monday said the murder of Willie Joe Sanford should be investigated ‘from stem to stern ... and let the chips fall where they may.’ Sandford’s body was found submerged in Limestone Creek, a few miles from here, on March 1 after he had been missing for nearly a month. the Negro had been stabbed, bound with wire, and tied to undergrowth in the creek. Authorities are seeking a motive for the murder. ‘Whoever mobbed and killed the Negro did your city, your county, your state and the entire Southland a distinct disservice,’ Judge Whaley said. ‘By their conduct they have magnified a trying situation.’ Whaley urged the grand jury to ‘let the world and this mob in particular know we stand for law and order.’” According to the Kingsport News, Sandford was a sawmill worker who had been dead for about 30 days—he disappeared on 2 February and his “knifed body” was found on 1 March, and reports this from Judge Whaley, “Only a frenzied mob could have accomplished it.” The 3/27 Dispatch & News reports that “Clothing Found In Sanford Case” but no other leads. From the Plaindealer, “Hawkinsville, Ga. —Dixie’s split personality has been put on display in this village of 2,200 souls where the violent death of [illegible] to [Willie] Joe Sandford [illegible]. One group of townsfolk whisper in hushed tones that Sanford’s death was a lynching. Another group says that Sandford might have been murdered, but he certainly was not lynched. There are others who maintain that the entire thing is just a ‘whole lot of mess over nothing,’ that Sandford is ‘just another dead n_____.’ The weird story has unfolded here about a month ago when a fisherman, H. H. Vickers, discovered the nude corpse of Sandford stabbed, bludgeoned, trussed-up and tied to undergrowth on the bottom of a creek. Arthur King, a friend of the late Willie Joe, was subsequently held as a material witness and sent ‘up North’ to Macon for safekeeping, where he remained until Friday before the released by Pulaski County Sheriff Hill, who announced, ‘We couldn’t find any evidence in the case, so I didn’t feel in fairness to the man that he should be held any longer.’ Whatever King told his captors has not been revealed. What is more important is the fact that the citizens of Hawkinsville have, seemingly, for the most part shunned the implication that Sandford was a victim of a lynching. However, there are those who think otherwise.”

notes:
According to the Record, “J. C. Farmer, 26, negro, was killed by officers in Wilson [Wilson Co.] Saturday [27th] night after he allegedly ran beserk [sic] and wounded Deputy Sheriff Ves Bissette.” The Herald reports, “Josh Farmer, 27, Negro, ex-GI of near Wilson, was shot to death in a tobacco-field gun battle with ABC Officers Dave Barnes and Joe Beamon late Saturday after Farmer allegedly has wrested Deputy Sheriff Fes Bissett’s gun from him and shot the deputy twice. The ABC officers joined in the search for Farmer after Bissette said the Negro took his gun when he attempted to arrest him at Sims [Wilson Co.] for an alleged disturbance in connection with the slain man’s attempt to board a Trailways bus. Bissette said Farmer shot him twice and then ordered the driver and all passengers out of the bus at gun point, later leaving the scene afoot. Barnes and Beamon said they came upon Farmer in a tobacco path and when, they said, he opened fire on them they returned it, felling Farmer with two shots in the chest. Bisset’s wounds in the hand and leg were not serious.” According to the Plaindealer, “An armed posse of 20 or 25 men led by supposed ABC (alcohol beverage control) officers hunted down and shot to death J. C. Farmer, 20-year-old farmhand who lived with his parents on the Thad Sharpe plantation close to Bailey, a small town near here [Wilson], last Saturday after a fracas between the youth and a constable. ... [description of the altercation] ... A mob was formed and between 20 and 25 armed white men in seven or eight cars began a hunt for the youth. They ambushed him close to his home and killed him while his other, Mrs. Mattie Farmer, looked on from her porch .... Mrs. Farmer said that although the ex-GI still had the constable’s gun, he did not attempt to use it when he was surprised by the mob and shot from ambush. No inquest was held.” From the Press, “Near Bailey in Eastern North Carolina, J. C. Farmer, an ex-GI who tilled a white man’s farm, was shot by a posse by 20 to 30 men in eight cars, while his mother stood helplessly a hundred yards away. Farmer, who worked with his parents on the Thad Sharp farm near Bailey, was lynched after a scuffle with a police who attacked him. .... [Resulting in the cop getting a bullet wound in the hand] ... The posse killed Farmer an hour later.” The Handbook states that this is a suspected lynching by the NAACP around 3 August in Bailey, N. C.; “reputedly shot by an armed mob estimated at 25 white men, after having been accused of shooting a constable in the hand during a scuffle.”

Note: USGS lists a Bailey in Nash Co., which is directly north of Wilson Co., both in eastern NC. Suspected police lynching, or police assisted lynching.

notes:
According to the PBS account, Willie James Howard, 15, sent a Christmas card/letter to a white girl. On 2 January, the girl’s father, Phil Goff and two other white men, went to Howard’s home, captured him, and took him to the Suwanee River where they bound his arms and feet and pushed him in the river. His body was found the next day. Goff claims that Howard jumped into the river in order not to be whipped.

EJI sent their notes: The January 22, 1944 Florida Tattler (Jacksonville) states that “The Facts in the case still remain a mystery, but it was reported that a 17-year-old Negro was lynched after being releases from jail.” The “youthful Negro wrote a love letter to a Live Oak white girl” and “the girl’s father got the letter and had the boy arrested.” The charge was dismissed and he was told to go home, but “It appears as if a pre-arranged scheme was in the air and the boy had gotten only six blocks from the jail when a mob got hold of him and lynched him.” His body was found in a lake face down a few hours later.  17 Year Old Negro Reported Lynched in Live Oak, Florida, Florida Tattler (Jacksonville), Jan. 22, 1944.  This web site also has copies of affidavits signed by the victim’s mother as well as the white men involved that also strongly indicate it qualifies as a lynching: http://www.pbs.org/harrymoore/terror/howard.html.

From the Civil Rights and Restorative Justice Project web site: Willie James Howard was fifteen years old when he was killed by three white men. His crime was to pursue a youthful crush on a white co-worker, Cynthia Goff, who was the same age as Howard. In the Christmas of 1943 Howard sent cards to Cynthia and other employees at the dime store where he worked. He signed Cynthia’s card “with L” (love). It appears Cynthia was upset by the card or told her father about it. On New Year’s Day Howard delivered a second note explaining the card and asking Cynthia not to be mad. At the bottom of the page a few lines were added: “I love your name, I love your voice, for a S.H (sweetheart) you are my choice.” The next morning, January 2, Cynthia’s father Phil Goff and two of his friends came to the Howard home. At gunpoint the men dragged Willie from the arms of his mother. They then collected the boy’s father, James Howard, and drove to an embankment on the Suwannee River. Willie Howard was bound by his feet and hands and made to stand at the edge of the river where, according to his father’s testimony, he was told he could either jump into the river of his own accord or be shot. Willie jumped and drowned. Later that evening Goff and his accomplices provided the sheriff with a signed statement alleging they had taken Willie Howard from his home intending to discipline him. They admitted binding his feet so he would not run away, but claimed that the boy became hysterical and jumped into the river, drowning himself, to avoid a whipping administered by his father. Under threat for his life James Howard signed the statement, supporting Goff’s version of events. Three days later the Howards sold their house and fled to Orlando.

City policeman, Doris Rhodes, arrested Jesse Thornton Saturday afternoon on June 31st [21st] and was carrying him to the city jai., when the boy broke and ran away from Rhodes. ... The death of Thornton, who was lynched by a police-led mob because he had ‘forgotten’ to refer to a white police officer as ‘Mr.’, marked the fifth authenticated lynching this year. ... On June 22, Jesse Thornton, a farm worker, went downtown to a barber shop. ... [in front of the barber shop, a white cop, Doris Rhodes, walked by and Thornton didn’t refer to the officer as ‘Mr. Rhodes’, and Rhodes beat him with his blackjack and was taken toward the jail where Thornton escaped before being apprehended by a mob and dragged into a swamp] ... Shortly shorts were heard. Members of the mob returned from the wooded section near the swamp. Jesse Thornton did not come out.”—his body was discovered in Pataylagga River on 28 June.

From the Civil Rights and Restorative Justice Project web site: “On June 21, 1940, Jesse Thornton fell victim to racial violence when he was lynched by a mob in Luverne, Alabama, Crenshaw County. One day, Jesse Thornton made a trip to the local black barbershop. In typical fashion, Thornton and a few of his acquaintances were standing in front of the barbershop talking. As an officer came along, Thornton said to his friends, “There comes Doris Rhodes, Boys.” Officer Rhodes overheard the remark, turned to Thornton and said, “What did you say?” When Thornton realized that he had been overheard by the officer, he hesitated to make a reply and tried to recant his statement by saying, “Mr. Doris Rhodes.” The officer said, “No you didn’t Nigger.” In response, Thornton said, “I did say Doris Rhodes.” Officer Rhodes immediately struck Jesse with his black jack and knocked him down to the ground. Following the violent attack, Rhodes arrested Thornton and walked him to the local jail. At the jail door, Rhodes slightly relinquished his grasp of Thornton to unlock the jail door and Thornton attempted to get away. By the time he tried to escape, bystanders were already crowding around the jail and began to throw brick, bats, and stones at Thornton to prevent him from running away. Despite the resistance, Thornton attempted to escape again from the rapidly forming mob. As Thornton ran away the second time, five shots were fired at him as he gained ground. He ran for approximately three quarters of a mile before he fell from exhaustion due to the loss of blood. After resting, Thornton made an attempt to continue running when he saw that the mob was still chasing him, however, he gave up in sheer exhaustion as the mob finally captured him. The mob put Thornton in a small truck, carried him to a “dead-end street,” and then dragged him from the truck to a swamp where more shots were reportedly fired. Seven days later, a local fisherman found Thornton’s body eaten by vultures and buzzards in the Patsaliga River near Tuskegee Institute.”

notes:
Howard states that Theodore “Buckie” Young was accused of attacking a white woman in Greenville area. A mob took Young from his mother’s home, and riddled him with bullets—the mob kept his body for two days before giving it to a black mortician. From the Plaindealer, “Greensville, Fla.—(SNS)—Taken into custody by a mob of 40 infuriated white persons the past week end here for undetermined reasons, 36-year-old Theodore Young, son of the well known local minister, Rev. G. W. Young, was shot down in cold blood, his body riddled with bullets. At home Friday [11th] evening about 6:30 o’clock with his mother, Mrs. G. W. Young, the murdered man was mobbed and, before he had time to speak or act in his defense, was ganged and a short time later dropped to death with a barrage of shots fired from shotguns at close range. For two days, the mob refused to allow the dead man’s body to be removed. However, it was turned over to a local colored funeral home early Monday and was buried quietly and unceremoniously.”

The 9/13 World  reports that Finch was shot three times by Det. B. W. Roper as he tried to escape from the cop’s car. Another cop was driving. The 9/14 edition of the World gives a different story. According to Finch’s father, the cops came to his house and took Finch away—he said that there were five cops outside of the house in addition to the cop who took Finch. The father also said that Finch had been badly beaten and shot more than three times. The NAACP was asked to investigate. The 9/20 edition of World gives a small article about Finch being buried in Mt. Zion Church in Maxey’s. In a very brief story, the Constitution reports that Tom Finch was killed by city Detectives J. W. Cody and S. W. Roper while trying to escape after being arrested—he was shot 3 times. Couldn’t find any follow-up in the Constitution. 

Note: interestingly, the Daily World of 12/25 gives another killing of a black man as he tried to escape by Det. Roper. That victim was also accused of attacking a white woman. Based on the C.I.C. report, going to classify this as a probable lynching. Suspected police lynching, or police assisted lynching.

notes:
From the NAACP  “December 4: Laurel, Mississippi: (Memphis, Tenn., Press-Scimitar, December 5) J. B. Grant, 17, was shot to death by a mob. After his body was riddled with more than a hundred bullets, it was tied to an automobile and dragged through the streets, then hanged to a trestle.” From the Times, “Laurel Miss., Dec. 7.—(INS)—Officers were confronted with the apparent lynching of a young Negro whose body was found hanging from a railroad trestle less than half a mile from the Laurel business district. A coroner’s jury decided the young, J. B. Grant, 17-year-old employe of a local tourist camp, had met death ‘by strangulation at the hands of parties unknown.’ The boy’s belt had been used to hang him, officers said.” The Echo report adds nothing. From the Star, “Laurel, Miss., Dec. 5. (U.P.)—The body of a 17-year-old Negro, J. B. Gant, was found hanging from a railroad trestle today. He had been hanged by his own belt. There was little evidence to indicate whether he had been lynched or committed suicide. Negro suicides are extremely rare.” From the Plaindealer, “Laurel, Miss., Dec. 11—(Special)—The State of Mississippi, running true to form staged a pre-Christmas lynching celebration to climax 1936 ... the white ‘citizens’ of Laurel turned out to murder and lynch 17-year-old J. B. Grant. ... According to what information could be received, the usual story was circulated as to the motive behind the action, ‘insulting a white woman.’ ... After riddling the youth with more than a hundred bullets, the body was tied to an auto and dragged through the streets where thousands of white men, women and children cheered madly. At intervals along the route the car dragging the body halted so that little children using their parents’ pistols and guns could pour more lead into the body ....” In a second story on the same page, “Washington, D. C., Dec. 11.—The United States was asked this week to probe the lynching of 17-year-old J. H. Grant who was found hanging from a railway trestle on the outskirts of Laurel, Miss., Saturday [5th].

Note: there are some inconsistencies: the Star and Times report that Grant/Gant was found hung from a railroad trestle but make no mention of bullet wounds or evidence of being dragged.

Moore and two deputies...” Although they mob was unmasked, none of the officers recognized any of the lynchers. The Robesonian reports that Govan “Sweat” Ward was hanged by a mob near Louisburg on the 30th. Ward had been accused of decapitating a prominent farmer with an axe and assaulting two other persons. The NAACP report states that a National Guardsman cut off Ward’s toe “as a souvenir”—this was mentioned in the long Observer account as well.
According to the Henderson Times-News, Govan Ward, 25,—also called Sweat Ward in the news story, was taken from the authorities: “The mob took Ward away from officers four miles out of Louisburg [Franklin Co.] as they were rushing him from Henderson [Vance Co.] to Nashville [Nash Co.] for safekeeping. More than 100 men in cars surrounded Constable E. C. Wrenn and his two deputies and snatched the prisoner. Ward was hurried bak though Louisburg toward the scene of the crime. The mob stopped at a wooded section ten miles out of Louisburg and hung the negro to a tree. Bullets were fired into his head, chest and stomach.” The 7/31 Burlington Times-News states that Govan Sweat Ward attacked a white farmer, Spurgeon Ayscue, white, who fled and then he beheaded 67 year-old Charles G. Stokes, white, farmer.

Note: the NC Death Index lists a Govan Ward, black, age 30, died on 30 July in Franklin Co. The North Carolina Death Certificates list his death by lynching 30 July in Hayesville Township, Franklin Co. The 1920 Franklin Co. census lists a Govan Ward, mulatto, 15, living with his parents Tom, 64, and Fannie, 45, and many siblings in Haynesville. The 1940 Franklin Co. census lists a Spurgeon Ayscue, 29, who was living in Hayesville, Franklin Co. in 1935; 1930 Franklin Co. census lists a Charles G. Stokes, 58, farmer, living at Hayesville in Franklin Co. with his wife Isabella and their children. Charles G. “Charlie” Stokes is buried in the New Bethel Baptist Church Cemetery at Epsom, Vance Co., but Find-A-Grave notes that he died on 30 July in Hayesville Township, Franklin Co.

naacp: Jim Meriweather, 8/22/1935, Lowndes County, Leader of the Sharecroppers Union
notes:
From the NAACP, citing an NAACP investigation, “Jim Meriweather, leader of the Sharecroppers Union and of the cotton pickers strike, was arrested by a sheriff’s posse which took him away and killed him. The posse gave the excuse of “self defense”. From the Eagle, “The deputy sheriff said that Jim Pre[illegible] Meriwether, Negro, was killed near Sandy Ridge yesterday he he broke away from a posse and grabbed a shotgun he had hidden in a ditch. The officers said Meriwether had fired on a Negro woman, wounding her with birdshot, because she went to the cotton fields after being ‘warned’. Another Negro, Jim Lassick, was wounded when fired upon from ambush as he worked in the fields on the Robert Herlong plantation. First reports were that Lassick was killed.” The Star mentions that a black man was killed at Sandy Ridge, but provides no further details. From Kelley, “That evening [apparently 19 August], [Sheriff] Woodruff [of Lowndes Co.] organized a posse which scoured the county, committing atrocities against strikers and nonstrikers along the way. Jim Press Merriweather and his entire family, all union members, were among the posse’s first victims. ... Then on the night of August 22, Jim Merriweather was captured by the posse, accused of shooting a strike breaker, and summarily executed. According to police reports, Merriweather miraculously broke away from four fully armed men, jumped into a nearby ditch, and picked up a shotgun which he had allegedly planted there earlier. When he fired at the ‘officers’, claimed Sheriff Woodruff, his captors retaliated and killed him. Forcing their way into Phillip Merriweather’s home, the mob continued its reign of terror against the rest of the family. Phillip broke from his captors and escaped down an embankment, but Jim’s wife, Annie Mae, was not so lucky. She was stripped, possibly raped, and beaten with a knotted rope while she hung from a wooden beam.” It is clear from Kelley’s analysis of the activities in Lowndes Co. that “Sheriff Woodruff and his posse” was much more akin to a mob on a rampage against the SCU. The Afro American reports that Ed Bracy, Jim Merriweather, and Smith Watkins were killed by mobs in “Lowens [Lowndes Co.]” for participating in the sharecroppers strike. “The first victim was Smith Watkins, an alleged organizer, who was slain while en route to the jail when he allegedly jumped out of the posse car. He was shot down in cold blood. The second man slain was Ed Bracy, who was shot in the back when he attempted to escape from his home, when two carloads of men drove up to the house.

naacp: Joseph Shoemaker, 12/9/1935, Tampa, White, Political activities
notes:
According to Howard, Shoemaker and two others, Sam Rogers and Eugene Poulnot, were arrested on 11/30 by the police and questioned, and then released. They were abducted right in front of the police station and taken ten miles east of Tampa. Rogers were stripped, tied over a log, flogged, and hot tar poured on the wounds, his stomach, and his genitals; Poulnot was flogged and then tar and feathered; Shoemaker was flogged to the point of mutilation. Rogers and Poulnot lived but Shoemaker died in the hospital as a result of his flogging and mutilation on 9 December. Ingalls gives the location as Brandon [Hillsborough Co.], 14 miles east of Tampa. Later six police were indicted for kidnapping but were found not guilty. The Express reports that Shoemaker was the most seriously injured; “His doctor said the man was ‘horribly mutilated’ and added, ‘I wouldn’t beat a hog the way that man was whipped.’” W. F. Poulnot was in serious condition and Sam Rogers was recovering. The Light and the Herald report that Shoemaker died on the night of the 9th from his injuries from the flogging, tarring and feathering. The Eagle notes that a grand jury is investigating Shoemaker’s death. The News reports that five police officers have been charged with the murder of Shoemaker.

Note: Shoemaker was tortured and beaten on 30 November but didn’t die until 9 December.

Six men have been arrested in connection with the lynching. The News states that three men have been arrested in conjunction with the lynching of Scott. “Officers ... said the three were stragglers who were captured after the main body of lynchers had scattered.” Scott’s body was found hanging, and riddled, “two miles south of VIcco tonight about two hours after he was removed by a mob from the Perry county jail.” The Times reports the mob size as 150-200 men and that Scott was hanged and shot in a graveyard in Knott County—the same report appears in the Advocate. Moving him that distance suggests a Knott Co. mob. It is clear that Johnson was attacked by Scott in Hazard on Saturday night but that doesn’t mean that Johnson was from Perry Co. notes:
From the 6/9 Times, “Huntsville, Tenn., June 9 —Armed men forced their way into the Scott county jail last night and carried off Jerome Boyett and Harvey Winchester, both held on murder charges. Winchester’s body, riddled with bullets, was found today about 200 feet from the road between Huntsville and Helenwood [both in Scott Co.]. Boyett has not been found. Boyett was charged with the murder of Sheriff Winningham and his son of Pickett county about three weeks ago. ... Winchester, officers said, was charged with the murder of Namon Perry and Esker_ Thompson at Winfield [Scott Co.] several months ago. Soon after Sheriff Winningham and his son were slain, Boyett’s father was taken into custody and a reward offered or his son. The elder Boyett was released from jail when he said he thought he could locate his son. The next day his body was found and his death has remained a mystery.” The News reports that “The body of [Jerome] Boyett was found late yesterday 150 yards back n the woods from where Winchester’s body was found early in the day. Indications were that Boyett, after being stripped naked, had been turned loose and shot to death as he darted in the moonlight through the woods.” From the Enquirer-Sun, “Huntsville, Tenn., June 9.—(AP)—Riddled with bullets, the body of Jerome Boyette, who with Harvey Winchester, a fellow prisoner, was taken from the Scott county jail last night by armed men, was found today forty feet from where the bullet-pierced body of Winchester had been found earlier. Both were white prisoners and held in jail on murder charges. ... Boyette was in jail charged with the murder of Sheriff G. B. Willingham and his son, Floyd Willingham, of Pickett county and Winchester was charged with the murder of Namon Perry and Esker Thompson at Winfield [Scott Co.]. ... Sheriff Esau Lexton said the prisoners were taken from jail near midnight last night by 25 masked, armed men, who overpower the jailer and took his keys.”

TN. The 1930 census lists Ransom Boyatt/Bayatt, age 58, and his wife Poppie, age 45, and children in Scott Co.; Gerome Bayatt/Boyatt, age 19, is living with his nephew, Mitchel Burk, in Scott Co. Neither Ransom or Jerome/Gerome appear in the 1940 Tennessee census.

(AP)—A negro accused of attacking an aged white farm woman was dragged from the Somerset county jail tonight by a mob of more than 1,000 men, women and children, and was lynch to his neck, and pulled him behind an automobile through the main streets of the town. As the mob made its slow progress toward the scene of the hanging, various members leaped at the negro, screaming and cursing, and repeatedly knocked him down. He apparently was dead when the crowd finally reached the oak tree. Later, the body was cut down and taken to the public square where it was burned. The rope was cut into small pieces and distributed among members of the mob as souvenirs. ... In breaking into the jail, the mob overpowered a detail of 25 state police who had been sent to Princess Anne to guard Armwood. ... The hanging occurred next to the home of Judge Robert F. Duer, who had attempted to dissuade the crowd early tonight when it first formed at the jail. ... The march to the final scene of the hanging was wild in the extreme. The mob members seemed crazed, continually leaping on the negro, even after he fell to the ground and was unable to rise. One boy, about 18 years of age, slashed the negro’s ear almost off with a knife.” The Star reports that the state police had used tear gas, which stopped the mob for a while; in a second report in page 2, the mob size is estimated as between 1000 and 2000, and the reports gives more details. From the Observer, “Warrenton, Va., July 19.—(AP)—Fauquier police and citizens sought today Shadrack Thompson, former negro convict, for an assault upon a white woman, Mrs. Henry L. Baxley, and her husband yesterday morning. See also the 7/20 Leader. The body, found by a white man, employed on the Miller place, about 200 yards from his home in a dense undergrowth, was badly decomposed and before officers, summoned from here, could reach the spot, a large crowd had gathered and had attempted to set fire to it. Officers and a physician who went to the scene last night expressed belief the negro’s death was by his own hands. Police said it was their opinion that when the chase became so hot immediately after the attack, the negro fled and hanged himself. Mr. and Mrs. Baxley were attacked the morning of July 12 ....” The essentially the same story appears in the 9/16 Leader, Mail, Herald, and other newspapers. The Afro-American includes this as a lynching in 1932 and gives the location as Warrenton. Interestingly, the Bee reports, dateline Warrenton, Va., Dec. 28, that “Fauquier county law enforcement officers” were protesting the listing of Thompson’s death as a lynching by the NAACP; the commonwealth’s Attorney, C. W. Carter, said “... the rope from which the negro was found hanging was known to have been in his possession previously.”—but that doesn’t preclude him being hanged with his own rope by others.

notes:
From the Advocate, “Senatobia, Miss., Oct. 17. (AP)—Three negroes were slain and two other probably fatally wounded near here last night by a posse hunting Jesse Williams, 45, another negro, who officers said, shot and killed Deputy Sheriff Walker Williams, Sunday afternoon. County Jailer J. T. Dixon said that when the posse surrounded the home of a negro, Judge Crawford, shortly before midnight, two shots were fired from the house. The posse members sent several shots into the home, killed Crawford and two of his sons, and wounding Crawford’s wife and another son. Details of the shooting were lacking today since the posse was in the Tate county hills, west of here, continuing their search for Williams. ... Deputy Williams, a son of Sheriff A. C. Williams, was slain with his own gun, the jailer said after he had arrested the negro Williams, on a robbery charge.” Essentially the same story appears in the Herald. According to the Register-Republic, the 75 man posse was led by Sheriff C. A. Williams; the posse approached the Crawford home, looking for the murderer and then “Crawford, answering the posse’s peremptory summons, refused to admit the men, opening fire with a pistol. Max Lloyd, a deputy, fell, struck in the head by a bullet from the Negro’s gun. The posse returned fire, riddling the frame dwelling. Crawford, his wife, Annie, two sons, one 14 years of age, and a son-in-law feel fatally wounded under the savage barrage of pistol and rifle fire. Williams, the negro slayer, was not found in the residence.
From the World, “Memphis, Tenn., Oct. 24.—Judge Crawford, who with two of his sons were shot to death by an angry Mississippi posse last Sunday night, a week ago, during a search for a Negro slayer of a deputy sheriff near Senatobia [Tate Co.], Miss., was a law abiding citizen and a minister of the gospel, according to Rev. B. F. Graham of this city who is personally acquainted with the Crawfords. Rev. Graham, who spent his childhood days in Senatobia, added further that he has known all the parties connected with the North Mississippi tragedy, Sheriff A. C. Williams of Tate county, his slain son, Deputy Walker Williams, and the hunted Negro slayer, Jesse Williams, 45, as well as the Crawfords. ... Judge Crawford and his family were living at the time the posse, in search for the colored slayer, came and riddled their home with bullets.” The Times-Picayune reports that the District Attorney will investigate the killing of three men at the Crawford home—Jesse Williams has not been caught but his 15 year-old son, Steve, was taken to a different jail for safekeeping. The News states “The posse then opened fire on the negroes, killing four of them and probably fatally wounding a fifth. Judge Crawford, Algie [Algiers] Crawford, a son, and another son of Crawford [Earnest], and Tom Scott, a son-in-law of Crawford, died of their wounds. Annie Crawford, the wife, is expected to die. ... Williams’ daughter [Mattie] and niece are in jail here [Senatobia].” According to the Defender, dateline Senatobia, 28 October, Judge Crawford and six of his family were killed by lynchers: Judge Crawford, his wife, Annie Crawford, three sons, a daughter, and his son-in-law [seven victims] were shot by a “... mob of blood-thirsty white men, women and children”; “Each of the seven persons had been shot at least six times. Fingers had been cut from most of the dead, evidently by those who wished to have souvenirs of the lynch hunt.”

notes:
From the Advocate, “Senatobia, Miss., Oct. 17. (AP)—Three negroes were slain and two other probably fatally wounded near here last night by a posse hunting Jesse Williams, 45, another negro, who officers said, shot and killed Deputy Sheriff Walker Williams, Sunday afternoon. County Jailer J. T. Dixon said that when the posse surrounded the home of a negro, Judge Crawford, shortly before midnight, two shots were fired from the house. The posse members sent several shots into the home, killed Crawford and two of his sons, and wounding Crawford’s wife and another son. Details of the shooting were lacking today since the posse was in the Tate county hills, west of here, continuing their search for Williams. ... Deputy Williams, a son of Sheriff A. C. Williams, was slain with his own gun, the jailer said after he had arrested the negro Williams, on a robbery charge.” Essentially the same story appears in the Herald. According to the Register-Republic, the 75 man posse was led by Sheriff C. A. Williams; the posse approached the Crawford home, looking for the murderer and then “Crawford, answering the posse’s peremptory summons, refused to admit the men, opening fire with a pistol. Max Lloyd, a deputy, fell, struck in the head by a bullet from the Negro’s gun. The posse returned fire, riddling the frame dwelling. Crawford, his wife, Annie, two sons, one 14 years of age, and a son-in-law feel fatally wounded under the savage barrage of pistol and rifle fire. Williams, the negro slayer, was not found in the residence.
From the World, “Memphis, Tenn., Oct. 24.—Judge Crawford, who with two of his sons were shot to death by an angry Mississippi posse last Sunday night, a week ago, during a search for a Negro slayer of a deputy sheriff near Senatobia [Tate Co.], Miss., was a law abiding citizen and a minister of the gospel, according to Rev. B. F. Graham of this city who is personally acquainted with the Crawfords. Rev. Graham, who spent his childhood days in Senatobia, added further that he has known all the parties connected with the North Mississippi tragedy, Sheriff A. C. Williams of Tate county, his slain son, Deputy Walker Williams, and the hunted Negro slayer, Jesse Williams, 45, as well as the Crawfords. ... Judge Crawford and his family were living at the time the posse, in search for the colored slayer, came and riddled their home with bullets.” The Times-Picayune reports that the District Attorney will investigate the killing of three men at the Crawford home—Jesse Williams has not been caught but his 15 year-old son, Steve, was taken to a different jail for safekeeping. The News states “The posse then opened fire on the negroes, killing four of them and probably fatally wounding a fifth. Judge Crawford, Algie [Algiers] Crawford, a son, and another son of Crawford [Earnest], and Tom Scott, a son-in-law of Crawford, died of their wounds. Annie Crawford, the wife, is expected to die. ... Williams’ daughter [Mattie] and niece are in jail here [Senatobia].” According to the Defender, dateline Senatobia, 28 October, Judge Crawford and six of his family were killed by lynchers: Judge Crawford, his wife, Annie Crawford, three sons, a daughter, and his son-in-law [seven victims] were shot by a “... mob of blood-thirsty white men, women and children”; “Each of the seven persons had been shot at least six times. Fingers had been cut from most of the dead, evidently by those who wished to have souvenirs of the lynch hunt.”

The American reports, “Sherman, May 10.—(Saturday)—A mob ruled Sherman yesterday, burned its courthouse, killed a negro who confessed to having attacked a white woman, dragged his body through the streets, and early this morning made him a funeral pyre of a two-story drug store in North Sherman, negro district. The negro was George Hughes, 41, who was to be sentenced Friday in district court for his crime. He was being guarded in court by four Texas rangers and Grayson county peace officers, under orders from Gov. Dan Moody to hold their prisoner but avoid trouble. The mob sought to take him from the officers shortly after noon, but failed. Three rushes at the courthouse were repelled with tear gas bombs. On the fourth rush, the mob dumped ten gallons of gasoline in the basement of the building, applied the torch, and then chopped up fire department equipment to prevent any effort at extinguishing the flames. Everyone in the courthouse escaped but the negro, who was locked in the district clerk’s vault for safe keeping when the mob fight began. His body was found in the vault when it was forced open at midnight. The mob leaders [names/ages listed] and at least four soldiers were injured in a clash between national guardsmen and the mob late in the day.” In a second story, same page, it’s reported that Hughes did not die of burns but was killed when the vault door was dynamited, blowing the heavy door in and striking Hughes, “...there was a large hole in the side of the negro’s head which indicated the door, blown inward by the force of the blast, had struck him and probably killed him, indicating that it appeared the negro  was stranding up across the valut from the door when it was blown from its hinges. The belief that he was alive until the explosion was strengthened by the fact thgat the body was not in the slightest stiff, indicating that if Hughes had been dead before the blast it was for a very short ime. The door weihed several hundred pounds and was blown the lentht of the valut. Several bars toward the black of the valut were broken off by the impact and tables inside were overturned.” After Hughes body was recovered it was dragged behind a car toward the black section of town, North Sherman, placed in a building housing several businesses, and torched. The Herald gives the mob size as “several hundred”; the Sun says 700.

naacp: Johnnie Cornish, 5/6/1922, Kirvin, Negro, Murder of 17 year old white girl, Burned
notes:
The News reports, dateline Kirvin, 6 May, that “Snap” Curry, John Cornish, and Mose Jones, all black men, were “... mutilated and then burned alive, one after another, at daylight here his morning by a mob estimated at 500; they were accused of assault and murder of 17 year-old Eula Ausley on the 4th; they were jailed in Fairfield [Freestone Co.] but were taken by the mob back to Kirvin arriving around 4:00 a.m.; “A large plow was obtained and placed on the square. ... Curry was first brought to the plow and strapped and chained to the iron seat. He was then mutilated and crude oil and kerosene poured over him. He then cried out to burn the other two negroes and started singing as the match was applied to the pyre. Jones and Cornish did not confess to participation in the crime. They were also mutilated before being burned.” According to the Gazette, the victims were: Snap Terry, 26; Morse Jones, 44, and John Cornish, 19. The Post notes that “... a number of women and children witnessed the close of the executions.” The Statesman lists seven persons lynched in May, four of which were connected to the rape/murder of Eula Ausley: Snap Curry, Mose Jones, and John Cornish burned in Kirvin on 6 May, and Shed Green who was hanged at Kirvin on 7 May. The Sun gives their ages as: Mose Jones, 43; Snap Currie, 20; and Johnnie Cornish, 18; and says “Mose Jones probably suffered the most. He was thrown on the fire several times and would roll off to one side to lay there and groan with pain until he was against [again?] cast into the torturing flames to gain added misery. After five unsuccessful attempts, he was placed permanently on the burning time and lay there, the flesh of his legs, his waist and hips a charred mass, still conscious and declaring he knew nothing of the affair for which he was dying. Losing total control of the lower part of his body, the negro used his hands to wipe the sweat from his blistered face and to tear away the collar of his shirt that had caught flame. ... For several minutes he lay there, struggling with his hands to ward off the approaching death. Some one in the crowd grew tired of the ghostly performance and threw gasoline on the wood and man. ... Another dash of gasoline, another weird groan followed by a crumpling of the elbows and the man fell chest down in the pit of the fire and related his life to avenge another. The men were burned individually, Currie and Jones being mutilated before being pitched to the fire.” The Herald lists the victims as J. H. Varney, Mose Jones, and “Snap” Curry, as does the Times.

Note: Shadrick/Shattucks/Shadow Green, aka Tom Cornish, was lynched in Freestone Co. on 7 May in connection with this murder/rape.

notes: Based on the Times-Picayune reports, F. Watt Daniel and Thomas F. Richards and three other men (relatives) were taken from Richard’s garage on the 24th by 20-30 masked men. The relatives were released and they assumed that Daniel and Richards would be released after a whipping. The mob is referred to as a “vigilance group”. Daniel and Richards were apparently from fairly well-to-do families: Daniel’s father had been a planter and Richard’s owned his own garage. On 12/22 their bodies were dragged from a lake. Both men had been badly tortured: their heads and hands had been cut off, their brains extracted, the missing limbs/head apparently were removed by some sort of machinery, the bones in their arms and legs were broken at 3.5 inch intervals, the skulls were crushed and all their ribs broken, and they had been castrated. Autopsy reports showed that they were alive during all of the above. Daniel’s watch was recovered and it had stopped at 10:00. On 12/27, the former mayor of MerRuge, Dr. McKoin (MD) was arrested with several other KKK members, who apparently was the leader. Possible motives for the lynching are a fight McKoin had with Richards when the KKK was using a room attached to his garage for a meeting. On 12/27, McKoin denied killing the men and said “all I know is that both men who were killed were on the bad side—the side of bootleggers, gunmen, and men who associated with negro women.” From the Advertiser, “Old Age Claims Klan Chief Once Held For Murder. Monroe, La., Aug. 20.—(AP)— Death of old age yesterday claimed Capt. John K. Skipwith, veteran of the War Between the States and the chief of the Morehouse Parish Ku Klux Klan a decade ago when its members were accused of kidnapping and murdering two men at Mer Rouge. National guardsmen patroled the town of Bastrop at the court hearing but there were no conviction. The picturesque captain, whose hair was white at the time he was leader of his klan group, known as a ‘wrecking crew,’ died at the age of 85. ... The disappearance in 1922 of Watt Daniels and Thomas F. Richards, after they were said to have been kidnaped with ‘Tot’ Davenport and Daniel’s father by a hooded band, brought State and Federal investigation of klan activities in that section. Davenport and the elder Daniels were released by their abductors. Fragments dynamited from a lake near Mer Rouge were said to have been parts of the bodies of the two missing men, but was not officially established.”

notes:
From the Tribune, “Vicksburg, Miss., Dec. 10.—One white man, whose name officers have not learned, Jake Stevens, a negro labor agent, and three other negroes are reported to have been fired on and killed at Duckport, La., by a crowd of men on the wharf there, who objected to the negroes leaving to work on a plantation near Vicksburg, according to a report by William Wooten, a fisherman and A. Memes Dangerfield, a negro, who were bought to a hospital here early today suffering from gunshot wounds they say received in the attack. According to Wooten’s statement, he took his launch with a small barge attached to Duckport to get the negro laborers, who had been engaged by Jake Stevens. When the negroes began to board the barge, Wooten said, about twenty men on the levee began firing at them. He cut his launch and made his escape but was wounded when a short distance from the bank. He was picked up and brought here. The trouble was said to have arisen over objection by Duckport citizens to the leaving of negro labor.” Essentially the same appears in the Journal (and other newspapers) with a Vickburg, 9 December dateline. The Appeal states that some of the reports of the Duckport murders are conflictual but all agree that an unknown white man, Will Crofton, black, and Jake Stevens, black, were killed and three men (two white and one black) were wounded by “Fifteen or twenty white men and negroes” that “opened fire with automatic guns and pistols. Jake Stevens had a revolver and returned the fire. A second fusillade of shots from the shore bourght Stevens and two others down.” On the other hand, the Item lists the dead as three black men: Will Crafton, Jake Stevens, “... and a negro known as ‘Red’”; two white men wounded: Bill Wooten and Mego Dangerfield. From the Post, “So far as learned the body of the man called ‘Red’ killed in the battle and whose body is reported to have been thrown in the river, has not yet been recovered.” According to the Herald, “It was reported that the negro Will Crofton, of the [Jake] Stevens party, had been killed, but this was erronous, as the negro made his way to Mound, La., and from there to Vicksburg. ... The body of Jake Stevens ... was buried yesterday afternoon at 2 o’clock. ... The interment was made in the National cemetery, as Stevens had served in the World War.”

notes:
From the Herald, “Four Negroes Killed By Mob. Wharton, Texas, June 30.—Two negroes were shot to death and two others hanged by posses early this week in this county, it became known here today. They were wanted in connection with the killing of deputy sheriff S. C. McCormick last Saturday [26th] night, Washington Giles and his brother, who was accused of firing the shot that killed McCormick, were shot by pursuers late Tuesday [29th] afternoon near Diamond Mound. The bodies of Jodie Gordon and Elijah Anderson were found Tuesday morning hanging from trees six miles east of Wharton. Officers here assert they have no clue as to the personnel of the posses. It is understood 250 men participated. Gordon and Anderson, it was said, admitted they assisted the Giles brothers to escape.” According to the Statesman, two black men, Washington Giles and his brother, were shot to death at Damon Mound on the afternoon of the 29th when they refused to surrender to a “posse.”; Jodie Gordon, aged 34, and Elijah Anderson, about 30 years of age, both negroes were found dead Tuesday morning hanging from trees six miles east of Wharton. Gordon and Anderson had been taken by the pursuers Monday and admitted they were aiding in the escape of Washington Giles and his brother.” According to the Post, the posse that killed Washington Giles and his brother was “... composed of Damon Mound citizens. The negroes were given the opportunity to surrender but refused and were killed in the shooting that followed when they tired to make their escape. Sheriff Kemp and posse of Wharton were in the vicinity at the time the negroes were shot but both negroes were dead before they came up. ... Brooks is in the county jail.” From the Item, “Mob Pursuing Deputy, Negro. Officers Spirit Prisoner Out of Miami Jail Toward Jacksonville. Miami, Fla., July 31.—A mob of more than 1200 men surrounded the Dade county jail here this morning in an effort to obtain Henry Brooks, arrested on the scene on a charge of attacking a 55-year-old woman. The local authorities spirited the negro away. A committee from the mob was permitted to search the jail to ascertain that the negro had been taken away. The mob refused to permit Sheriff D. W. Moran to make a statement, hooting him each time he tried to speak. Finally the mob quieted down to listen to the reading of an order signed by Judge H. H. Branning, authorizing the removal of the prisoner. Deputy sheriffs who returned to this city early this morning after accompanying Brooks on the first lap of his trip north, stated that he was being taken to Jacksonville jail for safekeeping. When this reported was received, about 25 automobiles started north in pursuit of the prisoner. The deputy sheriff in charge of the prisoner had a half-hour start on his pursuers.” From the 7/31 Herald, “Deputy Sheriff B. C. Williams, who accompanied Herbert (or Henry) Brooks, colored, on the first lap of his journey to Jacksonville for safety, returned to Miami on the early morning train today, and stated that Deputy Sheriff Guilford Green was still traveling north with this prisoner. Rumors that a for-hire chauffeur carried the prisoner north set the mob to searching through the street for him, and nearly 50 automobiles loads of men tore through the streets, going here and there in their efforts to secure information regarding the spiriting away of the negro. ... The mob returned to the court house yard about 1 a. m., and after a short consultation, headed their automobiles toward the northern part of the city. ... Five hundred white men, who began assembling between 9:30 and 10 o’clock, surrounded the county jail last night and at a late hour a small party of them was still conducting a search though the jail and courthouse for Herbert or Henry Brooks, negro .... The search resulted in no trace of the negro being found. ... Deputy Sheriff Bob Simpson, who attends to the clerical work of the sheriff’s office, was questioned and an attempt made to force the information from him, but he refused to tell. Reports that mobs were storming the county jails at Ft. Lauderdale, Palm Beach and Ft. Pierce proved unfounded, telephonic assurances being received by The Herald from those points that everything was quiet at 12:45 this morning.” According to the 8/1 Herald, Herbert Brooks was accused of raping white women in Miami and had been arrested and “... he was being transported [by train] to Jacksonville for protection from the mob of white men which Friday [30th] night and yesterday [31st] morning surrounded the county jail. ... Brooks was taken to Ft. Pierce in an automobile Friday night, by deputies from the sheriff’s office who left at dusk. He was turned over to Sheriff Monroe and he started on the first north-bound train for Jacksonville. While details were lacking yesterday afternoon, it was believed that the negro heavily handcuffed took the one chance for life and sprang form the moving train. This chance was one for life and a thousand for death, and he pitched headlong to the ground.”

Note: the alleged attacks on white women happened in Dade Co., but he jumped from the train near Ormond in Volusia Co. This is a difficult case that rests on whether he would have jumped from the train in the absence of the white mobs. If that’s true, then this is no lynching. The 3/16 News states that on Thursday [13th] night, a son of Sam Cage, in the Ralph neighborhood, was found cut to pieces, being killed by parties unknown, on account of his actions toward a young lady of the neighborhood, when he attempted to pull her from her horse.” According to the 3/18 News, “Doubt Death of Cicero Cage Is Freely Expressed. ... Is Cicero Cage dead? This negro boy attempted to pull a prominent young lady from her hose, in the western part of the county, one day last week. There seems to be a serious doubt about his having been cut to death, although Sam Cage, Cicero’s father, who was in the city on Saturday [15th] last, informed Hon. Walter D. Seed that his son was dead. Sam Cage went to tell Mr. Seed that his son was literally cut to pieces.” The 3/19 News reports “Mystery Deepens Regarding Fate of Cicero Cage, Negro. Reported Killed Thursday [13th]—Gentleman Says Negro Worked In Garden Last Saturday [15th]. The mystery of what has become of Cicero Cage, the negro boy reported to have been lynched, deepens as time passes. On Tuesday [18th] Sheriff Hughes and two of his deputies went to the Parks-Mill neighborhood, where the killing is said to have taken place, and could find no trace of the missing negro boy. A representative of the The News talked to a gentleman form that neighborhood, and he said that Cicero Cage worked for him on Saturday last. ... [apparently it was raining on that Saturday, thus discounting the garden story] ... Sheriff Hughes says he and his deputies could get no trace of the missing negro and he is of the opinion that Cicero is dead, as his father reports, and that the matter is being kept quiet by those who killed him. It is pretty certain he has not been buried and it is supposed that after he was killed, his body was sunk in some deep hole in the creek ..... There is a deep mystery about what has become of the negro and it may never be cleared up.” From the unidentified news report, “For the past few days there has been a good deal of suppressed excitement in the Parks’ neighborhood, three miles beyond Ralph. The story has been kept quite, as the people of the neighborhood were trying to get their hands on a negro youth by the name of Cicero Cage, son of Sam Cage, who attempted an assault on one of the most prominent and popular young ladies of that neighborhood. She was riding along a road, some distance from any residence when Cicero ran out from a clump of bushes and places his hands on her before she could whip up her horse and get away. He made a dash and head the horse off and made another attempt ....  [she escaped] ... She knew the negro and reported the matter and a watch has been kept for Cicero, the outraged men of the neighborhood swearing vengeance if they could lay their hands on him. ... [after avoiding the law and others] ... Cicero thought there was no danger and came back to his old haunts, with the result that his head body was found Friday [14th] morning, with his throat cut and many stabs in different parts of his body. The matter has been kept so still that very few people at Ralph, only three miles from the scene, knew anything about the attempted assault or the death of the negro boy at the hands of parties unknown. Late Saturday afternoon Sam Cage, the father of Cicero, was in the city and confirmed the above rumor that his son had been killed. He says he was literally cut to pieces. He related the killing to Hon. Walter D. Seed, who knew Sam and so the story of the death of the negro is a factor, instead of being a rumor.” Whitaker just says that Cage was “cut to pieces” on the streets of Tuscaloosa—this is probably based on the 3/16 News story.

notes:
According to the 7/25 Constitution, Berry Washington killed a white man who was assaulting a black woman and her two children. He turned himself into the police and was put in jail in McRae. Later a mob took him from the jail and brought him to Milan, hanged him, and riddled his body with bullets. One report says that the mob of 75-100 men while another says 10. The 7/27 Constitution story reports that the governor will pay $1000 for information on Washington’s lynching that happened on 5/25 at Milan. Also it notes that Washington was “... inoffensive and highly respected old Negro...” and that the mob was composed of 10 men. Interestingly, it also reports that the local papers did not report the lynching and that it was covered up. The 5/29 Times-Journal story gives name as B. W. Washington. The 8/28 Constitution gives the judge’s charge to the Telfair grand jury to investigate the lynching The 8/11 Telegraph and 8/14 Times-Journal report that the Mayor of Milan denies that the white man accused of assaulting that black woman didn’t do it.

Note #1: From Dorsey, “County No. 1. Case No. 1. July, 1919, two white men, drunk, went to the negro section of a town in this county [unspecified] at night. An elderly negro, got his gun and went into the streets, it is claimed, to protect the women of his race. In the shooting, which followed, one of the white men was killed. The negro was placed in jail. The sheriff let him there, with no guard, to go to another place to get a prisoner. A county commissioner hearing that a mob was coming went to the jail to remove the prisoner, but could find no key to unlock the door. The mob had the key. They lynched the negro.” The Post-Search Light reports Governor Dorsey’s reward of $1,500 for the lynchers of Berry Washington, 72, and then writes “On the night of May 24 two white men are alleged to have invaded the negro section at Milan and threatened inmates of several house. Washington came out with a shot gun in hand, and words and an exchange of shots followed in which one of the white men was killed. The negro surrendered and was put in jail at McRae, near by. A mob removed him early on May 23 [25th], carried him back toward Milan, hanged him to a post and then fired shots at his body.”

Note #2: Suspected police lynching, or police assisted lynching based on Dorsey’s statement. The Governor’s Statement says July probably because there were many newspaper reports of the lynching in their July editions.

notes:
While reporting on racial conflict in Longview in mid-July, the Times reprints a story that appeared in the Chicago Defender in early July, “’Longview (Tex.) July 4.‚—Despite the fact that every effort has been made by officials here to keep the outside world from learning of the lynching of Lemuel Walters at this place June 17, the news has leaked out. Walters was taken from Longview jail by a crowd of white man when a prominent white woman declared she loved him and if she were in the North would obtain a divorce and marry him. No charges were preferred against Walters other than the statement made by the white woman to her personal friends. ... Walters was taken to the outskirts of the town and shot to pieces. His nude form was thrown near the roadside.’ The facts in regard to Walters and his lynching as given by local white citizens here differ materially from the account published in the Defender. It is stated that Walters was found in the room of a daughter of J. S. King of Kilgore [Gregg Co.]. ... [he was captured] ... The negro admitted his guilt and stated that he was in the house for the purpose of robbery. It was suggested by Mr. King ... that inasmuch as the negro was half-witted, the best thing to do with him was to put him on a train and send him back to Louisiana, where he came from several months ago. The negro was brought back to Longview and that evening a ticket was purchased and he was put on the train, according to those who should be in possession of the facts. The next morning after Walters had been placed on a train bound in the direction of Louisiana the lifeless body of a negro was found near the highway south of Footes Switch. An inquest was held over the body, the verdict being that an unknown negro had met death by shots from a gun in the hands of unknown parties. It is said the body was never identified and it was buried by negroes of that community. It is stated that [S. L.] Jones [a black school teacher] and a negro physician, Dr. E. P. Davis, interested themselves in the lynching of the unknown negro and identified the body as being that of Walters.” In the Messenger reprint of the Defender story, his name is Lemmel Walters and that he was taken from jail by a Kilgore mob, carried to the outskirts of Longview, and shot, see page 3. According to the Express, “About the middle of June, a colored man was found in a white family residence at a late hour of the night, not, however, in Longview, but about sixteen miles away, near the little town of Kilgore. For this offense he was arrested and landed in Longview jail. A few nights thereafter, unknown parties forced the locks on the jail and the culprit was killed, his body being found hanging in the woods near the place where he is alleged to have committed his offense.” From the Morning News, “Kilgore, Gregg County, Texas, July 15.—In compliance with the order of the Governor, National Guardsmen and rangers began today the disarmament of the citizens of this place. They will finish this work today. ... The negro Shag was executed north of here. Out of this grew the trouble at Longview, as it was followed by the publication of the article in a negro paper to which exception was taken.”

Couldn’t find a death certificate for a Walters in Gregg Co. in 1919. Footes was a small community 4 miles SW of Longview in the eastern part of Gregg Co. See the Marion Bush incident, 13 July. Caldwell-DeLord have the wrong month for this incident.

They admitted having killed 15 of the number.” Second story, same page, “El Paso, Texas, Feb. 7.—An investigation of the killing of 15 Mexican citizens at Porvenir, Texas, 40 miles northwest of Presidio, January 13, has been ordered by the state department at Washington, and is being made by the military stationed in the Big Bend district of Texas, where the killings occurred. .... the 15 men were taken from their homes by armed men and shot to death. The reason given was a suspicion that they had participated in the Brite ranch raid Christmas day.”

It is clear that Texas Rangers from Company B, U.S. Troops from Company G of the 8th Cavalry, and ranchers murdered fifteen Mexicans at Porvenir. But was this massacre a lynching or something else—that’s an arguable issue. See Texas Senate Proclamation No. 80 in Honor of the Porvenir Massacre.

From the Advocate, “Monroe, La., March 16.—The body of George McNeel, one of two negroes arrested yesterday suspected of implication in the assault of a young white woman here Thursday [14th] was found hanging to a tree in the court house yard early today. It was stated at the sheriff’s office last night that the sheriff and deputies had started in automobiles for Shreveport [Caddo Parish] with McNeel and John Richards, the other suspect.” The Journal reports, “Monroe, La., 16.—A mob of armed citizens, supposed to be from this city took George McNeal and John Richards, negroes, suspected of robbing and assaulting a young white woman here last Thursday [14th] from Sheriff Grant, at Choudrant, Lincoln parish last last night while the sheriff was on his way from Monroe to Shreveport with the negroes for safe keeping, lynched McNeal and possibly made away with Richards. McNeal’s body was found early today [16th] handing from a tree in the courthouse yard here [Monroe]. There were many rumors that Richards also had been lynched, but his body had not been found up to noon and his fate was unknown to the authorities. ... Late today the authorities expressed the belief that the mob had released Richards, advancing the theory that the lynchers may be obtained a confession guilty from McNeal. The News-Star gives the names Johnnie Richards and George Neal and writes: “Official confirmation of the release of Johnnie Richards, held as a suspect in the Strozier assault case, was obtained this afternoon. Apparently Richards was released, first by the mob and then by the police, on the strength of information that he was not guilty of the assault.” The Herald states “Monroe, La., March 16.—The body of George McNeel, one of two negroes arrested yesterday, suspected of implication in assault upon a young white woman here Thursday was found hanging to a tree in the court house yard early today.”—no mention of what happened to the other black man. According to the States, George McNeal, 26, and John Richards, both black, were taken from Sheriff Grant at Choudrant on the night of the 15th, and McNeal was found hanged on the 16th; “The sheriff does not know what became of the other, John Richards. ... Later Saturday the authorities expressed the belief that the mob had released Richards, advancing the theory that the lynchers may have obtained a confessional of guilt from McNeal.” The Times-Picayune says that George McNeal and Johnnie Richards were taken from officers in Lincoln Parish and brought back to Monroe. The woman identified McNeal and he was hanged near the Monroe courthouse. Richards was freed. From the Post, “Monroe, La., March 16.—A mob of armed citizens, supposed to be from this city, took George McNeal and John Richards, negroes, suspected of robbing and assaulting a young white woman here last Thursday [14th], from Sheriff Grant at Choudrant, Lincoln Parish, late Friday [15th] night while the sheriff was on his way from Monroe to Shreveport with the negroes for safekeeping, lynched McNeal and possibly made away with Richards. McNeal’s body was found early Saturday [16th] hanging from a tree in the court house yard.”

notes:
Internet: “Memphis, Tennessee, 1917: Lynching: On April 30, Antoinette Rappal, a sixteen-year-old white girl living on the outskirts of Memphis, disappeared on her way to school. On May 3 her body was found in a river, her head severed from it. On May 6 a Negro woodchopper, Ell Person, was arrested on suspicion. Under third degree methods he confessed to the crime of murder. The grand jury of Shelby County immediately indicted him for murder in the first degree. The prisoner was taken secretly to the state penitentiary at Nashville. It was known that he would be brought back for trial to Memphis. Each incoming train was searched, and arrangements were made for a lynching. On May 15 the sheriff disappeared from Memphis. He returned on May 18, announcing that he was informed that several mobs were between Arlington and Memphis. The men were reported to be drinking. "I didn't want to hurt anybody and I didn't want to get hurt," he said, "so I went south into Mississippi." The press did nothing to quell the mob spirit, and on May 21 announced that Ell Person would be brought to Memphis that night. Thousands of persons on foot and in automobiles went to the place that had been prepared for the lynching. With a knowledge of these conditions, Person was brought back from Nashville, guarded only by two deputies. Without difficulty he was taken from the train, placed in an automobile, and driven to the spot prepared for his death. The Memphis Press reported the lynching in full. We give a few of its statements. "Fifteen thousand of them—men, women, even little children, and in their midst the black-clothed figure of Antoinette Rappal's mother—cheered as they poured the gasoline on the fiend and struck the match. They fought and screamed and crowded to get a glimpse of him, and the mob closed in and struggled about the fire as the flames flared high and the smoke rolled about their heads. Two of them hacked off his ears as he burned; another tried to cut off a toe but they stopped him. The Negro lay in the flames, his hands crossed on his chest. If he spoke, no one ever heard him over the shouts of the crowd. He died quickly, though fifteen minutes later excitable persons still shouted that he lived when they saw the charred remains move as does meat on a hot frying pan. 'They burned him too quick! They burned him too quick!' was the complaint on all sides.”

Note: there were threatened lynchings of Persons on 8 and 16 May in Shelby Co.

notes:
From the Advertiser, “Tuscaloosa, Ala., July 17.—News reached Tuscaloosa today that an unknown negro was taken from policeman Gunter and Adcox near Reform [Pickens Co.] last night between 10 and 11 o’clock and strung up to a tree. The negro confessed to having entered the home of a farmer named Price, living about four miles from Reform for the purpose of committing an assault on Mr. Price’s daughter. The capture was made early last night. Fearing lynching, the officers attempted to carry the negro with another suspect to the Pickens county jail at Carrollton. They had proceeded but half mile from from when the mob stopped them and took the negro.” Apparently the other black man was not molested. The Constitution reports that Hibbler was arrested near Reform, Alabama, and it was when he was en route to Carrollton that he was taken from a deputy sheriff and lynched. From the Post, “Columbus, Miss., July 24—News reached here tonight of the lynching Monday of Poe Hibbler, a negro, in Pickens county, Ala., for an attempted crime against the daughter of a prominent citizen of that county. The negro was taken from the sheriff who was enroute to Carrollton, Ala., with the prisoner, and hanged to a tree.” According to the States, Poe Hibbler was accused of entering the bedroom of the daughter of a prominent citizen; he was arrested in Reform and was being brought to Carrollton when taken and hanged; the report ends with “Another negro, implicated by Hibbler, was given a hearing at Carrollton and acquitted.”

Note: it is clear that Poe Hibbler was the unknown negro in the Advertiser report and that the reported lynching of Hibbler on 
23 July was a duplicate of this 16 July lynching near Reform.

He is survived by his wife and nine children.” According to the Herald, a dozen “possum hunters” [nightriders] went to the home of Pedro Mohundro on the night of the 12th, near Lovelaceville, and riddled his body with bullets; “The negro, residents say, had been warned to leave, but he did not heed the warnings.” From the News, “Lexington, Ky., Jan. 14.—Posses are today scouring the hills for 20 masked night riders who last night assassinated Peter Onohund, a negro tobacco grower of Ballard County. ... The Journal reports “just as we finished writing this article, we understand that Peter Fambrough, the negro who is said furnished fire arms and ammunition to [James] Jackson and misled the officers in the hunt for him has been killed.” No mention of Fambrough in the Gazette or Local stories. The 7/15 News and Herald reports that Peter Fambo and “a man named Jackson” were killed by a posse and that another man, “Jeems [James] Jackson”, was killed after resisting arrest. naacp: — Jackson, 7/21/1915, Cochran, Pulaski Co., Negro, Accessory to murder
notes:
The Journal reports that James Jackson killed his white plantation overseer in Bleckley Co. and then went  to his brother’s house in Pulaski Co., some 7 miles from Cochran and 3 miles from Hawkinsville. There he was surrounded by a sheriff’s posse. He then shot and killed a white sheriff and another white man. Apparently the posse, at this point, was made up of men from both Bleckley and Pulaski counties. They then dynamited the house and shot Jackson down. The Journal states that it was not a mob but a legal sheriff’s deputy that killed Jackson However, according to the Gazette, Gene Jackson was killed by “a posse of several hundred citizens and county officers” after they dynamited his house. The Local reports that after the unnamed negro killed his white supervisor, he barricaded himself in his house 3.5 miles from Hawkinsville. When the sheriff tried to arrest him, he shot the sheriff and an unnamed negro assisting the sheriff. Then, a group of men dynamited his house — “The enraged posse then took the negro and lynched him to a tree nearby.” The 7/14 News reports that the posse “lynched” James Jackson. The 7/15 Constitution doesn’t imply a lynching. No mention of this Peter Jackson in the 7/15 Constitution, Gazette or Local stories. He may be the brother of James Jackson mentioned in the Journal article. The Journal reports “just as we finished writing this article, we understand that Peter Fambrough, the negro who is said furnished fire arms and ammunition to [James] Jackson and misled the officers in the hunt for him has been killed.” No mention of Fambrough in the Gazette or Local stories. The 7/15 News and Herald reports that Peter Fambo and “a man named Jackson” were killed by a posse and that another man, “Jeems [James] Jackson”, was killed after resisting arrest. The 7/15 Constitution notes that Peter Fambrough has been arrested but the 7/16 edition says that Peter Jambo and “another named Jackson” were killed by a sheriff’s posse.

notes: According to the Times-Union, there had been a town meeting where it was decided to order Dr. H. M. Owens and Mrs. McGuire (at whose house Owens resided) to leave Trenton. On the 20th., 100 shots were fired into the house by “a number of persons”. No one was injured. On 21 July, Owens and two men exchanged gun shots. “The fusillade attracted the attention of the other citizens and in a few moments the entire community had arrived at the scene, the town marshal going to the barn [on Mrs. McGuire’s property] and ordering Owens to surrender. Owens shot at the marshal who retreated. An attempt was made to dynamite the barn but that failed. The barn was then set afire. Owens stayed in the barn until the flames/smoke drove him out. He came out of the barn firing his gun randomly. He was then riddled with bullets from the crowd. “It is said that Dr. Owens was in the county jail for several months, he having been charged with the alleged murder of a man at Tyler, in this county. His case went before the court and resulted in a mistrial, and at the last term of the circuit court the case was nolle prossed by the state’s attorney.” From the Ledger, “Jacksonville, Fla., July 22.—The series of incidents that had stirred the town of Trenton, Fla., culminated late yesterday in the killing of Dr. H. M. Owens, by several citizens, according to reports here today. Dr. Owens and Mrs. Elizabeth McGuire, with whom he boarded, had been requested, it is said, by a committee of citizens to leave the community. they demurred. A few nights ago shots were fired into the house. Yesterday two men were called to pack the household goods. On arrival they were fired upon from the house. The shots attracted the citizens. They fired at Owens as he left rear door. He hid in a barn and continued firing. The barn was fired and Owens rushed out, when he was shot to death. A coroner’s verdict read: ‘At the hands of unknown parties.’ Mrs. McGuire was taken to Gainesville for safe keeping.”

Driver, who prevented a lynching here a week ago [of Crum and Kenyon], was out fishing, a mob of 15 men entered the county jail here this afternoon and shot to death Andy Crum, accused of instigating the murder of Sheriff S. D. Mauldin on Island 37 in the Mississippi River on July 31. ... Crum was brought here today from Marion, Ark., where he was held with Bert Spring, a negro who shot Sheriff Mauldin. Bert Spring, the negro who did the shooting when Sheriff Mauldin was killed, died last night from the effects of wounds received at the hand of the mob which burned many structures on Island 37 following the murder of the sheriff. notes: The Constitution reports that Henry Russell and “Kid” Jackson were lynched at Hope Hill, ten miles from Montgomery by a masked mob. They took the two men from their homes, riddled their bodies with bullets, and threw them into a ditch. They had been tenants on the McLain plantation but had been replaced by white tenants. Later they were accused of poisoning some of McLain’s mules and burning a barn—they had been arrested and jailed but where released on bond until their trial when the lynching took place. notes:
From the Statesman, “Sulphur Springs, Texas, Aug. 30—Sulphur Springs was quiet today following yesterday’s excitement which culminated in the burning of two negroes, Joe and King Richmond. The negroes early Sunday [29th] morning shot and killed Deputy Sheriff Nathan A., Flippen and seriously wounded Sheriff J. B. Butler when the officers attempted to arrest King Richmond on a minor charge. Joe Richmond later was killed and King Richmond seriously wounded in a fight with posses. The former’s dead body was burned with his brother in Buford Park here. ... As soon as the news of the negroes attack on the officers became known yesterday 1500 armed men and boys began to scour the country for the murderers. The negroes were surrounded in a wood six miles southwest of Sulphur Springs, and while the negroes fired at their pursuers, their fight was of short duration, as the posses poured volleys of shots into the hiding place, killing Joe and seriously wounding King Richmond. The dead and wounded negro were brought directly to this city, where a crowd of several thousand were waiting. Despite the pleadings of influential men and peace officers from this and adjoining counties, the mob, with little ceremony and in an orderly manner, placed both negroes on a pile of wood in Buford Park and burned them.” According to the Post’s account, the posse brought the dead Joe Richmond and fatally wounded King Richmond into Sulphur Springs at 5 p.m. and were greeted by a mob of 6000 persons. The Courier-Gazette story adds nothing. The American, characterizes the posse as a mob: “A mob surrounded the negroes in the woods, killing one and wounding the other. The body of the dead negro and the prisoner were brought to town. Thousands of people had gathered on the public square and when the prisoners arrived they were burned at the stake.” The News’ account states that “peace officers from this and adjoining counties” were in the posse that shot the Richmonds.

Note: if the posse that shot Joe Richmond was really a mob intent on murder, they would have also killed King Richmond at the same time. It seems likely Joe was killed in the fire fight with the posse, but King was definitely lynched in Sulphur Springs.

With these Mexicans in jail were two others, Daniel and Ben Longoria. ... About two miles out of San Benito, according to reports to the authorities here, the three prisoners jumped from the machine, attempting to escape. They were shot and killed.” ... One of these Mexicans, Turner said, was Y. Rincones, a boy of 16, whose mother was a widow living on his ranch.
