notes:
From the website <https://refusingtoforget.org/the-history/> “Texas Rangers played a key role in these atrocities. On September 28, 1915, for example, after a clash with about forty raiders near Ebenoza, Hidalgo County, the victorious Rangers took about a dozen raiders prisoner and promptly hung them, leaving their bodies in the open for months. Several weeks later, on October 19, after a dramatic attack derailed a passenger train heading north from Brownsville, Rangers detained ten ethnic Mexicans nearby, quickly hanging four and shooting four others. Cameron County sheriff W.T. Vann blamed Ranger Captain Henry Ransom for the killings. Vann took two suspected men from Ransom and placed them into his custody and likely saved their lives. Both proved to be innocent of any involvement.” From the Caller, “Brownsville, Texas, October 19—Ten Mexicans have paid with the lives for their supposed complicity in the wrecking last night of the St. Louis, Brownsville and Mexico railroad train on the outskirts of Brownsville and the killing of three Americans and the wounding of four others by Mexican bandits. ... Four of the Mexicans executed today were hanged to trees. The others were simply shot down by their captors.” In a second story, same page, “Five [Mexicans] were reported killed by soldiers of Troop A, Sixth Cavalry, in a running fight staged between Los Indios [Cameron Co.] and Galveston Ranch [Cameron Co.] late this afternoon [19th].” In connection with the train wreck and murders, the Statesman reports, “He [Sheriff Vann] said he has reports of nine Mexicans killed yesterday [19th] and that five of these were slain in the Los Indios [Cameron Co.] section, more than twenty miles from the wreck. He said he did not know whether these five killings were connected with the wreck.” The same appears in the Post. From the Times, “Brownsville, Tex., Oct. 20.—The border resumed quiet today for the first time since the train wreck, robbery, and murder by Mexican bandits Monday night. No further execution of Mexicans since yesterday [19th] is reported. There were not over ten executions.” From the Herald, “4 Men Killed Are Identified. Bodies Founds Near Brownsville Identified as Rancheros Living in District. Relative and friends yesterday identified the four bodies found in the vicinity of Monday [18th] night’s [train] wreck as Santiago Salas, Trinidad Ybarra, Jesus Ybarra, and Severo Garcia, all four of whom they said were rancheros living in the neighborhood of where the wreck occurred. the killings were due to the wreck and murders of Monday night. ... The bodies were all found in what is known as the Flor de Mayo, near the Hughes farm, about four miles from Brownsville, and buried where found. The justice of the peace return no verdict, but that the only possible verdict in the cases would be that the four deceased met their deaths as the result of bullet wounds by parties unknown.”

Note: can confirm only four lynching victims: Santiago Salas, Trinidad Ybarra, Jesus Ybarra, and Severo Garcia. Could find no definitive evidence that there were 5-6 other victims—no report of bodies recovered or names, etc.

notes:
From the website <https://refusingtoforget.org/the-history/> “Texas Rangers played a key role in these atrocities. On September 28, 1915, for example, after a clash with about forty raiders near Ebenoza, Hidalgo County, the victorious Rangers took about a dozen raiders prisoner and promptly hung them, leaving their bodies in the open for months. Several weeks later, on October 19, after a dramatic attack derailed a passenger train heading north from Brownsville, Rangers detained ten ethnic Mexicans nearby, quickly hanging four and shooting four others. Cameron County sheriff W.T. Vann blamed Ranger Captain Henry Ransom for the killings. Vann took two suspected men from Ransom and placed them into his custody and likely saved their lives. Both proved to be innocent of any involvement.” From the Caller, “Brownsville, Texas, October 19—Ten Mexicans have paid with the lives for their supposed complicity in the wrecking last night of the St. Louis, Brownsville and Mexico railroad train on the outskirts of Brownsville and the killing of three Americans and the wounding of four others by Mexican bandits. ... Four of the Mexicans executed today were hanged to trees. The others were simply shot down by their captors.” In a second story, same page, “Five [Mexicans] were reported killed by soldiers of Troop A, Sixth Cavalry, in a running fight staged between Los Indios [Cameron Co.] and Galveston Ranch [Cameron Co.] late this afternoon [19th].” In connection with the train wreck and murders, the Statesman reports, “He [Sheriff Vann] said he has reports of nine Mexicans killed yesterday [19th] and that five of these were slain in the Los Indios [Cameron Co.] section, more than twenty miles from the wreck. He said he did not know whether these five killings were connected with the wreck.” The same appears in the Post. From the Times, “Brownsville, Tex., Oct. 20.—The border resumed quiet today for the first time since the train wreck, robbery, and murder by Mexican bandits Monday night. No further execution of Mexicans since yesterday [19th] is reported. There were not over ten executions.” From the Herald, “4 Men Killed Are Identified. Bodies Founds Near Brownsville Identified as Rancheros Living in District. Relative and friends yesterday identified the four bodies found in the vicinity of Monday [18th] night’s [train] wreck as Santiago Salas, Trinidad Ybarra, Jesus Ybarra, and Severo Garcia, all four of whom they said were rancheros living in the neighborhood of where the wreck occurred. the killings were due to the wreck and murders of Monday night. ... The bodies were all found in what is known as the Flor de Mayo, near the Hughes farm, about four miles from Brownsville, and buried where found. The justice of the peace return no verdict, but that the only possible verdict in the cases would be that the four deceased met their deaths as the result of bullet wounds by parties unknown.”

notes:
The 12/31 Constitution reports that six black men were killed by a sheriff’s posse, four shot and two burned alive, but the story only lists five: Granison Goolsby and his two sons (unnamed), Early Hightower, and Jim Burton. According to the 12/31 edition, Goolsby, his sons, and the others were barricaded in a house and exchanged gun fire with the posse. The posse set the house afire and Goolsby and one black man were gunned down as they tried to escape. The two sons escaped to another cabin but that was set afire and they were burned up. How the other one/two died isn’t reported. The 12/31 Telegraph reports Granison Goolsby, Mike Goolsby, Ulysses Goolsby, Hosh Jewell, Charlie Holmes Jim Burton, and Early Hightower killed. The 1/1 Telegraph notes that Ed and Precious Law were killed, and that Simon Goolsby, brother of Granison Goolsby, was killed too - posses were still looking for Mike and Ulysses Goolsby. The 1/1 Constitution reports that two more blacks were killed: Ed Law and his son, Precious Law but no mention of a Simon Goolsby. The 1/2 edition of the Constitution and Telegraph note that posses are still looking for Mike and Ulysses Goolsby; Charles Holmes was placed in custody. Couldn’t find any follow-up thru 1/6. The 1/6 News reports that a mob cornered Grandison Goolsby in the loft of the home of Charlie Holmes. They set the house on fire and when Goolsby fled, he was riddled with bullets. The News further reports that Goolsby’s two sons, Mike and Ulysses Goolsby, had escaped. Much of the story is missing but there’s some indication that two black men, Ed and Precious Law, were killed “...making the sixth victim of vengeance.” The story’s headline is “Several Negroes Killed and Lodges Burned.” Couldn’t find any follow-up in the News.

A coroner’s jury returned a verdict that ‘a white man, unidentified, had been murdered by persons unknown.’ Around the neck was a short section of small rope, tightly drawn, which apparently had been cut. Another portion of the rope was discovered tied to a limb of a tree under which the body was found. The theory that before the murder the man had been tortured, was advanced by authorities, as one leg was broken and a hand missing. Letters addressed to Joseph Todd, Hickory, Miss. were found in the coat pocket, but at a late hour tonight it had not been established  that the body was that of Todd.” The News reports, “A Lynching Mystery. Hickory [Newton Co.], Miss., Dec. 30.—(Special.)—The skeleton of an unknown man was found today about six miles south of Hickory .... However, nothing as to the identity of the dead man could be found. When found the skeleton had a rope tied around its neck, apparently having been cut in two, as the other half of the rope was found about the limb of a nearby tree. The body was found near the public road, some little distance in a thicket. Nothing of the corpse, however, was left except the bones, as the buzzards had eaten all flesh from the bones. The clothes of the man were found near the body, and brought into town. There was a letter found in the pocket of the coat, but it seems that nothing could be learned from the letter to ascertain his identity. The officers think the man must have been hung four or five months ago. It seems to be a complete mystery, as no clue whatever can be unearthed.” According to the Item, “Man Tortured to Death”, the man, Joseph Todd, was found near Kelly Creek and was murdered “several weeks ago”; “The body found today [29th] bore signs of inhuman treatment, and the man had evidently been tortured before death. One of the hands was missing.” The Times-Picayune states, dateline Hickory, 30 December, that the dead man was not J. D. Todd of Hickory; “Mr. Todd stated that the man had visited his home during the early part of September. He stated that he was en route south from Missouri in search of work. According to Mr. Todd, the man was without a coat and explained its absence by the statement that it had been stolen at Mehan Junction. Mr. Todd gave the stranger one of his own coats, failing to remove letters from the pocket which were found on the dead man and which led to the belief that he was a member of the Todd family of this section.”

Note: the man must have been killed between early September and December. September is a guess.

notes:
According to the Appeal, Pat Bowers murdered his wife and later opened fire on a constable and two other men who had come to his house. He killed two of them and fatally wounded the other. “The negro returned to the house and on the arrival of Sheriff Swain the house was entered after an exchanged of shots. The negro was found in an upper room dying from a wound about the heart. In the room were found three pistols, a pump gun and a plentiful supply of ammunition.... ... the subsequent chase of the negro, who barricaded himself in his home and took his own life rather than be captured by the mob.” From the Star, “Little Rock, Ark., Sept. 12.—Two white men and two negroes are dead and a third white man is severely wounded as a result of a murder and subsequent race riot at Carlisle, Ark., twenty-eight miles east of here, today. Jack Bowers, a negro, shot and killed his wife in the outskirts of Carlisle. Bowers fled to the home of his father in the country. He was pursued by Constable Thomas Burnett, D. W. H. Crawford, Chester Crawford, a son of the physician, and Deputy Constable Jim Johnson. The posse was met by Bowers and his three brothers. Doctor Crawford fell with a bullet through his side. Johnson fell with nearly a hundred buckshot wounds. Both died within a few minutes. Chester Crawford fell with bullets in his arm, side, wrist and leg. Constable Burnett escaped unhurt. One hundred white men rushed to the scene and charged the house. Jack Bowers was killed and his brothers surrendered.” The Truth states “... the posse which had increased to 100 white men, caught up with Bowers and riddled his body with bullets.” From the Sun, “Carlisle, Ark., Sept. 12.—Two white men are dead, a third is dying and two negroes are dead here, the result of the murder by her husband of the wife of a negro, Pat Bowers, early this morning, the subsequent chase of the negro, who barricaded himself in his home and took his own life rather than be captured by the mob.”

Note: although Bowers killed himself, he did so because a mob was attempting to kill him. Thus his death was the result of mob action.

He was accused of murderous assault on a white merchant of Whitehaven, Shelby Co., TN.  Same story appears in the Telegraph. From the Plain-Dealer, “Memphis, Tenn., Nov. 3.—Tom Burns, a negro, was taken from a deputy sheriff today near Hernando, Miss., and lynched. The deputy was on his way to jail with the prisoner, who was charged with attacking a white merchant at White Haven.” From the Item, “Memphis, Tenn., Nov. 3.—After taking Tom Burns, a negro, from a deputy sheriff who was escorting him to the jail at Hernando, Miss., a posse of 10 men lynched the negro from the Horn Lake road bridge at the Tennessee-Mississippi state line early to-day. The negro was arrested for an alleged murderous assault on T. B. Miller, a merchant at White Haven.” This report appears in many newspapers including the Southron.

Note: based on Google Maps, Horn Lake road bridge would be a bridge over Horn Lake creek in DeSoto Co., MS. The 1910 census lists a Tom Burns, black, 24, living in DeSoto Co. and he does not appear in DeSoto Co. in 1920 census; the 1910 census lists a Thomas B. Miller, white, 37, living in Civil District 12, Shelby Co. with his family and children—no info on occupation; he was born in Mississippi, as were his mother and father. Couldn’t find this person in the 1920 Tennessee census. Going to assume that Tom Burns was a resident of DeSoto Co. and was arrested in DeSoto Co. for a crime allegedly taken place in White Haven, Shelby Co. TN. He was being taken to Hernando by Mississippi authorities before being transferred to Memphis. Also assuming that the mob was primarily composed of persons from Shelby Co. TN where the crime took place. Strangely couldn’t find in the Memphis Commerical Appeal 1-7 November—perhaps a page was missing.

notes:
The Times reports that Watkins Lewis, 59, was taken from jail at Shreveport at 11:30p by a mob and taken away. The Constitution reports that Watkins Lewis was burned at the stake near Sylvester after being taken from the jail. He was the 5th black man to be lynched in connection with the murder of the white postmaster, Charles M. Hicks, at Sylvester. The Times-Picayune states that Lewis was taken from jail in an automobile by a mob “and carried off presumably for the purposes of lynching him.” The Gazette states that a mob of 200 tied Lewis to a tree and burned him alive—apparently he was taken from the jail in Shreveport and taken to a “giant tree near the Texas line.” From the Record, “Shreveport, La., Dec. 12.—Watkins Lewis, a negro accused of complicity in the murder of Charles H. Hicks, postmaster at Sylvester, La., was burned at the stake, last night, by a mob, according to information received here, today. Lewis was the fifth negro to be lynched in this vicinity within ten days, and the eighth within a year. Two were put to death last week for alleged implication in the killing of Mr. Hicks, and robbing his store. Two others were lynched last night, after, as was said, they confessed to the killing of Cyrus Hotchins, an oil field worker. All here hanged except for Lewis. Lewis was taken from the Caddo parish jail by five men, who gained entrance through a window and overpowered the jailer.”

Note: there was a threatened lynching of Lewis on 2 December in Caddo Parish.

notes:
According to the 12/22 State, “Anderson, Dec. 21.—Two negroes were killed and four white men wounded in a battle between the four white men and a party of negroes at Fairplay, in Oconee county, last night. ... Allen Green and Green Gibson are the dead negroes. ... It is said that a negro burned a barn near Knox’s bridge in Oconee county Saturday afternoon and that Magistrate McClure, Woodrow Campbell, John McDonald and Paul Marrett went to the suspected negro’s house and, carrying him to the place where the barn was burned, gave him [Tom Speights] a severe whipping. Returning they are said to have been attacked by a part of negroes led by Allen Green. Green was killed in the fight which followed, and Green Gibson died later from wounds received in the battle. None of the white men is believed to be fatally wounded.” The 3/3 State gives a more complete and detailed report. On Saturday, the 19th, white men “severely whipped” Tom Speights, who was suspected of burning a barn. On Sunday, five white men went back to the home of Speights and started with him toward Fairplay. They also brought along three unnamed black men. On the way that party met a buggy of three negroes. They took George Gibson, “a young negro” and “beat him over the head with a pistol ...” They then took Gibson and Speights to Fairplay. There they were joined by a sixth white man and continued on to Knox’s bridge “where they crossed the river to the Georgia side”. There “... the defendants made two of the negroes brought along hold George Gibson and Tom Speights and the third negro beat then. Some of the defendants also beat them.” At that point, “old Green Gibson and two other negroes came up with shotguns and asked what these negroes (Gibson and Speights) had done to be whipped. A general firefight broke out. “George Gibson died the next day and Speights some days later in Georgia.” “Green Gibson then came back toward Fairplay, was pursued and was overtaken near the home of a negro, Mose Williams, and was shot. He fell, arose and fired upon his pursuers and started to run. He was shot and beaten to death.”

While en route under custody of Constable Ed Odom to the Harrsion County jail here, Perry was seized by a small mob and killed.” The Messenger states that Robert Perry and George Redden were shot by a mob about 11 miles north of Marshall by a mob while being brought to Marshall from Karnack by Constable Ed Odom; Perry was killed and Redden severely wounded.

Even though both Anderson and Perry were lynched on the same day, in the same county, they seem like two different incidents: Karnack and Elysian Fields lie at opposite ends of Harrison County.

From the Herald, “Greenwood, Miss., June 14.—A mob of more than 1,000 men, who attempted to capture and lynch Jim Williams, a negro, set fire to the house where he had barricaded himself today and watched him shoot himself when the flames reached him. Williams killed the cook of a white family of Greenwood and threw her baby out of a second story window. He escaped, and bloodhounds were placed on his trail. ... [He was found in a cabin] ... When the mob charged the house, Williams fired upon the leaders, wounding two of them. Unable to get close enough to take him, the mob threw lighted torches at the cabin until it caught fire. His charred body was found after the fire had been put out.” The same report appears in the Post and a briefer version in the Tribune and Star-Telegram. notes:
The Constitution reports that Will Norman was hanged from a telephone pole “at the most prominent street corner of the business district”. He was taken by the mob as he was being brought to jail. Norman was accused of killing the daughter of former Circuit Judge C. Floyd Huff. From the Appeal, “Hot Springs, Ark. June 19 — Garland Huff, the 14-year-old daughter of Judge C. Floyd Huff of this city, was brutally murdered here this morning in her father’s home by Will Norman, a negro servant in the house, while defending herself against a bestial attack by the black. ... The negro made his attack on the person of the girl and she resisted. He had a large wooden potato masher in his hand which he used as a club and with that tried to intimidate her, and when she could not weaken he struck her on the head.” The Gazette notes that he was stripped naked, hanged, and later his body burned. The Post states that the mob was composed of “prominent citizens of Hot Springs” and that “the negro was dragged to a conspicuous place and hanged. As soon as his feet swung clear of the ground volleys of bullets were fired into his body, almost riddling it.”
From the World, “Cut Hole In Jail Roof To Save Prisoner. Negro Taken From Building That Way to Escape Mob in Arkansas. Little Rock, Ark., Nov. 4.—Hot Springs officers last last night cut a hole in the roof of Garland County jail and removed Robert Bluthenthal, a negro alleged assailant of a white girl. Fear that a mob would get the negro led to the action. Bluthenthal was rushed to Little Rock in an automobile. According to Hot Springs officers, Harry Poe, a negro, lynched two years ago, died protesting innocence and charging Bluthenthal with having committed the assault, of which he was accused.

Note: suspect Norman/Poe was tortured.

The Journal reports that 120 men were in the mob but only 30 came to the jail and removed Burrell Hardaway, apparently a black male, Gene Arrington, an unnamed negro, and Dusty Crutchfield. notes:
From the Messenger, “Two Negroes Were Hung. Mob Near Elysian Fields [Harrison Co.]. Strung Up Man and Woman Who Furnished Gun With Which Strange Was Killed. ... Mary Jackson and George Sanders were lynched Tuesday night by parties unknown as a result of the killing of Paul Strange on the night of January 29th by the negro, Tennie Suted [Tennie Sneed]. The lynching occurred in Panola county, a mile or more beyond the Harrison county line, judging from description of the location. ... This man [who reported the lynching] stated the two negroes were found Wednesday morning hanging to one limb. They were discovered by Prof. Stranger, a brother of the dead man and a former candidate for county superintendent in this county. ... He notified the officials and an inquest was held, the verdict of which was that the negroes came to their deaths by strangulation at the hands of parties unknown. Their necks were not broken. ... He have the location as three miles south of new Elysian Fields and about a quarter of a mile from the place where Paul Strange was ambushed and killed by Tennie Sneed. ... [apparently a mob came to Marshall on Tuesday, 13th, looking for Sneed and learned that Sneed had lived in the same house as Sanders and Jackson] ... Sanders was about sixty years of age and always considered a good negro .... The woman was about forty years of age.” The Eagle notes, dateline Marshall, 15 Feb., that George Sanders and Mary Jackson “... were lynched by hanging to the same limb of a tree in Panola county Tuesday.” The Statesman, dateline Marshall, gives the location as “just across the Panola County line [separating Panola and Harrison counties].”

Note: Tennie Sneed was tried in late February in Marshall, Harrison Co. for the murder of Paul Strange. Likely that the mob that lynched Sanders and Jackson were from Harrison Co,.

notes:
The Talk states, dateline Tallulah, 15 February, that Lewis Andrews has been arrested at Rayville charged with being one of the two black men who killed J. Key Oakes, and that Anderson will remain in Rayville until the other man is arrested. From the Post, “Tallulah, La., Feb. 27.—The lifeless body of Lewis Andrews dangling from a rope’s end from a telephone pole at the street corner where he helped to murder J. Key Oakes and then robbed the body on the night of Feb. 13 sets aside the indictment returned against the negro yesterday by the Madison Parish grand jury, which had been called in special session of Judge F. X. Ransdell to consider his case.” The same report appears in the Times with more details: the mob captured Anderson in Rayville and then brought him back to Tallulah for lynching. The Times-Democrat, on the other hand, says that Anderson was being brought from Rayville and when the train arrived at Tallulah, the mob, “a large crowd”, took Anderson. From the Citizen-Times, “Vicksburg, Miss., Feb. 25.—Louis Anderson, negro, accused of complicity in the killing of Key Oakes, a young planter, who was shot to death at Tallulah, La., several weeks ago, was hanged by a mob at Tallulah tonight, according to a despatch [sic] received here. Andrews, the despatch [sic] continues, was captured at Rayville, La., and confessed, it is alleged, that he had part of the killing. He was to have been lodged in the Tallulah jail tonight to await trail but when Andrews and his guard stepped from a train they were seized by members of a mob. The guard was detained while the negro was dragged to a telegraph pole and hanged.”

According to the Constitution “Mobile, Ala., June 19.—Tom Jackson, a negro, 70 years old, who shot and killed Deputy Sheriff Coate, of Clarke Co., was taken by masked men from Clarke County officers near Jackson Wednesday morning and has not been heard from since.” The 6/20 Advertiser gives the name of the lynched man as Ebb Jackson. The News report ends with “Officers found him [Jackson] this morning and were taking him to Jackson when intercepted by the mob.” The same story appears in the Telegraph. According to the 6/20 Democrat, Deputy Sheriff Chalmers Coats was killed by Tom Jackson, black, 5-6 miles from Walker Springs on the 18th; added to the first story: “... it was learned that the shooting of Deputy Coats was done by Munsey Jackson, a negro about seventy-five years old, the father of Tom Jackson. ... Wednesday [19th] morning ... he was arrested by Deputy Wilson and carried to Jackson [Clarke Co.]. Just before reaching Jackson Deputy Wilson had to protect his prisoner from a mob which had formed. After stopping in Jackson a brief time, he left for the County jail at Grove Hill, but had gone only a short distance before a second mob took the negro away, swung him to a limb and riddled his body with bullets. However, the Alabamian says “Ben Jackson, a negro murderer, was taken from a guard of about a mile from Jackson Wednesday about half past one o’clock, strung up to a tree and his body riddled with bullets. The work was done by a body of masked men numbering over one hundred. ... Tom Jackson escaped and at the time of going to press is still at large. ... Several rumors that he has been lynched are without foundation.”—apparently Deputy Coate had a warrent for Ben’s son, Tom Jackson; there was an altercation and Ben Jackson shot and killed Coate. The 6/27 Democrat reports that Tom Jackson has been arrested near Sunflower [Washington Co.] and clarifies that the man who killed Coate was Ben Jackson, not Munsey Jackson. The 9/12 Advertiser story reports on the inquiry into this lynching, and states that Jackson was hanged from a tree near Grove Hill.

Note: Tom Jackson, Ben’s son, was threatened with lynching on 26 June 1912 in Clarke Co. 1910 Clarke Co. census lists a Benjamin Jackson, 71, living at Salt Works, with his wife Everline Jackson, and two young men named Hilliard. Bet this was a police lynching, or police assisted lynching.

notes:
According to the Advance, a mob of “several hundred” broke into jail and riddled Ed Collins with bullets. His body was then mutilated with a crowbar, taken to the town square and hanged from a telephone pole. There were 4000 spectators, according to the Advance. The News and Constitution stories add nothing. In the Banner report the lynch victim is unnamed. From the Times, “Cumming, Sept. 11.— ... The county jail was stormed yesterday by a mob who riddled Ed Collins, a negro, with bullets after which he was hung to a telephone pole in the court house square. Collins was arrested yesterday with three other negroes in connection with the killing of a young white girl Sunday. It is alleged that he assisted Ernest Cox, the negro who confessed the crime, in hiding the body. Cox was taken to Atlanta for safe keeping.” From the Journal, “Cumming, Ga., Sept. 12.—Further lynching as a result of the recent fatal assault by negroes on the young daughter of a prominent planter near here was narrowly averted yesterday afternoon. Three negroes, Oscar Daniels, Delia Daniels and Ed Collins, confessed that they were implicated in the attack on the young girl. As soon as the news became public a mob was formed to hang them to the same telephone pole on which Robert Edwards, a negro who confessed to the assault, was hanged Tuesday [10th]. Sheriff Reed and his deputies learning of the mob being formed, rushed the three negroes from the jail to an automobile and took them to Atlanta to be placed in jail. The mob then dispersed when it learned that its intended victims were no longer within reach.”

Note: Collins may be an alias of Robert Edwards who reportedly lynched on 10 September, or vice versa.

notes:
According to the Constitution, Yarbrough had been arrested and was being taken from Americus toward Oglethorpe for safe-keeping. A mob of “enraged citizens” followed the sheriff and over took him 15 miles from Americus. They hanged Yarbrough from “a bridge at a point in Macon county near Oglethorpe.” Seems reasonable to assume the “enraged citizens” were from Americus, Sumter Co. From the Times-Recorder, “Within four hours after ‘Babe’ Yarbrough, an Americus negro, attempted a felonious assault upon a little girl of twelve or thirteen years here [Americus] Saturday [5th] afternoon he had been tried and convicted in Judge Lynch’s court, sitting in special session, his body filled with bullets and the terrible incident of the day ended amid the usual excitement characterizing such tragedies. Vengeance came swiftly and surely, and, despite Yarbrough’s protestations of innocence of the charge, there was no doubt in the minds of the avengers that he was the guilty man, and they acted accordingly. Seeing that the trouble was brewing rapidly, and believing that the jail would be stormed, Deputy Sheriff Fuller sought to save his prisoner by spiriting him away to another county, but the avengers were aware of his plans and frustrated them before he had gone fifteen miles towards his destination [Oglethorpe]. ... It was the first lynching here [Sumter Co.] here in a long while, although in fact the killing of Yarbrough occurred beyond the county line in Macon county.” From the Caucasian, “Babe Yarborough, a negro railroad workman, who is alleged to have attempted assault on a twelve-year-old white girl, at Americus, Ga., was taken from the sheriff late Friday [4th] afternoon and hanged by a rope to a bridge near Oglethorpe. His body was then riddled with bullets.

notes: The Picayune reports that Silas Jimmerson, Mood Burks, and Jim Hurd were enroute to Benton for prison. On each man, a warning was hung: “This is the end and will always be the end of any nigger who forgets his place and assaults or attempts to assault white people in this part of the country.” From the Dispatch,”Shreveport, La., November 29.—That a portion of the mob which hanged three negroes near Bossier City last night had secured three other negroes and were hurrying to the scene of the lynching, intending to inflict similar punishment, but were overtaken by Sheriff Brumlow and forced to release their prisoners was learned tonight. Hurd, Jimmerson and Burk, the three negroes lynched last night, beat a jail attendant into insensibility several months ago and escaped from the Bossier Parish prison. The three rescued by Brumlow are said to have kept the men in hiding and aided the escape. They were captured in Bossier City to-day by the mob. Brumlow followed in an automobile, drove the lynchers into the woods and brought the three negroes to the parish jail at Bossier City. The negroes lynched were being taken overland from an adjoining parish, where they were captured, to Bossier City when the mob overpowered the guard and hanged the men in a swamp.”

notes:
The 11/30 Constitution reports, dateline Cordele, 29 November, “Armed men, determined to lynch Chesley Williams, a negro, accused of shooting and wounding the wife of a prominent planter near Rhine [Dodge Co.], Ga., and of then assaulting her 18-year-old daughter, tonight are pursuing in automobiles another automobile containing the negro and a police escort. The negro was captured early tonight [29th] by the Dodge county sheriff in a small frame building near the home where the crimes were committed last night. Fearing that the accused man would be summarily treated by enraged citizens, the sheriff place the negro in an automobile and, with five deputies, left for an unknown destination to place the negro in jail. Residents of the vicinity where the assault and shooting occurred, and who had been searching for the negro on their own accord, learned of the action of the sheriff a half hour after he had left with the negro. Other automobiles were obtained and, following the general direction taken by the sheriff, are tonight racing to overtake him and obtain possession of the negro. It is believed the sheriff started for McRae [Telfair Co.], Ga., or some other point on the Southern railroad.” In the 12/1 edition, the Constitution reports that Chestley Williams was taken from the authorities in McRae at 3:00 a.m. and riddled with bullets. According to the Times-Journal, Sidney Williams was taken from the Telfair Co. courthouse at McRae, carried a short distance, and riddled with bullets. The Times-Journal also notes that reports in the Savannah Morning News and Macon Telegraph that the lynching took place in Dodge Co. by Dodge Co. citizens was incorrect. Further that the planter lived in China Hill, Telfair Co.

notes: From the Times-Picayune, “Jackson, Miss., Dec. 17, 1912. Officer J. S. White, of the Jackson police, the oldest member of the force, to-day suffered a flesh wound in the leg during a round with Joe Beeman, a cocaine-laden negro. Beeman was terrorizing the negro neighborhood and submitted to arrest, but after a call was turned in for the patrol wagon Beeman seized the officer’s pistol. A scuffle ensued, during which the weapon was discharged, the bullet taking effect in White’s leg. The negro then got away and shut himself in a house, firing indiscriminately, but without effect. A posse reached the scene quickly after a riot call was turned in and the house was surrounded. Beeman refused to come and surrender and a fusillade of shots was fired during which the negro was fatally shot.” From the Telegraph, “Jackson, Miss., Dec. 17.—An unidentified negro, who shot and slightly wounded Patrolman Joseph White, after wrestling a pistol from the officer , was killed by a mob here today. After the shooting the negro took refuge in a nearby house. The house was set on fire and he was shot to death while attempting to escape the burning structure.” The same story appears in the Sun. From the Democrat, “Jackson, Miss., Dec. 18.—To avoid being burned to death in a house which had been set on fire by a mob to smoke him out, Ellis Wilson, an ex-convict, negro, dashed out and was shot to death by his pursuers. Previously he had shot and wounded Patrolman Joseph White white resisting arrest. The negro overpowered the officer and shot him with his own pistol. The mob then took up the chase. Wilson is said to have previously killed five men. He was shooting  when the patrolman attempted to arrest him. The fire department attempted to disperse the mob and a riot call brought out the whole police force, but they were powerless.”

A posse gathered and he was strung quickly up to a limb and his body filled with bullets, after which the crowd dispersed. Smith, although a preacher, was a notoriously bad negro. He was an old man with hoary head and was toothless. He was somewhat of a leader among the negroes, being a little above the average in intelligence.”

The mob was searching for Dick Odum, black, who give Charlie West [first name given in the Early County News] money to escape — presumably West was thought to have murdered Marshal Newberry. In a second he was riddled with bullets. ... The trouble which has resulted thus fatally grew out of a dispute Sunday between [Samuel] Stribbling and a negro named ‘Ruddy’ over wages. Ruddy shot and killed Stribbling, and Sunday night Deputy Sheriff Matthews was killed by either Ruddy or one of the Ellis negroes when the officer, at the head of a posse, had surrounded a house to which bloodhounds had trailed the murder of Stribbling. The county was aroused, and hundreds of citizens heavily armed have scoured the country for the past twenty-four house. To-night several hundred of the men came into Palmetto ... and reported that the two Ellis brothers, negroes, and Ruddy had been killed and their riddled bodies left in the swamps. Sam Ellis, one of the two negro brothers ... was riddled with bullets by a posse to-day, however, however, before he and his brother, Wade Ellis, had mortally wounded Deputy Sheriff J. B. Moran and seriously wounded Deputy Max Burnette. ... The negro Ruddy was killed single-handed by Henry Wasgame, a member of the sheriff’s posse, last night in the edge of a swamp near the negro’s house. notes:
From the El Paso Herald, “Houston, Texas, July 30.—Reports from Palestine, Texas today say 15 negroes were killed and one white man badly wounded in a race riot near Clocum, Anderson county late yesterday. ... Palestine, Texas, July 30.—Meagre reports received here by telephone from that section between Elkhart and Slocum today state that fifteen negroes and two whites were killed in a race riot which became general following trouble between a white man and a negro, growing out of an attempt of a white man to collect a debt .... “ The 7/30 Daily Herald says between 12 and 15 blacks and one white man were killed. According to the Reporter, 23 black men and 4 for white men were killed; the white men were “Dick Stubblefield, deputy sheriff. Sam Wolfe, Constable. E. E. Rains, prominent white farmer. Unknown white farmer. A deputy sheriff of Houston county is reported fatally wounded in this afternoon’s fight and a dozen men injured on both sides.”—names of black victims not given. The 7/31 Post says 18 black men killed, none named, and no white men have been killed. The 8/1 Daily Herald gives the list of eight dead black men: Cleve Larkin, 18; John Hays, 30; Alex Holley, 23; Sam Baker, 28; Ben Dancer, 70; Jeff Wilson, 18; Dick Wilson, 45; Will Burley, age unknown. The wounded: Charley Wilson, 15 and Lusk Holley, 18. The missing: Ned Larken, Abe Wilson and his son, Ned Forman. Also noted is that four white men, named, have been arrested and other arrests are expected. Cleve Larkin was killed and Charley Wilson and Lusk Holley wounded on Friday [29th] morning by 6-7 white men; Alex Holley was killed Friday 10-11 p.m. by 18-20 white men. The Messenger lists the dead as, all black men: Cleve Larkin, 18; John Hays, 30; Alex Holly, 23; Sam Baker, 28, Ben Dancer, 70; Jeff Wilson, 45; —Burley; wounded: Charley Wilson, 15; Lusk Holly, 18. Missing: Abe WIlson and a young son; Ned Larkin and William Forman. The 8/4 Post lists the names of thirteen white men who have been jailed in connection with this incident. The Statesman reports that Lusk Holly and Charles Wilson were taken before the grand jury in Palestine on 17 August; the story also reports that seven white men, six names listed, were indicted for killing five black men in Anderson Co.; “The indictments returned for the Anderson county killings cover only five negroes killed, there being no indictments returned for the killing of John Hays and Alex Kelly.”—that would be consistent with the seven dead listed by the Messenger, but the Statesman also states that those men are charged with killing an unnamed black man in Houston county—that would make 8 black men killed. The 8/18 Post carries the same story and notes that Abe Wilson is still missing. The News says that John Hays, Ben Dancy, Jeff Wilson, Dick Wilson, Sam Baker, and Cleveland Larkin were killed two miles from Slocum by mobs of white men.

Note: the many reports are confused and often based on wild rumors. There seems to be some agreement that Cleveland/Cleve Larkin, John Hays, Alex Holly/Holley, Sam Baker, Ben Dancer/Drancy, Jeff Wilson, and Will Burley were killed; Dick Wilson may have been killed. There’s no evidence that Charley WIlson, Lusk Holly, Ned Larkin, Abe Wilson, Wilson’s son, or William/Ned Forman were killed.

From the 8/1 Times-Union, “Latest reports from Dady is that only one negro was strung up by the mob.” He was accused of the rape and murder of little Bessie Morrison. Apparently the lynching took place on Saturday, 30 July.

Then the crowd dispersed and the night’s stillness was again unbroken.” The same story appears in the Advocate and other Texas newspapers. notes:
From the Tribune, “Three Negroes Slain By Mob. Fort Worth, Tex., April 30.—A mob lynched three negroes early today at Marshall, Tex., The negroes had killed a deputy sheriff. The militia, which had been guarding the jail for three days, was relieved at midnight and the citizens immediately formed a mob, taking the authorities by surprise. The Post, however, reports, dateline Marshall, 30 April, that only Matt Chase and Creole Mose Hill were hanged and that Pie Jesse Jefferson was left in his cell. Similarly, the Wise County Messenger states that Mose Hill and Mat Chase were lynched by 30-40 men between 2:00 and 3:00 a.m.; “Jejsse [Jesse] Jefferson was not molested by the mob.” Ditto for the Light and the 5/1 and 5/4 News.

Note: it seems clear that two men were lynched, not three: Mat/Matt Chase and Mose Hill—the question is does “Creole Mose” = Mose Hill or does “Pie” Hill = Mose Hill. From the Messenger, “Tyler, May 3.—JimJim Hodge was lynched by a crowd of 1000 men at 12:05 o’clock Saturday [1st] Saturday afternoon. From a huge derrick used for hoisting stone in the building of the new Smith County courthouse .... There was no excitement; no howling mob; no evidence of anything except determination. ... There was no attempt at disguise. Those who took part in the lynching went about it just as they went about their daily business. ... The Crime. Winnie Herman, eighteen years old, was attacked by a negro man Friday evening in her yard two miles east of town.” According to the 5/2 Post, “Tyler, Texas, May 1.—Jim Hodge, a negro 25 years old, was taken from the Smith county jail at noon today and lynched on the court house square. Hodge had been arrested on the charge of having attacked and attempted to criminally assault Miss Winnie Harmon, 18 year-old daughter of M. J. Harmon, a truck grower living three miles southeast of Tyler, yesterday between 5 and 6 o’clock p. m. ... By 10:30 [a.m.] more than 3000 people had gathered.  At 11:30 after the International and Great Northern form Palestine arrived and it was found no soldiers were abroad, the jail doors were broken down and the mob soon had the negro.”—given the mob size and the alleged offense, it’s a wonder that he wasn’t tortured or his body desecrated. The 5/3 Post raises the possibility that Jim Hodge was not the man who attacked the girl because the girl didn’t give a definitive identification. According to the 5/4 Reporter, nineteen persons have been accused of participating in the lynching of Jim Hodge; no names listed. The 5/6 Reporter lists seventeen persons accused of participating. The 5/9 Reporter says that charges against six persons were dropped but the other eleven are held over.

Note: this would be an interesting case to follow-up on to find out what happened to those charged.

notes:
According to the 6/23 Post (very, very difficult to read), nine black men have been killed; on Saturday [20th] midnight a mob of 150 men removed six black men (Jerry Evans, 22; Will Johnson, 24; Mose Spellman, 24; Cleveland Williams, 27; William Manuel, 25; Frank Williams, 22) five were hanged from the same tree and the sixth, Frank Williams was shot as he tried to escape. Apparently the same mob killed two other unnamed black men whose bodies were found riddled with bullets in a “creek bottom near Hemphill”; further Rabbit Bill McCoy, was shot on the 22nd “... while standing at the gate of A [illegible] Johnson, the victim of Saturday night’s murder. A loaded pistol, [illegible] cocked, was found by his side—number of killers unreported. Two additional black men, [Perry] Price and Johnson [Wright], who were accused of the murders were taken to Beaumont for safe-keeping. The Times story is also almost illegible and doesn’t seem to add anything. The Star-Telegram list: Jerry Evans, 28; Will Johnson, 20; Moss Spellman, 22; Clevel Williams, 20; Will Manuel, 30 years—they were taken from jail about one mile and hanged—no mention of Frank Williams or two unknown black men being shot; “’Rabbit’ Bill McCoy, a negro about 40 years old, was killed last night in front of the home of Arle Johnson.” The News states they were taken at 1:00 a.m. by 200 men and taken one mile from the courthouse for involvement in the murder of two white men: Hugh Dean and Arle Johnson; “The body of Hardy Evans, one of the principals of the Dean murder, is reported as having been found on the Hemphill and San Augustine road, about half-way between the two places. A negro whose name can not be ascertained is reported as being killed, but there are many wild rumors afloat of other negroes having been killed in the county. At the present time these nine are the only ones whose names can be given with any degree of certainty.” The 6/24 Post gives a more detailed account, but almost illegible; Bill McCoy was shot by a “large number of men” Sunday afternoon at the gate to the Arle Johnson house; Jerry Evans, Will Johnson, Moss Spellman, Wm. Manuel, Cleve Williams were lynched Sunday night after being taken from the jail—Si Williams, also taken from the jail but ran away and was shot at, five times, by the mob but “Williams was traced for about a mile, when all traced of him was lost.”; the Post also notes that Hardy Evans and __and Roberts escaped. According to the Democrat, dateline Houston, 22 June, six unnamed black men were taken from jail at Hamphill [Hemphill], five were hanged and one shot down trying to escape; “This afternoon Burgha Singleton, Hardi Evans and Henry Thomas, all negroes, were found dead on the roadside between Hemphill and Geneva, their bodies riddled with bullets.”—could only find this report.

Note: the reports on this incident are confusing but it seems clear that Jerry Evans, Will Johnson, Mose/Moss Spellman, Cleve/Clevel/Cleveland Williams, and Will/William Manuel were hanged and that “Rabbit” Bill McCoy was shot. The most detailed account, the 6/24 Post, doesn’t state that Frank/Si Williams was killed, and there’s no mention of other victims.

notes:
According to the 6/28 Constitution, Walter Wilkins and Albert Baker were arrested for raping a young girl — in Wayne Co., I think — and were brought to jail in Waycross. Later they were taken to be transported back to Wayne Co. (the jail in Jesup). A mob of 1000 took the two men from officers. Using a chain, they hoisted one of the men to a limb while the other, being handcuffed to the hanging man, clasped the tree trunk. Both men were then riddled with bullets. The story also says another black man was lynched in Hickox in connection to the same rape. The 6/29 Constitution reports that many of the tree’s limbs were taken as souvenirs, and that a mob from Hickox had gone to Jesup [Wayne Co.] to await Wilkins and Baker. The Weekly Journal and Weekly Herald report that the mob was mostly from Wayne Co. with some from Ware Co. observing, and it reports that an unnamed black man was lynched at Hickox. The Monitor report is consistent and reports the third, unnamed black man, was lynched near Nahunta [Wayne Co.].

Walker had cursed a white woman and threatened a white man with a pistol, it is said. When the mob of about fifty men ordered him to come from his house he replied with a shot. The torch was then applied and as the occupants came out they were shot down.” From the News, “Hickman, Ky., Oct. 10.—The wife of Dave Walker, shot by the night riders, died and was buried late yesterday afternoon. As the men approached the house, Padgett and some others in the house,opened fire and killing one man and wounding others. The men riddled the house with bullets killing Padgett and his 10 year-old daughter, and wounding two of his sons. Later a crowd attacked the house capturing Padgett’s wife and son, both wounded, and started for Reidsville. They were overtaken by a mob 75 men who took Padgett’s wife and his son and riddled them with bullets. The 5/23 edition reports that Padgett’s wife confessed to killing one of the 15 men attacking their home and that Arthur Padgett, the son who escaped, surrendered and was in jail in Savannah. The 5/24 Constitution reports that a second Padgett son, Melvin Padgett, was in jail in Savannah. The 5/22 Chronicle reports that Flem Padgett and his daughter were killed and his wife and a son lynched. The 5/23 edition of the Chronicle says that Flem was lynched and the 5/24 edition reports that Melvin Padgett has been taken to Savannah. The Post states that Padgett’s son was 21 years-old.

From the Dealer, “Memphis, Tenn., Aug. 16.—Will Clifford, a negro, was arrested at Tiptonville, Tenn., and confessed to assaulting Mrs. Mary Cowan, white, and throwing her body into the river, also that he killed another woman a year ago. From the Ardmoreite, “Memphis, Tenn., Aug. 16.—Constable Burris of Tiptonville, Tenn., was overpowered by a mob last night at Maple, Ky., and Will Clifford, a negro prisoner, was taken from him, carried to within one mile of Clifton [Clinton, Hickman Co.] and hanged. ... Wednesday [14th] night a mob stormed the jail but the prisoner could not be found. Sheriff J. A. Corlew told the mob that the prisoner had been taken to Dyersburg [Dyer Co.]. Thursday night the negro, who had been concealed in the barn of Squire Lambert, was taken secretly by Constable Burris toward Maple. Farmers along the road telephoned back to Tiptonville, were a mob of one hundred mounted men were soon formed.”

KY—that’s several counties east. Couldn’t find any non-redundant reports in Ancestry.com. There was a threatened lynching of Clifford on 14 August in Lake Co.

notes: The 5/30 Constitution reports, dateline Tallulah, that Robert T. Rogers was taken from the jail and hanged from a telephone pole. The Post notes that five of the masked men were recognized including the murdered man’s brother, a Dr. Brown. The News reports that Dr. Frank Brown, a wealthy planter of Ouachita Parish, and brother of the murdered white man, Jesse Brown, is under indictment for organizing and leading the lynch mob. The Picayune gives the size of the mob at 25. He was accused of killing a white merchant at Girard, Richland Parish. The Post reports that Rogers' widow filed suit against the railroad for $100,000; the story states that the railroad brought a mob from Monroe to Tallulah to lynch Rogers. The 3/6/12 Constitution reports, dateline New Orleans, that a jury may consider whether the Vicksburg, Shreveport, and Pacific Railroad was a “co-conspirator” in the lynching of Rogers in Tallulah in 1907 [1906]. The railroad chartered a special train to take the mob to the jail. The 6/7/12 Constitution says that the suit is now to the Supreme Court; also that the mob was from Monroe [Ouachita Parish] and the victim’s name was William Rogers. From the Post,”A civil suit of extraordinary interest, involving the legal liability of a railway system chartering a train to be used by a mob, will be called for trail at the May term of Federal court which convenes in Jackson next Monday. The suit is that of Mrs. Alice Rodgers vs. Vicksburg Shreveport & Pacific Railway, plaintiff asking $50,000 damages because her husband was lynched by a mob at Tallulah, La., the mob having been carried to that place from Monroe on a special train chartered especially for the purpose.”

From the Star, “Inverness, Fla., June 8.—Jim Davis, alias Dago Jim, was lynched here between the hours of 8 and 12 last night. The Brooksville Rifles arrived at 12 o’clock after the trouble was over, and returned on the 4 o’clock train this morning.” The 8/5 Constitution states that Governor Howard suspended Sheriff George R. notes:
The 8/7 Constitution that a mob of 3000 stormed the Rowan Co. jail and carried away Jack Dillingham, Nease Gillespie, and John Gillespie, despite the presence of Rowan Rifles (local military company whose rifles were loaded with blanks). The 8/7 Post reports that the men were “cuffed and slashed with knives by their captors” before being hanged. The 8/8 Post states that “Following the lynching ... thousands of people visited the scene. Some of them cut off fingers, ears, and other parts from the dead bodies and carried away the grewsome souvenirs.” The 8/8 Constitution reports that the leader of the mob, an ex-convict from Montgomery Co. named George Hall, has been arrested. There’s a brief story in the 8/10 Constitution that the barn of the white family that was murdered, was burned down — apparently in retaliation of the lynching of the Gillespie’s and Jack Dillingham. The white family was the Lyerly family (Isaac, his wife, and their 2 children) who lived at Barber Junction according to the Courier. The 8/10 Landmark notes that the lynch mob of 2000 were from multiple counties. The 8/14 edition states that four white men have been arrested: three “low-class” textile mill workers and a tenant farmer — the story names the men and describes them. The Star reports that the Supreme Court of North Carolina had denied a new trial to George Hall who was convicted of being one of the Salisbury lynchers—he was sentenced to ten years.

Note: John Gillespie, Nease Gillespie [a.k.a. Mitchell Graham], and Jack Dillingham/Dellingham were threatened with lynching on 14 July in Rowan Co.

After shooting and seriously wounding both, the negro told them that he thought they were members of a posse and assured them that he was very sorry he had fired on them. Later about 25 men with dogs started on Kinneys trail. A few members of the searching party finally located Kinney in a bottom near Doella, a plantation postoffice. Nash sent a bullet into the negro and he tumbled over dead. notes:
From the 9/10 Times-Picayune, “Sumner [Tallahatchie], Miss., Sept. 9.—The disappearance on Friday of Ed James, a negro tenant, from the plantation of Hon. Earl Brewer develops into circumstances of a murder. Charred fragments of a human body were found in an ash heap yesterday, a mile from the scene of the killing, and were identified as the remains of the negro, James. ... Ike Loftin, his brother, Baz Loftin, and Jake Hutchinson are charged with the murder, and John Melton and a negro, Ed Brown, are charged with being accessories after the fact. The suspected murderers are white men, and are transient croppers and laborers. They are alleged to have been bootleggers and craps shooters among the negroes, and are said to be a lawless element that has demoralized and terrorized that portion of Tallahatchie County. Brown was taken into custody Thursday, and Melton was arrested and placed in jail here to-day. The Loftins escaped to the swamps toward the hills at the beginning of the investigation.” From the 9/13 Times-Picayune, dateline Jackson 12 September, “As was stated in the Picayune of Sunday Governor Vardaman has been called on to offer a reward for the arrest and conviction of the murderers of Ed James, a Coahoma County negro. The negro was murdered and his body burned to ashes in his house.” Three white men, Ike Loflin, Ray Loflin, and Jake Hutchinson shot Ed James on the 4th because they feared that he would report them to the officials for selling moonshine whisky at black festival on Saturday, the 2nd, near Vance [Quitman Co.]. They then enlisted the help of another white man, John Melton, and a black man, Ed Brown, to carry Ed James’ body into the woods and burn it. The Loflin’s and Hutchinson have disappeared but Melton and Brown are in jail and confessed. The Banner reports, dateline 14 September, that Will James, living in Tallahatchie county, “... was taken to the woods by three white men and shot to death, after which his body was burned.” From the Landmark, “They kill and burn negroes in Mississippi with very little provocation. The other day in Tallahatchie county, Miss., three white men shot a negro to death and then burned his body, all because the negro had bought some whiskey from one of the whites and afterwards informed on him. These white men are guilty of deliberate murder and out  to be hanged.” This incident does not appear in the Post’s 1905 inventory of Mississippi lynchings.

Note: depending on how one wants to define it, the number of the mob was either 3 or 5. The 1910 census lists a Earle L. Brewer, 40, a lawyer, living with his wife Minnie, at Clarksdale in Coahoma Co. That same Earl Brewer is listed as living in Water Valley, Yalobusha Co. in 1900. The Times-Picayune stories mention that Earl Brewer was a District Attorney, apparently in Coahoma Co.; in 1906 he was a candidate for Governor. Couldn’t find in 1900 census any Loftin/Loflin, John Melton, or Ed Brown in Coahoma, Tallahatchie, or Quitman counties. 1900 census lists a William James, 31, living in Beat 5, Coahoma Co., but no Ed James. 1895 Atlas places Vance in Newton County, but USGS lists a Vance in Newton Co. and a Vance in Quitman. Quitman is directly adjacent to both Coahoma and Tallahatchie counties. Newton Co. is a very long distance from either.

notes:
The 2/4 Constitution reports that Luther Holbert, Halbert in the headline, and three/two other unnamed negroes are being hunted in connection to the murder of John Eastland, “a wealthy plantation owner”, and Albert Carr, a black tenant farmer. Apparently Holbert shot Eastland—when a “posse” arrived at the plantation there was more shooting and a black man named John Winters was killed. The 2/8 Constitution states that Luther Holbert and his wife were burned at the stake “before a church” in front of a mob of 1000. Also, that John Winters had been killed by Eastland. Further, that three/two unknown negroes had been killed by the posses: both were killed on the 6th near Belzoni, Yazoo Co.—mistaken identity. Interesting follow-up, the 9/11 Constitution reports that W. C. Eastland, brother of the murdered planter, has been charged with having caused the burning of Luther Holbert and his wife. The 9/23 edition notes that the charge against C. C. Eastland was dropped by the court. Shay (p. 103-105) describes the torture of Mrs. Luther Holbert, citing the Vicksburg Evening Post. The Post reports that the Holberts were beaten, had their fingers and ears cut off. From the Item, “Indianaola [Sunflower Co.], Miss., Sept. 21.—The trial of W. C. Eastland, charged with the burning of Luther Holbert, was taken up by the Circuit Court here yesterday. The special venire of fifty was exhausted, and one of the regular juries was almost exhausted before a jury could be secured.”

Note: 1900 census lists a Luther Halbert, black, 48, and his wife, Anne, 48, living in Scott Co. with their children. Couldn’t find this family in 1910 census in Mississippi.

notes:
From the Constitution, “Columbia, S. C., March 1.—(Special.)—South Carolina has just had another lynching, the story of which makes one of the most remarkable and unique chapters in the criminal history of the state. On Saturday [27th] morning last a strange negro, giving in turn the names of Richard Johnson, John Brown and Joe Swinson, arrived in the town of Holly Hill, Berkeley county, and made his appearance upon the streets. ... As the day wore on the negro became very obstreperous and was finally arrested for disorderly conduct. He was so violent after his arrest that it became necessary in order to subdue him to handcuff him and tie him securely with ropes after he was placed in the town calaboose. The authorities of the town thought no more of the matter until Sunday [28th] when the dead body of the negro was found in a vacant tenant house some distance from the town, the body having seven bullet holes in it, sitting erect by the side of the wall still wearing the handcuffs.” From the Tribune, “Strange Negro Shot Full of Holes by Lynchers in South Carolina.” The rest of the report is the same as the Constitution. From the Courier, “Murder At Holly Hill. A Negro, who had been Put in the Town Prison for a Trifling Offence, Found in an Unoccupied Outhouse Dead, with Six Bullets in his Body. Magistrate McCoy Trying to Find the Guilty White Men. Bowyer, Berkeley County, March 1.—Special: The citizens of Holly Hill [Berkeley Co.] were aroused last Sunday [28th] morning on hearing that a man had been found dead in an unoccupied house, just outside the incorporate limits—presumably a negro, who had been incarcerated in the town prison the previous night [27th]. Investigation so far shows that a negro man, apparently about 25 years old, of medium height ... arrived at Holly Hill at a late hour on Friday [26th] night, and procured lodging with on Luke Emanuel, saying that he haired from Summerville, that his names was Robert Williams, and that the once worked under a Mr. Scarf, who had charge of a working train on the Southern Railroad. ... [On Saturday morning he went out on the street and created a mild disturbance and was approached by the town marshal and ordered to leave; a bit later he created another disturbance and he was arrested and tied up in a building.] ... It is a clearly demonstrated fact that the unfortunate human was taken from the guard house, the lock which was opened carefully being taken away. He was forced down the railroad several hundred yards, shot and thrown into a deep ditch, out of which he succeeded in climbing after travelling up in for some distance. Tracks of two people were found leading away from the scene of the murder, along which trail was found the lock belonging to the guard house door. ... [He made his way to a cabin and reported that he had been shot by some men; the marshal was notified but refused to come to the cabin and the man died soon after.] ... Suspicion is strong against several persons, and it is so far a well-established fact that the prisoner was not interfered with by his own race of people ....” From the State, “Holly Hill, March 7.—The coroner’s jury in the case of Richard Johnson, the negro taken from the guard house at this place and shot on Sunday morning, Feb. 8, rendered a verdict this morning after deliberating at three different sessions. In the opinion of the jury there was sufficient evidence brought out to warrant holding of the marshal D. A. Hart, for further examination before the court of general sessions. ... Considerable suspicion is attached to one or two other persons, but sufficient evidence was not brought out to hold them.”

Note: this is likely a police lynching, or police assisted lynching.

notes: The Post writes, “A lynching party took a negro, John Maynard, from officers at Montgomery. Result of robbery and murder.” From the Star-Telegram, “Houston, Texas, March 21.—(Special.)—John Maynard, a negro, was lynched by a mob early this morning at Montgomery station on the Santa Fe railroad. He was charged with on of a party of negroes who robbed several Bohemians, and after eating them killed one. Two other negroes are under arrest.” The same story appears page 1 in the Enterprise. On page 6, of the Enterprise, “Montgomery, Texas, March 20.—About midnight last night a party of three Greeks, working in an extra gang at Montgomery Junction of the Santa Fee, were turning to their boarding cars from Montgomery were set upon by two or three negroes and beaten and cut with knives and robbed. One of the men died today. The others identified a negro, John Maynard, as one of their assailants. He was placed in the calaboose by the officers. Late this evening a mob gathered and forced the jail, took Maynard to the woods, where it is rumored he confessed and implicated another negro. As Maynard has not returned it is supposed that he was hanged.” The News, dateline Montgomery, 21 March, confirms that Maynard was killed by a mob “last night”, i.e., the 20th, for a murder on Saturday night—he was hanged from a telegraph pole.

A crowd again collected to make sure the negro was dead. Some one cut off his right ear. notes:
According to multiple, vivid articles in the 8/17 Constitution, Paul Reed and Will Cato were taken from troops at the courthouse in Statesboro, taken 2 miles and burned at the stake. The articles reports that local deputy sheriffs aided the mob — the 8/23 story describes how the sheriff opened the jail cell doors for the mob. Cato and Reed had been convicted of the murders and their execution set for 9 September. The article has photos of Reed and Cato before the lynching. Reed and Cato were tied to a tree stump, wood piled around them, and then soaked in kerosene. They begged to be shot or hanged as the flames reached them. After the original murders, 20 blacks were rounded up and some whipped. They were the “Before Day Club”, “a black mafia” according to the Constitution. In Reed’s confession he implicated Preacher Gaines, — Rainey, Big John Hall, — Talbot, Handy Bell, Kid Young, and — Cato. The 8/31 edition of the Constitution reports on the inquires into the mob violence. The 9/1 edition indicates members of the mob might be indicted. The 8/31 Post has a long article on an investigation into the lynchings; the 9/7 Post reports that the Methodist Episcopal Church passed a resolution condemning the lynchings; the 10/25 Post notes that “Georgia Judge Declares Lawless Element Is Composed of ‘Good Citizens’”. The Chronicle has a long editorial condemning mob violence and the lynching of Cato and Reid.

Note: the most relevant issue of the Statesboro News, 8/16, is missing from microfilm. The issues of 8/2, 8/5, and 8/12 have reports on the trial of Reid and Cato. Paul Reid/Reed/Reese and Will/William Cato were threatened with lynching on 31 July in Bulloch Co.

notes: According to the 9/8 Constitution, a mob routed state troops and took Maples from jail to a public square and hanged and riddled. Fingers and other body parts cut off for souvenirs. Some members of the mob were indicted but never convicted. The 9/9 Constitution reports that Acting Governor Cunningham is investigating the lynching. According to the 9/19 edition, many Huntsville preachers denounced the lynchers. The 9/20 edition of the Constitution (and the Advertiser) reports that a grand jury wants to impeach Sheriff Rodgers and the Huntsville mayor for “neglect of duty” in failing to prevent the Maples lynching. The 9/21 Constitution reports that some of the troops who where supposed to have protected Maples, hid because they were so frightened. The 10/12 edition reports on more repercussions from the failure to protect Maples, including calls for congressional action. notes:
From the Item, “Woodville, May 9.—About 5:20 yesterday fire was discovered in the big brick store of C. Schaefer, in Woodville. In a short time this building, together with the frame stores of G. A. Wetlin and Monroe Brown, with their contents were entirely destroyed. ... The fire is supposed to have been the work of an incendiary, and a reward of $500 has been offered by the citizens of Woodville for the arrest of the guilty persons.” The Appeal writes “About the quietest lynching that has ever taken place in Mississippi was the one recently pulled off in Wilkinson county, near Woodville. So quiet, indeed, was the affair that the details of it have just come to light, and it was so effectually managed that even the name of the negro seems to have perished with the victim. The offense for which this man suffered was the accidental setting fire to a store while in the act of committing a burglary, causing loss of property nearly $50,000 worth of property. The first occurred on May 8 last ...” From the Truth, “Citizens of Wilkinson county, Mississippi, have lynched a negro burglar who confessed to setting fire to a store in Woodville.” According to the Republican, “Jackson, May 25.—It was learned here today that a very quiet and successful lynching of a negro incendiary took place in Wilkinson county, near Woodville, recently. ... [description of the fire] ... ‘I [the sheriff] am told that the negro no longer lives in this county.’” [sarcasm]

notes: The Times-Union reports that he was taken from the jail and lynched. He was carried about a half mile from the city and lynched in what is known as the picnic grounds. He was tied to the same tree from which two negroes [James Denson and has step-brother] were lynched last Christmas a year ago.

notes: According to the Picayune, a sheriff named Riddle left the prisoner with another sheriff. After a time, a man came to the latter sheriff with a note from Riddle, and George Kincaid was handed over to the man. A mob then took Kincaid to a swamp and hanged him. From the Item, “Cleveland, Miss., June 24.—The body of George Kincaid, the negro who seriously wounded John Breck and George Stoakely, five years ago, has been found hanging in the swamps. A mob gathered at Ruleville [Sunflower Co.] Saturday [20th] to lynch the negro, and he was spirited to this place [Cleveland, Bolivar Co.] by Deputy Sheriff Riddle.” From the Republic, “Cleveland, Miss., June 23.—The body of George Kincaid, a negro who seriously wounded John Beck and George Stokely five years ago, has been found hanging in the swamps. A mob gathered at Ruleville Saturday to lynch the negro, and he was spirited to this place by Deputy Sheriff Riddle. Deputy Sheriff McGuire was unwilling to take the negro, even for a few hours, but agreed, on Riddle’s promising to come back and remain with the prisoner. Riddle failed to appear, but instead came an order duly signed by him that the prisoner be delivered to the bearer, one Jackson, which was done. The discovery of the body in the swamps today followed. While nothing definite can be said, there seemed to be a plot to shift the blame for the lynching on the officers of Bolivar County, as it is alleged that an armed body of men were seen less than ten minutes behind Deputy Sheriff Riddle, with every opportunity to overtake the negro within the bounds of Sunflower County.”

notes:
The Constitution reports that Cato Garrett has been arrested in connection with the murder of a young white farmer, Harry Stout, 4 miles south of Vicksburg. “... there are fears of a lynching.” The 7/5 Times-Picayune reports that Harry Stout, a prominent Warren Co. planter, was killed by Cato Garrett, 18. “By this time the murder of Mr. Stout became known pretty generally, and there was bitter feeling brewing on all sides. Judge George Anderson and Sheriff Brennan, fearing that the negro might be taken from the County Jail and lynched, co-operated to prevent such action by having Garrett hurried in a carriage from the jail to the westbound Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific train .... The prisoner was taken across into Louisiana, and now his whereabouts is unknown ....” The 7/8 Times-Picayune states that Garrett was being taken by train to be jailed in Vicksburg. When the train stopped in Stouts Crossing, a mob of 15 masked men entered and took Garrett. He was then lynched. From the Herald, “Vicksburg, Miss., July 7.—Cato Garrett, the negro who stabbed Henry Stout to death last Saturday [4th] morning, was hanged by a mob near the scene of his crime this afternoon. Garrett was taken to Natchez Saturday. Sheriff Brennan fearing an assault on the jail here. This morning a special grand jury found a true bill against Garrett, and Sheriff Brennan notified the Adams county sherif to bring the negro to this county. Sheriff Paul, with the negro, took passage on the train due here at 5 o’clock this afternoon. At Stout’s crossing, a flag station six miles south of this city, the train was held up by five masked and heavily armed men, who took the negro and hanged him.” From the Item, “Vicksburg, Miss., July 8.—Cato Garrett, the negro who murdered Harry Stout on July 4, was taken from an officer and hanged at Stout’s Crossing, about four miles below this city, last night. Garrett had been in the jail at Natchez since Saturday night, and yesterday morning an officer started to Vicksburg with the prisoner.”

Note: there was a threatened lynching on the 4th.

According to the Statesman, dateline Beaumont, 23 July, Mooney Allen, black, shot and fatally wounded a white policeman, Walter Stansbury and fled but was captured and returned to Beaumont; A crowd gathered and pursued him. The negro refused to halt, but turn and was in the act of firing on his pursuers when a fusillade of shots went in his direction, seven taking effect in his body and producing instant death. Negroes and whites were all gratified at the termination of the affair. Racial feeling had nothing to do with the matter, as Allen had long been a terror to respectable men of his race and they rejoiced at his taking off. Late this evening Officer Standsbury was still alive and resting well, but hopes of his recovery are very slim.” The 7/23 Enterprise states that Allen was being pursued by a “crowd of men, many of whom had pistols, started in pursuit of the negro. Some of them kept up a constant firing. ... He fell dead on Cedar street half way between Pearl and Main streets. ... Several citizens shot at him as he down the street [Cedar] and it is probable that one of these killed him.” According to the 7/24 Enterprise, Allen was shot four times, and gives the location as the same as did the American story. The 7/25 Enterprise states that Allen, after being wounded in a shoot out with the officers, was shot four times by “an old man” on Cedar street: “The old man fired four shots and another man ran up and shot at in twice. The last man who shot was drunk. The crowd gathered and the negro was hauled to the undertaking establishment. There were cries of ‘burn him,’ but the body was hauled off.”

Note: the contrast between the early reports and the 7/25 Enterprise account moves this into the “probable” category, and maybe even into the “possible” category.

From the Herald, “Hattiesburg, Miss., Aug. 8.—Amos Jones, a negro, was hanged tonight by a mob for the shooting and probable mortal wounding of Jailer M. M. Sexton. Jones and another negro of the name of McEllery disarmed Sexton and Jones shot him, inflicting three wounds that are said to be fatal. Here a man climbed a telegraph pole, and the negro was hoisted high up to a cross-arm and a volley of pistols shots fired into his body.” From the Advertiser, “Mobile, Ala., Aug. 8.—A special to the The Register from Hattiesburg, Miss., says: A negro, Amos Jones, was hanged by a mob at Hettesburg tonight for shooting and mortally wounding jailer M. notes:
The Journal reports that an unknown negro man was probably lynched at Rocky Ford on the night of the 11th; he was accused of attempting to assault a white girl of Portal [Bulloch Co.]. He was arrested and given to the constable of Bulloch Co. Later the constable accompanied by several men took him away and later shots were heard. This next morning there was no body but a lot of blood on the edge of a swamp. The Morning News reports that he was captured and told to run for his life, and then two loads of buckshot were fired. He lived and the next day he showed up in Rocky Ford and placed under arrest. Further, “tonight a crowd of people” from Bulloch Co. are in Rocky Ford and undoubtedly there will be a lynching. Couldn’t find any follow-up stories in the Morning News. The Constitution reports that Kennedy Gordon was taken from the constable by a “large posse” and later gun shots were heard but no body was found. The 4/19 News reports that Kennedy Gordon went to Rocky Ford and has since disappeared and thought to have been lynched. He was buckshot by the girl’s father and later arrested, apparently in Screven Co., and was being brought back to Bulloch Co. When the constable entered Bulloch Co. his prisoner was taken by a “large posse” — soon afterwards a large number of shots were heard and the next day a blood trail was found leading to the river. It was theorized that Gordon was shot and his body pitched into the river.

notes:
The Constitution reports that Abe Barrett was hanged by a mob 0.5 miles from Gulfport for allegedly assaulting a white girl. No other details. From the Times-Picayune, “Gulfport, June 18.—Abe Barrett, the cowardly negro brute who attempted to criminally assault Miss Anna Ladner, the 15-year-old daughter of a prominent citizen in Hancock county, was captured shortly after daylight this morning, nine miles above Gulfport, taken down to that town on the Gulf and Ship Island train, and then started across the country for the scene of the crime. A message had been sent to the people of Hancock county that the criminal had been captured .... This message reached Pass Christian about 10 o’clock in the morning, and the word passed along the entire coast. ... [It was decided to move Barrett out of town in a wagon] ... About 1 o’clock the little party [Barrett and his guards] started out of Gulfport and across the country. ... Three miles from Gulfport, about a mile outside the limits of the town, a big crowd of people [from Hancock county] was seen on the road. They had waited long for Barrett and his guards, and soon took charge of the entire party. The guards were quietly disarmed. They did not care to resist under the circumstances. A piece of cotton line ... was produced, and the negro’s hands and feet were tied. An old towel was used as a lash. Then the wagon was driven a short distance  up the road and under an oak tree. The end of the rope was thrown over the limb and made fast. The negro was made to stand up in the wagon, and the horse whipped up and the vehicle driven from under him. The rope and the negro’s neck stretched to such an extent that Barrett’s toes touched the ground. The wagon was backed up again and the negro put back into the vehicle. This time he was made to stand on the seat, and the rope was tied up short. The horse started with a run, and the negro went dangling in the air. A rifle shot rang out and a ball penetrated the left temple and found its way though the right side of Barrett’s head. ... Then the body was riddled with lead. ... By 3 o’clock the buzzards had taken up their position on the limb of the tree, silent watchers over the terrible scene.”

Note: the Times-Picayune’s report is very detailed and vivid.
