notes:
From the Times-Picayune, “Clinton, La., Aug. 30.—A lynching occurred in the upper part of the parish yesterday evening. A negro by the name of Sam West attempted to assault a white woman, and, being caught in the attempt, he was hanged immediately by unknown parties. The crime for which the negro was hanged occurred a few miles across the line in Mississippi, but the negro’s body was found on this side of the line.” From the Register, “New Orleans, Aug. 29.—Sam West, colored, who lived on the Caulfield plantation in a parish of East Louisiana, was lynched near the Mississippi line last night. The negro went to the house of a farmer named Caulfield and attempted to assault his wife. Caulfield happened to be at home and, aroused by his wife’s screams, captured the negro. He was turned over to a mob, which took him to a convenient tree and lynched him.” From the Item, “Clinton, La., Aug. 31.—Sam West, a negro, who attempted to assault Mrs. Caulfield near here yesterday, was given a short shift. A few hours after the act his body was bound by Sheriff Bennett hanging to a tree. The negro lived on Caulfield’s place, four miles from the Louisiana State line in Amite county, Miss. From the information Sheriff Bennett could gather, the negro thought Mr. Caulfield was not at home and went into his residence and made an attempt to attack his wife, who screamed when the negro took hold of her, which attracted the attention of Mr. Caulfield, who went to her assistance. The negro got to Mr. Caulfield’s gun first and held him off until a near neighbor ... came to his assistance, when the negro was capture. ... He [West] was hung about ten feet this side of the Mississippi State line.”

Note: based on these reports, it is most likely that the mob was from Amite Co., MS, where the attempted assault took place. The 1900 census lists several Caulfield families, white, living in Amite Co., Mississippi, including three families in Beat 2; also lists Jones and Cindy West, black, living in Beat 2, Amite Co., but no listing for an adult Sam/Samuel West in Amite Co.

notes:
According to the American, three unnamed black men and one black woman were shot by whitecaps in retaliation for a black man shooting at one of the whitecaps. Apparently a group of 35 black men and women were walking home from a festival and came across several whitecappers. One whitecap demanded to know the name of one of the blacks, the man in question then fired at the whitecapper. At that point the rest of the whitecappers started shooting into the crowd of blacks, mortally wounding four and seriously wounding 15. The Appeal story adds little. According to the Herald, 35 black men and women were returning from a dance at Caney Springs; “They were halted at the end of a bridge by men wearing white masks and armed with shot-guns and pistols. The name of each negro was demanded, and upon answering, several were allowed to pass. Finally one, instead of giving his name, fired on his questioner. The white cap fell and his comrades poured a volley into the negroes, who fled, leaving the wounded behind. The white cappers, after the fusillade, left in buggies, carrying the wounded member with them.”—15 blacks were wounded, 4 fatally. The same report appears in the People and other newspapers.

Note: this is the whitecapper version of the story.

notes:
From the Record-Herald, “Mob Scares Woman to Death. ... Shelbyville, Ky., Oct. 8.—Mrs. Ben C. Perkins, wife of the jailer at this place, died to-day as the result of shock and fright suffered Wednesday morning when a mob attacked the jail and lynched two negroes [Jimbo Fields and Clarence Garnett]. At the time Mrs. Perkins was ill with a nervous attack, and Dr. W. F. Baird, her physician, declares that the raid of the lynchers is responsible for the woman’s death.” The same story appears in the Telegraph. From the Journal, “Mrs. Ben C. Perkins, wife of the jailer of Shelbyville, died as the result of shock and fright suffered when a mob attacked the jail and lynched two Negroes.” The Courier-Journal states that Mrs. Ben C. Perkins died on the 5th; “Dr. W. F. Beard, her attending physician, claims that the visit to the jail by the mob which hanged Jimbo Fields and Clarence Garnett, two negro boys, Wednesday morning, hastened her death. ... Dr. Beard says that her fright in her weakened condition was so great that she was almost moribund when he reached her, and it was impossible to rally her during the four days she lived. Her death, he says, was caused by nervous prostration.”

Note: Jimbo/Jumbo Fields and Clarence Garnett/Garnet were lynched 2 October, but Perkins did not die until the 5th 1900 census lists a Benjamin Perkins, a jailor, living with his wife Catherine, 48, and three children, in Shelbyville.

According to the 5/15 Constitution, William W. Wilson was taken from a train at Grovetown and carried into the woods, hanged, and riddled with bullets. Since the murder took place in Augusta, and the lynchers came to Grovetown by train and auto, the mob was mostly likely from Augusta. The 5/14 Chronicle gives his name as William B. Wilson. The Chronicle 5/15 gives a very long and detailed report on this lynching. Wilson was taken off a train at Grovetown [Columbia Co.] and was being brought back to Augusta where the murder occurred. The 5/16 edition reports that Wilson was buried in at the Thankful Baptist Church [presumably in Augusta] where he was a member. The was accused of killing Aleck/Alex Whitney on a street car in Augusta. The Banner reports that the grand jury failed to return any indictments against members of the mob, even though the judge stated that the lynching was an “‘inexcusable instance of mob violence,’”.

notes: According to the Picayune, a group of 10 masked black men came to Jefferson’s house, 6 miles from Houston, planning to hang him. Instead they beat him to death with paddles and clubs. He was accused of being “unpopular with a certain element of his race.” From the Herald, “A Negro Mob Beat to Death a Member of Their Own Race. ... Houston, Texas, July 10.—Without giving any reason, except that they did hot like him, a mob of negroes beat Henry Jefferson, a negro, to death, six miles north of here.” The Messenger reports, dateline Houston, 10 July, “A negro was put to death by a mob Sunday [8th] evening at Jules Hirsch’s woodyards on Grena bayou, five or six miles from Houston. The victim was Henry Jefferson, and his assailants are supposed to have been men of his own race. The mob consisted of ten men, all well masked. They appeared at Jefferson’s home about 8 o’clock. Without ceremony, they burst open the door and rushed in. ... It had evidently been the intention to hang him, but this programme was abandoned and the lynchers adopted a more cruel means of accomplishing their purpose. The beat Jefferson with clubs and with their fists, and the blows could be heard at the camp commissary, fully 100 yards away. ... It is said that Jefferson had been guilty of no special offense, but that the mob had decided to get rid of him on general principles. He was a married man, and besides a wife, had several children. ... He was about 40 years of age, and a very good workman.” The Post prints the confession of one of the black men, a W. A. Williams a.k.a. W. A. Long, who was accused of murdering Jefferson.

notes:
According to the Tribune, dateline New Orleans, 4 August, “News has just reached this city from Bayou Vidal, La., of a negro lynching at that place with some few variations from the accustomed formula. An old farmer of the neighborhood was murdered last week, and his body sunk in the Bayou, the object being robbery. A strange negro, seen wandering in the neighborhood, was suspected of the crime and put to torture to force a confession. A chain, the same he had used in weighing down the body [of the old man] was fastened about the colored man’s waist, and he was repeatedly sunk in the Bayou, being hauled out before death resulted. At last the negro gave up, and acknowledge the crime. Thereupon he was forced into a sack, which was sewed up, heaving weighed and dropped into the water at the place where his victim had been found.” The Times-Democrat states that the black farmer was murdered on Thursday, presumably the 2nd (but could have been 26 July), and that “a crowd” of black men captured “a strange negro” and tortured him by repeated simulated drownings before being killed by drowning, as described in the Tribune account. From the Herald, “A negro mob lynched a negro for the murder of a negro farmer, at Bayou Vidal, La.” On the other hand, from the Post, “New Orleans, Aug. 4.—A few days ago a white farmer living in Bayou Vidal, in Concordia parish was murdered and the body sunk in bayou with stones attached. The people of the neighborhood suspected a strange negro named Scott of the crime. Today Scott was arrested and taken to the scene of the murder .... [description of the water torture and his final drowning.]” The same story appears in the Register. This account implies a white mob, not black.

notes:
From the News, “Shot Down By a Mob. Lake Charles, La., Sept. 28.—While defending the parish jail about 11 o’clock last night from the assault of a mob, Paul Sloane, Deputy Sheriff and jailer, was struck by a fusillade fired from the outside, receiving injuries which proved fatal an hour later. Early this morning Ross Johnson, Will Daniels and W. W. Davis, were arrested, charged with killing of Sloane and taken to Crawly for safe keeping.” The mob was after an unnamed black man. From the Times-Recorder, “Lake Charles, La., Sept. 28.—All day there were rumors of the probable lynching of Pierce Scott, a negro in jail here, charged with criminally assaulting Miss Oswald, aged 73. About 9 o’clock [last night] an unmasked crowd gathered at the courthouse. One of the crowd called for Sheriff Perkins and demanded the keys to the jail. In the meantime Judge Miller addressed the crowd and told them the punishment of criminals must be left to the courts. ... On this promise [that the judge would immediately hear the case] the crowd broke up and it was thought there would be no further attempts by the mob. At 11 o’clock, however, a fresh outbreak was made by the mob, which advanced toward the jail with an iron battering ram. D. S. A. Harmon and Paul Sloan, deputy sheriffs inside the jail, warned them to come no further and then shot over the heads of the crowd when some one in the mob shot at the deputies. Paul Sloan was fatally wounded. He died at 1:15 o’clock [on the 28th]. The sheriff and deputies outside the jail then dispersed the crowd at the point of pistols and the members of the mob began to call for the arrest of those who shot Sloan. Several members of the mob, known to have been armed, were arrested.” From the Times-Picayune, “Lake Charles, La., Jan. 14.—... Sheriff John A. Perkins and Deputy Ben Foster, of Starks, left this morning for Baton Rouge with Robert and Will Austin, Will Daniels and Ross Johnson, who are to be confined in the penitentiary for life.”

Note: the authorities were protecting Pierce Scott who had been accused of criminal assault on a 73 year-old unmarried white woman.

Some of the crowd took charge of Sheriff Hardin, when the others took the two negroes, placing them on mules, with ropes around their necks, the other ends to a tree, driving the mules out. H. Cleland. News has just reached here that Cleland, a stock farmer who lived about twelve miles east, was found dead in his room. ... At noon today a posse of 200 determined citizens secured possession of the two negroes and quietly hanged them to a tree. The mob then dispersed in an orderly manner.”

notes: From the 7/18 State, “White Rock [Lexington Co.], July 17.—One of the ugliest crimes that ever disgraced this county was committed last Saturday [15th] afternoon in the Piney Woods section, only about a half a mile from the Newberry line. Mr. Pat Bowers of that of that section was shot form ambush and instantly killed while traveling the public highway in the peaceable pursuit of his business. ... Bowers was alone in his buggy,. coming from from Little Mountain. When about half way, about 2 o’clock in the afternoon, three gunshots were heard, half a mile across the county line. on the Lexington side. ... It is supposed that three persons did the shooting.” Another story in the same edition gives the location as two miles from Little Mountain. The Constitution reports (dateline Columbia SC 8 August) that Patrick Bowers was riddled with bullets three weeks ago, presumably mid-July, and his head almost blown off. Ten white men have been arrested in connection with the killing. The story states “They belong to some of the old Dutch Fork families.” The story also lists their names. The Monitor story adds nothing. The 8/12 State reports that ten are being held and has this headline: “Neighbors Coveted Bower’s Property. Something About the Lexington Murder Case for Which Ten Farmers Are imprisoned.” The 8/24 State reports that six men have been let out of jail on bail while a 7th is still in jail.

notes:
From the Star, “Salisbury, Md., May 26.—Garfield King, a negro, aged about eighteen, was taken from the jail at this place early this morning, hanged to a tree and almost shot to pieces. He was awaiting trial on the charge of having deliberately shot Herman Kenney, a white boy about the same age as the negro. The shooting was done on Saturday night last and Kenney died yesterday. Last night about 2 a.m. a number of men from the neighborhood in which Kenney’s parents live rode into town and demanded the keys to the jail, which Sheriff Dashiell refused to surrender. The lynchers then broke the jail doors down, forced open the cell in which King was confined and dragged him out, the negro all the while fighting desperately and pleading for mercy. A light clothesline was tied about his neck, thrown over a limb and the unfortunate boy was strung up. The rope broke, and he fell seemingly unconscious. After lynching in his condition for a few minutes he regained his feed and made an effort to escape. His captors shot him though the body and beat and kicked him without mercy, then placed the rope around his neck and strung him up a second time. As he dangled in the air at least fifty pistol bullets ere fired into his body, which was left dangling in the air while the lynchers dispersed.” A somewhat less detailed report is in the World-Herald. According to the Sun, 100 “quiet, determined men” attacked the jail at 12:35 a.m. and took King away to be shot and hanged—over fifty bullet holes were found in his body. According to the Inquirer, the State Attorney is preparing to prosecute the persons who lynched King, and the State knew the  names of the leaders of the mob.

The first tragedy in the history of Plano happened at 1:50 o'clock this morning [14th] at the home of Jake Cebron, colored, on Main Street, second house south of the cotton belt [railroad] depot. A party of white cappers who had visited every Negro cabin in town, giving the inmates 4 to 10 days to leave town, appeared at Cebron’s house at the time above mentioned. ... [a party of white cappers tried to enter Cebron’s cabin but he met them with a rifle; when they saw the gun, they opened fire wounding, slightly, Cebron but killing his wife, Laura] ... Charley Gunter and Bob Cummings, both white, were arrested this afternoon charged with murder on warrants emanating from the justice court and taken to McKinney jail. Other arrests will likely follow in a few days. The city marshall [sic] tracked four of the mob and is doing everything possible to bring the guilty parties to justice.” The same story appears in the Eagle. The Democrat says that “a band” of whitecappers visited the home of Jake Cebron in Plano at 1:00 a.m. on the 14th and opened fire when Cebron appeared at the door with a rifle—Cebron’s wife was killed; “Two young men of Plano were arrested and landed in the jail here.” The Times story adds nothing new. According to the News, “It is said the members of tjhe party were all the way from five to twenty. All their faces were blackened.”

Note: it not clear that the white caps came to the home to kill Cebron but they didn’t hesitate to shoot; it could be argued that Laura Cebron should be classified as a “Coincidental death”.

Birmingham, Ala., July 15.—Near Coaling, where on Wednesday Sidney Johnson, colored, was lynched for assaulting Mrs. Hodges and attempting to assault Miss Cobb, a 16-year-old white girl, serious race troubles are threatened. There was great indignation among the negroes at the lynching, and John S. Durrett, a notorious negro character, threatened to organize a band of blacks to kill whites and burn their homes to avenge Johnson’s death. notes: The 11/2 Citizen-Times reports that “last Wednesday [26th] afternoon” 18 year-old Manly McCauley, black, eloped with Mrs. Milton Brewer, “wife of a substantial farmer of Orange county”; “On Friday [28th] a posse, headed by the husband of the woman, set out in pursuit. The negro and the woman were overtaken beyond Jonesboro [Moore Co.] and taken into custody by the posse. The negro was taken part of the distance back to Chapel Hill, but ‘disappeared,’ as those who were along put it, before he reached Chapel Hill. Although his fate is shrouded in mystery, it is believed that he was lynched. The woman was brought back to Chapel Hill and is now at the home of her father ....” According to the Record, citing the Durham Sun, the woman’s name was Maggie Brewer; “They passed through Pittsboro’ and were followed by seven armed men, who caught them at Lemon Springs, in Moore county, at the house of the man’s father. They all returned through here [Durham] Sunday [30th] afternoon.” From the Press, “The negro Manly McCauley, who eloped with the wife of a white farmer near Chapel Hill, was lynched. That the woman could stoop so low as to elope with a negro seems impossible. But the woman was born of a family who winked at social equality, and thought that the day when the white man and negro would be socially equal was not far distant. She married a man who entertained the same views, and they lived happily together. But one day the man came home to find that his wife had eloped with a negro farm hand. The woman is now at the home of her parents in Orange county, and the negro returned to his community to be lynched by a mob of indignant white men.” According to the Review, “Not Lynched by the Posse. If Manly McCauley, the negro seducer, who eloped with Mrs. Brewer, of Chapel Hill, was lynched, as is practically certain, it was not by the possee [sic] which went in pursuit of him from that place, but he was taken from the posse and lynched by others—probably neighbors of Mr. Brewer.” The 11/11 Citizen-Times writes, “—Chapel Hill telegram to Charlotte News: The body of Manly McCauley, the negro who ran away with Mrs. Brewer, was found Sunday evening, hanging to a tree. near the public road, some three miles from here.”

notes: From the Times-Picayune, “Early Thursday morning there was a quiet little lynching in St. John parish, and a notorious negro thief from this city was abruptly removed from the ranks of criminals. This negro for months has been systematically robbing the stores and residences of both St. Charles and St. John parishes. ... [Apparently there were two thieves, one from New Orleans and one from St. Charles, working together] ... Wednesday the St. Charles negro made a confession to Sheriff Ory. ... Early Thursday morning a mob quietly rode to the jail where the two negroes were kept, and, breaking open the door, dragged the New Orleans negro to a shed only 100 yards away and quickly strung him up. The body was left dangling, and the St. Charles negro was allowed to remain safely in jail. ... At the late hour at which the information of the lynching came to hand it was impossible to secure the names of the negroes.” According to the News,”Revolting Crime in Louisiana. Edward Gray, a negro from New Orleans, was arrested in St. Johns parish about a year ago with Charles Morrelle, another negro, and charged with a series of burglaries which had been committed in and around the parish. The authorities released Gray recently because there was no evidence against him. This lack of evidence was partially due to the fact that a mob took Morrelle from the Edward [Edgard] jail in November last and hanged him to a tree in the courtyard. Gray has been very sick during his incarceration, and when the order for his release was signed Sheriff Hart intended to send him to the Charity hospital in New Orleans.”—he got as far as Reserve where he stopped to spend the night, during which a mob found him and hanged him from a tree.

The Star reports that Otis Miller was tracked to Dunnellon [Marion Co.] and placed in the lock-up there prior to being transported to Ocala. However, “[S]ome time during the night a body of masked men, took out the prisoner and left as silently as they came. Just where they went with him no one seemed to know or if they did they would not tell. All that could be learned today concerning the matter was, that he had been sent to join his companions [Gilmore, Miley, and Holmes]. ... Later—Two reports were received late this afternoon. One was that the body of Miller was found this morning hanging on the same limb of the same tree where the other three were hung yesterday. The other was that he had been tied hand and foot and thrown into the Withlacoochee river at a point not far from Dunnellon.” From the Dealer, “Tallahassee, Fla., March 15.—Three negroes, Jim Gilmore, Jim Miley and Otis Miller, were taken from the sheriff today by fifty armed men, strung up to trees and their bodies riddled with bullets. The crime for which they were lynched was the murder of John Barefield, postmaster at Blue Springs [Marion Co.], and his assistant, John B. Turner, on March 3. ... Since that time a posse has been on the track of the negroes and yesterday they were captured by the sheriff of Orange county.” This same report appears in several newspapers. The State, however, lists the three victims as Ed Holmes, Jim Miley, and Jim Gilmore who were lynched at Blue Springs station. From the Athens Weekly Banner, “Ocala, Fla., March 18.—Otis Miller, the fourth negro implicated in the murder of Postmaster Barfield and Turner, his clerk, on March 3, at Juliette, was arrested and taken to Dunnellon jail for safe keeping. In the night an armed mob broke open the jail, took Miller out and disappeared with him. His cries were heard in the village, but no one cared to go out of doors just then. It is rumored that he was taken to the river and drowned by the lynchers. The other three negroes were lynched at Blue Springs by hanging.” From the Ocala Weekly Banner, “...Section Master Reamer was positive in his identification of Ed. Holmes as one of the parties he saw in the store on the night of the tragedy. On last Monday Holmes was overtaken and placed in custody. He broke down under examination and made a full confession and implicated as his confederates in the foul crime, Jim Gilmore, Jim Miller and Otis Miller. A party at once started in search of these negroes and soon had all of them except Otis Miller under arrest. They made a full confession and that night were swung to a limb within sight of the store where the tragedy depriving young Barfield and Turner of their lives...” They were accused of murdering J. B. notes:
According to the Traveler, on the 28th, “... near Harleton [Harrison Co.], Texas, masked men waylaid and shot three negro men, killing one, and wounding two others. The one killed at the first fire was Russell Wright. At the inquest, about two hours later, Hal Wright, who was one of the wounded, was shot and killed. No one will say who did the shooting. A man walked up near the crowd, shot his pistol off twice and said: ‘Look out there,’ and opened fire on Hal Wright, killing him at once. The other negro, who was wounded, was Bob Brown.” The Statesman reports, dateline Marshall, Tex., 28 April, that Hal Wright, Russell Wright, his son, and Bob Brown on their way to Harleton; two miles from Harleton at 9a-10a on the 27th, the posse was attacked by five masked men, killing Russell Wright and wounding Hal Wright and Bob Brown; Justice Jones of Harleton held an inquest over the body of Russell Wright at 2 p.m. when a man walked up and shot the wounded Hal Wright killing him. The News report is consistent with the note that Bob Brown was “seriously wounded”. From the 4/30 Messenger, “Marshall, Tex., April 29.—There is no clew as to who the men were that composed the mob that assassinated Hal Wright and his son and fatally shot Bob Brown on Tuesday morning while on their way to court.” According to the 5/6 Messenger, there was an altercation between a white man named James Walker and Hal Wright; Walker swore out affidavits against Wright for assault to murder; while Hal Wright, his son, Bob Brown, Richard Thomas and Wash Wright, Hal’s brother, were coming to court in Harleton they were fired upon 2 miles from town, killing Wright’s son and wounding Hal and Bob Brown; the rest of the story is the same as the other accounts—no mention that Brown was killed.

Note: couldn’t find any definitive evidence that Robert/Bob Brown died through June. If he died, he would be victim #2.

notes:
According to the Register, dateline Houston, 30 April, “For the murder of an old man in his dotage, a child in its nonage, and a woman in the first flush of young womanhood, the ravishment of two girls, burning the home of their victims, two of the bodies being consumed in the flames, six young negroes were last night sent to their doom at the hands an infuriated mob of negroes, the victims also being negroes, at Sunnyside, Waller county. ... [description of the murder of Henry Daniels, Marie Daniels and a y 7 year-old Daniels and the capture of Fayette Rhome, 27; Will Gates, 45; Louis Thomas, 20; Aaron Thomas, 13; Jim Thomas, 14; Benny Thomas, 15; and Will Williams] ... About 12 o’clock the guards were overpowered by a strong body of men and the prisoners taken towards the Brazos bottom north of here. A little later forty or fifty shots were fired; and all was quiet. This morning, dangling from the limbs of a large oak tree, were found the bodies of six negroes, limp and lifeless. ... All of them there except Williams, and he is not to be found, but the shots probably explain his absence. ... As far as can be learned, the mob was composed of white and black men, with the colored element largely predominating,” The 5/1 Post lists the victims as: Louis Thomas, 18; Aaron Thomas, 16; Jim Thomas, 14, and Ben Thomas, 12; Will Gates; Will Williams, and Fayette Rhoan. According to the Statesman, dateline Hempstead, 30 April, the mob of 40-50, white and black, took the men/boys around 11:00 p.m.; the lynching site was 1.5 miles west of Sunnyside and 1.5 miles west of the Hempstead and Paterson road; the six men who were hanged: Fayette Rhoan, 21; Will Gates, 35; Louis Thomas, 20; Aaron Thomas, 13; Jim Thomas, 15; and Ben Thomas, 16-17; “All of the bodies were riddled with bullets and the clothing of Will Gates and Louis Thomas was burned off from the waist down, the flesh being almost cooked, indicating that torture had been resorted to to extort a full confession, though the clothing may possibly have caught [fire] from the shots of the crowd at close range. ... A curious fact about the lynching is that Will Williams was not hanged with the others, nor is there any one up to this time who seems to know what became of him.” The Weekly Statesman states that it is now thought that Will Williams either escaped the mob or was released, but that he is alive.

notes:
According to the Messenger, dateline Nacogdoches, 14 May, “Thirty-five miles east of here is the town of San Augustine, not on a railroad, but connected by telephone, and twelve miles east of here in the edge of Sabine county, much bloody work has been done within the past forty-eight hours, and more is expected to result, causing great excitement. ... [there was an altercation between a white family named Johnson and a black family named White; on Tuesday [11th] there was some kind of fight at the Johnson home] ... The parties involved were William and John White, colored, George, Aaron, Jim and Red Johnson, Theo. Nobles, and Mrs. Johnson and daughter, all white. Theo. Nobles died Wednesday [12th] from gunshot wounds. George Johnson was knocked senseless with a gun. Aaron was wounded in several places. Red, a one-legged Confederate, was shot in the arm and leg. William White was shot in the body and knocked in the head, and on Wednesday [12th] night he was shot to death by unknown parties. John White fled, and at last accounts was being pursued, and a lynching is predicted for him. The Johnsons and the Whites have heretofore been regarded as peaceable farmers.” The Eagle account adds nothing, except that one of the persons named is identified as Fred Johnson, not Red Johnson. From the Weekly Statesman, “Nacogdoches, Tex., May 15.—(Special.)—Nothing further has occurred in the Sabine county disturbances, and the wounded are reported doing fairly well. The fugitive negro, John White, is still at large. ... He and his late brother, William, have been in trouble here, both for insolent deportment toward white ladies. John White narrowly escaped lynching on one of these occasions and was warned to leave. It is said that there were only two men in this lynching [of William] and they were disguised. Sheriff Spradley does not fear any attempt at lynching John White in his custody. He will resist and will thwart it if made.” From the Times, “William White, colored, lynched in Sabine county.” The Post account, dateline San Augustine, 12 May, makes it clear that the incident was in Sabine county; in regard to William White, “Later news received here tonight is that about 4 o’clock a crowd of well-disguised men went to White’s house and rushed in on him and fired forty or fifty shots into his body in the presence of his family, and scouting parties are scouring the country in every direction in search of John White, who will doubtless go to see his brother William on a free ticket.” According to the Advocate, “The parties all live in Sabine county.”

Note: based on the Post account, this would be a lynching because “a crowd” but based on the Weekly Statesman story, there were only two killer and this would not be a lynching. 1880 census lists a George Johnson, 47, family living in Sabine county; wife, Sarah A., daughter, Mary, and two sons: Aaron and James C., both 10 months. A John White, age 4, black, and William White, 13, black, are found in the household of Harry and Hariet White in San Augustine Co. in 1880.

From the Gazette, “Jackson, Miss., June 24.—At 5 o’clock this afternoon Lieutenant Governor Jones received a telegram asking that a military company be sent to Crystal Springs to prevent the mobbing of a negro murderer [William Moseley in the story]. The telegram stated that the presence of the troops was imperative. ... A telegram received late tonight from Crystal Springs says there is great danger of a lynching. At 10 o’clock an unsuccessful attempt was made on the jail.” There was no indication that troops were sent. From the Times-Picayune, “Jackson, Miss., June 24.—The sheriff of Copiah county wired to-night for fifty troops to protect the life of the negro who murdered old man Strong near Crystal Springs. The Capital Light Guards are in readiness to go, but up to a late hour to-night Acting Governor Jones ... had not been heard from giving the order. ... Word comes from Crystal Springs at 9:45 p. m., saying that he mob was surrounding the jail, and that the negro would probably be lynched before midnight.”
According to the Picayune, “When the door of the jail was opened to admit a negro preacher, a surging mass of humanity poured in and seized John Moses ... and putting a rope around his neck, he was quickly dragged to the southern suburbs and hanged on a tree.” This was a few yards from the place Jack Yarborough was lynched on 23 November 1895. According to the Times, Moseley was accused of killing a white farmer John Strong near Crystal Springs, and despite being protected by 100 troops, he was lynched —he was taken from jail and “dragged through the streets to a tree near the railroad and hanged. He was dead or nearly so when they reached the place of hanging.” The Age-Herald report adds nothing. The Clarion-Ledger says he was taken from the jail by a mob of 400 at 9:45 a.m., and dragged through the streets about 1.5 miles from the railroad depot, and “... hung on a tree near where Jack Yarbrough was hung some eighteen months ago.”

notes:
From the Times, “An Alabama Negro Preacher Lynched by a Raving Mob. Chattanooga, July 17.—A special from Florence, Ala., says that the negro preacher, named Edmonson, who assisted Anthony Williams, the murderer and ravisher of Miss Rene Williams, in making his escape, has been caught and lynched by a mob of 400 men. The preacher was overtaken by the mob this morning. He was stopping at the home of another negro, who denied that Edmondson was near. A search was made, however, and the man was found hidden under a bed. He was dragged from the house and met with the same fate of Williams. He was beat to death with rocks and clubs, and was then shot to pieces. Whether the body was burned or not is unknown. The wildest excitement prevailed at the scene of the lynching, and many of those engaged in it were in favor of lynching the negro woman who had concealed the preacher.” From the Inquirer, “Chattanooga, Tenn., July 17.—Rev. Edmondson, a colored preacher, was lynched and burned early this morning near Florence, Alabama, by a mob of 150 infuriated citizens. The offense for which Edmondson paid this penalty was shielding Anthony Williams, colored, who was shot to death and burned two days ago for the murder of Miss Rene Williams, a respectable white girl of that neighborhood. ... It is probable that he would have been left off with a whipping, but reaching a dense patch of woods the man, almost frightened to death, made a made dash for liberty. No sooner was the act observed than a pistol shot rang out, and he fell wounded. One member of the party jumped upon him and almost stamped him to death. A rope was a hand and the body quickly was hung to a large chestnut tree. Here it was left for some hours, and latest reports from the scene say that about half the party went back and burned it in the woods.”

Powell in this place, attempted an assault last night upon Mrs. Powell in her bedroom, and was captured after a fierce struggle, by her husband. He held his captive while other members of this household went for help, and in a short time nearly 50 of his neighbors, armed with guns and pistols, arrived at the scene of the assault. They took the negro from Powell and carried him some distance down the road, where it was finally decided that he should be shot in military fashion. After being given an opportunity to pray, he was placed against a pile of rocks and the mob drew up in semi-circle in front of him. At a signal from one of the leaders every trigger was pulled and a shower of lead found lodgment in the negro’s body. He was killed instantly.”

notes: From the 8/25 Telegraph, “Pine Bluff [Jefferson Co.], Ark., Aug. 24.—T. L. Johnson, a prominent white man, who was stabbed last Saturday at a negro dance at Kendall [Cleveland Co.], died here yesterday morning. ... Yesterday afternoon the deputy sheriff captured two of the negroes connected with the bloody work near the scene of the crime. The party started to place the two brothers in jail, when one of the negroes broke away and, although he was shot the second time, he made his escape. The officers then continued their way with the other one, whose name was Douglas. Near Anderson, the negro was taken from the men late in the night and strung up to a bridge on the Cotton Belt railroad, where his body was found this morning. It is given out that a mob of negroes hanged Douglass, but it is generally believed that the mob was composed of white citizens. ... A well authorized report reached here ... that six other negroes, who have been connected with the affair, have been arrested and placed in jail at Rison [Cleveland Co.]. The jail is not considered very safe and it is the general opinion that before tomorrow all six will be lynched. Excitement in about Anderson and Kendall is a fever heat and more trouble is expected.” The same story appears in the Appeal and the News with the spelling Bill Wiley Douglas. From the 8/26 Telegraph, “Little Rock, Aug. 25.—The reported [wholesale] lynching in Cleveland county proves to have been premature, though it is liable to occur at any time. It seems that the ring leaders in Saturday’s riot at Kendall’s mill have not yet been captured. ... a special dispatch to the Gazette as follows: Rison [Cleveland Co.], Ark., Aug. 25.—Joe Smith, Frank Matthews, Frank Wright and George Callahan, the main actors in the murder of T. J. Johnson, near Kendall [Kendall’s mill], on Saturday last, are still at large. There is no mistake about the murderous participation in this bloody affair of the negro Wiley lynched on Sunday night [22nd].” In other newspapers it is clear the “reported lynching” refers to an erroneous report of “wholesale lynching”. The Gazette confirms there was no wholesale lynching and reports “Tuesday night Bill Wiley, one of the ringleaders, was captured and officers started with their prisoner on a hand car for Rison. When they reached a trestle half-way between the Bluff City Mill and Kendall’s, the car was stopped by a mob who took the prisoner, tied a rope around his neck, fastened the other end to a crosstie, bound the negro’s hands and feet and pushed him off the trestle. The negro feel seven feet and his neck was broken by the fall.”

notes:
According to the 9/13 Telegraph, Charley Gibson, “diabolical brute”, raped a white girl and killed a black man. He was shot by a “posse” of men in a swamp near Peter’s pond and then tied to a tree and riddled with bullets. The Constitution report gives the site as “3 miles ..o.th of Macon” [north? south?]. They also report that his body was possibly burned after being riddled with bullets. The Banner gives the posse size as 150 in “the swamp near Peters’ pond” where he was riddled with bullets. The 9/18 Telegraph gives his age as 27. The News reports that Charley Gibson had been wounded three times before being hanged and riddled with bullets—not mention of any burning.

According to the news reports Gibson was shot three times by the officers, and then, from the Times, “A large crowd soon gathered at the scene of the shooting, and, in the momentary absence of the sheriff and deputies, swung the negro from a tree.” In some reports, the sheriff and deputies had left the scene to get a vehicle to bring Gibson into town. In any regard, Gibson was left to the mercy of the crowd and he received none.

This would seem to be a case of the authorities abetting the lynching.

notes:
The Age-Herald reports, dateline Wesson [Copiah Co.], 9 December, the murder of Mrs. Brown Smith and her children at their home at “the edge of Simpson county....” According to the 12/11 Telegraph, he was accused of assaulting the women and then murdering her and the children; after being arrested, apparently in Lawrence Co., he was taken to Monticello, the county seat. At 7 p.m., he was taken “... to the scene of the crime, where he was fully identified by the little girl [3 years old and the sole survivor]. It is said he was promptly lynched after the identification by a large crowd of infuriated citizens who had joined in the search.” In a second story on the same page, the Telegraph notes that Lewis is a mulatto, 23 years old, and married, that two black men, Will Powell and Andy/Andrew Smith, who were implicated in the murder, may be lynched as well. According to the 12/12 Telegraph, there was to be a trial at Bankston ferry but he was taken by a mob of 200; a plow line was tied around his neck and he was placed on a horse with the plow line secured to a limb and the horse driven away. After strangling a few moments he was cut down, revived, and then hanged “in earnest”. It is clear from the Times-Picayune report that the mob was composed of men from Simpson and Lawrence, and possibly other counties.

Note: Simpson Co. lies adjacent and north of Lawrence Co. in some early news reports, with a dateline of Wesson, the victim of this lynching was Charles Jones and the location is “near this place [Wesson, Copiah Co.]. Surprised no report of any torture. 1900 census list a Brown Smith, age 30, living in Simpson Co. with his daughter Stella, 5, and his mother, and others. He married a Nellie Mullen in 1885 in Simpson Co.—she does not appear in 1900 census.

notes:
From the 5/10 Journal, “Fulton, Ky., May 9.—This afternoon three negroes attacked City Marshal Jesse Walker. Two of them held him while the third cut him seriously four times with a knife. The negroes then escaped. Blood hounds were immediately put on their track and one has been captured. There is much excitement and the negro will probably be lynched.” From the News, “Fulton, Ky., May 10.—A negro implicated in the cutting of City Marshal Jesse Walker was lynched here tonight by a mob of about 600 citizens. The negro was arrested by the telegraph operator at Arlington [Carlisle Co.], a few miles north of Fulton [county], this morning, who, in the attempt to arrest him, shot him just about the left lung. The negro was carried into Fulton and was met by the mob. He remained in the mob’s hands until the arrival of Sheriff Purdue of Albion [Obion] county, Tennessee. Upon his arrival and immediately he had taken charge of the negro the mob rushed madly upon the negro and swung him up several feet in the air, and his last words were: ‘O, O, God save me, I am an innocent man.’ However, he confessed to the crime at Arlington this morning. The two other negroes who did the cutting are yet uncaptured, but are being hotly pursued by a large posse of Fulton citizens assistant by several well trained blood hounds. they re expected to be caught to-night. The one lynched to-night held the marshal while the other two did the cutting. The lynching of the two uncaptured will certainly follow their arrest immediately. Marshal Walker is not expected to live.” The same reporta appears in the Progress. From the Ledger, “Paducah, Ky., May 11.—Marshal Jesse Walker, of Fulton, was stabbed by a Negro at Fulton, and will probably die.” From the 5/11 Journal, “Fulton, Ky., May 10.— ... The negro was brought to Fulton and taken in charged by Sheriff Purdue but the mob which had gathered at the depot rushed upon the negro and swung him up. The negro confessed his guilt while under arrest at Arlington.” Essentially the same report appears in the Kentuckian. According to the Courier-Journal, Paschall was captured in Carlisle Co., Kentucky—accused of attacking Marshal Jesse Walker of South Fulton, Tennessee. When Paschall was being brought back to TN, “an angry mob of both Kentuckians and Tennesseans had formed and started in pursuit. The mob overtook the sheriff’s party at a dark spot in the Tennessee woods and demanded ... Paschall.”

Note: it seems reasonably clear that the marshal was stabbed in Fulton, Fulton Co. KY, and that the mob was probably composed of men from both Fulton Co. KY and likely Obion Co. TN. According to the USGS, the city of South Fulton is in Obion Co., TN while the city of Fulton is in Fulton Co. KY. They are adjacent counties. Other than the Courier-Journal report, all others suggest that he was lynched in Fulton Co. KY. Couldn’t find any reference to a Paschall in ChroniclingAmerica.loc.gov, Ancestry.com or GenealogyBank.com.

He made a confession and was strung up to a tree and his body filled with lead.” From the Times-Picayune, “Franklin, La., June 9.—Walter T. Starks, a negro about the age of 21 years, paid the death penalty at the hands of an infuriated mob at Vacherie plantation, in this parish, for the despicable crime to-day. Starks came to this parish about six months ago from Atlanta, Ga., and was employed by Mr. Alfred P. Tabor, the section boss, and the husband of the culprit’s victim. Mr. Tabor left his house this morning to put his men to work at about 5 o’clock. Mrs. Tabor and her infant child were the only persons in the house. At about 6 o’clock Starks entered the house, and, seizing a pair of scissors, rushed upon his victim and stabbed her repeatedly about the face, throat and breast. He soon brought her to insensibility and then robbed the house of about $200 in cash, a pistol, watch and other articles. The [illegible] colored servant came in a few minutes after, and found the poor dying woman at the window, gasping and beckoning for assistance, while the baby lay dabbling and playing in its mother’s blood. ... Starks was caught early in the afternoon at Jeanerette .... He had purchased a ticket for New Orleans, and was waiting for the eastbound train. ... ... when brought back to the Vacharie plantation, Mrs. Tabor, to his utter surprise, was still living, and at once identified him. Starks was then taken to an oak tree on the place, was hauled up to a limb, and volley after volley of lead from pistol, rifles and shotguns poured into his head and body, and just ten minutes after the hanging, the lifeless form of the most heartless brute of the age, fell to the ground. Very little excitement prevailed, and even the negroes, in large numbers, came to view the body, and express their approval of the mob’s action. Mrs. Tabor is yet living, and there is a possible chance of her recovery.”

notes:
From the News, “Chattanooga, Tenn., June 21.—On Friday night last Bessie, the 9-year-old daughter of Gwin Puckett, a prominent farmer living near Hartselle, Ala., was kidnaped by Leon Orr, a negro farm laborer. She was later found in the woods where the brute had assaulted her and left her in an unconscious condition. Orr was captured yesterday near Danville and confined in the courthouse an hour. At an early hour this morning a mob broke into the building, strapping the negro to a horse and took him to the scene of the crime, where they hanged him to a tree and riddled his body with bullets. Orr confessed his guilt.” From the Montgomery Advertiser, dateline Birmingham, 22 June, “News reached here today of the lynching of Leon Orr, a negro, near Hartselle, Morgan county, at an early hour yesterday [21st] morning. ... About midnight Saturday night, so the story goes, a mob visited Moulton and secured the negro. There were forty to fifty men men in the mob and all were masked and mounted. The negro was taken back to the scene of his crime where he was hanged to a tree, after he had confessed, and his body was then riddled with bullets.” The Herald account adds nothing. According to the Moulton Advertiser, “On Thursday evening last [18th], Lewis Orr raped Miss Helen Puckett, who is not yet 8 years old. ... [He was arrested and brought to Moulton] ... He was apparently about 21 years old ... Saturday [20th] night 250 undisguised men ... reached Moulton and after a diligent search found the brute hid away in the cupalo [sic] of our temp of justice, under the care of a deputy. The officer was overpowered, and the trembling prisoner seized by the infuriated men who disposed of him in accordance with their pre-arranged plans. He was marched to the colored Methodist church, just beyond the corporation limits, and swung up to a limb within 15 feet of the building. After riddling his body with bullets, the crowd mounted their horses and quietly dispersed. ... Sheriff Ethredge, apprehending trouble, hid the negro out both nights [19th and 20th] but there were evidently spies in town who kept up with his movements.” From the Tribune, “The negro, Orr was not lynched __ [at] Hartselle, as was reported, __ [but?] at Moulton [Lawrence Co.], 24 miles from __rtselle.”

Note: found in 1900 census a Gwin Puckett, 32, living with his wife, Agnes, living at Oakville, Lawrence Co., with children Mary H. Puckett, 12, Mabel M. Puckett, 6, and a baby, Gwin Puckett. Likely “Mary H.” = Bessie = Helen. Oakville is near the line with Morgan Co. It is likely that the mob was from both Lawrence and Morgan counties, given the proximity of the Puckett residence to the Morgan county line.

[After leaving the plantation she failed to return home] ... A searching party was organized at once, and the body of the unfortunate woman was found late yesterday evening about 250 yards from the road, where she had been dragged and outraged and killed by a negro named Hirman Weightman, aged about 30. The weapon used to take her life was a double-barreled shotgun, loaded with small shot, one barrel of which he discharged at close range into the back of her head. The negro brute was arrested yesterday, and the evidence, though circumstantial, was so convincing that he finally confessed and his guilt and was speedily put to death.” (2) “Gilbert [Franklin Parish], La., Aug. 4.—The Picayune correspondent has just learned that the negro who brutally outraged and murdered the white woman, Mrs. Bertha McDonald, near Cooter Point, in Franklin parish, an account of which was published in these dispatches, was taken from the sheriff’s posse and hanged last night near the place where he committed the deed by a large and determined body of men, who were bent on protecting the honor and virtue of our women.” The 8/6 Times-Democrat says that an unnamed black man was arrested for the rape and murder of a white girl. He was taken from the sheriff and hanged in southern Franklin Parish, date: before 8/5. According to the 8/7 Times-Democrat, Henry Waite was hunted down, burned alive, and shotl near Coulter Point. He was accused of the rape and murder of a white girl. From the 8/9 Times-Picayune, “St. Joseph [Tensas Parish], La., Aug. 8.—... The reported burning of the negro murderer, Henry Waite, at Couter Point on Thursday last was erroneous. After confessing his horrible crime he was hung to a tree and his body riddled with bullets.” The News states, dateline St. Joseph [Tensas Parish], that a white tramp was accused of outraging, murdering, and mutilating “a respectable white women employed as a domestic in a prominent family on the border of Franklin Parish ..... ... The infuriated crowd bound the brutal wretch, staked him to the nearest tree and burned his body and riddled it with bullets.” The same story appears in the Times, Gazette, Journal and other newspapers. notes:
From the Citizen, “Titusville, Sept. 16.—About a week ago a negro named Harris, employed as a section hand on the Jacksonville, Tampa and Key West railroad, committed an assault on the little 7-year-old daughter of Section Foreman Bruce at Maytown, in Volusia county, and was [taken to Titusville, Brevard Co.] by the little girl’s father.... Harris was placed in the city jail for safe keeping. Sheriff Bowman apprehended trouble, and took the prisoner out of jail Tuesday night, intending to remove him to Volusia county secretly. The sheriff had got only as far as Mims [Brevard Co.] when he was overtaken by a crowd of about eighty men, who demanded the prisoner. Harris was taken from custody and lynched at Wolf’s railroad crossing, at LaGrange [Brevard Co.].” From the Times-Union, “DeLand [Volusia], Fla., Sept. 19.—News has just reached here of a lynching in the southern portion of this county, near the Brevard line. The victim was Charles Harris, a negro, and his crime was committing criminal assault on the 7-year-old daughter of Mr. Bruce, a section foreman on the J.T.&K.W. railway, between Titusville and Enterprise. ... [He was taken from the authorities at Mims] ... Here the negro was taken away from the officers of the law and brought back to the railroad crossing just this side [north] of LaGrange, where short work was made of him, the body soon dangling from the road crossing sign. ... An inquest was held on the body of the negro and a verdict of death at the hands of unknown parties was rendered. After being hanged the negro was riddled with bullets.”—no mention of any other victim. From the Herald, “Charles Harris and Anthony Johnson criminally assaulted the 7-year-old daughter of J. D. Bruce, their employers, at Deland [Volusia Co.], Fla. The men were captured, but a gang of masked men took the prisoners and lynched them.” The same report appears in the Tribune and other newspapers. He met the party search for the man who had at 7 o’clock the same night assaulted Mrs. Glancey. The bloody work was done by a faction opposed to Crocker remaining in the country any longer. Two years ago Crocker’s house was burned. Last Winter Mrs. Crocker killed a man and on the afternoon of the day of the killing a member of the mob fired on Crocker and was thereupon killed by the Crockers. One is said to have made a full confession.” According to the Herald, the Crockers were killed on Sunday night, that would be the 19th, and notes that seven men, names listed, have been arrested. It is supposed that they were implicated in the killing of Johnson, the murdered pumper of the Houston East and West Texas railway at that place. notes:
The Gazette reports that a mob of blacks quietly took him away and hanged him. From the Herald, “Portland, Ark., June 21, 1895.—The Rev. Frank King, a negro preacher of local celebrity, preached his own funeral sermon here last night and then went straight to glory, if his antemortem testimony is good for anything. King stood in the centre of a mob composed of about one hundred and fifty persons of his own race. ... According to the Rev. William Tony, also colored, there had been an undue intimacy between his wife and King. The men met and quarrelled on Monday [17th]. King shot Tony twice and ran away. The wounded man, who is not yet dead, was very popular with his race, and an organized search for King was made. He was caught and lodged in jail here, but the jail was soon forced by friends of Tony. The victim was taken to the door of his own church and there permitted to talk thirty minutes. ... The rope had already been placed around his neck. One end of it was thrown over a cross piece of the frame work on which a bell is erected outside the church, a red handkerchief was tied over his eyes, and he was lifted into a wagon. The wagon was driven from under him and he fell about three feet. His neck was not broken. He died hard, suffering intensely.” From the Dealer, “Little Rock, Ark., June 20.—A shooting affray at Portland, Ark., Tuesday resulted in the fatal wounding of one of the participants and the lynching of the other. Rev. Frank King, colored, became infatuated with Deacon William Toney’s wife and trouble arose between them. When they met on the street the preacher pulled a pistol and shot the deacon in the abdomen. King was locked up and after dark a mob of infuriated negroes repaired to the lockup, took King to a tree and lynched him.” Essentially the same report appears in the News.

Note: from these reports it is not clear whether he was lynched on the 17th or the 20th.

notes:
The 7/26 Constitution reports that Tom Johnson, who was accused of killing a white woman (Mrs. Hartfield) and her daughter and assaulting another daughter, was put into jail in Hattiesburg. On the night of the 24th., a mob broke into jail and carried him away — he was wounded in the process — 14 miles to the scene of the killings. On the 25th some of the mob leaders claimed that Johnson had escaped but given that were was an estimated 1000 persons in the mob, that seems unlikely. “From all stories told of the affair, Johnson was burned at the stake.” The Picayune story says that he was given the choice between being shot or hanged — he was then riddled with 700 bullets. Also implies a date of 26 July. The 7/27 Constitution states that “... his body was riddled with buckshot.” The Sun reports that Johnson was killed at noon on the 26th by a mob of 300 men from Marion, Perry, and Jones counties at the Hartfield farm, 14 miles from Pervis—apparently a larger mob had taken him from jail but he escaped and was recaptured and then another took him to the Hartfield farm and riddled his body with bullets.

Note: Forrest Co. wasn’t created until 1906 - Hattisburgh was in Perry Co. until then. Couldn’t find a “Pervis” in 1895 atlas; USGS lists a Pervis Lake in Warren Co.

After shooting his several times the parties poured coal oil over an old bagging sack, set fire to it, threw it into the room, where the dead body lay, examined the body, saw that it was dead, then shot his wife, seriously wounding her also, shot his little boy 7 years old, seriously wounding him, and then fled. There is no clew to the murderers.”

Sunday [25th] forenoon, Messrs. West Stewart, James McDaniel and John Barber, who were old residents of Chilton County, but who now live in Elmore [Co.], having heard of the presence of a suspicious negro in the neighborhood, concluded to search for him .... Reasoning that he negro would be likely to cross the Coosa River, and that he would avoid all public ferries ... [the three men mentioned, and likely another found Hendricks on bank of the Coosa river 0.25 miles upstream from Calloway’s Creek and 4.5 miles south of Wetumpka; when the men approached Hendricks, he jumped into the Coosa and drown without struggling] ... The coroner was summoned on Monday [26th] morning, and also the Sheriff of Chilton County. the wounds on the body fully identified the man as the ‘third negro’ engaged in the murder of Mrs. Rucker near her home in Chilton County. He was brought to town and turned over to Sheriff English, who placed him in jail. Public sentiment was so outraged by the heinousness of the offense that a demand was made on the sheriff for the keys, but he refused and matters apparently quieted down. As a safeguard, however, the sheriff called upon the Greene Rifles to guard the jail, which they did and dispersed a crowd Thursday night. At half-post five this morning the guard was dismissed, and at about half-past ten o’clock a crowd, supposed to be from another county, came in and demanded the keys from the sheriff, who again refused. But the crowd were too determined to be baffled, and after a short delay took sledge hammers and crow-bars and broke down the door. A rope was quickly placed around the brute’s neck and he was led from the jail, while the sheriff and mayor begged the crowd to desist. The negro was carried beyond the incorporate limits and strung up to a pine tree. Before death came his body was riddled with bullets.” The 4/11 edition of the Constitution reports that the mob was also composed of men from a “neighboring county” — thought to be Morgan Co. notes:
According to the Constitution, Worley, a citizen of Murray Co., had been at war with a “gang of desperadoes.” Worley had been the leader of a group of Murray Co. whitecaps. He was hanged but was not killed. Later he was shot while plowing on the 19th. From the Argus “News of a brutal murder in Gilmer county, just across the Murray [county] line, reached Dalton yesterday. Henry Worley, well known in Dalton [Whitfield Co.], was found dead in his field, where he had been at work, Thursday morning. His body was still warm when found. His breast was perforated with several balls supposed to have from a Winchester rifle. His face was also riddled with wounds made by either buck or duck shot. Footsteps of three men led from the woods to within about ten steps of where he was lying. ... At the time of his death, Worley was under $1,000 bond to appear at Gilmer court on charge of kukluxing.” From the 4/21 Telegraph, “Murdered By White Caps. ... Atlanta, Ga., April 20—Henry Worley, a prominent Murray county farmer, was shot and killed in his field yesterday by whitecaps. ... Worley was formerly a member of the band, most of whose leading members are moonshiners. They suspected him of treachery, and last week took him out at night and strung him up. One of the gang slipped back, gave him a knife, and Worley cut himself down. He was fired on as he ran away. He declared that he was coming to Atlanta to give Governor Northen the names of 100 members of the gang.” The Journal report adds nothing of substance except that he lived “near the line of Gilmer and Murray counties”. The 1/14/1895 Telegraph notes that Judge John Edmondson, 70, of Murray county, has been indicted for implication in the killing of Worley, and that five others are under indictment for that murder. From the Enquirer, “Atlanta, Ga., April 9.—The Federal court jury in the hanging branch of the Worley murder case was completed today and two witnesses were examined. Henry Worley  was one of the informers murdered by the Murray county white-caps one year ago. Worley was first hanged, but that did not kill him, and a week later he was shot dead. Several attempts have been made to try the leaders of the gang, but W. C. Glenn, counsel for the defense, has knocked out the previous indictments on demurrers. One of the witnesses examined today stated that when Worley was taken from his home his mother denounced him as a traitor and declared that he deserved his fate. James A. Dixon, who was in the party who made the unsuccessful attempt at lynching, stated that A. McIntyre drove the mule from under Worley and left him suspended from a limb.” According to the 4/4/1895 Telegraph, Henry Worley was a well-to-do farmer of Gilmer county. The Herald reports on whitecap/ku klux/regulator activity in Murray, Gordon, Whitfield and Gilmer counties; “The two crimes which have made the regulators most notorious were the attempted murder of ‘Will Roper’ and the brutal killing of Henry Worley. ... the story of the Worley tragedy has been told in the Herald. Worley was, by his own account, ‘the gamest man in the mountains,’ and after making his escape in a marvelous manner from the lynchers’ noose he was shot down in cold blood by four agents of the gang. Worley’s own mother, wife and brother are said to have had a hand directly or indirectly in his death.”

Note: no Gilmer Co. newspapers for 1894 available on microfilm. Relevant issues of the Calhoun Times and North Georgia Citizen are not on microfilm. There was a failed lynching of Worley on or around the 12th of April in Gilmer Co. 1880 census lists a Henry Worley, white, 21, living with his wife Melissa and one child in Gilmer Co. Apparently the heart of the kukluxing area was Murray Co.

The State yesterday obtained the details of an exceedingly ugly affair which occurred in the upper portion of the State, just across the line dividing the counties of Abbeville and Edgefield, in the first named county, on Friday [6th] night last. notes:
From the Advertiser, “A sensational killing occurred near Barksdale [Laurens Co.] on the Greenville Railroad on Wednesday [29th] night last. At about 10 o’clock parties came to a cabin occupied by one Clem Davis and wife, colored, on the lands of Mr. Butler Putnam. The demanded that the door be opened which was refused. The mob claimed to be 75 strong but the report suggest it was smaller, at 35 or less. From the Union, “Minden, La., Sept. 9.—Link Waggoner, a noted desperado of North Louisana and Eastern Texas, was shot to death in his cell in the parish jail by a mob last night. For the past five years he had been a terror to the country. Innumerable murders are laid to his door, and his robberies were most daring. He was captured about a year ago at Nacogdoches, Tex., and brought to Homer, in Claybourne county and tried on a charge of murder. The case was not proven .... While at Homer an attempt was made by a mob to kill him, but single handed, having in some unaccountable manner obrained possession of a pistol, he kept the whole mob at bay until assistance arrived. Last night the jail here was broken into by a mob of seventy-five who shot him dead in his cell and then dispersed.” The News has a long account of Waggoner’s criminal career.

notes:
From the 12/20 Constitution, “A Sensation at West Point. Two Brother Kill a Professor Who Insulted Their Sister. A gentleman who was in the city last night from West Point, Ga., said that on last Saturday [15th] night two brothers shot a negro preacher named Turner, who had written an insulting letter to their sister. Yesterday [19th] they learned that Turner was not dead, so they took a friend and went to the house where Turner was being nursed. A negro woman met them at the door and brained one of the men with an ax. She and Turner were then killed. An effort is being made, so the informant stated, to suppress the story, as the brothers are prominently connected. It was impossible to learn their names.” Essentially the same story appears in the Star, Dispatch, and other newspapers. According to the Herald, “A Mob That Lacked ‘Sand.’ Atlanta, Dec. 21.—A special to The Journal states that a mob attempted to kill a negro named Liceus Turner at West Point, Ga. The negro wrote an insulting letter to a young lady, and he was decoyed and filled with bullets. He crawled to a house and the mob attacked him. The leader was struck down while the others fled. The negro was taken to Lafayette, Ga., for protection. No one was killed.”—Lafayette GA makes no sense. The 1/8 Constitution states, “Lafayette, Ala., January 7.—(Special.)—Lucius Turner, the negro who wrote an insulting note to a prominent young lady at West Point a few days ago, died in jail here last Saturday [5th]. He was terribly wounded by gunshots at the hands of the mob. He was brought here for protection.” From the Times-Picayune, “Death of a Negro Who Had Been Shot by a Mob. West Point, Ga., Jan. 8.—(Special.)—News comes from Lafayette, Ala., of the death there of Lucius Turner, the negro who was shot near here by a mob of would-be lynchers, headed by the brothers of a prominent young lady, whom the negro insulted. In escaping from the mob he received gunshot wounds, which have proved fatal. He was taken to Lafayette (AL) for safe-keeping.”

Note: Lafayette, AL is just across the GA-AL line from West Point. Apparently the black woman was not killed. Turner was shot on the 19th but didn’t die until 5 January.

At 12 o’clock Saturday night two shots were fired through the windows of the house ... instantly killing the old man. The murderers then pillaged the store and attempted to burn it and the residence. ... Suspicion pointed to a negro named Dan McDonald and a half-breed Indian named Will Carter, who previously boasted of having slain two negro men and an Indian woman. Before the posse reached McDonald’s house they were joined by Carter, who, by his overzealous efforts to implicate McDonald, sealed his own fate. notes:
From the Times-Democrat, “Kosciusko, Jan. 27.—Report reaches here that last night [26th] a mob of masked men went to the house of Tom Carr, a negro, who lives in beat 5, this county [Attala Co.], and assassinated him, and shot his wife, seriously wounding her. The perpetrators of the foul deed have not been discovered as yet.” The 1/29 Picayune says that Riley Horn, a farmer in the area, came to the home of Tom Carr and shot him. From the 2/1 Picayune, “Kosciusko, Miss., Jan. 31.—(Special.)—Riley Horn, who was arrested and jailed here last Saturday on suspicion as the murderer of Tom Carr, an account of which appeared in the Picayune, was today brought into court and succeeded in waived trial and gave bond in the sum of $1500 dollars for his appearance at the March term of the circuit court.” From the Commercial, “Kosciusko, Miss., Jan 31.—Riley Horn, the alleged leader of the White Caps who murdered Tom Carr, colored, twelve miles southeast of the his place Thursday night last, was arraigned before Justices Jennings and Terry today. He waived examination and his bond was fixed at $1,500, which he promptly gave. ... The fact that Horn had previously been reported by the murdered negro for a misdemeaner is supposed to have been the motive. No other arrests have been made yet. It is supposed several others are particeps criminis.”

Note #1: couldn’t find in a Mississippi newspaper or follow-up in Newspapers.com or GenealogyBank.com thru 1893. The question is  one of number of killers: only Riley Horn, a white cap leader, or that multiple white caps were involved with Riley Horn being the one who shot Carr. The Commercial account implies the later and is consistent with the Times-Democrat report.

Note #2: 1880 Attala census lists a Tom Carr, 18, (ca. 1862), black, living with his parents Jack and Mille Carr and many sibs. In the 1870 Attala census he’s listed as 9 years old and as living with same parents in Beat 5.

chicago_tribune: Not in Chicago Tribune inventory

eji: Not in EJI inventory
naacp: Not in NAACP inventory
notes:
The 8/1 Constitution reports, “Macon, Ga., July 31.—(Special.)—John Thomas is dead, and the men who are alleged to have killed him will be defended by Mr. Marmaduke Bayne ... well-known Macon lawyer. The case is an interesting one in which white caps figure. Thomas as a ‘Smart Aleck’ kind of negro, dudish and insolent. Last February in the lower part of the fifth district of Houston county, Thomas called at the house of a highly respectable lady and her daughter, took a seat, and made himself quite at home, and was insolent in his talk. ... That night a number of white caps attacked Thomas and gave him a severe beating, from which it was thought he would not recover. At the last term of Houston superior court the grant jury found a true bill against the Leverett boys, Willis Franklin and Watson, all young white men for assault with intent to murder. ... The information has reached Macon that Thomas died a few days ago, and the coroner’s jury rendered a verdict against the Leverett boys, Willis Franklin and Watson of voluntary manslaughter. Watson, however, is dead, having died several weeks before Thomas.” Essentially the same story appears in the News. From the Journal, “In the case against Willis Franklin, Charlie, Jim and Emmett Leverett, charged with murder, a no bill was returned. This is the case in which a negro man on the farm of Mr. J. T. Walker was so severely whipped by a number of men at night that he afterward died.” From the 10/7 Constitution, “The White Caps Dismissed. Willis Franklin, Charlie, Jim and Emmett Leverett, well known white men of Houston county, were charged with beating a negro so severely one night that he died from the effects of the injuries. The case became characterized as ‘a white cap outrage.’ ... The news reaches Macon today that the grand jury of Houston county, which is not in session, found no indictments against the so-called ‘white caps.’”

Note: Thomas was attacked in February but didn’t die of his injuries until July. Couldn’t find an earlier report in Newspapers.com or Georgia Historic Newspapers.

notes:
The Appeal-Avalanche reports that Neal was hanged by a mob of 400-500 persons near Germantown. It states that Neal said before being hanged “never under any circumstance have anything to do with a white woman, no matter how poor or humble she might be.” [This sounds contrived.] He was accused of raping a white woman, Mrs. Smith, of Forest Hill, Shelby Co. The Commercial gives his name as Richard Neal, the location as near Forest Hill, and the time as 3:00 p.m. on the 11th—no indication of mob size. From the Review, Thomas Neal, a negro, was lynched near Memphis a few days ago. The cause was the usual one. Colored men assisted the whites in this lynching. The reports say that ‘Preston Roberts, a prominent negro, who was a member of the mob and who assisted in the execution, made a speech to the crowd stated that justice had been done and that Neal had met his just doom.’” The Observer, however, dateline Memphis, 11 February, states that Neal was not lynched; a “party” started with Neal into the woods with the intention of lynching him but “A messenger overtook the party, however, with the information that Mrs. White was inclined to doubt that Neal was the person that committed the deed. This morning two other negroes were captured. If Mrs. White identifies either of them he will be lynched. Neal is still in custody of the posse. Sheriff McLendon, of this city, was called on by the law-abiding citizens of Collierville to come to their relief and free the prisoner from the mob. He is organizing a posse and will start at once. If he comes in contact with the mob there will be a desperate fight. The mob is composed of determined men and McLendon is a fearless officer.” The same report appears in the Telegraph. But the Ocean notes that the editor of the Memphis Appeal-Avalanche commented favorably on the lynching of Neal in Shelby county. The Journal reprints this editorial from the Appeal-Avalanche, “No unseemly anger was shown. It was the will of the people that a man whose existence was a menace to the community should die, and he was slain. The voice of the people is the voice of God. There is one crime that is punishable in the South with death without trial. It was committed by Neal. Neal is dead.”

notes:
According to the 4/25 Constitution, Peterson was accused of raping a young white woman. Peterson heard that he was a suspect and went to Governor Tillman in Columbia, claiming that he had witnesses that could provide him with an alibi. Governor Tillman give him to a constable and sent him back to Denmark. There Miss Bessie Baxter could not identify him as her attacker but the mob took Peterson a short distance up the railroad track, tied him to a sapling, and riddled his body with bullets. The article speculates that Peterson was innocent. From the Telegraph, “Augusta, April 24.—John Patterson, a negro, was lynched at Denmark, S. C., tonight by a mob. He was convicted of criminal assault on a young white girl by a vigilance committee organized for the purpose. He was hanged on a pine tree near the scene of the outrage and shot to death. Five hundred citizens participated on the lynching.” The State’s report starts with headline: “An Innocent Man Lynched. Gov. Tillman Accessory Before the Fact” and then gives a detailed account of the lynching. The 4/26 Constitution has a strong editorial criticizing the lynching of an innocent man. Note: there were many newspaper articles/editorials condemning this lynching, both inside and outside of the south. 

Note: the Recorder notes that Tom Peterson, a.k.a., Tom Peters, the brother of John Peterson, was arrested for murder in October, 1895.

notes: According to the 7/8 Republican, 7,000 watched Charles J. Miller being hanged from a telegraph pole next to the train depot after being taken from the jail. He was accused of killing the Ray sisters of Bardwell. The 7/10 edition notes that it is now known that Miller was innocent of the charges. The News reports that a second man has been arrested at Milan, Tenn., in conjunction with the murder of the Ray sisters, and that Miller may have been innocent. The paper states that Miller was lynched by a “mob composed of nearly every white man in Carlisle county.” From the Daily Journal, “Bardwell, Ky., July 12.—A number of the most active workers in the capture and lynching of S. J. Miller have gotten together and prepared a statement which will be given the public. It establishes the guilt of Miller beyond all question.” The Times reports, dateline Cairo, Ill., that “Wrong Negro Hanged by the Bardwell, Ky., Avengers”. Miller was accused of killing the two Ray sisters near Bardwell. He fled and was captured in Missouri and brought to Wickliffe [Ballard Co.] for questioning, and then taken to Bardwell in custody of a sheriff. A huge mob awaited Miller; Miller argued that he was from Springfield, IL. and completely innocent. The sheriff was allowed to take Miller to the jail until 3:00 p.m. At that time the mob took Miller, stripped him naked (tied a shirt around his loins) and paraded through town to a place near the train depot. There he was hanged and shot and his body burned. The Republican says that Miller was also known as “Glass-Eating Joe”, and that he was hanged and burned at the stake. According to the Banner, citing the Macon Telegraph, states that the lynching of the murderer was justified but that Miller was innocent.

According to the Constitution, “Carrollton, Ga., August 11.—(Special.)—News received here is that there is one less negro in the community between Brooks station [Fayette Co.] and Senoia [Coweta Co.] tonight than there was this time last night. Dug Hastleton, a burly black negro, got very angry at Mr. Gul Hicks, a farmer, living in the community, and went to Hick’s home last night for a row. On his arrival Hastleton found Hicks at Brooks station, attending the preliminary trial of Walter Reeves, who was being tried for an assault on a young lady. Hicks soon got home and a band was organized and went in pursuit of the negro. It is reported that the posse caught the negro on Line creek, but what was done with him cannot be learned. Your correspondent was informed by good citizen of that community tonight that it was his opinion that there was one less negro in that vicinity. Hastleton was a bad character.” The Telegraph reports, citing the Griffin News, that an unnamed black man was found drown in Flint river, “near Line Creek district, was found drown on Wednesday [9th] and two others are missing. These negroes had had some trouble last week with Mr. Hicks ... who lives in Fayette county. On Tuesday [8th] they went to Mr. Hicks’ house, but did not find him at home. They talked very threateningly and insultingly to his wife, and told her that if her husband had been at home they intended to kill him. The ringleader was found drowned yesterday, and the others have not been seen since. Very probably in attempting to cross the river the flood was too much for them all. Providence acts very quickly in some of the neighborhoods of Georgia, if not mysteriously.”
