eji: Rufus Bigley, 9/8/1893, Monroe Co., Black, Other
naacp: Rufus Beagley, 9/15/1893, Jackson, Hinds Co., Negro, Alleged well poisoning
notes: According to the Appeal-Avalanche, Lou Carter (Ben Jackson’s mother-in-law), Mahalia/Mohaly Jackson (Ben Jackson’s wife), Rufus Broughs (listed as Rufus Dayles in the 9/15 edition), were lynched on 14 September for being accessories to the poisoning of a well that killed three family members. The News states that Rufus [illegible] was found hanging to a tree on the 14th. The Enquirer-Sun states that two children of the Thomas Woodruff family died. The Star lists this victim as Rufus Bayles. Apparently Broughs/Beagley/Dayles/Bayles was accused of giving the Jacksons’ the money to buy the poison. From the Herald, “Aberdeen, Miss., Sept. 11, 1893.—Two weeks ago Thomas Woodruff and five children, living near Quincy, were taken violently ill, and two children died. He and the others still linger, with little hope of recovery. Examinations of the well on the premises disclosed three packages of rat poison in it, and suspicion pointed to a negro. Ben Jackson, who was arrested and taken by a crowd of unmasked men from the officers during the inquest and hanged [8 September]. The jury next day examined Mehaley Jackson, Ben’s wife, and Lou Carter, his mother-in-law, who testified to a knowledge of Ben’s intention to purchase poison for that purpose, but the jury discharged them. A crowd of armed men also took them out and hung them as participants in the conspiracy. Mehaley Jackson also testified that Rufus Broyles, a well known negro of the neighborhood, had furnished the money to buy the poison and after the first lynching he hid away and eluded discovery until yesterday. He was seen at Woodmill, a few miles from the scenes of the other tragedy, and this morning his dead body was found hanging to a limb in that vicinity.”

notes:
From the Telegraph, “Birmingham, Ala., Sept. 19.—Riley Gulley, a negro 23 years old, was lynched yesterday at Pineapple, below this city, for attempting an assault on Mrs. Nored, the wife of a highly respected farmer residing near Pineapple. He was taken from Pineapple jail by a large crowd of angry citizens and strung up in the jail yard. The body was riddled with bullets.” From the News, “Birmingham, Ala., Sept. 20.—Riley Gulley, a negro 23 years old, was lynched at Pineapple, below this city, for attempted to rape Mrs. Nored, the wife of a highly respected farmer residing near Pineapple.” From the Star, “Birmingham, Ala. Sept. 22.—The negroes friends of Ned _____, who was lynched a few days ago near Pine Apple in Dallas county for criminally assaulting a white woman living near there, made another attack yesterday upon the whites. From the best information received the news ... [illegible] ... Two negroes were killed and several badly injured.” The Democrat gives the name Ned Gully and that he was lynched “near Pine Apple, in Dallas county...” “a few days ago”. The Times also states “near Pineapple, in Dallas county.” The Advertiser says that he was taken from the authorities “When about ten miles from town [Pine Apple, as he was being taken to Camden, Wilcox Co.] they were overtaken by a mob of determined masked men about fifteen or twenty in number, who demanded the prisoner. He was taken some distance in the woods and when found his lifeless body hung from a tree mutilated with bullets.”

Note: 1895 Atlas and USGS puts Pine Apple in Wilcox Co. Wilcox is adjacent and south of Dallas Co.

notes:
The Gazette reports that Robert Smith was hanged and riddled with bullets on Ninth Avenue SW in Roanoke after being taken from the jail by a mob of 20 men—”They left a placard on his body, ‘This is Mayor Trout’s friend.’ ... Thousands of people visited the scene of the lynching between daylight and 8.50 o’clock when the body was cut down. After the jury had completed their work, the body was placed in the hands of officers, who were unable to keep back the mob. Three hundred men tried to drag the body through the streets of the town, but Rev. Dr. Campbell, of the First Presbyterian church, and Capt. R. B. Mooreman with pleadings and main strength prevented them. Capt. Moorman hired a wagon and had the body put in it. It was then conveyed to the bank of the Roanoke [river], about one mile from the scene of the lynching. The dead negro was dragged from the wagon by a rope about two hundred yards and burned on a pile of dry lumber in the presence of an infuriated man [mob] of over 1,000 men. The mob threatened at one time to bury the negro in Mayor Trout’s yard. Threats of vengeance have been openly made against the Mayor and and militia for attempting to maintain the law. Capt. Bird, commanding the militia has left the town. Mayor Trout has also disappeared ....” He was accused of assaulting and robbing Mrs. Henry Bishop. The 9/22 Roanoke Times account is very detailed and gives the lynch victim’s name as Thomas Smith. The Richmond Times states that Thomas Smith was 21 years old, and that Mrs. Sallie A. Bishop was from Botetourt county—the alleged assault (non-sexual) and robbery happened in Roanoke. The Chattanooga Times reports that Edward Page, one of the lynchers, was acquitted “by the jury today [15th] after a short deliberation. ... The trial of J. Frank Sheppard and W. S. Bone [Boone], indicted as principles, and Chief of Police Terry and Sergt. Griffin as accessories before the fact, is set for tomorrow. Boone has been out of the city since the indictments were found. The others are out on bail.” According to the Dispatch, Sergeant A. H. Griffin was reduced in rank for “conduct unbecoming” and
a Hugh M. Dyer was appointed as the new chief of police. According to the Spectator five men, names listed, were tried in Hustings Court of Roanoke on the 22nd charged with burning the body of Thomas Smith; one was acquitted, four were convicted with three fined $5, and one person was fined $100 and sentenced to one year in prison;”The grand jury has so far found forty-four indictments.”

* Note #1: Apparently only 20 men were engaged in the actual lynching, but a mob of 300 took Smith’s body and burned it with many more (1,000?) being spectators. On the 20th there was a threatened lynching of Smith by a mob of 100s and they attacked the jail; the Planet says nine of the mob were killed when attacking the jail, however, the 9/22 and 9/27 Roanoke Times lists just eight. There was also a threatened lynching of Mayor Henry S. Trout in connection with this lynching.

Note #2: the grand jury handed down 19 indictments on 24 October, including Walter S. Boone, Edward Page and Frank Sheppard, “as principals” and A. H. Griffin, “sergeant of police”, and J. F. Terry, “chief of police”—Vergennes (VT) Enterprise and Vermonter 11/3/1893, p. 4 (Newspapers.com)

notes: From the Star, “A special from Drake’s Branch, Charlotte county, Virginia, says: Notorious Abe Redmond, the worst man that ever lived in Charlotte county, came to his death last night at the hands of a mob. It being night, Constable Crutcher was ordered to take the prisoner to his house, which was on the way to the court house, under a guard of three men. They arrived at Crutcher’s house without any sign of disturbance. Redmond was taken from an officer at night by a small party of men, carried off into the woods, and hanged. He was a notorious character, and the people seemed to have determined to rid the county of him.” In the 12/9 Times report on the indictments in connection with the lynching of Abner Redmond, the men were Toney Robinson, black; Abner Harrison, white; Dudley Hamilton, white. notes:
From the Birmingham News, “Nashville, Tenn., Nov. 4—News has just received here of the triple lynching near Lynchburg, Tenn., last night [3rd] of Ed Wagner, his son-in-law and daughter, all negroes. It is said they were hanged by other negroes for barn burning.” The Constitution reports that Ned Waggoner, Will Waggoner (his son), Mary Motlow (his daughter), and Sam Motlow (son-in-law) were hanged one mile from Lynchburg, on the farm of Jack D[illegible]. The story states that they had the reputation of being “desperate characters and had recently been warned to leave the country ...” They were suspected of barn-burning in Moore and Lincoln counties. The Banner reports, “Fayetteville, November 6.—The jury of inquest empanelled by Coroner H. B. Morgan on Saturday [4th] to inquire into the cause of the death of Ned Waggoner, William Waggoner, Sam Motlow and Eliza Motlow, the negroes who were lynched on Friday [3rd] night last, has returned the following verdict:” [Ned Waggoner was hanged and shot 0.25 miles from the courthouse on the Booneville road by a mob of 200 “between the hours of 11 p.m. on the 4th and 5 a.m. on the 5th day of November”—this can’t be right because the inquest was held on the 4th] ... The verdict in all the other cases was substantially the same as the above, save as to the manner of death. The necks of Sam Motlow and Will Waggoner were both broken, and the woman, Eliza, met her fate by strangulation. ... Ned Waggoner was 50 years of age; Will Waggoner, 25; Sam Melton [Motlow], 25, and his wife Eliza, 22.” They were buried in the black cemetery in one grave in Lynchburg.

Note: this could have happened late on the 3rd or in the very early hours of the 4th. Brundage does not list these lynchings in his Virginia inventory.

notes:
According to the 11/9 Times-Union, Henry Bogue was taken from a sheriff’s posse, carried off a quarter of a mile, and riddled with bullets. He was accused of complicity in the murder of W. J. Duncan at Lake City Junction ... was taken from the sheriff’s posse last night [8th] at the doors of the town jail, carried off and riddled with bullets. The sheriff is keeping the others accused in hiding. “The town is full of angry, excited men and more lynching may follow.” According to the Constitution, citing the Times-Union, Henry Bogue was taken from the authorities late on the 8th and riddled with bullets 0.25 miles from Fort White; “Judge Murrell had just had a preliminary trial over Bogue and two others supposed to be implicated, and had adjourned the court until 10 a. m. tomorrow [10th]. In less than fifteen minutes Bogue was a corpse. The sheriff is trying to keep the others hidden out. The town is full of angry, excited men, and more lynching may follow.” The News makes no mention of any other victims and says that two others were being hidden by the sheriff. The 11/12 Times-Union reports that a rag was stuffed into his mouth and the mob began cutting on him, gouged out his eyes, and sewed up the sockets. The paper asserts that there is a “general opinion here that three, if not four, were lynched.” The Globe-Democrat describes, dateline Columbia [Co.] Fla., 12 November, Henry Boggs [Bogue] torture and lynching and reports “... Of the mysterious fate that befell three other negroes [later described as ex-convicts] who disappeared little can be learned, as no one has been at Fort White since the lynching [of Boggs/Bogue], and even if they had, the fear of getting into trouble would prevent any one here giving any details. ... As to the other two, perhaps three, implicated, they got away from the officer having them in charge Thursday [9th] night. Some say, with an incredulous smile, that they really did make their escape by breaking apart the handcuffs which bound them together, taking to their heels under fire. It is the general opinion here that three, if not four, where lynched, and tortured. The Sheriff has not yet returned from the scene.”

Note: if the “town is full of angry, excited men” that would suggest at a level 3 (50-99) mob. There are a great many newspaper accounts of the lynching of Henry Bogue.

notes:
The report in the Constitution in Ancestry.com is a fragment: a black man named Nelson was hanged and riddled with bullets and burned at Varn__ by negroes. According to the 11/15 Gazette, Nelson was taken from jail at 11 p.m. by a mob of masked black men. He was shot over a dozen times and was thrown on a small brush pile and attempts were made to burn him. It was raining so he was only slightly parched. From the Star, “A mob, consisting exclusively of colored people, broke down the jail at Varner, Ark., and took a negro named Nelson, who a week ago murdered another negro, hung him to a tree, riddled his body with bullets and then burned it.” The Banner gives the mob size as 500. From the Patriot, “Little Rock, Ark., Nov. 14.—Word has reached here of the execution of a negro named D. T. Nelson at Varner last night by a mob of negroes. Last week Nelson murdered Ben Betts, a negro, and since then he has been confined in the small jail at Varner, a little station on the Iron Mountain railroad in a sparsely settled country. The friends of the murdered man broke down the doors and tied a rope to the murderer’s neck and dragged him to a tree, where he was quickly swung up. As soon as his body was fastened to the tree the mob fired a volley of bullets into it. They gathered a lot of wood and set fire to it. The mob then withdrew but the rain which was pouring down quenched the flames and saved the body from incineration.” According to the 11/18 Gazette, dateline Varner, 17 November, “Judge John M. Elliott issued his warrant today for the arrest of Stros Tinsley, Abraham Washington, Yancey Hawkins, Edmund Taylor, Jr. William Moore, Jim Elis and Milton Greenler and two others not in custody, charged with the killing of D. T. Nelson, taken out of the jail at Varner November 13, 1893. Yancy Hawkins, the leader, was first arrested and he broke down and told everything, implication Tom Boydin, J. K. Hubbard, a Justice of the Peace for this Choctaw Township, Tom Riley and all arrested except Jim Ells, who will be able to prove his innocence. The Sheriff and posse of this county are after all implicated. Edmund Taylor is the Constable of this Township and Yancy Hawkins, Deputy Constable.” The 2/23/1894 Gazette reports, dateline Pine Bluff, 22 February, that Yancy Hawkins, Edmund Taylor, Colburn Ashley and Tom Riley, all colored, were yesterday indicted by the Grand Jury of Lincoln County for the murder in the first degree. They were members of the gang who took David Nelson from the jail-house on the night of the 13th of November and shot him to death. Tom Boydin, Steve Tinsley and Abe Washington are held as accessories.”

Note: suspected police lynching, or police assisted lynching

The Journal reports that a mob killed Mrs. Martin, “an innocent old negro woman”, at Henderson [Chester Co.]. The two sons were unwounded and fled the county. From the Daily News, “Nashville, Tenn., Feb. 4.— Another bloody chapter was added to the Berry barn-burning matter near Hendersonville [Sumner Co.]. Two negroes named Martin were tired last fall at Gallatin [Sumner Co.], where they were acquitted and warned that they had better get away from the county. They returned on Christmas. Last night a mob went to the cabin of their mother and called them out. This was refused and the mob shot through the windows and the old mother was killed instantly. The Martins remained in the cabin until daybreak, when they fled.” The same story appears in the Tribune. One of the accused arsonists, Frate Haynie, was lynched in Sumner Co. on 2/13/1891 — noted in the Star report. The Pensacola News gives her name as Juda Taylor, the mother of Countz and Check Martin, who were accused of barn burning but acquitted; according to this story, the mob was masked. This same story appears in the Leaf-Chronicle.

The Negro hearing the noise and learning their intention had armed himself with a small club, about an inch in diameter and twelve or eighteen long, and as the men with the keys came to unlock the door of his cell, he ran the stick through the bars and punched the leaders in the eyes and face. This kept them back for a quite a while, but the crowd from behind pressed forward, and the door was finally opened. Then they seized the Negro and rushed him out into the open air, when a half hundred guns were fired at him. Again and again the deadly rifles belched forth their death-dealing contents, and Harris sunk to the ground with seventy bullets in his body, twenty-two of which had passed through the immediate region of the heart. ... The crime for which Harris met his terrible death was the brutal killing of E. T. Parker, a sewing machine agent, on the 3rd day of December last.”

From the Light, “Lithonia, Ga., April 4—The party which sent in search of the two negroes who had assaulted Postmaster Brown’s daughter yesterday has returned and reports that there was no use in further pursuit as the two men were ‘lost’. What this means is generally understood.” The same story appears in the Northwestern, Times, and Tribune, and other non-southern newspapers. From the Constitution, “The little town of Lithonia ... had a little sensation of its Saturday afternoon. The main features of the sensation—the grabbing hold of a little girl on a lonely road by two black negroes and running into a dense swamp with her, the subsequent finding of the child with her clothes badly torn, and frightened halt to death—were told in yesterday’s Constitution. The child was Miss Newell Brown, the pretty little ten-year-old daughter of Postmaster Brown, of Lithonia. ... [a friend of Newell Brown screamed that Newell was being carried off by two black men. A group of white stone cutters ran toward the swamp when a black man fled from the swamp and was chased. Apparently others joined in the hunt. Later the marshal brought bloodhounds to track down the black man] ... But when the trained canines ... reached Lithonia, the men had already returnef rom their pursuit of the negro, but without him. ‘It is useless,’ the marshal was told, ‘to put the bloodhounds after the negro. The trail is too cold.’ ‘And,’ the men added, ‘if we had caught the negro he would be cold now, too.’ So the search was given up and the bloodhounds were sent back. The search was not renewed yesterday by the citizens of Lithonia. ‘If those fellows,’ said Marshal Crawford yesgteray, ‘had laid their hands on him, that negro would have lived about six seconds, I guess.’ If that negro is dangling to a limb of one of DeKalb county’s sturdy oaks, he but suffered the doom he deserved. notes:
According to the Journal, “A tall oak tree near Goodlettsville, Tenn. tonight bears human fruit. The cold inanimate form of Henry Grizzard is swaying in the breeze and is a mute argument with negroes to let white women alone.”

APRIL 29 1892, Goodlettsville. Henry Grizzard, an African-American, was identified by his victims Mary and Connie Bruce the night before. He was taken away from Davidson County Sheriff Hill by a mob composed mostly of Sumner countians to a bridge over Mansker's Creek. There he was lynched on the Sumner County side of the creek, protesting his innocence to the end. According to the Nashville Daily American: "The deed was witnessed with evident satisfaction by the assemblage of vigilantes. Some one pinned an envelope on the hanging negro 's breast. On the envelope was written 'Death to the man that cuts this rope before 12 P.M.'" Another black, Mack Harper, was to be hanged as well but the mob could not agree as to his guilt and so he was surrendered to the Sheriff after several ministers and prominent citizens pleaded with the mob to let the law take its course. Harper was taken to Nashville along with Eph Grizzard, Henry's brother and two other suspects. According the Nashville Daily American, the black community in Goodlettsville was split, one group composed of "the better class of negroes" condemning the rapes and approving of the lynching, while "[t]wo negroes had early in the morning made threats of what the colored people would do if any of their race should be hanged. They were told to leave the State and that unless they left within twenty-four hours they would summarily be dealt with. They ... left during the day." The coroner's jury rendered the following verdict: "That he came to his death by a party unknown to the jury." Henry Grizzard had served a term in the state penitentiary for attempted rape in and "house-breaking." He was survived by a wife and child.

notes:
APRIL 30 1892, Nashville. Eph Grizzard, a black man, who along with his brother Henry, was accused of raping the Bruce sisters of Goodlettsville, was lynched. A large and restive crowd had gathered in the town square with the intent of lynching Eph, his brother having been murdered in Goodlettsville the day before. Later the crowd attempted to rush the jail but two deputy sheriffs shot into the crowd and wounded an indeterminate number. A crowd estimated at 6,000 grew to 10,000 many of whom were armed. At noon Governor Buchanan's proclamation asking the crowd to disperse was met with jeers and heckles. Meanwhile the prison guards attempted to remove Eph from danger by dressing him as a woman but it was too late. With the cry "remember your wives, daughters and your mothers!" the mob rushed and took the jail. According to one newspaper account: "He was jerked down and dragged over the rough cobblestones, his eyes and tongue protruding." He was quickly taken to the Cumberland river bridge with a noose around his neck and dropped fifteen feet. Although he was dead the frenzied mob hauled him up and dropped him one more time while countless bullets struck his body. It was said that over 50,000 people had witnessed the lynching. Afterwards, his body was taken to Goodlettsville so the Bruce family could see the mobs handy work, after which his body was burned to ashes in a large bonfire. As the Sunday Chattanooga Daily Times explained: "While everybody condemns mob law, no man can ravish a Southern girl and live a day after it is proven on him."

notes:
From the Times, “Little Rock, Ark., May 14.—Maggie Dixie, the 5-year-old white girl outraged by the negro, Henry James, who had hanged by a mob at 2 o’clock this morning at the corner of Fifth and Main street, died of the effects of her injuries received an hour after the hanging occurred. The details of the lynching, which were briefly told in these dispatches last night, are as follows: Late in the afternoon a mob was organized, but the prisoner was removed just in time to the penitentiary. About midnight a second mob formed, and at 1:15 this morning 1,000 men armed with Winchesters and revolvers demanded admittance to the penitentiary. The authorities refused to let the mob in but admitted that the prisoner had been taken by them for safekeeping and declared that they would turn him over to the sheriff at 8 o’clock this morning. The mob with sledge hammers then broke open the great iron gates, entered the penitentiary and, having secured the prisoner, started with him to Johnson’s house, some distance away,w here Johnson identified him. The mob grew in numbers to an immense throng as it then marched to Fifth and Main streets, in the heart of the city, opposite the Masonic temple. There the wretch was given several minutes to pray and contest. He at first denied his guilt, but finally admitted it. A rope was then thrown across the crossarm of a large telephone pole and James was soon swinging in midair and was riddled with hundreds of bullets.” According to the Democrat, the first mob, about 10 strong, came to the city jail at about 10p on the 13th; six of the mob were permitted to search the jail for Henry James, who had been removed to the penitentiary for safe keeping; in the very early hours of the 14th by a mob of 300. notes:
From the Herald, “Mobile, Ala., June 21, 1892.—Christian Chalma was hanged to a tree Saturday between Healing Springs and Buckadunn. Chalma lived near the Mississippi line, and short time ago his house was burned and he accused William Woods of arson. Chalma was considered a bad character. ... [After attempting to kill Woods] ...  He was overpowered and a posse decided to take him to jail at Winchester, Miss. On the way Chalma threatened to murder all the guards and at Red Creek the posse lost their temper and hanged him.” A brief version appears in the Enquirer. From the News, “Christian Chalma was lynched near Buckadunna, Ala., by a posse set to guard him.” From the Telegraph: “Hollinghead is not dead. Mobile, Ala., Oct. 22.—The report that John Hollinghead, who turned state’s evidence in the cases of the parties charged with lynching Chris Chamberlis, had been riddled with bullets near his home, in Washington county, is denied by a neighbor who left there yesterday morning.” From the Weekly, “Sam P. Williams and William Woods have been sentenced for life at St. Stephens, Washington county, Ala., for lynching Christoper Chamblis in 1892. This make three who have been given life sentences in this case, and there are five others awaiting trial.” According to the Bee, Chris Chamblis was killed in late July [June] by twelve members of the Farmers Alliance; Chamblis was an outspoken critic of the Alliance and his house was burned; he accused a man named Wood who was arrested and acquitted; Chamblis was “seized, held all day and at night lynched. The twelve men were immediately arrested and later were indicated for murder.” From the Journal, “Montgomery, Ala., Dec. 7.—The celebrated Chambliss lynching case began at St. Stephens to-day. The parties on trail are Will Wood, J. L. Copeland, Buck Hare, Sam Wilkins, Bishop Cupp, M. J. Cupp, L. B. Beckton, E. S. Williams, J. L. Hambrick, T. J. Button, J. W. Holllingshead and D. E. McRae.” From the Intelligencer, “The Alliance people of Washington and Choctaw counties, Ala., are excited about a trial of 12 of their number who are charged with lynching Chris Chamblis because he publicly denounced the Alliance. As a warning his house was burned. He had a man arrested on suspicion but he was acquitted. Soon after that Chamblis was arrested and held in custody all day and killed at night. For this murder they are now up for trial.” In a brief story, the 10/21 Constitution reports that the four men who lynched Charles Chandler in Washington Co. “At the last election” have been sentenced to 10 years at hard labor by a court in Clarke Co. They are in jail at Selma and will be carried to Coalburg. Apparently, Chandler was a Democrat; “Kolbites” hung Chandler. The 10/24 Constitution states that “... in a remote precinct in Washington county, Alabama, the only democrat was lynched by a band of populists.” Twelve of the lynchers have been found guilty and are headed for the penitentiary. The 4/25 Constitution reports that Alabama Governor Jelks pardoned a Tom Jordan, “the youngest of the Washington county lynchers, some dozen of whom were sent to the penitentiary for the killing of Arthur Chambliss in 1892. Chambliss was a democrat and the mob were populists, the crime having been political. Jordan was a mere boy at the time and his youth gets him out of the penitentiary.” The 6/14 edition reports that the governor pardoned three more men who had been found guilty of the Chambliss lynching, and that seven in total had been convicted. The 11/30 edition states that the pardoning board recommends the pardon of James and Jerry Tew and gives the lynching as 1892. The 12/12 Constitution notes that Governor Jelks pardoned the last two men, William and Jerry Tew, convicted for the Chambliss lynching—this story gives the year as 1899 when “a populist mob lynched Chambliss, who was a democrat.” However, the Age-Herald, “Bill and Jerry Tew, Washington, murder; refused [pardon].”

notes:
The 6/28 Tribune reports, dateline Galveston, 27 June, that “Three negroes were shot to death at Spurges Friday [24th] evening. They had confessed to having outraged Mrs. Beasley and her daughter near that place the night before.” According to the 6/30 Tribune, Prince Woods, Tom Smith and Henry Gains, all black men, were taken from the authorities about one mile from Spurgis on Friday by a mob of 50 masked men and riddled with bullets.” From the 6/30 Tribune, “Galveston, Tex., June 29—A dispatch from Colmes Mill says that three negroes, Prince Woods, Tom Smith, and Henry Gains, arrested on Friday for outraging three white women near Spurgis, confessed to having committed the crime. After the confession ten men were deputized to convey the negroes to Woodville [Tyler Co.] jail. ... When about a mile from Spurgis they saw some red flags in the roadside bushes, behind which were fifty masked and armed men, who demanded the release of the negroes, emphasizing their demand by leveling their guns upon the guards. The guards were told to retrace their steps a few paces, which they did. A few moments a volley from the guns of the masked men told the fate of the negroes. When the deputies returned to the spot they found the bodies of the three negroes riddled with bullets. Prince Woods, the leader of the negroes, was a former convict.” A somewhat expanded account appears in the Daily News with the correct spelling, Spurger. According to the County News, the authorities were given the three men on Friday afternoon but started for Woodville at 8:00 a.m. on Saturday, the 25th, when they encountered the mob one mile from Spurger—this info came from one of those authorities, a R. H. Jordan.

notes:
The 7/13 Telegraph reports that a black man named Flowers was found mangled on the rail tracks 1 mile north of Jesup. Flower’s son told the paper that three men came to their home and took his father away. The paper hypothesizes that Flowers was killed on the 8th and then put on the tracks. According to the Constitution, on the night of 7 July Issac Flowers was killed and his body placed on a railroad track, with a sign that read “Death to the South Carolina negroes; Jesup shall be rid of them.” No reason was given for the lynching. Apparently, some men were arrested but a mob formed to rescue them. The military was called in. The article in the Journal was very brief stating that the men were arrested for murdering Flowers in Jesup four weeks prior. Similarly, the Courier and 8/12 Telegraph reports added little but names some of the men arrested and suggests that Flowers was mutilated prior to being put on the tracks. The News states that Charles Warren, Tobe Little, and an unnamed black man were arrested in connection with the murder of Ike Flower; “The cause which led to the murder was the supposed part that Flower took in the Jesup riot two years ago.” According to the State, at least some of the men who shot Flowers were ku klux.

notes: From the News, “Paris, Tex., Sept. 6.—At an early hour this morning a messenger arrived in the city with the intelligence that three negroes had been found hanging to a limb by the roadside nine miles southeast of the city. The testimony [inquest] showed that a party of twenty or thirty armed and masked men went to he house of Gilbert Daniels about midnight and took Ransom and put a rope around his neck and told him they wanted him to go with them and them where other negroes lives who had been doing mischief in the neighborhood. About 2 o’clock this morning they went to the house where Armor and Walker were living and forced an entrance to the house, and dragged them both out, placed ropes around their necks, and in company with Ransom, marched them in the direction of the woods.”—the reason for the lynching seems to grow out of altercations between whites and blacks over the murder of “a notorious negro desperado [Jarrett Burnes] by John Ashey [presumably white]”. Last night about 11 o’clock a masked mob twenty-five strong went to Gilbert Daniels’ ... and ordered the door opened. ... The mob then went in, and finding John Ransom hid under a bed took him off with them .... About 12 o’clock they appeared at the house of William Armor ... where Jack Walker, a young unmarried negro, lived with Armor.”—they then hanged all three. The County News account adds nothing.

notes:
The Journal lists: Mose Johnson, Mose Jones, Jim Packer and Handy Packer
The Constitution gives the victims as: Moses Johnson, Burill Jones, Jim Packard, — Packer
The Times gives the victims as: Mose Johnson, Mose Jones, Jim Packer, and Jim’s brother
The Telegraph gives the victims as: Mose Johnson, Burrell Jones, Jim Packer, and his brother
The News lists: Mose Johnson, Mose Jones, Jim Packer, and Handy Packer
The Advertiser gives: Moses Johnson, Moses Jones, Jim Packer, Handy Packer

The four men were taken from jail, taken Graham’s Bridge over Flat Creek, hanged and while still choking, riddled with bullets. Then their limbs were torn apart by the mob and their bodies burned, according to some early accounts. They were accused of killing Richard L. Johnson and his daughter Jeanette, and burning their bodies. The Advertiser says that the mob numbered 200 and they were taken to Graham’s bridge, over Flat Creek, and riddled with bullets; “... their bodies were left where they fell and were neither burned nor mutilated. The oldest of the four was about nineteen years old.” Essentially the same account appears in the Constitution. On the other hand, the Journal says that 40-50 men broke into the jail and riddled with bullets 50 yards “above” Graham’s bridge and that “The negroes were only about eighteen or twenty years old.”—no mention of any mutilation. Some out-of-state papers, e.g., Pottsville (PA) Republican and Herald 10/15/1892, p. 3 (Newspapers.com) state that after being killed, their bodies were “torn to pieces” and then burned but this was denied, see Montgomery Advertiser 10/10/1892, p. 4 (Newspapers.com).

Note #1: 1880 Monroe Co. census lists a Burrel Jones, black, age 25, living with his parents and several siblings, including a Moses Jones, age 9, and Burrel Jones, age 3 at Bells Landing (the younger Burrel is listed as the grandson). That same census lists a Jim Packer, black, age 13, living with his mother and siblings—his only brother is Willis Packer, age 11, in Bells Landing. Couldn’t find a Mose/Moses Johnson/Johnston in Monroe Co. in 1880 but there were two Frank Johnson’s living at Bells Landing: Frank #1, age 19, born 1861, and Frank #2, 25, born 1855, and married to Chenney, age 23; in 1900 Monroe Co. census, Channie Johnson, 34, widowed, is living at Bells Landing with six children. In the 1920 census, there’s a Frank Johnson, 60, living at Bells Landing with wife—this must be the 1861 Frank Johnson. It is possible that the Frank Johnson, born 1855, is the same as Mose/Moses Johnson but he would seem to be too old. Neither Jim nor Willis Packer appears in 1900 Alabama census.

Note #2: 1900 Monroe Co. census lists a Handy Packer, black, age 14, living with his parents in Keinpville, and a Burl Jones, black, age 22, living with his wife at Bells Landing—this is the Burrel Jones that was 3 in 1880.

naacp: Henry Sanders, 3/13/1891, Lavernia, Wilson Co., Negro, Rape
notes:
The Evening Star story states that Henry Sanders has been accused of raping a 16 year-old girl, presumably white, around Christmas. On 11 March a mob went to his home, dragged him from bed, and “hanged him to the limb of a tree with 200 yards of his house.” From the Register Gazette, “Milan, Tenn., March 13.—Last Wednesday [11th] night a mob dragged Henry Sanders, aged 20, from his bed and lynched him to a tree near his house, for an assault committed on Miss Aggie Belton, aged 16, last Christmas. After committing the crime he escaped to Texas but was taken back and returned home to receive the care of this family. The relatives of the girl waited till he recovered and then avenged her.” From the Kalamazzo Gazette, “Milan, Tenn., March 3.—The ending of a fearful crime and its awful sequence took place Wednesday night about four miles north of Lavinia, Carroll county. Last Christmas Miss Angie Belton, a 16 year-old girl, was dragged from her horse and criminally assaulted by a neighbor named Henry Sanders, aged 20. A posse was organized to lynch Sanders, but he escaped to Texas where he remained till a few days ago. ... ... Wednesday night a mob went to his home, dragged him from his bed, and heedless of the screams of his mother and sisters, hung him to the limb of a tree within 200 yards of his home.” Essentially the same report appears in the Leaf-Chronicle, the Chronicle, and other, primarily non-southern, newspapers. However, the American has a story (actually two stories) that a the St. Louis Globe-Democrat published a report of a lynching in Lavinia, “... a small village near Milan.”, that was bogus: “It [the report] was painted in glowing colors and gave the name of the victim and the causes which led up to the tragedy. The Globe-Democrat embellished the story with glaring headlines and gave it the post of honor on its first page. .... A visit to the neighborhood of the alleged lynching demonstrates the fact that the story is a lie out of whole cloth; that there were no grounds whatever for such a fiction, and that the people, are very much exercised over the great outrage which has been perpetrated upon them.”

Note: couldn’t find any follow-up in Newspapers.com or ChroniclingAmerica.loc.gov or any report of the December assault. The American denial seems to place the lynching in Gibson County, but Lavinia is in Carroll Co. 4 miles N of Lavinia would still be in Carroll Co. but if the lynching was a bit NW, then it could have been in Gibson Co. Found both some Sanders and Balton/Belton families in Carroll Co. 1880 census but no one with a first name of Henry or Aggie/Angie/Annie. It’s odd that the details were so precise—wonder if the original report got the state wrong.

notes:
The 3/16 Picayune reports that Antonio Bagnetto, Joseph P. Macheca, Pietro Monasterio, Antonio Scoffedi, James Caruso, Rocco Gerachi, Frank Romero, Antonio Marchesi, Charles Traina, Loretto Comitz, Manuel Politz were killed by mobs. Last year Hampton was suspected by his white neighbors of complicity in a hog stealing case, and they went in a body one night to his house to chastise him. He warned them off, and when they persisted in the attack he shot and killed one of the members of the party. This dispersed the crowd for the night. The next day Hampton was arrested for the killing. An attempt was made to enter the jail and lynch him, but the plans of the mob were thwarted by the prompt action of the sheriff. ... [Hampton was later arrested, convicted of hog stealing and served a term in prison] ... Upon his arrival in Claiborne he was met by an armed mob, who took him from the constable and burned him to death. The next day nothing could be found of Hampton except a heap of ashes and a pair of handcuffs.”

notes: According to the Times, a mob of 2000-3000 took Clarke from the jail in Bristol and carried him to Lindsey’s Grove and hanged him from a chestnut tree. The Star says Clarke was a “boy”. From the Advocate, “Bristol, Tenn., June 15.—The city is intensely excited over the lynching that occurred here at 1 o’clock Saturday [13th] afternoon. A horrible outrage was committed on the person of Mrs. John Warren, a respectable white lady last Sunday morning about 3 o’clock. ... Tuesday night Bob Clark, a colored boy 20 years old, was arrested on suspicion. ... The evidence was very damaging. He was bound over to court Saturday morning and was sent back to jail. The great crowd that attended the trial had no idea of dispersing, and soon the news spread all over the city that Clark would be lynched before noon. In an hour hundreds of people, all colors, ages and races, gathered around the jail. Prominent men of the city made speeches loud and long, begging the excited people to disperse and let the law take its course, but they would not listen to it. At last one man obtained an ax and told the crowd to follow. The jail door was broken down and a stream of angry men filled the jail. The negro was brought out amid shouts and cheers. By this time, over 3,000 men had assembled, and as soon as the leaders started to the woods it seemed as if the whole population of Bristol was in pursuit. The excited crowd carried him to Lindsey’s Grove, a mile from town, and swung him to a limb of the nearest. He body fell once or twice, but was finally secured. It hung for four hours when it was cut down by the coroner's jury.”

For this two of the rescuing part were lynched. Bailey Sims was killed by a deputy marshal, and James Sims was lynched by a mob of Choctaw County men. Robert Sims became a fugitive from justice.” The Times-Picayune gives a long and very detailed report on this incident, including a description of the hanging of Jim Sims by a mob of “over 100, and all were armed with Winchester shotguns, revolvers or knives.”

Bowling, and a second mortally wounded, Fred Wilkerson. Three men (Charles Miller, John Scott, Robert Burton) and a 16 year-old boy (William Morton) were arrested and jailed in Clifton Forge. The mob then returned to the jail and took Robert Burton in a cart (his leg was broken) to the slaughter pen and hanged him. The following day another man (Robert Lewis, who was described as “a sober industrious colored man”) was found dead on the railroad tracks, and believed to have been murdered. notes:
According to the Gazette, “Queen City, Cass County, Tex., Oct., 26.—The negro brute, Lee Green, who murdered the family of Farmer Lowe seven miles west of this place Saturday [24th] ... was arrested at 9:30 o’clock last night near Kildare and hurried to jail at Linden. A crowd appeared at the jail at 5 o’clock this morning and demanded the keys from the sheriff’s wife who was forced to deliver them. ... They took him about twelve miles north to the scene of the tragedy and turned him over to the husband of the murdered woman, who obtained a full confession from him. [bet he was tortured]. ... All day long men from the adjoining counties, as well as from all parts of this [county], continued to arrived at Mr. Lowe’s farm. At 2:30 o’clock a trace-chain was placed about his neck and fastened to a persimmon tree so as to hold him in a standing position. At this stage of the proceedings forty-six negro men piled fagots high up around him, and an old negress touched the match to it. In a few minutes his soul passed into eternity .... It is variously estimated that the crowd numbered from 500 to 1000, both black and white. Mrs. Lowe and child were buried side by side in a common grave. The other child is doing well and is out of danger.” Essentially the same story appears in the Weekly Statesman; in a second story, same page, it’s stated that Green is 19 years old. The News story adds no new details of the lynching. The Messenger reports that Lee Allen, mulatto, 18 years old was accused of murdering a Mrs. Lowe and her 2 year-old daughter, who lived near Douglasville; he was captured and taken to Linden but was removed by a mob and taken to Douglasville to be burned. According to the Daily Statesman, thirty of those involved with the lynching of Lee Green in Cass county on 26 October  have been indicted “... and others stand a good show of going the same road.”

Note: in some out-of-state newspapers, his name is Lee Lewis. Given the nature of the crime, the length of time he spent with the mob before being burned, and that after being turned over to the husband, he confessed—likely that he was tortured.

notes:
Indicted by a Thomas Co. grand jury for murder. Taken from guards in Meigs [Thomas Co.] by mob, but the Democrat (11/5) hints that the jail “guards” may have turned over Nix willingly. According to the Times-Enterprise, dateline Cairo, 2 November, Larkin Nix was taken from the Meigs jail Saturday night between midnight and 1 a. m., and shot to death. The Post-Dispatch notes that the lynchers of Nix have been arrested. The Herald says six men were arrested. The Dispatch reports, dateline Macon, 25 March, “For the first time in the history of Georgia a lyncher has been convicted for the crime of murder and will suffer the death penalty for his offense. The murderer’s name is Barney White, and the tragedy for which he must suffer was the lynching of Larkin Nix last Fall. Nix had a wife and daughter. The mother induced the daughter to accept the attentions of a man named Mize. ... [this did not sit well with Nix so he killed Mize] ... Nix was arrested, but a mob of Mize’s friends too him out and shot him to death in Mitchell county. The preceding events took place in Thomas county. Barney White and six others were arrested and are now on trial. ... One of the leading witnesses for the State, William Davis, was shot to death by a mob of Mize’s friends in the county last night.” According to the Constitution, “A Lyncher Convicted. And One of the Witnesses Against Him Shot By Assassins. Camilla, Ga., March 25.—(Special.)—The conviction of Barney White, charged with the murder of Larkin Nix, is one of the first cases of the conviction of a lyncher on record. Six other prisoners are awaiting a like fate. ... One of the witnesses against the lynchers, William Davis, was shot last night near town. It was the work of the friends of the criminals, who wished to put the witness out of the way.”
The 7/27 edition of the Democrat, citing the Camilla Clarion, has a brief article on the arrest, and subsequent escape, of Barney White, one of the ringleaders of the mob that lynched Nix—apparently he had escaped from Camilla jail 18 months ago.

Note: apparently some early reports say that Nix was tortured and mutilated but later accounts refute this, e.g., Atlanta Constitution 1/22/1892, p. 2. See Thomasville Daily Times-Enterprise 12/3/1891, p. 3 (South Georgia Historic Newspapers) and the Thomasville Daily Times-Enterprise 4/3/1892, p. 1 (South George Historic Newspapers) for details on the acquittal of four of the alleged lynchers.

notes: According to the Times-Picayune, “Meridian, Miss., Nov. 30.—(Special.)—Saturday night about midnight, Arthur Ramsay, an old negro, was murdered and his cabin burned down over his dead body by a band of outlaws. The tragedy occurred on Mrs. Cook’s plantation, nine miles north of Meridian. ... The inquest brought out a bad state of affairs. It was in evidence that Ramsay was an inoffensive old negro, and, no one was able to surmise any cause for the dead. On Saturday afternoon went to a neighboring store and bought provisions. After his arrival home, the old man asked his oldest boy who had been to the cabin. On the boy saying no one, the old man said he had seen several white man riding away from the cabin. The old man and his little family lay down, and, about midnight, some one knocked at the door. The boy got up and stuck a light, and Ramsay grabbed an ax, refusing to open the door. notes:
From the News, “Mobile, Ala., Dec. 26.—A man named John Savage, who is supposed to be one of the Sims gang, has been captured.” According to the Journal, “... it is said that John Savage, who was arrested the day before Christmas on the charge of being a member of Sims’ gang, was hanged to a tree at ten o’clock the same night.” From the Repository, “Mobile, Ala., Dec. 28.—Bob Sims and two members of his bloodthirsty gang named Thomas and John Savage were lynched in Choctow county Saturday [26th] night by a mob.”—they were taken from the sheriff, hanged, and riddled with bullets.” From the State, “Mobile, Ala., Dec. 26.—Bob Sims and two members of his blood-thirsty band, named Thomas and John Savage, were lynched in Choctaw country last night by a mob.” From the Sun, “Robert Sims, Thomas Savage and Young Savage, a nephew of Sims, charged with the murder of the McMillan family, have surrounded to the sheriff in Choctaw county, Ala. ... The promised him protection, but the posse in charge of the prisoners were overpowered on the way to Butler Friday [25th] night and the three were hanged. It is reported that another of the Savage boys were hanged at the same time. This is in addition to John Savage who was hanged Christmas eve.” The Journal states that “The body of Bob Sims and the three Savage’s were taken down Saturday and thrown over the wall into the grave yard. John Savage still hangs suspended.”

In summarizing the incident, the Herald states “The citizens hanged him [Bob Sims], ‘Tom Savage, ‘Willie’ Savage and Tyree Savage. ‘Con’ Savage and ‘Harry’ Hinton were captured the same day and hanged to the same tree. The remaining Simsites left the country and Neal Sims has never been captured. Thus came the end of the Simsites, and with the destruction of the ‘Hell at the Breach’ gang Choctaw and Clarke counties breathed easier.”

According to the Statesman, dateline Houston, 29 July, William Hawkins, black, was not killed but a black man named John Walton was killed at the home of William Hawkins, in Houston, on the 28th by four white men: J. Sellers, W. Fox, C. Roth, and J. Buvinghausen, “... all from the vicinity of Cypress [Harris Co.]. Erichson that the negro Walton had displayed a large amount of money at Mr. Fred Kessler’s store, went in that vicinity, and meeting the posse from Cypress assisted in locating the negro. Wichman went under the house and drove the hiding negro out. No sooner out than the negro Walton ran, when several shots were fired by the Cypress party, one of the balls hitting Walton in the back of the head and coming out in the vicinity of his mouth, from the effects of which he died. On preliminary examination the four Cypress men were put under $1000 bond each to appear and answer to a charge of murder at the next term of the criminal district court.” The 7/30 News gives the location as the home of William Hawkins, “near the corner of Bradley and Summer streets” and the time as between 1:00 and 2:00 a.m. on the 29th.—this is a very detailed report.

notes: In a two sentence story, the Constitution reports that Willis Alexander was lynched near Baton Rouge for attempting to outrage a young girl. His body was found hanging from a tree by the roadside. The Picayune states that Alexander was in jail and was bonded by a Mr. Bogar who said he need him to pick cotton. Bogar said that on the way out [of town] he was overpowered and Alexander was taken. His body was found hanging from a tree. From the Times-Picayune, “Baton Rouge, La., Aug. 22.—(Special.)—Willie Alexander, a mulatto, about 17 years of age, was hung last night on the Greenwell Springs road, in the Tenth ward, just beyond the Comite bridge, for the attempted rape of the little 11-year-old daughter of Mr. Carmena, a prominent resident of the Third ward. The crime was committed six weeks ago, when Alexander, at 2 o’clock at night, climbed through a window of the Carmena residence into a room where two little girls were sleeping. On being aroused the girls made an outcry, which caused the negro to flee in such haste as to leave his hat behind. This led to Alexander’s identification, and on being arrested four or five days alter at Zachary, he admitted that he had entered the room but claimed that he went there to play with two little boys, and discovered his mistake when the alarm was given. Alexander was brought to Baton Rouge and lodged in jail where he remained until last evening when he was bonded by Mr. Bogar, a young man from the Tenth ward, who stated he wanted him to pick cotton. Mr. Boger returned to town last night and informed the law officers that on the way out [of town] he was overpowered at the point designated and forced to give up the custody of Alexander, who was taken off. He did not know what was done with him. Parties coming in town to-day say the dead body hanging from a tree by the roadside.” From the Review, “New Orleans, La., Aug. 23.—The Picayune’s Baton Rouge special reports the lynching is Willis Alexander, colored, aged 17, in that parish Thursday night. Alexander was accused of attempting to rape an eleven-year-old white girl.” The Advocate reports that coroner’s inquest: “Testimony of witnesses taken under oath at an inquest held over the body of an unknown colored man [William Alexander] near Comite bridge, in the tenth ward of this parish, on the 22nd day of August, 1890 ....”

They lynched him at the edge of Big Black swamp. The News adds little except that he was hanged near the scene of his attempted crime. From the Times-Picayune, “Vicksburg, Miss., Feb. 22.—(Special.)—The excitement cause by the attempted outrage of Miss Penkston by the negro Wesley Thomas on Wednesday [20th] last has not diminished in the least this morning, but as time passed it was known that Deputy Sheriff Rainwater was alone with the negro somewhere in the county under pretense of protecting him from being lynched. This seemed to enrage the public, as fears were expressed that he fiend would make his escape. Telegrams were sent in all directions to watch the trains and public roads. Deputy John Rainwater left with the prisoner yesterday [21st] at 12:30 p.m., designed to lodge him in the Port Gibson [Claiborne Co.] jail. ... Thinking that he was being sent to Raymond, a party went there to intercept him, but retuned at night on a freight train baffled and disappointed. ... He and the officer were seen at Glass station last evening, and the news soon reached the city. A few resolute men, divining the intention of the officers to send him to Port Gibson, left for that place by the Valley Route at 1 o’clock this morning [22nd]. It was reported early this morning that Thomas was taken from the officers, who had him in charge, near Port Gibson by a a large party of men, who led the prisoner up the railroad track, there to expiate his attempted crime. . About noon to-day a party of men, sixteen in number, chartered an engine and car from the Louisville, New Orleans and Texas Railroad and left for Port Gibson to meet the party that had him in charge. ... It was the intention of the party on the train to bring Thomas back to Vicksburg and hang him. About 5 p. m. Coroner Auter received information that the body of Wesley Thomas, the negro fiend, was hung to a trestle of the Louisville, New Orleans and Texas Railroad a short distance below the tunnel, about two miles above [north] this city [Vicksburg].” In a second report, same page, “Port Gibson, Miss., Feb. 22.—(Special.)—Wesley Thomas, wanted in Vicksburg for assault on Miss Pinkston, was apprehended here to-day concealed in a box car and in charge of a deputy sheriff from Warren county. He was quietly taken from the car by four or five men ... who quickly yanked off [illegible] to the railroad. The posse disclaim any intention of harm to him here, but that a just desert awaits him in Vicksburg no one doubts. He is now concealed from the hand of the law, and will be carried into Vicksburg and thence to eternity to-night.” From the Post, “Port Gibson, Miss., Feb. 1:20 p.m.—Reports of the lynching of Wesley Thomas here are untrue. He is in custody of friends of the Pinkston family and will not be hurt, it is said here, but will be taken back to Warren county. ... [the authorities took their prisoner to the woods for safe keeping].”

notes:
From the Herald, “Abingdon, April 3, 1889.—At a country dance in Russell county, about four weeks ago, Perry Courts, a white man, became involved in a difficulty with Martin Rolland, the colored banjo picker of the occasion. The result was that the white man was killed with a stick of wood. Rolland was arrested and placed in the County Jail at Lebanon. The race feeling ran high, and a lynching bee was threatened but the Sheriff outwitted the mob by spiriting the negro away and conveying him to the jail of Washington county for security until the time of the trial. Rolland remained safely here until the day before yesterday, when he was taken back to Lebanon for his trial .... A mob armed with guns and pistols entered the town on horseback about twelve o’clock last night, firing their weapons ... Then, without even the preliminary of a demand, they forced the jail doors, entered the prisoner’s cell, struck the irons from his limbs with sledges and hurried him to a point more than a mile away. There he was hanged on the limb of a tree, the mob emptying their revolvers and repeating rifles into the body of their victim. There have been no arrests.” The Dispatch reports that an unnamed black man was taken from the jail by a mob of 25-40 men at 10:30 p.m. and carried 1 mile east of town and hanged to an ash tree off the Fincastle Turnpike. He was also shot in the legs, chest, and head.” From the Patriot, “Martin Rolland, colored, awaiting trial for the murder of a white man named Courts, was taken from the jail at Abington [Abingdon, Washington Co.] , Va., the other day by a an armed mob and hanged in the woods.”

notes:
From the Register, “New Orleans, July 17—News is received from Graysport, Grenada Co., Miss., an isolated place, of a shocking and uncalled for murder. At the last term of the circuit court Jim Tillman, a negro, reported quite a number of parties as violators of the gaming laws. They swore vengeance, and the negro was murdered and his body thrown into the Yallabusha River. It was recovered yesterday morning. A number of arrests have been made, and there is much excitement in the county.” Essentially the same story appears in the Patriot and the Star but with the name Zim Filman. According to the American, dateline Memphis, 27 January, a black man named Jim Tilghman, of Grenada Co., was murdered and body sunk in the Yallabusha River on a Sunday [14th] in July 1889; “Suspicion fell upon M. J. Cheatham, a merchant, and James Lemmons, a farmer and miller, both white. After some investigation Cheatham was arrested, and two days later Lemmons was found in the woods, where he had endeavored to hide. Three negroes, Cornelius Robinson, Lee Irwin and Jake Irwin were also arrested. They had their preliminary trial at Graceport and were bound over to the Circuit Court without bond. At the August [1889] term of the Circuit Court Cheatham was tried, and Lee Irwin and Cornelius Robinson made a full confession. ‘They admitted they, together with Cheatham, Lemmons and Jake Irwin, were present at the killing of Tilghman, which was on the roadside, and that Cheatham did the shooting and that they carried him to the river, a distance of a few miles. The reason that they killed Tilghman was that Tilghman had given them away in a game of cards and Cheatham had been indicted by the grand jury on Tilghman’s evidence. ... [Cheatham was convicted and sentenced to hang; Jim Lemmons, Cornelius Robinson and Jake Irwin were convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 25-30 years in prison] ... It is considered certain that the Supreme Court of the State will affirm the decision of the lower Court in Cheatham’s case. In that event Cheatham will be the first white man ever hung in Mississippi for killing a negro. It is due to the white people of  Grenada County to say, however, that they were hot for lynching Cheatham, and it was on that account that he was removed from Grenada to Oxford jail for safe keeping.”

One negro was killed outright and another badly wounded.” According to the Times-Picayune, dateline Augusta, 26 December, “Chief of Police Twiggs arrested seven negroes for crating a riot and while carrying them to jail a mob of white men, crazed by liquor and maddened by the outburst of the negroes, shot and mortally wounded A. F. Twiggs, a turbulent negro who was in the crowd.” From the Telegraph, “Augusta, Dec. 30.—(Special.)—Tom Young, also known as T. Wiggs, the negro man who was shot by the crowd on Datnignac street Christmas day, died in the hospital this afternoon. Twiggs was leading a crowd of negroes, ..., when he became boisterous and began to strike in the crowd of whites with a big stick, he was shot some some unknown party among the whites, knocked down and left for dead on the sidewalk.” From the Chronicle, “Alfred Twiggs, also known as Tom Young, is dead. He was drunk and carried in his hand a big stick. When the infuriated crowd of whites made a rush from the police and their charges, Twiggs started forward to meet them. He was met by Lieut. Desmond, who saw his danger and said to him: ‘For God’s sake, go back.’ The officer pleaded and threatened, but without avail. When Twiggs encountered the whites as was expected, a difficulty arose. In an instance sticks were being used with a vengeance, the negro using his with telling effect. Then came four or five pistol shots and Twiggs fell to the ground unconscious, blood oozing from a ragged hole in the left ear. The wounded man was taken to the Freedman’s hospital, and given every attention. ... He died Sunday [29th], however, just before noon. ... the jury rendered a verdict that deceased came to his death ‘from a gunshot wound in the head, inflicted by the hands of some one unknown to us.”

notes:
From the Enquirer-Sun, “Birmingham, Ala., Dec. 27.—(Special.)—A special to the Daily News from Fayette Court House, seventy-five west of here, says that night before last a negro named Bud Wilson entered the house of James Fowler, a well-to-do farmer who resides in the northern part of Tuscaloosa county, and attempted to outrage Mrs. Fowler, her husband being absent. ... A posse was formed and pursued him. He was overtaken ten miles from the scene of the crime yesterday and hung to the nearest tree. His body riddled with bullets. It is said Wilson made a full confession before he was hung. He was a bad character.” From the Star, Bud, Wilson, a negro accused of an assault upon a white woman, was taken from a party of officers near Tuscaloosa, Ala., Wednesday and lynched.” This story appears in several newspapers including the Despatch. From the Light, “Bud Wilson, a young colored man, arrested for attempting to assault a white woman, was taken from the officers at Fayette Court house, Ala., hanged to a tree and riddled with bullets.” The Times-Picayune states that Wilson was taken from the authorities “... by an armed posse of 50 men.” However, according to the American, “Bud Wilson, a negro, was lynched in Fayette County, Alabama, about ten days ago, but the fact did not leak out until to-day. It is believed the officers who had the negro in charge were in thorough sympathy with the lynching party, if they did not have a hand in it, which accounts for the matter being kept so quiet.” The same story appears in the Constitution.

Note: since Fayette Co. is directly north of Tuscaloosa Co., the actual location of the lynching could be southern Fayette Co., as suggested by the American; also the date could have been 16 December if the American account is accurate.

Spanish Camp is composed of Mexicans, negroes and desperate whites, and is remote from railroads and telegraph lines, and on this account only meagre accounts are obtainable. Sunday [26th] morning at 6 o’clock a negro cabin was set fire, and the occupants brutally shot down as they ran half naked from the burning house. Batley, was found yesterday hanging to a tree and it is thought was hung on the same night that the others negroes were shot. The affair is said to be the outcome of a suit over the title of the land where the negroes resided and had purchased. The suit was decided in favor of the negroes at the last term of the district court in Wharton. So far no arrested have been made, thought the sheriff and posse are on the ground.” In the 2/29 Gazette account, at 2:00 a.m. five black men were shot as they fled the cabin and two other black men were shot in the house; the eighth victim, William Battle was found hanged. The 3/1 Gazette provides more details but no mention of a William Battle/Batley. The Times story adds nothing. The News says five black men were killed and “It is also rumored here that the body of a negro by the same of Wm. Battle was found in the upper portion of Wharton county, about twelve miles below [south] here [Eagle Lake, Colorado county], this morning [29th] hanging to a tree, where he had probably been for several days. If this report is true it is thought that the hanging was been done by some of his own colored, with whom he was very unpopular.” The 3/24 Gazette says only six blacks were shot down, not seven; ditto for the 3/25 Times.

Note: going to assume that all the men in/near the cabin were black and the cause of death was being shot. Given the later reports, going to assume that only six men were shot and killed. Also going to count the reported lynching of Battle as a separate incident because of the News account.

notes:
From the Statesman, “Horrible Butchery. A Negro Cabin Fired and the Occupants Shot Down. Houston, February 28.—News was received in this city this evening of the most horrible crime which has ever been perpetrated in this section of the state. The bloody tragedy was enacted at a settlement known as Spanish Camp, Wharton county, about 60 miles west of this city. Spanish Camp is composed of Mexicans, negroes and desperate whites, and is remote from railroads and telegraph lines, and on this account only meagre accounts are obtainable. Sunday [26th] morning at 6 o’clock a negro cabin was set fire, and the occupants brutally shot down as they ran half naked from the burning house. Five were killed out-right and one seriously wounded. Two Mexicans were shot in the house and their bodies consumed in the burning house. In the same neighborhood the dead body of one negro, Wm. Batley, was found yesterday hanging to a tree and it is thought was hung on the same night that the others negroes were shot. The affair is said to be the outcome of a suit over the title of the land where the negroes resided and had purchased. The suit was decided in favor of the negroes at the last term of the district court in Wharton. So far no arrested have been made, thought the sheriff and posse are on the ground.” In the 2/29 Gazette account, at 2:00 a.m. five black men were shot as they fled the cabin and two other black men were shot in the house; the eighth victim, William Battle was found hanged. The 3/1 Gazette provides more details but no mention of a William Battle/Batley. The Times story adds nothing. The News says five black men were killed and “It is also rumored here that the body of a negro by the same of Wm. Battle was found in the upper portion of Wharton county, about twelve miles below [south] here [Eagle Lake, Colorado county], this morning [29th] hanging to a tree, where he had probably been for several days. If this report is true it is thought that the hanging was been done by some of his own colored, with whom he was very unpopular.” The 3/24 Gazette says only six blacks were shot down, not seven; ditto for the 3/25 Times.

Note: going to assume that all the men in/near the cabin were black and the cause of death was being shot. Given the later reports, going to assume that only six men were shot and killed. Also going to count the reported lynching of Battle as a separate incident because of the News account.

notes:
From the 3/8 Courier-Journal, “Owingsville, Ky., March 7.—(Special.)—An entirely trustworthy report reaches here of the atrocious and cowardly murder of a young woman named Sallie Ohier, at the home of her father, Zach Ohier, near Yocum postoffice, not far from the Bath [Co.] line, in Morgan county, yesterday [Tuesday] afternoon. The details of the affair are very meagre. The girl’s body had sixty-three bullet holes in it, and she died pleading with her murderers for God’s sake not to shoot her any more. Four men, by the names of David, Joseph, Amos, and Alfred Lewis, are under arrest charged with commission of this deed and other unknown parties are know to have had a hand in it. There is much excitement over the matter in the community where it occurred, and especially as no one knows of any adequate cause for the four deed.” The Review states, “The murder of the young woman, Margaret Auxier, near Yocum, in Morgan county, Kentucky, is still being discussed in the neighborhood where it occurred. On Friday night a party of men rode up to the house and called to her father to come out. Instead of doing so, he sent his daughter, who asked the men what was wanted. In answer, they opened fire at short range, and her body was literally riddled with bullets. The neighbors are completely at a loss to account for any motive for the cowardly murder of the young woman. Joseph S. Amos, David Lewis, and Noah and William Long are still held on suspicion, but the only evidence against them is the statement of Auxier, that he thought he recognized one of the Lewises in the party.” The Bulletin notes that Joseph S. Amos, David Lewis, and Noah and William Long are being held on suspicion. From the Journal, “—In Morgan county a cowardly crowd went to the house of a man named Auxier and called him out. He sent his daughter Margaret instead, and she was literally riddled with bullets. Several men are held for the crime and lynching is talked of.” According to the 8/11 Courier-Journal, “Mount Sterling, Ky., August 10.—(Special.)—Dave and Al Lewis and another brother [presumably Amos], aged respectively sixteen, eighteen, and twenty years, were arrested yesterday, charged with the murder of Joe Lewis, a cousin, in Morgan county three weeks ago. Joe Lewis murdered Miss Auxier last spring and had been evading the law, but had returned and accounted the he would turn State’s evidence, when he mysteriously disappeared, and his body was found found until yesterday, when it appeared, from bullet holes in the back of the head, he had been foully dealt with, and circumstance pointed to the guilt of the arrested parties. The excitement is intense, and it will require an effort to keep down a mob.”

Note: it’s not clear that she was the primary target of the mob

That telegram says that last Tuesday afternoon on Bayou Martin, nine miles above [north[ of St. Martinsville, the whites had heard that the negroes were arming themselves with rifles, which had been secreted in the house of a negro named Albert Narcisse. Now note the rest: ‘About 250 whites surprised Narcisse and his brother working in a field. The two negroes ran to the house and attempted to barricade it. They were fired upon and compelled to surrender, after Narcisse and a 10-year-old boy had been shot. Thirty guns, all new, and heavily loaded with buck-shot were found in the cabin. notes: According to the 8/28 News, dateline Longview, 27 August, there was conflict between democrats, republicans and union-labor party (democrats v. all others), “... it was learned that a very influential negro named Harrison Spencer, living on the A. S. Taylor place one mile from here, was last night [26th] called out form his bed and taken away in night clothes, and it is reasonable to suppose, drowned. Anyway no trace of him can be found. His wife ... says her husband hearing a noise went out to see if the stock had not broken into his garden. Soon she saw a form pass the door; then another; then voices were heard sounding like over a dozen men, and she saw her husband forced to mount an animal from a stump near by and hurried off. ... There is no doubt but Spencer was murdered by his own color for political reasons. He bears the best name, and has been a peaceable farmer for a number of years ... The fact of his declaration on the streets of the place a few days since to support the democracy is the sole cause of his death.” Essentially the same story appears in the 8/29 Statesman. The 8/31 News reports, dateline Longview, 30 August, that “The body of Harrison Spencer, the missing negro, was found at 3 p.m. hanging to a small dogwood tree .... The supposition that it was a political murder has about been abandoned by most citizens, as he was not in any way a prominent of effective politician, but on the contrary, knew or said nothing much about politics. The reason for his taking away is a dark mystery, as not cause can be assigned for the act.” The brief report in the 9/1 Statesman says that he was founding hanging and “It is thought he was shot several times, but owning to the advanced stage of decomposition no examination could be had. The negro figured very little in politics and was one of the most honest and humble of his color. The true reason may never be known, as the murder was entirely uncalled for from any standpoint.” According to the Tribune, Harrison was “... forcibly taken from his home a few nights ago by a masked band of Ku Klux. Spencer had deserved the Union Labor party and announced his intention of supporting the Republican ticket. Reynolds [deputy sheriff] reported that he had found Spencer's body about three and half miles from this place [Longview], on the west bank of Harris Creek. ... He was evidently shot before the rope was placed around his neck. There is a bullet hole just behind the left ear and one in his left side, and he had been brutally mutilated.”—in some other out-of-state newspapers, it is said he left the Union Labor party and was supporting the Democratic party; for example, the headline in the World’s account asks “Was he Murdered for Being a Democrat?” The Evening News reports that “There is a bullet hole just behind the left ear, and one in his left side, and his person has been brutally and horribly mutilated. His shirt is torn from his back, and scars where he had been severely whipped are plainly visible.” The 9/4 Statesman reports that Governor Ross has offered rewards for the apprehension of the murderers of Harrison Spencer; “Harrison Spencer was kidnapped the night of August 27, and was found hanging in a decomposed condition three days after.”

The lynching party of to-day boarded the train at Carpenter [Copiah Co.], having learned by telegraph and Shortney was aboard, having been captured at Rolling Fork [Sharkey Co.]. Two miles out Conductor Gordin was ordered to stop the train. Shortney was taken out by the party.” The Post says Shortney was taken “... by a crowd who took him from the rain and no doubt hung him.”

notes: The Democrat reports, citing the Wilmington Star of 31 August, that Mrs. Simon Sasser, “an aged lady”, was assaulted by an “unknown” black man; “There is no clue to the perpetrator of the outrage; but if caught a lynching is probable.” According to the Star, “Lynching at Whiteville. A special dispatch to the STAR, printed elsewhere, gives particulars of a lynching affair at Whiteville, Columbus county last Wednesday night, the victim being a negro desperado named Sherman Farrior, who was charged with a brutal assault on an aged white lady in that county a few weeks ago—as reported at the time in the STAR. Another account of the affair, also received by telegraph, says that lynching party numbered, it is supposed a hundred or more. A colored prisoner confined in the same cell with Farrior testified at the coroner’s inquest that the lynchers were all colored men.” From the Messenger, “Whiteville, N. C., Sept. 13.—(Special Telegram)—A body of masked men, supposed to number a hundred or more, entered Whiteville, Columbus county, jail last night and demanded the keys from the jailer. At the point of arms he surrendered the keys to them, and they proceeded at once to the cell where Sherman Farrior, colored, was confined for an outrage committed on an aged white lady of this county, and took him and departed with him into the night. This morning, suspended to the limb of a large oak, about one mile from the jail, was found the body of Sherman Farrior with a placard pinned on his breast, bearing this inscription, ‘We Protect The Virtue Of Our Women. Beware!’ The negro was a man of bad character and had repeatedly been engaged in robbery. The crime that cost him his life was the outraging of Mrs. E. A. Sasser on the 29th of August.” The News states that Farrior was taken from the Whiteville jail at 1:00 a.m. on the 13th by 40-50 disguised men and hanged 1 mile from Whiteville, and says that a black prisoner in the jail reported that the lynchers were black.

notes: From the 9/17 Times-Picayune, “Breaux Bridge, La., Sept. 16.—(Special.)—An awful crime was perpetrated in this vicinity Friday [14th]. A gang supposed to be composed of five thus far unknown parties assaulted a negro cabin, and shooting through the walls mortally wounding a black woman, who died a few hours afterwards. From this place they went to another cabin, outraged a black woman and then whipped a black man. The negroes have made no affidavits yet. The white population is very much excited over this matter, and held last night an indignation meeting.” The Star report adds nothing. The 9/18 Times-Picayune reports that Sam Polk was charged with murdering the black woman and that he and four other men attacked the cabin, and with raping the black woman in the other cabin—Polk has fled the parish. The 9/19 Times-Picayune states that four men have been arrested, names listed, in connection with the murder but that Sam Polk was still free. From the Messenger, “A negro woman was brutally murdered by four white men about a mile from the town of Breaux Bridge during the night of Friday the 14th inst. The woman was pregnant of twins of 8 months, one of which had a bullet though the head. The particulars are about as follows: The murderers went to the cabin and called the husband of the women it is believe to whip him. He being afraid to open the door asked who was there when the reply came that it was the Sheriff. The name of the Sheriff reassured the woman who opened the door and as the moon was shining brightly she recognized one of the four murderers and slammed the door when she was shot though the belly with a rifle.”—Before dying she identified a Sam Polk, and the sheriff has arrested others thought to be involved: Vilmont Hollier, Detour Hollier, Didier Hollier, and Numa Boudreau. In a second story, same page, “The good people of the town of Breaux Bridge, shocked by the brutal murder of the colored woman Friday night, and other revolving crimes which have been committed by a gang or mob of assassins, held a meeting of indignation. Three hundred people were present and resolutions condemning these brutal acts and pledging protection to the colored people, and to bring the criminal to justice.” The Courier reports that 4 or 5 men “... whipped a black man, criminally assaulted one black woman and killed another.”

As soon as the street was reached, the leader started in the direction of Flat Rock, followed by this time must have numbered over three hundred, many of whom were spectators only. ... From the Globe, “Southern Regulators Hang One and Riddle Another With Buckshot. Meridian, Miss., Jan. 4.—In the neighborhood of the Roberts place, twelve miles northwest of the city, there has been great excitement since the Wednesday [26th] after Christmas. From the Repository, “Union City, Tenn., April 14.—(Special.)—John Thomas, colored, had a preliminary trial yesterday on a charge of assault on a little white girl Sunday last. John Thomas, a young married negro, was the victim. Last Sunday evening Thomas, who lived in the yard of Mr. Albert Turner, enticed little Bertha Turner into his cabin, while his wife was absent, and the girl’s parents were at church, and by threats and force outraged her. ... At 10 o’clock his preliminary trial was had before Justice Unistead Carter, Thomas Lawyer and A. J. Harpole represented the State. At the close of the testimony and before the court could render a verdict, a yell was heard, and in an instant Officers Sain Bratton and Dick Harrison were overpowered, though they bravely resisted. The negro was seized, a rope placed round his neck, and over a beam in the court-room, and a hundred hands drew him to a merited doom. Not more than two minutes were consumed in the act.” This lynching is reported in several newspapers.
