notes:
From the Star, “New York, May 9.—A special from Tarboro, N. C. to the [New York] Herald says: Much excitement prevails in this section over a lynching that took place Saturday night, the first in the history of the county. Ben Hart, a negro, 19 years old, was arrested for an attempted criminal assault on April 27, on a sixteen year old white girl in which great brutality was displayed. The feeling against him was so high that Judge Shipp, holding court, ordered him taken to Williamstown [Williamston, Martin Co.] for safe keeping. Time and distance only served to inflame the people, and Saturday night an engineer on a material train lying over at Rocky Mountain ... was compelled by sixty armed and masked men to take his engine and two coaches and convey the party to Williamstown. There some of the party surrounded the sheriff’s residence, to prevent any communication, while the remainder broke into the jail and dragged forth Hart. He was then brought back here and near the scene of his crime was hanged to a tree.” The same report appears in the Appeal. From the Courier, “When White was arrested Judge Shipp, of the Superior Court, for his better protection from the indignant friends of the girl, sent the negro to jail at Williamston, N. C. A body of men arrived there on a train on Saturday night, and some time after [mid]night picketed the streets, broke open the jail, took the negro to Tarboro and hanged him to a tree at a spot near where the crime was perpetrated.” The 5/12 Landmark report gives his name as Ben Hart. The story’s headline: “A Lynching Bee at Williamston, Martin County” — but the hanging did happen in Tarboro. On his body was the card: “We hang this man, not in passion, but calmly, with a due sense of responsibility we assume. We take executive power in this case and hang this man in accordance with the unwritten law provides no penalty adequate to the crime. And, be it understood, we who have done this act will repeat it under similar circumstances. PEOPLE’S COMMITTEE.” The 5/26 edition reports on the coroner’s jury investigation: a large body of armed and masked men took Hart. From the Wilmington Morning Star, citing the Fayetteville Observer, “The Observer is not in sympathy with those who take the law in their own hands. We wish to see the law upheld. But the recent case at Tarboro is an exception. ... The beast, for he was nothing less, was deserving of death, and a speedy one, and he received his deserts.”

Note: there was a threatened lynching of Hart in late April.

notes:
According to the Herald, Bias Robinson, who lived some two miles from Baldwin’s, was found going to Baldwin’s house with some ten or fifteen pounds of buckshot and several pounds of powder. It was at once decided he was going there to aid them to resist arrest. Some hundred citizens decided on Monday [27th] evening to hang him which was done about 5 p,.m., and if they obtained no more proof against those under arrest, they were to be turned loose Tuesday evening.” Most of the rest of the account is illegible. The 7/7 Times-Picayune cites the Morehouse Clarion of 1 July, a black man tried to break into the home of a Mr. Hathcock at Oak Ridge with the alleged intent on raping Hathcock’s wife’s sister and was arrested and jailed; “The incensed citizens naturally—as all southerners are—being fired with the noble ambition of defending the virtue of southern women, broke open the jail [on the 26th] and took the prisoner out, whom they whipped until they thought that life was extinct, and lighted a match to make sure. Then to their surprise a body of the swarthy blacks lying in ambush, with murderous intentions, took advantage of the opportunity made by the match light and fired into them wounding Mr. Gardner severely and several others slightly. ... The negroes fled almost immediately. ... [the next day, 27th, “a party” of citizens—no mention of a sheriff or other authorities— set out “to punish the cowardly would-be assassins”] ... They suspected at once the Baldwin negroes, who have always been known to be ‘white man haters,’ .... So they proceeded to go to Jerry Baldwin’s house. ... [when they approached, Baldwin and others opened fire, killing Geo. Higginbotham and mortally wounding John Conger; at that point about 18 other whites joined in the affray] ... But they (the negroes) fought like tigers until all of them had been laid powerless in the charge of death. Three more negroes were arrested on suspicious grounds of being implicated and carried back to the Ridge and placed in jail. Monday [27th] evening a large and justly infuriated mass of people from every part of Morehouse [Parish] had collect in the town, who made a thorough investigation of all the evidence against the parties arrested, and found that prisoner Bias Robinson was guilty of having taken a prominent part in instigating the trouble, and whom they hung in the corporation limits in open daylight, permitting any and everybody to be present that wished to. The negro who was left, as though, whipped to death on Sunday [26th] night, is reported as having been found to be alive on Tuesday [28th], and was hung on the same day. We learn that two more negroes were hung on Wednesday [29th] and several others severely whipped for having been ringleaders in bringing about this trouble, making ten negroes that have been killed. From the Journal, “There was quite a serious riot at Oak Ridge, Morehouse parish, last week. A negro had been arrested and, while being conducted to jail by the officers, a band of negroes attempted to rescue the prisoner, and fired upon the officers. Relief soon came to the officers and a posse, seeking to arrest the negroes who did the firing, were also fired on and two white men killed and others wounded. The fire was returned and six negroes killed, and a number of the outlaws captured, three of them publicly lynched. A negro was fatally wounded in Arcadia, and also one killed near Minden [Alex McLemore shot by sheriff’s posse on 30 June], while resisting arrest—both of whom belonged to the Morehouse rioters.” According to the Times-Democrat, four black men escaped the fire-fight at the Baldwin’s but were later captured and hanged; on Monday one of the two men in jail at Oak Ridge was hanged [Bias Robinson] and the other let go; also on Monday another black man was captured and “hung on the banks of the Bon Idee, near Oak Ridge.”

notes:
The 4/19 Telegraph notes that George Hart, charged with the murder and robbery of Charles Waldrup in November 1886, had been arrested near Birmingham and moved to Montgomery for safe keeping: “... he [Hart] would have been lynched if brought to Opelika.” The Times reports that George Hart was taken from the jail in Opelika by a mob of armed men and carried to Waverly, where he was hanged. He was accused of killing a young white farmer, Eddy Walcrop, of Waverly. An accomplice of George Hart was John Hart who was lynched in Lee Co. on 11/3/1886 for murder. According to the Advertiser, he was taken from jail between 11:00 and 12:00 Saturday [5th] by a mob of 15-20 persons and taken to near Waverly where he was hung in the early morning hours of Sunday [6th]. The 11/7 Constitution says a masked mob of 75 took Hart to Waverly, hanged, and a placard pinned to his back, “The person who cuts this man down will suffer the same fate.” There was no mention of John Hart. However, from the 11/29 Constitution, “Double Lynching, Which Took Place in Lee County, Alabama.” The story gives an account of the lynching of George Hart on 11/5 and the previous (undated) lynching of John Moss by, presumably, someone who was there. The men were accused of killing and robbing a young white farmer, Edgar Waldrup. Apparently Moss was lynched some time prior. The informant says “I am very familiar with the hanging of John Moss and George Hart and their confessions.”

Note: John Hart [Moss], George’s cousin, was lynched in Lee county on 3 November 1886. George was threatened with lynching on 11 April 1887.

notes:
From the Times, “Kidnapers Lynched. Rio Grande City, Texas, Dec. 9.—The sheriff of Star county to-day arrested Cecilo Barrea and Vivian Diaz, charged with kidnapping Senor Barrear last August. A band of Mexicans took the prisoners from him and lynched them.” From the News, “Rio Grande City, Tex., December 9.—The sheriff of Starr county arrested Cecillio Barrera and Vivian Diez on Wednesday and started with them to this place. When about eight miles from here Wednesday [7th] night, about 7 o’clock, the sheriff was waylaid by a band of from fifteen to twenty armed Mexicans, who took the two prisoners away from him and hung them both. The band of Mexicans then rode off toward the Rio Grande [river]. They are believed to belong in Mexico. The parties hanged where two of the men who helped rob Juan Garcia Barrera two months ago, and were bandits. Vivian Diez was a well-to-do ranchman, and both were residents of the Gruela ranch, in Starr county.” According to the Gazette, “The Sheriff of Starr county with three men, made a capture last Wednesday evening of two of the desperadoes who were in the bandit’s gang which spirited off Juan Barrea, a wealthy ranchman of Starr county and held him for $1700 ransom until the amount was paid. The capture was made some miles down the river from Rio Grande City. As night came on the officers started for that city with the prisoners. ... When the party reached a point about seven miles below [south] of Rio Grande City they were overtaken by a mob of masked men who demanded the two prisoners. ... The vigilantes then took them a short distance off the road to a tree and hanged them in plain sight of all who passed.”

Note: since the abducted man was from Starr county, going to assume that the mob was also from Starr County.

notes:
According to the Examiner, “A Case for Judge Lynch. Franklin, Ky., Dec. 12.—W. F. Holmes, an aged white man, living in this county, was found shot by a negro desperado named Tom Dess, Saturday night, and died this morning. ... The negro is now in jail here. A strong guard was placed around the jail last night in anticipation of a riot. It is thought the jail will be attacked to-night and the negro, who is a bad character, well known in Tennessee and Kentucky, swung up.” The same report appears in the Eagle with the name Tom Doss. From the Post, “Nashville, Tenn., Dec. 24.—(Special.) Tom Doss, colored, who recently shot W. T. March 1) that in Pickens, three black men (Bolton, Heyward, and Williams) were convicted 2/28 of lynching a “half-witted white mountaineer” for “outraging” a young black girl. Three other black men were acquitted. The paper notes that this was the first time that a black mob had lynched a white man in South Carolina. Also that white lynchers of blacks have never been brought to court. The same story appears in the News. The Times has an interesting editorial condemning lynching and arguing that if white men are not prosecuted for lynching blacks, then blacks shouldn’t be prosecuted either. The Telegraph reports that Wm. C. Williams and Harrison Heyward, both black, have been pardoned by the governor for the lynching of Waldrop

C., June 7, 1886—Alfred Long, one of the negroes implicated in the murder of A. J. McBride and wife, near Lexington, has been lynched by the indignant citizens of the community in which the outrage was committed. He was lynched at three o’clock last Sunday morning at the scene of the murder, about five miles from Lexington. The Democrat, citing the Greensboro Workman of the 7th, gives the location as near Reed’s Baptist Church, between Lexington and Tyro, and that 2000 people witnessed the lynching—that seems implausible.

Note: the Star report is incorrect: this happened in Lexington, Davidson Co., NC, not SC.

notes:
From the 6/18 Morning News, “Carbon [Eastland], June 17.—News renched [sic] town this morning that a man by the name of William Pruitt was hung by a mob of four men Monday [14th] night last, ten miles south, near Sipe Springs. The body was still hanging today. Full particulars could not be learned, buy it is said he was hung for attempting to murder and rob an old man named Hosetter.” The brief 6/19 Daily News report adds nothing. According to the Morning News and 6/19 Daily News, “A man by the name of Morrison had it made up with Pruitt, so it is alleged, to go to old man Hostetter’s and murder and rob him. Pruitt, being a boy of only 18 years of age. It seems Morrison was jealous of Pruitt, both having been paying attention to the same girl, a child only 13 years of age, and took this method of putting him [Pruitt] out of the way. ... About 9 o’clock Pruitt and Morrison went to Hostetter and asked for a drink of water. Pruitt went in first, and as Hostetter away him he broke to run, as if expected to be murdered. While Pruitt was drinking the four men came up with drawn revolvers and ordered him to throw up his hands, which command he obeyed quickly. He was soon securely tied and was led from the house by the mob. Morrison joined in the crowd. Nothing more was seen of Pruitt until Thursday morning, when he was found hanging, as reported last night. The body was cut down and inquest held by Justice Haley, of Cypress Spring. ... The County Attorney and several lawyers of Comanche were expected at Cypress Springs to be at the examining trial of the four men arrested.” From the Messenger, “Sipe Springs, June 17.—News was brought to town Tuesday that a young man by the name of W. P. Pruitt was taken from the house of I. O. Hostetter on Monday night by a crowd of men with his hands tied behind his back and a rope around his neck. Pruitt and one Morris had planned the murder and robbery of Hostetter, but before they put their plan into execution Morris gave the thing away, and on their arrival Pruitt met with the above reception. ... The body of Pruitt was found hanging to a tree two miles north of town [Sipe Springs] yesterday evening.”

Note: Sipe Springs is in the extreme northwest of Comanche Co. near the Eastland Co. line—2 miles north of Sipe Springs could be Eastland Co. Likewise, 10 miles south of Carbon could be in either Eastland or Comanche counties. Couldn’t find a likely Hostetter/Hosetter in 1880 or 1900 Texas census.

notes:
From the Herald, “New Orleans, La., July 3, 1886.—A Pearlington (Miss.) special says: —’News has just reached here of the lynching on Thursday [1st] last of George Parker, colored, who, on June 19, made a criminal assault on a white lady in the upper portion of Hancock county. The screams of the lady frightened the fiend off. A number of citizens started in pursuit of him, and eventually caught him in the neighborhood of Wakiah Bluff, on Pearl River, and there meted out to him summary justice.” From the Times-Picayune, “Pearlington, Miss., July 3.—(Special.)—It is reported here to-day that George Parker, a colored man, was shot and killed in Pearl River swamp, up about Walkiah Bluff, Hancock county. The News states that Parker, who was accused of criminal assault on a white woman in Hancock Co., was captured and hanged near Wakiah Bluff on the Pearl River. From the Light, “Lynching for attempted rape disencumbered the earth of George Parker, a resident of Hancock county, Miss.”

Note: according to the USGS, today Walkiah Bluff is in Pearl River county but would have been in Hancock Co. in 1886. Interestingly, in 1872, the state took parts of Marion and Hancock counties and created “Pearl” county, but in 1878, the state abolished Pearl county, and the land went back to Marion and Hancock counties. In 1890, the state again took land from Hancock and Marion counties and created Pearl River county.

From the 8/21 Southern Herald, “Silas Collins, a peaceful colored man, while riding along the public highway near Osyka, on Thursday [12th or 19th] evening of last week, was fired on by unknown parties and instantly killed.” According to the 8/26 Times-Picayune, “Two Negro Murderers Lynched. There is much excitement over the matter, but it is believed that substantial justice has been done, though by questionable means.” From the Herald, “Negro Murderers Lynched. New Orleans, Aug. 24—The Picayune’s Magnolia special says Last night an armed mob came to town, broke open the jail, took therefrom John and Leander Nelson, colored, charged with the recent murder of a negro named Collier, and hung them from the bridge near the town. There is much excitement over the matter, but it is believed substantial justice has been done.” The Gazette states that on Tuesday [24th] between 1:00 and 3:00 a.m. a masked mob broke into the jail in Magnolia and removed Leander Nelson, John J. Nelson, and Frank Nelson, a youth who they later released; Leander and John were taken to “the first bridge across Tangipahoa River” where they were hanged; as for the mob, “Neither Mr. McGowen [the jailer?] nor the boy Frank could recognize a man of the crowd—and they so disguised themselves when talking that they could not tell whether they were white men or negroes.” The 8/28 Southern Herald reports that the murdered man was Silas Collins and the lynching of Leander Nelson and his unnamed brother but little else. The 8/29 Times-Picayune gives a more detailed report, citing the Summit Sentinel and gives their names as Leander and John Nelsen, accused of murdering Silas Collins, black—they were arrested on Tuesday evening and “About 1 o’clock the night they were were incarcerated, a crowd of masked men, about thirty in number ... broke in the jail and took out Leander, John, and Frank Nelson. Frank was turned loose and ordered to report to the sheriff next morning, which he did. Leander and John were taken to the bridge across the Tangipahoa, near Magnolia, and there hung.”

Note #1: there is ambiguity whether this happened in the early morning hours of Tuesday, the 24th, or Wednesday, the 25th. Given that the murdered man was black, it is likely that the mob was also black. It would be very unusual for a white mob to lynch black men accused of murdering another black man.

Note: #2: the 1870 Pike Co. census lists a Leander Nelson, age 27, a farm laborer, living near Osyka with his wife Mary, 22, and baby son Frank. And a John Helson, age 17, mulatto, living in Osyka with his parents Joseph and Irman Helson—believe this is the Nelson family, not Helson. The 1880 Pike Co. census lists a Silas Collins, 21, living with his wife Jane, 17, no children. Couldn’t find him in 1900 Mississippi census.

Note #3: some newspaper reports have this happening in Magnolia, Louisiana.

Note: 1880 census lists a Saul B. Pue, 41, living with his family in Atascosa county; he has a daughter Ella, 13, and Axia, 11, among others. Somerset, Bexar Co. is close to the Atascosa county line. Couldn’t find a Pugh family in either Atascosa or Bexar Co. Couldn’t find a black Washington family in Atascosa Co., but there are such families in Bexar Co. There is some locational issue: was he being held in Somerset, Bexar Co. in anticipation of being moved to Anascosa Co. when he was taken and lynched, or was he being held someplace in Atascosa county and taken before being taken to Pleasanton? It seems reasonable to assume an Atascosa Co. mob, in either case. Going to assume that (a) Washington was a resident of Bexar Co. and he was incarcerated there; (b) he was taken by a Atascosa Co. mob and killed, likely in Bexar Co. but that it not certain.

From the Telegraph, “A Murder and a Lynching. Information was received here Wednesday [10th] evening that a dastardly murder had been committed near Oak Ridge, Morehouse parish, on that day and that the murderer had met with speedy punishment at the hands of an infuriated and outraged citizens. The victim of the murder was Mr. J. Pipes, a merchant and planter of Morehouse and and an estimable gentleman. The murderer was a negro whose name is unknown to us. From the meagre particulars we could learn it seems that two negroes were engaged in a quarrel in Mr. Pipes’ store during his absence and he coming in before it terminated, ordered them out, whereupon one of the negroes drew a pistol and shot him, the wound resulting fatally. Mr. A. S. Pipes, a prominent planter and merchant of the Fifth Ward, was shot and seriously wounded by Green Gardner, a colored boy, on Saturday [6th] night last. Mr. Pipes being disturbed by a noisy crowd in his store, went over from his house to quell the disturbance. He found Gardner in a difficulty with a white man and endeavored to quiet matters. His interference aroused Gardner’s ire and he deliberately turn upon Mr. Pipes and shot him in the left breast. Fortunately the bullet ranged to the left and did not penetrate the lung. Gardner, under the cover of darkness, at once fled, but a party of Oak Ridgers were seen on his track, and we have learned that they caught up with the fugitive and swung him to a limb. The lynching is only rumored, but we have little doubt of its truthfulness. The negro who wantonly and maliciously shoots down a white man who is acting as a peace maker deserves little sympathy, and the action of the men who meted out Gardner his just deserts is generally approved. Later.—We are sorry to learn that at last reports the doctors had small hopes of Mr. Pipes’ recovery as his wound was much more serious than at first thought. The body of Gardner has been discovered suspended to a tree in Boeuff River Swamp.”

H. From the Times-Picayune, “Two Negro Murderers Lynched. Grenada, Miss., July 7.—Our town was thrown into a fever of excitement this evening. After taking them across the Bogue Creek, one mile from town, Felix Williams confessed to the murder of two peddlers and implicated two other negroes beside McChristian, who were tried here yesterday and acquitted and who skipped. They were allowed to pray and sing a hymn, when the ropes were thrown across two limbs on the same tree, and they were swung into eternity. Their bodies still hang.” The Gazette reports the mob as 150. In the Spy report the victims being: Felix Williams and Perry McCristian. According to the Republican, Perry McChristian and Felix Williams were hanged near Grenada in connection with the murder of two peddlers. Two other men were also implicated: Bartley James and John Campbell. James had been hanged by a mob at Union Church, 10 miles from Grenada, and John Campbell was shot to death by a mob some where near Grenada. From the Herald-Tribune, “New Orleans, July 8.—A dispatch from Grenada, Miss., says: The mob yesterday, after hanging Perry McChristion and Felix Williams, started after two other men implicated in the same murder. Williams had confessed, stating that Bartley, James and John Campbell had assisted in killing the two peddlers. The mob found James at his house and carried him to Union Church, about ten miles from Grenada, and hanged him to a tree; they then went to Campbell’s house. Campbell fired upon the mob, wounding one of the them, it is reported, and then made his escape. At daylight this morning the mob overtook Campbell, who refused to surrender. They then shot him to death.” Thompson reports that Perry McChristian, Felix Williams, James Farthley, and John Campbell were white.

notes:
From the Times-Picayune, “Two Negro Murderers Lynched. Grenada, Miss., July 7.—Our town was thrown into a fever of excitement this evening. About 6 o’clock, as the officers were carrying Felix Williams, colored, recently sentenced to the penitentiary for life, to the depot for the purpose of sending him on the 6 o’clock train to Jackson, a crowd of about twenty-five from the country, backed by many others not visible but on hand, violently took Williams before getting to the train from the officers, and then proceeding to the jail got his accomplice, Perry McChristian, colored, sentenced to death, and carried them across the Bogue, on the east side of town. .. After taking them across the Bogue Creek, one mile from town, Felix Williams confessed to the murder of two peddlers and implicated two other negroes beside McChristian, who were tried here yesterday and acquitted and who skipped. They were allowed to pray and sing a hymn, when the ropes were thrown across two limbs on the same tree, and they were swung into eternity. Their bodies still hang.” The Gazette reports the mob as 150. In the Spy report the victims being: Felix Williams and Perry McCristian. According to the Republican, Perry McChristian and Felix Williams were hanged near Grenada in connection with the murder of two peddlers. Two other men were also implicated: Bartley James and John Campbell. James had been hanged by a mob at Union Church, 10 miles from Grenada, and John Campbell was shot to death by a mob some where near Grenada. From the Herald-Tribune, “New Orleans, July 8.—A dispatch from Grenada, Miss., says: The mob yesterday, after hanging Perry McChristion and Felix Williams, started after two other men implicated in the same murder. Williams had confessed, stating that Bartley, James and John Campbell had assisted in killing the two peddlers. The mob found James at his house and carried him to Union Church, about ten miles from Grenada, and hanged him to a tree; they then went to Campbell’s house. Campbell fired upon the mob, wounding one of the them, it is reported, and then made his escape. At daylight this morning the mob overtook Campbell, who refused to surrender. They then shot him to death.” Thompson reports that Perry McChristian, Felix Williams, James Farthley, and John Campbell were white. 

Note: of the 5 possible Felix Williams in MS in 1880 census, 4 are black or mulatto—none were listed in Grenada Co.; the census lists a Perry McCristian, 29, mulatto, living in Grenada Co. Couldn’t find a relevant Bartley James, James Bartley, James Bartly, or James Farthley in 1880 MS census, however, the overwhelming majority of James families in Grenada Co. were black or mulatto.

notes:
The Times reports that Cicero Green and John Figures were attacked in their jail cells and riddled with bullets. They were accused of murder and of “waylaying with intent to kill”. From the Picayune, “Minden, La., July 22.—Last night, about midnight, a mob of about one hundred armed men from the neighboring parish and Southern Arkansas entered the town from different points, placing all persons found on the streets under arrest. They then forced a citizen to show them where Deputy Sheriff Bailey slept, and forced him at the peril of his life to open the jail door. They then proceeded to the cell in which the two notorious negro desperadoes, Cicero Green and John Figures, were confined. Finding it impossible to open the cell, they fired into the cell and filled the bodies of their victims with buckshot. The mob then quietly mounted their horses and rode away. Cicero Green was convicted and sentenced at the last term of court to fifteen years’ hard labor in the State Penitentiary for lying in wait and shooting at with intent to kill. ... John Figures is the negro who murdered young Coyle in this parish last summer, and was recently arrested in Texarkana, Ark., and brought back and jailed to await trial at the next term of court.”

Note: some of the mob may have been from Arkansas.

From the 8/11 Constitution, “Cuthbert, Ga., August 8.—(Special.)—This community was shocked and is thoroughly aroused over the news which has reached here of a fiendish outrage, which was committed by Henry Davis, a negro, in this county. ... Little Sylvia Knight, aged nine years, and her smaller brother, aged seven, the children of Rev. John T. Knight, a Baptist minister and farmer of high standing, left their home for school, a walk which carried them two miles south of Ward’s station. ... After the children had progressed on their journey about three-quarters of a mile they were suddenly pounced upon by a burly negro, perfectly nude, who had been lying in wait behind a large stump by the road side. Seizing the little girl girl in his powerful grasp and commanding the little boy in thundering tones to remain in the road or die, he carried the victim, torn, choked, bleeding and frightened almost to death, to a place of concealment where he treated her in a horrible and most outrageous manner and escaped into the woods adjoining. ... The scoundrel proved to be Henry Davis, a desperately mean negro, about nineteen years old, and in the employ of Colonel H. Crittenden, of Ward’s station.” In a second report on the same page, “Cuthbert, Ga., August 9.—(Special.)—... At 1 o’clock this morning, the jailer was awakened by a large crowd of masked men, who demanded the surrender of Davis. They then proceeded to break down the doors, and securing the prisoner, they hustled him off to the railroad bridge near by, noosed a rope around his neck, threw the other end over the cross beam, and as the body was pulled up, it was riddled with bullets. Coroner Coleman held an inquest, and found that the act was committed by persons unknown.” From the Banner-Watchman, “A drummer was in Lumpkin last week who carried a piece of the rope with which a negro was lynched in Cuthbert in his vest pocket. From the Times-Picayune, citing The Pensacolan of the 28th, “A Colored Preacher Lynched in Florida. A colored divine, hailing from Greenville, Ala., called himself Albert Lee, was lynched by a masked mob at Milton on the night of the 22d inst. The crime for which Lee atoned for, at the merciless hands of Judge Lynch, was that of outraging two girls, aged 14 and 16 years, respectively, daughters of a quiet, inoffensive old colored man living near Yellow River, nine miles from Milton. About 11 o’clock on the night in question a party of between sixty and seventy-five men, marched to the gate of the wooden wall inclosing the jail, and by an original ruse practiced on Jailer Thompson, succeeded in getting him to open the gate, and when once inside the mob secured the keys to the jail and cell in which Lee was confined and carried him out near the graveyard, about a quarter of a mile from the town, and there hung him to an oak limb until all that was moral of Albert Lee had climbed the golden stair. ... After leaving them [the daughters] he made for Alabama, and was captured at McGowan’s Ferry, near the [state] line, and jailed in Milton on Thursday [20th], before being hanged Saturday [22nd] night. In the preliminary trial before Judge Chain, Lee acknowledged the crime charged against him, and claimed that he was inspired to do it though the suggestion of Divinity. He was about 19 years of age, and it is said met his death bravely ....” According to the News, “The Greenville (Ala.,) Advocate says that the negro Elbert Lee, recently lynched at Milton was known about Greenville as ‘Little Joe Payne.’ The Advocate further state that a negro was hanged at Greenville in 1862 or 1863 for a crime similar to that which cost Lee his life, and that Lee had stated that the negro was his father.”

From the Picayune, “The iron cage in the Murphreesboro, Ark., jail, in which the Polk brothers were confined on a charge of murder, was attacked by a mob, on Sunday night, who piled wood around the bars, set fire to the mass and literally roasted the prisoners alive.” According to the Republican, the victims were Henry Polk and Sylvester Polk. “Something over a year ago Sylvester and Henry Polk and Henry Kuykendall killed an old German peddler in Howard county, Ark., robbed him of his pack, and then to cover up their crime, piled fence rails on the body and set fire to them.” The Polks and Kuykendall were caught and tried. Note: there were attempted lynchings of Henry Polk and Sylvester Polk on 17 May 1884, 7 August 1885, and 26 August 1885.

notes: From the News, “Chained to a Tree and Burned. Mobile, Ala., Dec. 28—Yesterday afternoon at Gainestown, Clark county, Ala., Alexander Reed, a negro, who brutally murdered Miss Carrie Boyer at that place on the 18th instant, was chained to a tree at the spot where the crime was committed and slowly burned to death by a crowd of indignant whites and blacks.” The Times incorrectly puts this lynching in Clarke Co., Georgia. The Telegraph, citing the Montgomery Advertiser, “The negro, Alex. Reed, who murdered Miss Carrie Bover, near Gainstown, Clarke county, Ala., Friday week, was captured Christmas eve on the Rhodes plantation, near the county line. The entire population, white and black, had been for a week on his track. ... A guard of one hundred men was formed and the march to Gainstown made. All along the route the desire of the people was that Reed should be lynched, but the captors moved on to the point where the brutal murder was committed. The place was reached yesterday morning, and at 2 o’clock Reed was taken out on the road and chained to a tree at the place where Miss Boyer had been found dying with her head crushed in. ... The crowd then piled lightwood around the negro and set fire to it. Although he appealed for mercy, after he had roasted a while the fire was scattered and he was allowed to feel the full agony of burning. Then a new fire was built, and this in turn, after burning some time, was taken away. The process was repeated three times. Reed made no outcry, but his contortions showed that he suffered terribly. When it was found that he was dead the lightwood was piled thickly around and the corpse was reduced to ashes.” The Banner-Watchman also describes the torture of Dick Reed.

From the 2/4 News, “Crockett, February 3.—This morning about 1 o’clock a crowd of masked men, numbering between seventy-five and one hundred, took Sandy Robinson, the negro who killed James Lathrop, in Leon county, from our jail and hanged him near the graveyard, out near the edge of town; and it is supposed that he crowd came from a distance, as they came on horses. Late yesterday evening it seems that the sheriff got wind of the intention and summoned a guard of ten or more to stay at the jail, but there were only about six men besides the sheriff at the jail when the crowd came. No one was hurt. There were about ten other prisoners in jail at the time, none of whom were molested.” The same story appears in the Gazette. According to the Banner, “—The excitement at Crockett about the lynching of the negro, Sandy Robinson, has about died out, and people are turning their attention to other and more profitable matters.” The Ocean lists of lynch victims: “February [1884]. 3. notes: From the Tribune, “Brenham, Tex., April 14.—(Special.)—The little village of Lyons, twenty-two miles north of this place, was the scene Sunday [13th] night of a tragedy which for terrible details an scarcely be equaled in the annals of the Southwest. A negro named Gibbs was literally roasted alive at the stake and surrounded by a mob. This morning his charred remains, in a sitting posture, his arms hugging the stake, presented a sickening spectacle. Gibbs was an escaped convict. He hired himself to a farmer named Moore living in the vicinity of Lyons. Late Saturday evening, taking advantage of Moore’s absence, he entered the house and demanded a seat at the supper-table. Being remonstrated with by Mrs. Davis, he seized an ax, brained her, and fled. On the return of Moore a posse was organized, and, after a hot chase, the negro was captured, after being badly wounded, put in a wagon, and brought back to Lyons. Despite the piteous pleas of the wretch, he was pulled from the wagon, dragged to and chained to an impromptu stake, coal-oil poured on, and he was roasted alive. Bidwell as accessories before the fact—yesterday brought a verdict of guilty of murder against Bacon, Andrews and Bidwell, and cleared Hunter. The crime charged was the killing of Harrison T. Riley in August 1884. Two of the thugs, Cato and Disman, turned State’s evidence.”

The dead body and the wounded man were then taken on to Kingston where they were cared for. Leary, Ga., Dec. 23.—The case against the colored Kuklux, Allen Yancey and Abe Blocker, has resulted in the conviction of both for murder and their sentence to lifelong imprisonment. Abe Blocker and Allen Yancey were members of a party who one night, in the month of August of last year, went to the house of George Cuff, a negro living near the Clay County line, where they supposed they would find Ashley Cowart, a negro who had incurred their displeasure, and who, as it was shown, was to be murdered. Near George Cuff’s house also lived Ashley Cowart’s parents. Ashley Cowart, Richard Cuff, and two other negro boys were in the habit of sleeping in a house between George Cuff’s and the Cowart’s. ... About midnight Abe Blocker marshaled his clan and they proceeded to the house where they supposed Ashley Cowart was sleeping. The crowd numbered about eight men, and all were disguised except Abe and Allen. Reaching the house they immediately burst in and commenced an indiscriminate shooting, in which a boy, Richard Cuff, was killed , and Vince Cowart was shot through the arm. He was fired on form an out-house in the vicinity of the jail, as he was retiring from the mob, and as he had made no resistance [to the mob], it is generally supposed the shot was fired by a hidden negro.” The account in the Times says that attempted outrage happened on the 28th and that Riley was killed on Wednesday, which would be the 27th—inconsistent, and “George Hawes, one of the negro ring leaders [of the group of blacks around the jail], was shot and killed [by members of the mob]. Sweeney, one of the volunteer guards about the jail was mortally wounded by a bullet fired form the negro camp.” The Caller-Times reports, citing the Goliad Guard, that Bob Riley was in jail at Refugio on a charge of attempted outrage; “For several nights the negroes collected around the jail and made threats that they would liberate the prisoner. On Sunday night an attempt was made by firing from a rock wall on the two guards whom the sheriff had placed at the jail. One of the guards, a Mr. Sweeney, was shot down, seriously wounded though the thigh. The whites, who were expecting some trouble, assembled at the jail, where they were fired upon from behind the rock wall. Several rounds were discharged and the negroes dispersed. The crowd then went to the jail and shot the prisoner through the windows of the jail. ... On the outside, during the battle, two negroes were wounded, one of them it is supposed to be fatally.”

Note: Caldwell-DeLord state that Cornelius Sweeney died on 3 December 1884 but haven’t been able to corroborate.

A good deal of bitterness between the negroes and whites had grown out of the affair, and the negroes had been around in squads since the beginning, threatening to take Riley out of jail, and vengeance is he was molested. George Hawes, one of the ringleaders, was shot beyond recovery in attempt to bully the mob, last night, when they attacked the jail. Mr. Sweeney, one of the guards and an estimable citizen, was also seriously wounded in the leg, which, it is thought, will have to be amputated. He was fired on form an out-house in the vicinity of the jail, as he was retiring from the mob, and as he had made no resistance [to the mob], it is generally supposed the shot was fired by a hidden negro.” The account in the Times says that attempted outrage happened on the 28th and that Riley was killed on Wednesday, which would be the 27th—inconsistent, and “George Hawes, one of the negro ring leaders [of the group of blacks around the jail], was shot and killed [by members of the mob]. Sweeney, one of the volunteer guards about the jail was mortally wounded by a bullet fired form the negro camp.” The Caller-Times reports, citing the Goliad Guard, that Bob Riley was in jail at Refugio on a charge of attempted outrage; “For several nights the negroes collected around the jail and made threats that they would liberate the prisoner. On Sunday night an attempt was made by firing from a rock wall on the two guards whom the sheriff had placed at the jail. One of the guards, a Mr. Sweeney, was shot down, seriously wounded though the thigh. The whites, who were expecting some trouble, assembled at the jail, where they were fired upon from behind the rock wall. Several rounds were discharged and the negroes dispersed. The crowd then went to the jail and shot the prisoner through the windows of the jail. ... On the outside, during the battle, two negroes were wounded, one of them it is supposed to be fatally.”

Taylor was a cousin of the famous desperado Andy Taylor, hanged at London some time since.”

notes:
According to the 12/28 Times-Picayune, Jordan Parker and his son were arrested at Purvis [Marion Co.] station charged with train wrecking which resulted in the scalding death of the engineer and fireman—they were put on a train; “When the train reached Popularville [Marion Co.] the people and train men turned out en masse and took charge of the two alleged criminals. ... They both stoutly protested their innocence, but their pleadings and assertions fell on unheeding ears. They seized the son first and endeavored to frighten him into making a confession, but he refused; then they applied the torture, trying him up and burning his hands with coals of fire. ... [After confessing under torture] ... On this the mob turned their attention to the father and tied him up to a tree about five miles north of Highland Station and opened fire upon him with rifles, shotguns and revolvers, ridding him with bullets. They left him dead and returned to Poplarville with the son, and it was rumored last night that they intended to lynch him during the night. Jordan Parker is said to be a resident of Purvis Station and a hard case. ... At half-past 7 o’clock last evening there was a rumor circulated to the effect that the son of Parker had been hanged by the crowd, and as it was known that the excitement and indignation ran high, there was no doubt in the minds of the railroad officials but that the rumor was true.” The 12/29 Times-Picayune notes, in a very long and detailed report, that the engineer was white and the fireman was black—no indication that the Parkers were black. From the Messenger, “New Orleans, December 28.—Last Friday Jordan Parker, colored, and his son, Daniel, were arrested at Purvis’ station, charged with having placed obstructions on the Northeastern railroad track, wrecking a train and causing the death by scalding of engineer Turn and his fireman. A dispatch from Mobile last night reported the lynching of Jordan Parker by a mob near Highland station. The Times-Democrat this morning prints a long account of the lynching showing that a confession of guilt was extorted from Daniel Parker, a mere youth, by thrusting his hands into the flames in a hot stove, and keeping them there till they were burned to a crisp.” The Journal reports Jordan’s age as 65. From the Times, “One report of the lynching of the train wreckers, who wrecked the train near Purvis, states that the boy was tortured to make him confess. The torture is said to have been most fiendish, namely, the boy’s hands were trust [thrust] into a hot store, and literally burned off. The age of the child, for he was nothing more, was thirteen years. Such an act is unjustifiable. Nothing can justify such torture, or mitigate such an atrocity. For the man himself, he deserved anything. ... The report of the torture of the child is denied, and it is hoped, for the sake of ‘poor humanity’ that the report is not true.”

Note: USGS lists Highland as a variant name for Carriere Station in Pearl River Co. today Interestingly, in 1872, the state took parts of Marion and Hancock counties and created “Pearl” county, but in 1878, the state abolished Pearl county, and the land went back to Marion and Hancock counties. In 1890, the state again took land from Hancock and Marion counties and created Pearl River county. 1885 and 1895 MS atlases place Purvis in Marion Co. There is no “Lamar” county in MS until 1904. Both Williams and Thompson, Lynchings in Mississippi, say that Jordan Parker was White.

From the Journal, “James Tice, a clerk in Campbell’s store at Prospect, Tenn., and was killed with an axe on Tuesday night, and the store robbed. ... While the inquest was in progress a mob took Wesley Warren, one of them, out of jail and hung him, and others were released.” From the Bulletin, “Wesley Warren, a negro accused of the murder of young Price at Veto Station, Ala., was taken from jail Tuesday night by a large mob and hanged.” According to the Appeal and the Banner, Wesley Warren, Harry Reid, and Kyle Walker were arrested in connection to the ax murder of James Trice at Veto, AL. As a coroner from Athens, Alabama was questioning witnesses, a “squad” nabbed Warren and took him down the railroad track half a mile and hanged him. Henry Reid and Kyle Walker were released. The same story appears in the Bulletin. From the Enquirer-Sun, “Cincinnati, June 20.—The Times Star’s special from Prospect, Tenn., says: Jas. Tice, a clerk in Campbell’s store, was killed with an axe last night and the store robbed. Three negroes were arrested. While the inquest was in progress, a mob took one of the negroes, Wesley Williams, out of jail and hung him. The others were released.” According to the Times states that James Tice was from and murdered at Prospect, TN. Warren, Reed and Walker were held in custody and “... the Coroner of Athens, Ala., who was the nearest official, was sent for.” Soon a mob appeared and took Warren a mile away and hanged him. The Herald states that James Trice was the son of William Trice, and that he was found dead in his bed in the store in Prospect.

Note: Veto in Limestone Co., is right on the Alabama-Tennessee line. The 1880 census lists a James Trice, 39, farmer, living in Giles Co., TN with his wife and children. It also lists a James F. Trice, 15, born in TN, living with his father, William Trice, mother, and siblings in Limestone Co., AL. Given that Trice’s family was in Alabama, and likely had relatives in Tennessee, it is highly probable that the mob was composed of people from Giles Co., TN and Limestone Co., AL.

notes:
According to the Appeal, the Times, and the Banner, Wesley Warren, Harry Reid, and Kyle Walker were arrested in connection to the ax murder of James Trice. As a coroner from Alabama was questioning witnesses, a “squad” nabbed Warren and took him to the railroad tracks and hanged him in Giles Co. TN on 6/20. Henry Reid and Kyle Walker were released. The 6/23 edition of the American reports that Ky Walker and Harry Reed were re-arrested for the ax murder. A mob took them after they were released and hanged them a half mile across the Alabama state line. The 6/21 Herald states that James Trice was the son of William Trice, and that he was found dead in his bed in the store in Prospect [Giles Co., TN]. From the 6/23 Herald, “Pulaski [Giles Co.], Tenn., June 22, 1883. Kyle Walker and Harry Reed, both colored, who had been arrested for supposed implication in the murder of young Trice, at Veto, Ala., were released on Wednesday, but certain parties, believing them guilty, investigated into the matter, found proof of their guilt and rearrested them. By threats the fourteen-year-old son of Wesley Warren, who was lynched on Tuesday, was induced to disclose the particulars of the crime. Walker and Reed were taken from the jail last night and lynched.”

Note: Veto in Limestone Co., is right on the Alabama-Tennessee line. The 1880 census lists a James Trice, 39, farmer, living in Giles Co., TN with his wife and children. It also lists a James F. Trice, 15, born in TN, living with his father, William Trice, mother, and siblings in Limestone Co., AL. Given that Trice’s family was in Alabama, and likely had relatives in Tennessee, it is highly probable that the mob was composed of people from Giles Co., TN and Limestone Co., AL.

notes: The Times-Democrat reports, Lasater, Tex., Lynching of a Negro. ... Marshall, Tex., June 26.—Lacy, one of the negroes who outraged Mrs. Rodgers, in Marion county, last Wednesday, was hung by a mob to-day near Lasater, the scene of the crime. He confessed and said that the other negro concerned in the crime is named Douglas. A buggy was driven form under him, producing the fall. Five hundred people were present, of both races and sexes. No secret was made of the intended lynching. General notice was given of the exact hour of the hanging. It was first decided to burn him, as was done in a previous case in the same vicinity some time ago, but it being recollected that the law provides that hanging is the penalty for the crime, and it was finally determined to follow that course. ... Douglas, the negro implicated by Lacy, was arrested by the officers, and is now in the Jefferson jail. It is expected he will be taken out, and the same fate meted out to him at an early date, likely to-night.” The Herald says that Alex Lacy and Jasper Douglass were charged with assaulting a Mrs. Rogers, who lives 11-12 miles from Jefferson; “Lacy was hung on Tuesday [26th] about 11 a. m., in the presence of at least 500 people, a large number of them negroes. On Tuesday Douglass was placed in jail. That night between 11 and 12 o’clock, a mob numbering from 100 to 150, supposed to be citizens living in the neighborhood where the outrage was committed, came into town, overawed the jail, obtained the jail keys, took possession of the prisoner, pinioned him, and with a rope around his neck, started off with him. No tidings have been heard from him, but it is reasonable to suppose that ere this he has been hung.” From the News, “Marshall, June 27.—A Herald special from Jefferson, Tex, says two negroes, Alex Lacy and Jasper Douglass, who brutally outraged Mrs. Rogers, were both lynched. Lacy, who was still in the hands of citizens, was publicly hanged yesterday [26th] at 11 a.m. in the presence of 500 people, many of whom were negroes.” According to the Spectator, “Galveston, June 27.—The News’ Jefferson special says: Last last night a column of 150 horsemen suddenly galloped up and surrounded the jail containing the negro Douglass, guilty of assaulting the white woman, Mrs. Rogers, for which a negro named Lacy, was lynched yesterday morning. The deputy sheriff with guards attempted resistance, but was instantly ‘covered’ by the assailants and secured. The cell was unlocked and Douglass pinioned and placed on a horse. The band then disappeared as quickly and mysteriously as it had arrived. This morning two miles from the city the body of Douglass was found hanging from a tree, with four bullet-holes though his head.” The Times-Picayune gives the name Alexander Lacy and says he was hung at “Lacy’s Bridge, near Jefferson, on Tuesday.”—no mention of Douglas.

notes:
From the 8/2 Gazette, “Washington [Hempstead Co.]. August 1.—The negroes are on the war path in the northwestern part of our county. ... Yesterday [30th] one Bob Wyatt was surrounded and killed while plowing in his field. In defending himself he killed a negro by the name of Johnson Booker. The whites have organized to defend themselves. About twelve of the negroes have come in and surrendered.” The Republican reports that a white man named Wyatt was beating a black man after an argument over land. He was arrested and released. Local blacks, numbering 50-200, found Wyatt in a field and riddled him with bullets. From the Register, “In Hempstead County, Ark., recently, a white man named Wyatt and a colored man had a difficulty which resulted in a fight in which the latter was worsted. The negro subsequently collected a number of his friends, who attacked and killed Wyatt. The attempt to arrest the murderers brought on a small war of races. A fight was reported as having taken place between the posse and the negroes, which resulted in the killing of five of the latter and arrest of eighty.” The 8/4 Gazette reports that Wyatt was killed in Howard county and “Twenty-seven men implicated in the killing of Wyatt in jail at Center Point [Howard Co.], and three on the same charge and forty-four charged with riot, are in jail at Washington [Hempstead Co.].” The 8/5 Gazette states that Wyatt and Johnson were killed in Howard county, but the mob was from Hempstead county. According to the 8/11 Mansion, Wyatt [Wyatte in other parts of the story] beat a black man over a land dispute and later beat his daughter. “Last Monday [this would have to be the 30th] a crowd of colored men (twenty, sixty, or eighty-five) went into one Wyatt’s field (white.) and opened fire on him. He killed one of them. They shot Wyatt to pieces. This was about the woman beating.” The 12/8 Mansion says that Thos. Wyatt was a “Texas fugitive from justice”.

The Encyclopedia of Arkansas History and Culture gives the best description of the Hempstead-Howard counties killings. Thomas Wyatt, a white sharecropper, got into an altercation with two black men over a property line; two days later he solicited a young black girl and when she screamed, he hit her on the head with a fence rail—all this in Hempstead county. When the authorities took no action, a group of black men went to Wyatt’s home; Wyatt shot and killed Joe Booker and then he was shot by the black men—his body was found “in a cotton field just over the line in Howard County.” “Posses” hunted down Wyatt’s killers; “This posse, led by John Bell, killed Eli Gamble, a neighbor and carpenter building Booker’s coffin; his helper and relative, a young farmer named Alonzo Flowers; and a teenage boy named Abraham Booker, a bystander.”

1880 census lists a Thomas Wyatt, white, 30, farmer, living with his wife Mary at Mine Creek, Hempstead Co. Couldn’t find in 1900 Arkansas census. Couldn’t find a Robert/Bob Wyatt in Hempstead or Howard Co.

notes:
The Times reports that a mob of 500 men from six surrounding counties came to the jail for Miller McLean. Sheriff Bumpass took McLean into a nearby cornfield to hide. The mob surrounded the cornfield and killed Sheriff Bumpass, and then riddled McLean. McLean’s corpse was “subjected to all possible indignities”. The same story appears in the Telegraph. From the Gazette, “Nashville, Tenn., Aug. 24. Sheriff Bumpass, of Wayne County, was mortally wounded, and Miller McLean, a colored ravisher, riddled with bullets by a mob Wednesday night. Two weeks ago Miller McLean was arrested for an outrage on a white girl, and despite the warnings of a mob that short mercy would be shown him, he was taken to Waynesboro. On his trial before a magistrate he was acquitted, but was afterward indicted by the Grand Jury and kept in jail. Threats that mob law would end McLean’s life were circulated freely for several days. Monday [20th] night a mob was organized and made an ineffectual effort to get McLean. Tuesday fifteen of the ringleaders were arrested and required to give bonds. Wednesday one of the arrested parties was tried. In the meantime the feeling grew in bitterness, and the people of the surrounding country became more determined than ever to execute summary justice on the negro. A mob of 500 men from six surrounding counties gathered Wednesday night and proceeded to the jail, which is situated on the edge of a large cornfield. Sheriff Bumpass, on beholding the approach of the mob endeavored to lead McLean out through the cornfield. He was soon surrounded by the mob and forced to retreat. Scores of guns covered him, and demands were made for McLean. The Sheriff refused to give up his prisoner. The mob began firing from all sides. Bumpass ordered McLean to make his escape. Just as he gave the command a ball struck him in the neck, producing a fatal wound. The mob then opened fire on McLean, who was running across the field. His body was literally riddled, no less than one hundred bullets having struck him. The corpse was then subjected to all possible indignities.”

Note: there was a threatened lynching of McLean on 20 August in Wayne Co.

From the Daily Gazette, “Athens, Ga., Feb. 14—A colored man named Smeal, living on Thomas Dillard’s plantation, Guerney [Gwinnett] County, was suspected of stealing a horse. Last night a mob broke open the negro’s cabin and whipped him until he confessed to the stealing, and took the men to where the stolen horses was tied in the woods. The mob then hanged the negro to a black-jack limb, near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road. There the body was found hanging to-day.” The same story appears in the Ocean. From the Times, “A negro in Gedney [Gwinnett] county, Georgia, recently confessed to stealing a horse. A mob hanged him, and the body was found the next day.” According to the Messenger, citing the Oglethorpe Echo, an unnamed black man was found on Monday [13th] hanged by a chain “near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road, just over in the edge of Gwinnett county.” He was accused of stealing a horse from Tom Dillard. The Herald, citing the Jackson Herald, reports that “On last Monday [6th] a negro was found hung to a black jack limb, with a trace chain, near Jefferson and Lawrenceville road, just over in the edge of Gwinnett county. ... A horse was stolen in the neighborhood some time during the week, and this negro was suspected of having committed the crime. So a body of men organized themselves and went to Mr. Tom Dillard’s, where he was hired, and broke open a house and caught him. He was carried out and whipped until he confessed the crime and piloted them to where the horse was tied in the woods. He was then hung in the manner mentioned.” The same report appears in the Constitution. From the Summerville Gazette, “In Gwinnett county, on the night of Sunday, the 5th, a negro was hung by a party of whites, after having been whipped till he confessed that he had stolen a horse, and piloted them [the whites] to where it was tied out in the woods.” The Advance gives his name as Wm. Smeal.

notes:
From the News, “On Monday last a mob broke into jail at Tampa, took out a prisoner named C. D. Owens and hanged him on a shade tree in front of the court house. Owens, was was an Englishman, about thirty years of age, had the night before entered the house of a prominent citizen and, after securing a variety of plunder, entered the room of gentleman's daughter, whom he attempted to assault. Failing in his purpose, he stabbed the young lady several times with a bowie knife and left her almost dying. Suspicion pointed to Owens, who was pursued and captured.” The Journal story adds nothing. The Star reports, dateline Washington, 16 April, that the Supreme Court has denied a petition by J. B. As the constable having the wretch in charge was crossing Bonfouca Bridge [St. Tammany Parish] he was met by a crowd of sixty men, who took the prisoner from him. A halter was quickly placed around his neck, the other end fastened to the bridge, and Howard thrown over. The fall was so great that his neck was broken and death was instantaneous. ... The lynched negro was a preacher as well as a railroad worker.” From the Times-Picayune, “St. Tammany Farmer: St. Tammany parish is not a healthy summer resort for desperadoes. From the Chronicle, citing the Charlotte Observer, “Oscar Wilde ran across a lynching at Bonfauca, La. A negro assailant of a white woman had been taken out of jail by a mob, and Oscar saw the hanging from a [railroad?] car window. The negro was a preacher and his wild, eloquent appeals for mercy moved the aesthetic traveller greatly, but did not affect the lynchers, who quickly suspended him from a railroad bridge.” This report appears in other newspapers.

The old darkey, Gray, had been charged with killing a log belonging to a man named Trent, and on Saturday, Dec. 23, was taken to Mooresburg before a magistrate for trial. There being no proof of his guilt he was discharged. That night a crowd of men stoned his cabin but offered no further violence. Next night they surrounded the cabin and ordered him to come out and be sacrificed. This he declined to do, when a fusilade [sic] was opened on the shanty which was replied to from within. Of the lynchers, Jim Williams had the top of his head torn off by a charge of shot from the effects of which he died the next Friday. Mat. Orrick was badly shot about the face, one eye being put out. Upon the fall of Willliams, who seems to have been the leader, the assailants having had enough of it retreated in disorder. Gray was shot through the body and died the following Wednesday. His stepson was slightly wounded in the leg.” The same report appears in the American.

S. Laprade (of Sadlersville in Robertson Co.) in 8 September 1880. The American lists: James Higgins, Lock Mallory, Lum Small, Anthony Duffy, James Elder, and Robert Thweat.

Note: After the death of Laprade on 8 Sept 1880, James Higgins (”an old negro”) was placed in jail in Sadlersville in connection to the murder. A few days after his arrest, a mob broke into jail, tortured Higgins by burning his feet so badly that they had to be amputated; he admitted his involvement in the murder and named the others who were subsequently arrested. Two other black men, Jack Bell and Archie Jameson, were arrested and locked up in Sadlersville. On 16 Sept 1880 the mob came to the jail and carried the two men toward Laprade’s place and hanged them. The article further reports that on that same night, the mob shot and killed another inmate of the Sadlersville jail—a man named Ramsey (presumably white) for the murder of a woman, a Miss Holt. Higgins had been moved elsewhere or they would have gotten him too.

Note: Lark/Loch Mallory, Thomas/Lou/Lum Small, James Elder, Robert Thweat, and James Higgins were threatened with lynching on 14 February in Robertson Co. Jim Higgins, Wm. Murphy, Chas. Mallory, Andrew Duffey, Lou Small, and Lack Mallory were threatened with lynching on 15 September 1880; Robert Thweat, Charles Curley, and Jim/James Elder were threatened with lynching on 7 October 1880.

notes:
From the Telegraph, citing the Berrien County News, “Last week we gave our readers in a special from Dixonia [Ware Co.], an account of the robbing and burning of Mr. Dan Lott’s store in Coffee county, and the arrest of Willie Johns (an assumed name no doubt) who was charged with the crime. Thursday last we learned the following additional particulars: Soon after he was arrested Johns was placed in charge of five men, who left Dixonia with him. The fourth or fifth day afterwards the prisoner’s body was found at Indian ford, on Seventeen Mile creek. His head was literally shot to pieces and a large portion of his brain was found tightly grasped in one of his hands. The sight was a most horrible and sickening one. At the inquest, two of the men who had charge of the prisoner ... testified that they did not know who the firing party were, and a verdict was rendered that the deceased came to his death at the hands of an unknown party or parties. It is rumored that the guards were overpowered by a body of armed and unknown men, who sized Johns, and after taking him to Indian ford, shot him to death.” From the Constitution, “Lynch Law in Georgia. We print elsewhere from the Berrien County News an article that should attract the attention of the law-abiding people of Georgia. We gave recently from the same paper an account of the robbing and burning of a store in Coffee county. It was stated in this connection that a man named Willie Johns was charged with the crime, but it is to be presumed the evidence against against him was mainly circumstantial. However this may be, Johns was placed in the custody of five men, who carried him off. A few days afterwards, his body was found. He had been murdered. His head had been literally shot to pieces, and he presented a horrible and sickening sight.”

He was had been accused of felonious assault on his betrothed, Mary E. Taylor, of Franklin Co. He had been tried and sentenced to death but the Governor changed the sentence to 21 years. This was the third attempt to lynch him.” The Inquirer states that the mob was “thought to be from Franklin county, and to be friends of the murdered woman, Mrs. Emory, ...”

From the Evening News, “Houston, Texas, Aug. 23.—Eight Men Lynched. Eight desperadoes have been lynched at Orange. One of the gang, O. I. Delano, attempted to escape from jail and was shot [not fatally] by Deputy Wood. The rest of the gang went to the jail and demanded that Wood be given up. The gang, fearing arrest, began a series of outrages intended to draw the Sheriff out so they could attack him. Yesterday four of them, Charles Deluos and Dug. Harris, white, and Sam and Bob Saxon, colored, made a sham fight, cleared out a saloon and burned the building. ... [the sheriff followed Bob Saxon and was shot by someone] ... Michael is now unconscious at the jail, and is believed to be dying. The whole town rose up, and a public meeting was held. It was voted unanimously to lynch the offenders, and a committee of 150 was appointed. Early this morning [23rd?] four of the negroes were caught and shot in a field without preliminaries. Robert Garson, a colored leader, was captured, and a confession was demanded and refused. He was hung to a tree until unconscious and taken down and resuscitated five times before he made a full confession. He was then hanged a sixth time and left. Finding they were right as to the men they had hanged and that they were searching for, they captured Sam Saxon and Charles Deluos and put them in jail. After consultation it was decided to hang them and they were taken into the street. While ropes were being procured they attempted to escape, and were shot, their dead bodies left bleeding in the roadway. O. L. Duluos was then brought out and formally tried before Judge Lynch; he was dragged down the road with a rope about his neck, and hanged to a telegraph pole.” The 8/23 Herald reports, dateline Houston, 19 August, that “Robert [also Rob] Saxon was taken and hung to the limb of a tree; a rope was placed around his neck and he was hoisted up and then let down, and was tortured in this manner about an hour, when he finally confessed, the complicity of [Charles] Delano in the affair, and revealed the plot. He stated Delano had hired him for a pair of boots some eight months previous to assassinate Bill Bobcock, and in which attempt Mrs. Bobcock was shot. After making a full confession of his many crimes, he was hoisted for good, and they left him hanging. Another negro was hung to a tree over at the grove in the country, and the buzzards are using him this morning.”—it seems this happened on the 18th. According to the Chronicle, dateline St. Louis, 22 August, citing the Republican’s Houston “special” of the 21st, “Duke and Albert Delano, James Fort, Dug Harris and several negroes belonging to the gang of desperadoes, are still at large, but it is believed that they will be captured in a day or two.” The 8/27 Herald says, dateline Houston, 24 August, Sam Saxon and Robert Whaley were shot by the mob on Sunday, which would have been the 21st; [Charles] Delano was not killed and is scheduled for trial on the 25th; a black man named Odell agreed to turn state’s evidence and was “released by the lynchers”; there were 30 persons in the mob who hanged Bob Saxon “... to the big oak in front of Call’s store last week”—apparently Bob Saxon was not hanged on the same day that Sam Saxon and Duluos/Whaley were shot. According to the New York Times, Sam Saten and Robert Whaley were shot on Sunday [21st]. The Shreveport Times states that Charles Delno was bonded for $3,000 and fled the county.

notes:
Based on the very difficult to read report in the 8/19 Daily News, the “riot” at Orange when Sheriff Michel was shot might have happened on the 18th. From the Evening News, “Houston, Texas, Aug. 23.—Eight Men Lynched. Eight desperadoes have been lynched at Orange. It was the comparatively sober act of organized citizens determined to rid the county of a murderous gang of outlaws. The immediate cause was the attack of the gang on Sheriff George Michael. One of the gang, O. I. Delano, attempted to escape from jail and was shot [not fatally] by Deputy Wood. The rest of the gang went to the jail and demanded that Wood be given up. The Sheriff was overpowered and the jail searched, but Wood, who was in hiding, was not found. The gang found they had been deceived by the Sheriff and threatened the latter’s life. The guard was increased and the people notified to assist, and the plainsmen formed a volunteer guard. The gang, fearing arrest, began a series of outrages intended to draw the Sheriff out so they could attack him. Yesterday four of them, Charles Deluos and Dug. Harris, white, and Sam and Bob Saxon, colored, made a sham fight, cleared out a saloon and burned the building. ... [the sheriff followed Bob Saxon and was shot by someone] ... Michael is now unconscious at the jail, and is believed to be dying. The whole town rose up, and a public meeting was held. It was voted unanimously to lynch the offenders, and a committee of 150 was appointed. Early this morning [23rd?] four of the negroes were caught and shot in a field without preliminaries. Robert Garson, a colored leader, was captured, and a confession was demanded and refused. He was hung to a tree until unconscious and taken down and resuscitated five times before he made a full confession. He was then hanged a sixth time and left. Finding they were right as to the men they had hanged and that they were searching for, they captured Sam Saxon and Charles Deluos and put them in jail. After consultation it was decided to hang them and they were taken into the street. While ropes were being procured they attempted to escape, and were shot, their dead bodies left bleeding in the roadway. O. L. Duluos was then brought out and formally tried before Judge Lynch; he was dragged down the road with a rope about his neck, and hanged to a telegraph pole.” The 8/23 Herald reports, dateline Houston, 19 August, that “Robert [also Rob] Saxon was taken and hung to the limb of a tree; a rope was placed around his neck and he was hoisted up and then let down, and was tortured in this manner about an hour, when he finally confessed, the complicity of [Charles] Delano in the affair, and revealed the plot. He stated Delano had hired him for a pair of boots some eight months previous to assassinate Bill Bobcock, and in which attempt Mrs. Bobcock was shot. After making a full confession of his many crimes, he was hoisted for good, and they left him hanging. Another negro was hung to a tree over at the grove in the country, and the buzzards are using him this morning.”—it seems this happened on the 18th. According to the Chronicle, dateline St. Louis, 22 August, citing the Republican’s Houston “special” of the 21st, “Duke and Albert Delano, James Fort, Dug Harris and several negroes belonging to the gang of desperadoes, are still at large, but it is believed that they will be captured in a day or two.” The 8/27 Herald says, dateline Houston, 24 August, Sam Saxon and Robert Whaley were shot by the mob on Sunday, which would have been the 21st; [Charles] Delano was not killed and is scheduled for trial on the 25th; a black man named Odell agreed to turn state’s evidence and was “released by the lynchers”; there were 30 persons in the mob who hanged Bob Saxon “... to the big oak in front of Call’s store last week”—apparently Bob Saxon was not hanged on the same day that Sam Saxon and Duluos/Whaley were shot. According to the New York Times, Sam Saten and Robert Whaley were shot on Sunday [21st]. The Shreveport Times states that Charles Delno was bonded for $3,000 and fled the county.

Note: newspaper reports are confusing and inconsistent. Some early accounts give the other man who was killed along with Sam Saxon/Saten as Charles Delvos/Delno/Delano but he was not killed.

notes:
The New York Times, dateline Charleston, reports that there have been rumors that “a party of white men” are hunting an unnamed black man who was accused of outraging a white woman near Georges [Colleton Co.]. According to the News, Louis Kender was accused of an assault on a white woman named Boyd “near George’s Station, Colton [Colleton] county, fifty miles from this city [Charleston]. He was arrested and was being transported under guard from George’s Station to Walterboro [Colleton Co.] when he was seized. At 10:30 p.m. on the 1st, he was hanged and riddled with bullets. From the Orangeburg Times, “On Saturday morning [28th] an outrageous assault was made on Mrs. Byrd about six miles from Georges Station [Colleton Co.] by a one armed negro of desperate character. From the description he is believed to be the same person who committed a brutal assault upon another Mrs. Byrd near Branchville [Orangeburg Co.] about a month ago, an account of which has already appeared in our paper. ... On Saturday a regular hunt was organized and he was finally found about 4 o’clock Sunday morning. ... Some seventy men were present, and a vote was taken to decide what disposition should be taken of the prisoner. It being decided to let the law take its course, he was carried to Georges Station and lodged in the guard house. An unsuccessful attempt was made on Sunday [29th] night to take them out of jail, the party being repulsed. On Monday he was taken out jail to be sent to Walterboro [Colleton Co.]. When about one and half miles from Georges a party of seven or eight men took him from the officers, and carrying him to a secluded spot where a man was hung some fifty years ago, in the darkness of night by the light of a camp fires, a noose was fastened around the desperado’s neck, and the rope fastened to a convenient limb. At the word two men pulled the buggy away on which the prisoner was standing, and his neck was immediately broken. A few pistol shots were then fired though his body, and after a few minutes the crowd, consisting of about 100 persons who had gradually gathered at the spot, quietly dispersed.” The Review states that the mob was composed, largely, of the woman’s relatives. The Intelligencer notes, dateline Branchville, 1 March, that Kinder was lynched 1.25 miles from Branchville, and that Louis Kinder was also known as Moses, Fulton, Gaillard and Skinner.

Note: there was a threatened lynching of Kender/Kinder on 29 February in Colleton Co. In some early news stories his name is Lewis Skinner.
