notes:
According to the Courier, citing the Laurensville Herald 27 August,“The Mysterious Murder in Laurens. A rumor had been afloat in this vicinity in the early part of the week to the effect that two negroes had been found dead in Little River, just below [south] the Laurens line, in Newberry County ... On last Saturday evening an old black man named Henry Grier was fishing Little River, just below the Newberry [Laurens ?] line, near Floyd’s bridge, when he discovered the dead body of a man in the water.”—later the man’s body was recovered and it was Henry’s son, afterwards the body of the other son was found—both men had been shot and their bodies weighted down in the river. Some news reports state they were killed for attempted rape. From the Register, “The lynching of the brothers Grier, at Laurens, S. C., was conducted by the brothers Workman, whose sister they had maltreated. A mob of about fifty persons took the Griers from their house and tied them to two trees. Then the Workmans stepped forward with pistols and deliberately killed the offenders.” The Newberry Co. Coroner’s inquest (online) gives their names as Prue and Dorse Greir and date of death as around 16 August and location of their bodies as 300 yards “below” [south] of Floyd bridge. Apparently Dorse had had some issue with a white man named Hugh Workman on the 14th; apparently Prue and Dorse tried to get into/or look into a window of a Kate Johnson [Hugh Workman’s sister] who was living in Workman’s house. The date of the lynching is not clear: sometime between the 16th and the 18th.
 
Note: couldn’t find other non-redundant reports in GenealogyBank.com. Couldn’t find Dorsey, Prue, or Henry Grier/Greer/Greir in 1870 or 1880 census. The 1880 census lists W. Hugh Workman, white, 20, living with his wife Mary Lou in Hunter, Laurens Co., along with his mother, and sister N. Kate Johnson [Workman], 33, and her son M. Fate Johnson, 8. It seems likely that the brothers Grier/Greir were murdered in Newberry Co., but by a mob from Laurens Co. Below is the Coroner’s report for Dorse Greir, Prue’s report is similar: 

State of South Carolina, Newberry County

An inquisition indented taken at Mrs. J. B. Leonard’s Plantation in Township No. 6 in Newberry County the 24 day of August A.D. before E. C. Longshore Coroner for said County upon view of the body Dorse Greir then and there being dead by the oaths of A. J. Langford, J. A. Wallace, W. E. Longshore, J. W. Boozer, L. L. Hendrix, Mart Adams, Allan Andrews, Wiley Henderson, Whit Andrews, Anty Griffin, John Spraggin, Taylor Spraggins being a lawful jury of inquest who being charged and sworn to inquire for the State of South Carolina where and by what means the said Dorse Greir came to his death upon their oaths do say that the said Dorse Greir came to his death by a gun shot wound on or about the 16 day of August A.D. 1880 and that said shot was inflicted by some person or persons unknown to the jury and against the Peace and dignity of the Same State aforesaid.

In witness whereof I, E. C. Longshore aforesaid and the jurors aforesaid to this inquisition have interchangeably put our hands and seals the day and year above mentioned.
                                                                                                            E. C. Longshore Coroner.

A. J. Langford, foreman of jury, W. E. Longshore, J. A. Wallace, J. W. Boozer, L. L. Hendrix, Mart (X) Andrews, Allan (X) Andrews, Wiley (X) Henderson, Whit (X) Andrews, Anty (X) Griffin, John (X) Spraggins, Taylor (X) Spraggins

Henry Greir being duly sworn says: I goes off yesterday morning a week ago and I have not seen my boys to say I know them until Sunday morning. And then Saturday evening I goes fishing and I saw something moving in the water and then I left and went back home and got to talking about it from one to an other and they said it may be your boys there in that creek. And I went and spoke to my brother Fed Pitts and Peter Williams and Jerry Ducket and Lem Suber and we went to the river on Sunday morning between 8 and 9 o’clock and looked at the boys in the water and I swear it was my boys Dorsy and Prue that was in the river about three or four hundreds yards below the Floyd Bridge it was on Sunday the 22 of August.                                                           Henry (X) Greir

Lewis Pitts being duly sworn says: Me and Fed Pitts, Jerry Ducket and Peter Williams, Sam Philson, Dan Wheeler, went to the river on Sunday morning about 10 o’clock and saw Dorse Greir’s body in the river about 300 hundred yards below the Floyd Bridge and pulled him up to the bank and then felt for the other one who was his brother because we thought he was in there also. And we felt him in the water and we pulled some of rags from him with a hook and then left because we could not get him out without more help. We then went home and sent after Mr. Vance the trial Justice in Laurens County and I swear the man I saw in the water was Dorse Greir because I knew him by his clothes and when we drew the body to the bank a rock was fastened to his neck and tied to his body by a leather string. The rock would weighed about 25 or so pounds. I never heard no threats about the boys.                                                             Lewis (X) Pitts

Jerry Ducket being duly says: The old man said he was down there Saturday fishing and saw something on the water and when I got there I saw Dorse Greir on the water. We took a hook and pulled him to the bank and found who he was. We began to look for the other as he was missing too. Then I striped off and went in. Found him. I pulled at him but could not get him and I come out and left him and pulled Dorse to the bank. We found a string to his neck with a rock to it. The rock under his right arm. It was about 300 yards below the Floyd Bridge. We found him on Sunday the 22 day of August. Tom Greir told me Dorse and Mr. Hugh Workman had had a difficulty on last Saturday night the 14 of August as Mr. Workman thought he was trying to get in his mother's house.                                                                                                                     Jerry (X) Ducket

Lem Ducket being duly sworn says on Sunday morning the 16 of Aug. Mr. Hugh Workman measured mine and Dorsey's and Prue's feet because someone had tried to get in his house and he said the measure fitted Prue's track. Mr. Hugh Workman told me that Mrs. Kate Johnson saw some one come to the window of her room on the night of the 14 of Aug. and that she jumped and ran up stairs to Mr. Workman and he came down the stairs and shot and that she thought the person was Dorse.                                                                                                               Lem (X) Suber

Mary Glenn being duly sworn says: I live at Mrs. Nellie Workman's. I cook for her. I cook for all of her wages hands, five in number. I left Dorse in the kitchen on last Tuesday night Aug. the 17. He was eating supper with Prue. I missed Dorse on Wednesday morning. Dorse went to Clinton with Mr. Workman on Tuesday morning and came back on the same evening early. I asked Coleman and Jim if they had seen Dorse and Prue and they said no. Mrs. Workman told me after I had given the boys supper to go on to my house. She was not accustomed to tell me to go. I never stayed any later than usual. Mr. Workman measured Prue's and Dorsey's track as some one tried to get in the window on Saturday night and said it was Prue's track. Prue denied to me it was his track or that he tried to get in the window.                                                                                     Mary (X) Glenn

Emmaline Greir being duly sworn says: I saw Dorse on Tuesday morning and on Tuesday night I left home to go to see Dorse and Prue and on the road in a small patch of pines this side of Mrs. Workman I saw a number of horses & men about 40 or 50 I suppose. I could not see as it was dark. I met Lem Suber on this side of the horses and he went as far as the branch with me and then went back towards Mrs. Nellie Workman's saying he would go back as he was afraid they might get after him.                                                                                                                    Emmaline (X) Greir

Susan Greir being duly sworn says: On Wednesday morning Lem Suber asked me if my boys had come home last night and said that he saw a crowd of men in the pines this side of Mrs. Workman’s house and that three men rode inside of the fence and turned around and went back.
                                                                                                                         Susan (X) Greir.

W. H. Workman being duly sworn says: Dorse Greir was in my employment up till the and Prue Greir was in my employment up till the 17 of Aug. There was no company at my house that night. I was at home. I had heard no threats of his life. I saw nor heard no body pass my house that night. Mrs. Johnson was not at home on the 17 of Aug. 1880.                         W. H. Workman

Dr. D. W. Patton being duly sworn says: I proceeded on the 23rd of Aug. 1880 at the request of Coroner E. C. Longshore to examine the dead body of Dorse Greir. I found the deceased came to his death by 2 gun shot wounds one near his left nipple the other on the back between the scapula. Either wound would necessarily have proved fatal without the other on account of the close proximity of vital organs. Appearances of mutilation were the result of decomposition.

                                                                                                                        D. W. Patton.

From the Clarion-Ledger, “We learn by an extra from the Kemper Herald that a negro preacher named Maddox, met his death at Wahalak in that county, under the following justifiable circumstances: In the absence of Mr. Hampton, a citizen of Wahalak, Maddox went to the house and made improper advances to Mrs. H. On the 26th, Maddox “put on his Sunday clothes” and went to the home of Mr. Hampton, who was absent; Hampton’s wife made Maddox leave but he soon returned and said “... he wanted to talk with Mrs. H. a few minutes; and finally told Mrs. Hampton that he had come to take her for his wife; that he had been so directed by some higher power, &c.”. Mrs. Hampton shot at him with her pistol. “Nothing, perhaps, but a pistol in the hands of a brave lady saved her from a fate worse than death. While we do not approve of mob law, yet under certain circumstances it seems to be a necessary evil, and this is one of those instances. ... That night the guard was overpowered by a body of armed and unknown men, and Maddox was then and there riddled with bullets, and his spirit fled to meet in just reward.” From the Herald, citing the Meridian Mercury, “On Wednesday night, at Shuqualak, a negro was taken from custody and shot to death by a crowd of lynchers. His name was W. D. Maddox, a preacher. that day he had gone to the resident of Mr. T. H. Hampton during his absence, and made a demonstration upon the lady, whom he found alone, which she resisted by firing two pistol shots at him, which caused the lecherous villain to desist and run for his worthless life which he was soon to lose. The lady saved herself from outrage and probably death by her presence of mind and cool courage. An alarm was made, the negro pursued and captured, and it happened as above stated.”

Note: Shuqualak, Noxubee Co., is a few miles north of the Noxubee-Kemper Co. line, and Wahalak, Kemper Co., is just south of that line, almost in Noxubee Co. 1880 census lists a T. J. Hampton, age 30, living in Wahalak, Kemper Co., with his wife Callie, age 26, and three children. Going to assume that the actual murder took place in Shuqualak but the mob was from Kemper Co.

notes:
The News reports, dateline Dallas, 11 October, “Particulars of a Fannin county horror, resulting in the outrageous murder of the negress Easter and her young boy, and the dangerous wounding of her little girl, are gathered from conflicting and and fragmentary reports current in the county. Easter was a renter on John Aldridge’s farm, four miles from Orangeville. The day previous to the butchery her son Charley and two freedmen made an attack upon George Aldridge, who had charged one of them with theft, and but for the timely appearance of two white men would have beaten Aldridge. At 2 the following morning the house of Easter was visited by an armed party, who called for Charley; upon refusal to open the door the house was fired into, wounding the girl in the forehead. A freedman, Charley Justice, who was staying with the family, fired though the crack of the cabin, shooting one of the attacking party in the stomach. ... [the mob broke into the cabin] ... The ruffians, disguised by tying hankerkerchiefs over their faces, forced the old woman and children to come out; drove them off a trail; securing John Washington, another freedman, from an adjoining cabin, and were leading them in a southeastern direction, when Washington and the two boys  escaped, reaching a tree. The mode of death was debated and shooting determined upon . Charley was shot first, five bullets entering his back. Easter ran, some distance before she fell, her right breast being riddled with buckshot and balls. George Aldridge and Thomas Fullerton were arrested .... On the examining trial they were held in $2000 bail; in default of which they were committed to jail at Bonham. The morning after the butchery, Samuel Gilley was found fatally shot though the abdomen, which he claims to have accidentally done himself awhile out hunting. He has since died.” The Banner reports, “—A negro woman named Easter, and her young boy were were brutally murdered and her daughter shot and wounded near Orangeville, Fannin county, a few days ago. The murderers were committed by masked men and grew out of the woman being a witness. Two men were arrested and in default of $2000 bonds each were committed to the Bonham jail.” From the Messenger, “—A negro family, consisting of an old negress named Esther, her son, Charles, a young boy, a girl, and other children, rented, worked and occupied a cabin on a farm of John Aldridge, four miles from Orangeville, in Fannin County, Texas. George Aldridge, a son of John, accused Charley, Esther’s son, with stealing, when Charley and two other negroes attempted an assault on Aldridge, but were prevented by two white men. At midnight, old Esther’s house was surrounded by a party of armed and masked men. They called for Charley, but were refused admittance, when the maskers fired into the house, wounding Esther’s daughter in the forehead. Charles Justice, another negro who lived in the family, returned the fire, hitting one of the maskers, Samuel Gilley, in the stomach wounded him mortally. notes:
The Watchman reports that on Friday, the 24th of May, fifteen year-old Tom Hutton, black, made an attempted to rape the 2.5 year-old daughter of Mr. Richard Hill, who lived in the “vicinity of Beckville” [Panola Co.] ... A party at once pursued him but he was not captured until the Monday [27th] following, when he was brought to Carthage and lodged in jail, and the authorities in Beat No. 2, where the crime was committed, notified of the fact, and on Thursday last, the 30th ult., Constable Forsyth brought a warrant from Esquire Craig, and took the negro back to Beckville. At night the negro boy was confined in the back part of a store room, and a strong guard, three armed white men and two negroes placed over him. About midnight a large crowd of men came to the store and completely overpowered the guard, took the negro boy from their custody and that is the last that has been seen or heard of him, as the whole community was aroused and very much enraged at the fiendish deed that had been committed, it is not a difficult matter to tell the fate of the negro. He committed a most diabolical and heartless crime, and that he has paid the forfeit with his life, no one acquainted with the facts will question. His retribution was swift and sure.” From the 6/11 Statesman, “A negro boy in Panola county committed a rape upon a little child two and half years old. He was arrested and taken from the authorities by an excited mob and hung.” The Democrat account adds nothing. The 6/25 Statesman reports, citing the Mount Pleasant [Titus Co.] Patron, “Murders, rapes, robberies, etc., are on the increase; two recent rapes are unsurpassed for fiendish brutality, one in Panola county by a negro boy fifteen years old upon the person of a white child two and a half years old, the boy being caught and lynched; the other, a tramp at Dallas, upon a child three and a half years old; he is confined in jail.”

Note: it is not clear if he was lynched in the night of 30 May or in the very early hours of the 31st. Going to assume the 31st. Did they ever find the body? Going to assume he was killed even though could find a report of finding his body. Couldn’t find in GenealogyBank.com or ChroniclingAmerica.loc.gov.

Beach, of Palo Pinto, who passed though here last evening, direct from Albany, reports that on Sunday night, 23d ult., John M. Larn, ex-sheriff of Shackleford county, was killed by a mob, while under guard in a building used for the confinement of prisoners. .... the prisoner was held to await a preliminary examination before a justice of the peace, on a trail of murder, and it was reported that two men who had been in Larn’s employ were missing, and that two dead bodies (which were not recovered) had been seen floating in the Clear Fork of the Brazos. ... The mob numbered about twenty men who were dressed in india rubber overcoats and had handkerchiefs tied around the lower part of their faces. John M. Larn was a prominent stock man, and connected with some of the most prominent and best citizens of the county. According to the 7/13 Galveston Daily News, Jno. Larn was killed “Sunday night, June 23” and that he came to Shackelford county from Colorado in 1872 or 1873 at the age of 16—that would make him 21-22 years old when killed; the account outlines various suspicions that Larn was involved in stealing cattle and committing multiple murders. Oddly, the Statesman puts this in Alabama:  “John M. Larn, ex-sheriff of Shackelford county, was killed last month by a mob in Alabama. He was accused of murder.”

A negro man by the name of George Bullitt was arrested near this place on the 3rd inst. for outrageous conduct toward the family of Mr. S. C. Howey, a farmer, and was to have an examining trial the next day before Esquires Patterson and Peck. ... the trial was postponed until nine A. M. to-day. The prisoner was left under guard of Constable Enlow, S. E. Howey and James Crawley, who state that between twelve and one o'clock last night they all feel asleep, and the prisoner escaped, with his hands tied before him. At an early hour this morning the negro was found dead, hanging to a tree in front of the Baptist church, about one and half miles distant, with his hands cross and tied behind him. How this strange occurrence took place without any of the citizens knowing of it, and how all the guards happened to go to sleep at the same time, and after the prisoner made his escape how he happened to fall into the hands of a mob, are mysteries that have not yet been explained.” The same report appears in the Patriot. The Tribune report gives his name as Henry Burnett and he was lynched for threatening to burn a white man’s house.

notes:
According to the Telegraph, there was a rumored insurrection by blacks to burn the city of Monroe; “Justice Anderson, upon this affidavit [of a pending insurrection] issued warrents for the arrest of Aaron Randall, Garret Esau, Ike Randall, Wm. McGown, Dan Madison, John Wilson, Jordan Wilson, and Cook McGee; and the warrants were placed in the hands of Constable Hinson for service. Mr. Hinson arrested all of the accused, except the last-named three, who were not to be found ... Constable Hinson, with a posse of four gentlemen, left Logtown at half past four o’clock in the afternoon ... for Monroe. ... About half-way between Monroe and Logtown, the Constable and posse were ordered to halt by a number of men ... The prisoners were demanded, and the Constable and his men placed under guard. The prisoners were taken in charge by the waylayers, and marched off into the swamp, the captors saying that they proposed to give the prisoners a whipping, and if the Constable would wait a few minutes the prisoners would be returned to him. The Constable and posse waited a sufficient length of time, were discharged by their spectre of guards—the prisoners were not returned—and the Constable and posse came on to Monroe, and reported to Judge Slack in accordance with the facts here related. Nothing has been heard from the prisoners—where they are, or what became of them; but speculation seems to have settled down into the belief that they were carried away into the dense swamp and there either hung, or shot. At all events, the prisoners have not been found.”

notes:
According to the Independent, 36 Negroes were killed on the 15th in Goldman’s field, “four miles above Waterporoof”, in a fight with whites. Later in the same story, the number killed was reduced to 10 Negroes, and even later reduced further to 5 Negroes. The Times reports that seven unnamed Negroes were killed in Waterproof by white Democrats. From the Journal’s story in White League atrocities in Louisiana: “Such cases as that of Daniel Hill, of Ouachita Parish, who was riddled with bullets, and his assassination completed while upon his dying bed trying to make peace with his God; Herman Bell, of the same parish, taken from his home in the dead of the night, dragged to the woods and massacred, his body left to feed the vultures and the prowling beasts of the forest; Commodore Smallwood, Charles Carrol, John Higgins, and Washington Hill of Concordia Parish; Charles Bethel, Robert Williams, Munday Hill, James Stafford, Louis Postlewait, William Henry, and others, of Tensas Parish, were ruthlessly murdered in their different parishes for no other reason than of being republicans, and for attempting to exercise their rights as American citizens.” The same report appears in the Louisianian. From the Picayune, the testimony of Henrietta Williams before the Teller Committee, “Live in Tensas. On a Sunday, two weeks before the election three men came to my house. They surrounded my husband while he was approaching and arrested him. They took him to the swamps and hung him. Mr. Thos. Kemp was one of the men who arrested him, and that night he got a cart and brought the body back and buried it.” Painter lists a Robert Williams killed in Tensas Parish.

Note: the election was on 5 November. There are many newspaper reports on the political conflicts in Tensas Parish in mid-October but most do not report the names of the blacks killed. There were four Sundays in October: 6, 13, 20, 27—assuming the date was Sunday, the 13th.

He was left as one dead; but although shot in five places, mostly in vital parts, he disengaged himself from the tree and made his way to a friendly negro’s hut, where he remained until he was out of danger from his wounds. He was then taken by some negroes back to the county jail, they deemed it the safest place in the county. There he remained unmolested four days; on the fifth day forty-five men, ‘armed to the teeth’, marched to the jail, broke down the dungeon doors, took the prisoner therefrom and completely riddled his body with bullets.” The Messenger story adds no new information.

Soon after that a crowd of disguised men went to the house of Alfred Turner, a colored Baptist preacher, took him out to whip him and, upon his trying to escape, shot him dead, after which they took another negro from his house and beat him so severely that he was confined to his bed for three days. Johnson and other ringleaders in the negro riot have been tried and sentenced to the penitentiary, but no arrest have been made of the white murderers....” The Appeal says that eight whites have been arrested. From the Chronicle, “On the night of the 3d of April a crowd of disguised men went to the house of Alfred Turner, a colored Baptist preacher, on the plantation of Mrs. R. R. Mitchell, and took him out for the purpose of whipping him. He got loose from from and ran off and was shot by the crowd, and shortly afterwards died. The same crowd took out another colored man named Anthony Thurston, and whipped him with such severity that he was confined to his bed for three days. No one seems to know who did did these cruel and lawless deeds, or what motive impelled the lynchers to the commission of the crime, but there can be little doubt that Turner was murdered and Thurston beaten because of real or fancied connection with [Luke] Johnson and his schemes. No arrests were or have been made.”

Smith, Sheriff of Union County, is in the city, returning home from Mississippi, where he carried the murderer Latenear [indistinct], who was recently lynched on his arrival in Rankin County.”’ From the Telegraph, “Our readers will remember accounts we have published from time to time of the acts of Lattineer, alias Robbins, who some three weeks ago was taken through this place under arrest charged with the crime of murder committed in Simpson Co., Miss. Robbins was safely conveyed to the jail of Simpson county, and the key turned on him. The Westville (Miss) News furnishes us with recital of what has since transpired: Rumors having circulated that the prisoner, Ira D. Robbins, in jail, charged with the murder of Peter M. Dickerson, of this county, in 1873, and William T. Bass, of Covington, in 1875, and other crimes, was to be taken from the jail and hung, scores of men wended their way towards Westville at an early hour on Friday morning, the 10th instant.”—the report gives the mob size as 800 and implies that he, Commodore D. Latinneer, was hanged by the mob around 1:30 p.m. The Record, citing the New Orleans Democrat, states that Ira D. Robbins, a.k.a., Latineer, “barely 30”, was hanged at Westville by a mob of 600 from Lawrence, Covington, and Simpson counties.

He then surrendered and started off in charge of his captors, but soon darted out of the road into another swamp. He was closely followed, and pretty soon a great noise which sounded like guns was heard. Right here it is best, perhaps, that we should let the curtain fall. We will only add that Elbert Jackson will never attempt to outrage another woman.” The same report appears in the Telegraph. notes:
According to the Democrat, citing the Catahoula News, “On the night of December 17, a negro, Isaac Maxwell by name, while about to go on board the steamer Jno. Wilson near Trisler’s Landing, on Black River, was taken by a body of armed men, riddled with bullets, his pickets rifled and his body after being cut open and disemboweled, thrown into the river. William G. Dale, one of the murderers, last week voluntarily came before Mr. Henry Trisler, just of the Fourteenth Ward, and made a confession ....” The same report appears in the Chief but with the addition, “The reason given for the killing of the negro was that he was cohabiting with a white woman, and had failed to leave the country when ordered to do so.”, but the Chief also says that might have been a pretext and the real reason was robbery. There were four killers: William G. Dale, Duff Burley, John W. Crane and Stephen Fredericks. The Chief states that “None of the parities implicated live in Catahoula [Parish].”

Note: the Black River forms part of the boundary between Catahoula and Concordia parishes. The 1870 census lists two Henry Trislers: (1) living in Ward 14 of Catahoula parish, age 54, and (2) living in Ward 4, Richland Parish, age 30. The 1880 census lists a Stephen Frederics, age 28, living in Concordia Parish; there are multiple Burley families living in Concordia Parish in the 1870 and 1880 censuses. Gong to assume that the murder happened in Catahoula Parish but the killers were from Concordia Parish. Couldn’t find an earlier report or follow-up in Newspapers.com.

notes: From the Herald, “Louisville, Ky., Dec. 24, 1877. An unknown negro was hung near Nicholasville [Jessamine Co.], Ky., this morning, by a mob. [Denton was hit in the head with an axe.] ... The neighbors hearing the firing [Denton has shot at the fleeing man] ran to the store and after the murderer whom they identified by the bloody axe left behind. He was caught hiding in the neighborhood, arrested and held before a Magistrate to await the result of Denton’s wounds. Last night he was taken from the constable by parties unknown, and found this morning a ghastly victim of the rope, hanging to a neighboring tree.” According to the 12/25 Gazette, dateline Lexington, 24 December, on Sunday morning three black men entered the store of Jake Shutemen, at East Hickman, and one of them stuck him with an ax. Later on Sunday the three men were captured and brought to Shutemen for identification, which he did. One of the men was then “hung to a beam in an out house, and was still hanging their at 8 o’clock.” From the 12/26 Gazette, “Lexington, Ky., Dec. 25. The man Jake Shulemen, who was reported in a critical condition in yesterday’s dispatches, died this morning. John Nephew, the colored man hung by a mob of over one hundred men for committing the crime of striking him the blow with the ax which caused his death, was cut down down to-day, by order of a Magistrate of Jessamine County. A rumor was current on the streets late this evening that his two accomplices had been nabbed and hung. The report could not be traced to any reliable authority. It is a fact that the names of two colored men, whom Nephew stated, before he died, were with him at the time the murder was committed, are in the hands of the vigilance men in the vicinity of East Hickman [Fayette Co.], with every possibility of their speedy arrest.”

chicago_tribune: Chicago Tribune inventory covers the years 1882-1918

notes:
The 10/29 Times-Picayune states, citing a letter with a dateline of Clinton [East Feliciana Parish] 26 October, “Some sixty days ago, Emory Curtis, an esteemed young planter of this parish, was called to his quarters to adjust a domestic difference between a man and his wife. He entered into no altercation with the parties, gave some advice to the man in regard to the matter, and turned to go back to his house when the negro man turned upon him with the exclamation, ‘No d--d white man shall interfere in my business,’ stabbed him most brutally in the back, cutting the spine in two, from the effects of which wound young Curtis died. A posse was organized to pursue the murderer, and armed with a warrant they went to a house in East Baton Rouge parish, where he had sought refuge. As soon as the summons was made a shot was fired from the premises, and young Smith, another respectable planter, was killed. The arrest was then made and the parties taken to Baton Rouge. A constable from this parish [East Feliciana], called on the authorities in East Baton Rouge demanding the prisoner for trial; but he was refused, because his chances to escape the just consequences of his crime seemed more favor in that parish. The facts were duly noticed in our [Clinton] local paper, but they were not heralded by telegrams throughout the land, nor was any more notice taken of the matter.” According to the 1/10 Times-Picayune, “Lynch Law in Baton Rouge. Hanging of the Negro Burgess. Friday [7th] night last a man named Burgess, a prisoner in the Baton Rouge jail, was taken out of his cell and hung. Burgess, it appears, about two months ago, killed a man in East Feliciana, and while a posse were attempting to arrest him, he killed one of the posse. He was then secured, however, and locked up in Baton Rouge, and though apprehensions were early entertained that he would be disposed of by a resort to the law of Judge Lynch, it was only last Friday night that he met his end. Burgess was a negro, and the man he first killed a white man, the murder being perpetrated in obedience to the impulses of the green-eyed monster. The complexion of the Lynchers is not known.” From the Republican, “Another Victim of Lynch Law. Some weeks since a colored man named Burgess was supposed to have killed a white man in East Feliciana. A posse attempted to arrest him, and in resisting he killed one of the posse. He was locked up in the at at Baton Rouge. The public feeling was intense against him, and it was the general impression that he would be immediately taken out and lynched. As he was well guarded the attempt was not made and the feeling seemed to have died out, a desire to have the law take its course taking its place. notes:
From the 5/15 Times-Picayune, “Woodville, Miss., May 14.—On the night of the 11th inst., Mr. Ernestine was assassinated by a mob of armed negroes in the parish of West Feliciana [LA}, without provocation, whereupon the citizens of the parish and of Wilkinson county, Miss., executed two of the leaders of the mob.” From the 5/17 [morning edition] Times-Picayune, “The Aaronstein who was killed resided in the neighborhood of Laurel Hill. One night, not long ago, he detected four negro men in the act of killing some of his cattle. He informed upon them, and they were given 500 lashes by the colored people themselves. Several nights afterward, animated by a revengeful desire, they came to the house and shot Aaronstein and a colored man who stayed in the house with him, killing the first and wounding the latter in the hand. He recognized the murders and informed upon them, whereupon the whites in the neighborhood captured and executed the two leaders of the band of assassins.” From the 5/17 [afternoon edition] Times-Picayune, “Woodville, Miss., May 14, 1876.—About 11 o’clock on Thursday night, 11th inst., a mob of armed negroes, about (30) thirty in number, surrounded a store in front of Mr. Perkins’s house, where they knew Mr. Ernestine lodged. They, under disguise of friendship, asked admission; Mr. Ernestine requested a negro boy who waited on him to open the door. As  he opened it, one o the mob, supposing the door to be opened by Mr. E., fired and shot the negro [sic] in the left eye. Mr. E. seized his gun and spring to the door, when no less than fifty shots were fired, many of them taking effect in the breast and head of Mr. E. The decreased was an honest, respectable, law-abiding citizen. He has been a merchant in the parish of West Feliciana for several years. A few nights previous to his death, he, with several of his neighbors, whipped a negro man for stealing beef, which is the only possible provocation the negroes had for committing the brutal act. An indignation meeting was held by the citizens of West Feliciana parish and Wilkinson county, Miss., as the store was within a few yards of the State line. After a careful investigation and an impartial trial, which continued two days, the two leaders of the mob, Duncan Gaines and Ben. King, were executed.” Some newspaper accounts state that two unnamed black men were caught and hung, with no implication of a trial. From the Times, “A New Orleans Times special, dated Summit, Miss., May 15th. says: Information was received here last night of a row between negroes and whites at Laurel Hill, West Feliciana Parish near the Mississippi line. On Friday night about thirty negroes went to the store of a white man in that vicinity and called to the door riddled him with bullets. A posse from Bayou Sara went out on Saturday [13th] for the body. The negroes would not give it up. A fight ensued, and three negroes were killed. Two white men are missing. The negroes are gathering. Eleven hundred are said to be under arms. The whites are going down from neighboring counties in Mississippi. A serious fight is expected.” From the Agitator, citing a New York Times dispatch from New Orleans on the 17th, “From dispatches received from East Feliciana, in this State, and Wilkinson county, Mississippi, it is estimated that about sixteen colored men have been killed there during the past three days of trouble; also that one white man was killed at the beginning of the affair. Aaronson, a white man, had accused a colored man of stealing, and had whipped him. Aaronson was subsequently killed, and dispatches quite as trustworthy as any say he was killed by the white Regulators of Mississippi, being in bad odor and charged with buying stolen cotton at his store. The Picayune prints the report of the military commander’s on this incident which makes no mention of any hanging, but the sheriff’s report states “I heard a report of five negroes being hung; if so, it was done by unknown parties. The Baton Rouge Advocate charges the crime upon responsible parties from Mississippi.” From the Watertown Daily Times, “The New Orleans Republican records as a matter of current news that in a recent outbreak at ‘Point Pleasant Plantation’, Henry Martin was hung between the gateposts, Devin Foster and hanged and shot, and Wilson Rhodes and William Lewis were hanged—all colored; no whites injured.” The Cincinnati Daily Times publishes a list of incidents sent to them by a reader which notes that “Henry Martin, hanged on his own gate post. ... Levin Foster, hanged, and shot through while hanging. Wilson Rhodes, hanged. William Lewis, hanged.” The 6/24 Republican lists the victims as Levin Foster, a Baptist preacher, Henry Martin and Wilson Rhodes hanged; however, the 6/28 Republican references five black men lynched at Mount Pleasant—no names mentioned; the 6/30 Republican, “Henry Martin was one of the colored men hung between the gateposts of the Point Pleasant plantation; Levin Foster was hanged and shot; Wilson Rhodes and Bill Lewis were hanged. The bodies of these victims were ‘viewed’ and buried by the justice of the peace at Port Hudson, but for evidence reasons no inquest could be held.” From the 9/3 Republican, “We long ago published the names of the poor slaughtered negroes, and will do so once again, to satisfy our exacting neighbor [the Times]. They were Henry Martin, Wilson Rhodes, William Lewis, Levin Foster and one who could not be identified. Their bodies were officially ‘viewed’ by the justice of the peace, under his direction buried. The coroner, Ben Morgan, feared to hold an inquest, because he had been formally warned that he would be killed if he held inquests on the bodies of the bulldozer slain.”—apparently they had been hanged north of Baton Rouge.

notes:
According to the 8/5 News, two black men went missing on Saturday, the 29th; “The bodies of the two freedmen were found—one shot through the head, the other though the body—and were taken charge of by their friends.” Exact location not given but in Wharton Co. From the 8/11 News, “Eagle Lake, Aug. 10, 1976. On Saturday week [29th] last near the Wharton and Colorado county line, at a point known as Frazier’s store, in the afternoon two freeman stopped, and, after making some purchases, left. Their horses reach home at night without riders. Search was made for the men and, after a lapse of about three days, they were found some five or six miles from the store of Mr. Frazier, dead in the prairie. They were supposed to have been killed by some stockmen. The negroes being much incensed immediately congregated in large numbers armed, and threatened to destroy the property of Frazier and also kill him. Affairs became so alarming that armed white men congregated at Frazier’s from all directions. Subsequently six negroes, all of notoriously bad character, have been killed.”
From the 8/13 News, “The Columbus [Colorado Co.] Citizen gives the following version of the late troubles in Wharton county: ‘In our last issue we announced that two negroes had been killed on the East Bernard [apparently referring to Middle Bernard creek in Wharton Co. near the city of East Bernard], in Wharton county, while killing cattle upon the prairie. The bodies of the negroes were found, and showed they had been shot. As yet it is unknown who did the killing, but it is presumed to have been done by stockmen. After the negroes were missed, which, of course, was soon after they left for the cattle, the negroes in the lower end of our county [Colorado Co.] and upper end of Wharton, were excited, and scoured the woods in armed bodies of from fifteen to twenty in search of the dead bodies, which they finally discovered. A disreputable white woman, cohabiting with a negro man, reported that they had been killed by Dr. Smith and the Frazar brothers. ... Two negroes, said to be cattle thieves, were killed on Monday night or Tuesday morning [31st or 1st], an inquest held, and a verdict returned that they came to their death by violence at the hands of parties unknown.”  From the 8/20 News, “Colorado County. The names of the negroes to this county, killed in the late troubles on the border of Wharton [county], are Lewis Gaskin and Reuben Wheeler, the former of whom is reported to have kept a butcher shop from cattle stolen off the prairie, and of notoriously bad character. The latter is is said to have been a very good man, and the negroes do not think he was intentionally killed. The inquest failed to give the names of the parties who did the killing, but there is little doubt that stockmen did it in order to protect their stock.” According to the Tribune, “Eagle Lake, Tex., Sept. 1.—Following are the names of seven of the colored men murdered at or near Eagle Lake, within the past few weeks, by the supporters of Tilden and Hendricks: Lewis Yaskins, worked for John Matthews; Isam Davenport, farmed on old Battle place; Boney Cotton and Raymond Cotton, farmers; Zack Hughes, farmer; Felix Fonda, farmer. All of the above are know to have been good, peaceable, and industrious men, except Zach Hughes, who was charged with killing and skinning cattle. It was utterly false that any of them were caught in the act of skinning cattle. The two first killed, Zach Hughes and Lewis Yaskins, were returning to their homes from Eagle Lake on horseback, where they had been to purchase some groceries. They were shot on their horses, and allowed to lay on the roadside where they fell until found by some of their colored friends and buried. There are six more know to have been killed, but as yet I have been unable to ascertain their names. ... The Perpetrators of These Crimes. There is very little doubt here [Eagle Lake], either among white or black, as to who are the perpetrators of these crimes, or rather atrocities. If united States Marshal Phillips will do his duty under the Ku-Klux act, he will find that Jim Frazier, Will Frazier, Brant Frazier, grocery-keepers; Bill Beard, clerk for Watterson & Ficklin at Eagle Lake; Bill Lowry, whisky-seller; Jimmy Roan, loafer and desperado; Murray Watts, ditto; Lewis Fritz, loafer and whisky-guzzler; Henry Tracey, butcher, and Bill Murray, another drunken loafer and desperado; and perhaps a certain Dr. Smith, are the ringleaders. James Raymond, known as ‘Crip,’ if he is in complicity with this gang of thieves and assassins, is but a dupe and a tool,—no doubt a willing one, though.”

Note: couldn’t find a Frazar/Frazer/Frazier family in either Colorado or Wharton counties in 1870 census. East Bernard Creek forms the border of Wharton and Austin counties. Apparently this incident happened in Wharton county but near the border with Colorado Co. It seems likely that the killers were from Colorado Co., but also possible from Wharton Co. Date of death is uncertain: sometime between the 29th and the 2nd.

Dover, Thomas Gamely, John and Elizabeth Nelson, John and Lee Dover, and Clementine Dover were guilty of murder or accessories to the murder of Humphreys.

The case was worked up, and Steve Robertson, Sol. Ridge, George Veal, Burrell and Smith Jackson were arrested, the others leaving the county with the hooddoo doctor. Geo. Veal turned State’s witness. notes: According to the 2/21 Republican, citing the Iberia Progress, on the 14th a man named T. H. George was beaten and robbed by three black man who were directing him to a bordello—he died on the 17th; “A colored man named Vincent, charged with the commission of this crime, was arrested by the sheriff and lodged in jail about ten o’clock on Wednesday [17th] night. The next morning [18th] the parish judge was informed that a mob had surrounded the jail in which Vincent was confined and attempted to force an entrance. The judge went immediately to the spot and succeeded in dispersing the crowd by assuring them the prisoner should be tired, and if guilty suffer the extreme penalty of the law. Vincent was then brought before the judge, regularly tried on a preliminary examination and remanded to jail without benefit of bail. On the way to the jail Vincent was forcibly taken from the sheriff and hung.” The Sugar-Bowl reports, “Murderer Lynched. Last week we gave an account of the murder of Thomas H. George .... Fortunately, the principal was easily caught. ... [the was arrested on Wednesday night] ... The pistol which the murdered man had borrowed from the Pelican Saloon, and had been taken from him, was found on this man, named Sevin Sam, or Sevin Benoit. He was taken to jail .... Great excitement followed the announcement, Thursday morning, that the murderer had been arrested, and a large crowd assembled at the jail to lynch him. Judge Fontenlien and other officials attempted to quiet the crowd, by saying that the murder would be punished, and he was by the officers taken to court house, where a preliminary examination established his guilt, and Judge Fontenlieu, ordered that he be committed to the jail for trail at the next term of the District Court. Much excitement among the spectators was caused by this determination, .... When the Sheriff and Constable were escorting their prisoner back to jail, the crowd rushed upon them, a noose was thrown over his head, and with the rope in hands of a large number of men both white and colored, he was violently hung. So quickly was it done, that even the officers are now unable to tell who the lynchers were.” In a second story, same page, the Sugar-Bowl reports that two black men, Ceacare Joseph and his brother Basige, were arrested as accessories but were then released for lack of evidence. From the Review, “On the 18th inst., a colored man named Savan Benert was arrested at New Iberia, La., charged with assaulting a white man named T. H. George, who afterwards died. After examination, the Sheriff transferred him from the Court House to the jail. On the way, an infuriated mob, maddened with whisky, threw a lasso over Benert’s head and dragged him to the nearest tree and hung him. He was dead, however, before being hung, having been choked to death by the lasso.” In the 3/9 Republican, his name is Vincent Benoit. According to the Times-Picayune, citing the Iberia Progress of the 6th, “... several parties” have been indicted and jailed for the lynching of Vincent Benoit; on the night of the 3rd, or possibly a day or two later, a crowd of 150 presented the sheriff with a petition to remove the men from the jail, and, inexplicably the sheriff told the crowd to open the jail themselves and release the prisoners, and they did.

notes:
The Statesman reports, “Fort Bend County.—L. J. Jones is reported killed by two freedmen named Allen Brooks and Mitchell Brooks, who have been arrested.” From the 2/26 News, “Richmond [Fort Bend Co.], Feb. 25.—Have just learned that Mr. L. J. Jones was killed night before last [23rd] at Wharton by two freedman named Allen Brooks and Mitchell Brooks. The freedmen have been arrested. No particulars.”
From the 3/29 News, “Letter from Wharton—Three of the Brooks Brothers Killed. Wharton, March 26, 1884 [sic]. Eds. News—The three Brooks brothers (colored), Allen, Mitchell and Bird, who were implicated in the murder of L. P. Jones, a merchant and respectable white citizen of this county, were shot and killed, and another brother, Alex. Brooks, was shot [illegible] seriously, if not fatally wounded, about midnight on the night of the twenty-fourth, by unknown parties.”

The Louisianian prints a letter from the Governor, presumably of Texas, refers to “... the murder of the four young colored men named Brooks in Wharton county in March last, without any charge against them whatever ....” The Times prints a letter from a T. C. Barden, of Victoria, Texas, dated Wednesday, 30 August, that “In Wharton County only a couple of years ago, Gray Franks, an ex-State Senator, since killed in the streets of Wharton, himself led a gang of whites to the Brooks plantation near Wharton, and calling the four Brooks brothers, all negroes, and all intelligent, prominent colored Republicans, to their doors at the dead hour of midnight, shot them dead in the presence of their families; and therefore not a single indictment has never been found in any court, although the names of this murderous gang were well known. Franks, not long after was killed by Lee Lacey.”—the letter describes the conflict between Lacey and Franks. From the  Times-Picayune, “Texas. ... Gray Franks was killed in Wharton on the 11th inst. by Texas Lacey. Franks was elected to the Senate of the Thirteenth Legislature.”

Note #1: couldn’t find in GenealogyBank.com or other reports in Newspapers.com or NewspaperArchive.com. This incident could have happened on the 24th. Going to assume that Allen/Allan, Mitchell, and Bird were lynched, and that a fourth brother, whose name is uncertain, might have been killed.

Note #2: Caldwell-DeLord cite the Times, the Louisianian, and the Times-Picayune. 1870 Wharton Co. census lists Allan Brooks, 16, living with his parents, and male sibs: Joe, 17, Calvin, 11, and Rosco, 3; Bird Brooks, 25, living with wife; and Mitchell Brooks, 28, living with wife and two children—everyone in Beat 2 of Wharton Co. Couldn’t find an Alex Brooks in Texas in 1870 or 1880 census.; can’t find Joe or Calvin Brooks in 1880 census in Texas. 1870 Wharton Co. census list a L. D. Jones, planter, Beat 3, age 23, who doesn’t appear in the 1880 census.

notes:
According to the 4/28 Republican, Sunday [26th] morning between 8 and 9, a band of “vigilantes” found three men suspected of being horse thieves and a fire fight ensued. The end result was three dead suspected horse thieves and one of the vigilantes was killed. From the 4/29 Republican, “Boughton, April 27, 1874. ... We are called upon again to witness a scene of blood and death. The peace and quiet of our little town and community was yesterday morning completely demoralized by a bloody tragedy which was enacted about three miles from here. Three men named Walker Hollingsworth, David DeLanter and William Murray, who were noted for the skill in stealing horses, have paid the penalty of their crimes. They were entirely void of fear—they, only three in number, facing thirteen determined men, armed with double-barrelled shotguns. They stole some horses near Fort Smith, and were pursued from there into Clark county, where some more horses were stolen by them and sold. A posse was raised in Clark county which followed and overtook them about three miles from this place, where they met their reward.”

Note: USGS places Boughton in Nevada Co. Couldn’t find in 1895 atlas. Nevada co. formed in 1871.

On Thursday [14th] a mob took them from the jail [presumably in Shreveport] but were persuaded to return them to jail. However, on Friday [15th], “At midnight a party of fifty armed men attacked the jail, removed Jones and Hill, and hanged him to trees in the court house yard.” The Picayune reports that 30-40 took Hill and Jones from the jail at midnight—the date could be either the 15th or 16th depending. The Republican states that fifty masked men attacked at the jail at 10:00 a.m. Sunday [17th] morning and then hanged Jones and Hill from the trees in the court-house yard. The Times has a report of finding a metal coffin on the property of “Doc” Jones who was lynched on the courthouse square in 1874; it doesn’t appear obvious whether the skeleton is Jones, or some one who Jones may have killed at this “dive” which was on the property. The 5/24 Republican says that Jones was 48 years old and was born in Virginia, and Oliver Hill was 26 years old and born in Ohio.

Note: Ed. Lucas was lynched as an accomplice to the Elliott murder on 11 June near Shreveport

notes:
The 6/9 News states that Thad Smith and wife, citizens of Refugio county, were murdered on the 7th by, it’s thought, by Mexicans. According to the 6/12 News, “St. Marys [Refugio Co.], June 11, 1874. On Tuesday [9th] five young men went to a Mexican ranche, on the Blanco, in search of the Swift murderers, and were fired on by the Mexicans, and Dan Holland, of the party, was killed. ... When the sheriff of Goliad county came up the Mexicans surrendered, three in number, but the ones suspected of the murder were not among them. It is since reported that the three Mexicans were taken from the sheriff’s posse and two shot and one hung. No trace of those implicated yet.”—this must have happened on the 9th. From the 6/13 Statesman, “Victoria [Victoria Co.], June 10.—Intelligence has been received here from Goliad, through a gentleman direction from that section, that there were three Mexicans implicated in the murder of Swift and his wife, near Refugio [Refugio Co.], last Sunday [7th] night. He states that the three murderers separated, each taking a different direction. One of them was overtaken by a party of ten citizens at a house west of Goliad [Goliad Co.], wherein was two other Mexicans. The house was surrounded, and one of the pursuers advanced to demand a surrender, when he was killed instantly by a shot from the house. The citizen pursers, having secured reinforcement, the Mexicans were besieged and compelled to surrender. They were sent forward to Goliad under guard, but were met on the way by a band of about fifty white men, who fired upon the Mexicans, killing all of the instantly.” From the Express, “A special to the Telegraph from Victoria says that three Mexicans implicated in the murder of Thad. Smith and wife, near Refugio, were arrested near Goliad [Goliad Co.], and shot by a body of citizens.”

Note: apparently the house where the three men were located, was 12-15 miles from Goliad—12 miles south of Goliad appears to near the border with Refugio county. Going to assume that the men were killed in Refugio county and that the mob was primarily from Refugio County—the lynching site could have been, however, in Goliad Co. near the Refugio County line. Carrigan-Webb cite the San Antonio Express, 12-16 June 1874, but could not locate in any reports in those editions where the names of the three men were given.

From the Gazette, “Shreveport, La., June 11.—Ed. We further say that the letter id not state one-half that the White League is doing for hardly a day has passed in the last two months that it was not reported that a man was found dead. Further, we will name some few places where men have been killed by unknown parties. ... Seventh, a colored man hung to a dogwood tree at Fairfield, only three miles from town.”

Note: C. T. Jones and Oliver Hill were lynched in Shreveport on 15 May for this murder

notes:
From the News, “From Bryan. Shot and Hung Inside the Jail Yard. Bryan, June 26, 1874. Last night at about 12 o’clock a large crowd of men took Harry Cook, the assassin of James P. Farmer, out of the jail and shot and hung him inside of the prison yard. J. A. Nelson, his accomplicate, it is said, was told to leave the State at once. The jail was guarded by 43 men, but they were powerless to prevent the hanging of Cook against the large number of about 200.” A slightly briefer account appears in the Statesman. In the Herald’s account, the jail was guarded by 73 men and the mob was 200, but the Express says the jail was guarded by 13 men and the mob was 200—a guard of 13 is a more reasonable number.

Note: this could have happened in the very early hours of 26 June. The 1870 Brazos Co. census lists a Harry Cook, 29, born in England, occupation barkeeper, married to Sarah Cook, 29, also born in England. 1880 Salt Lake City census list a Sarah Cook, 39, born in England, widowed, dressmaker, and a child Melbian Coo,.

[the alleged perpetrators were caught and jailed] ... Four o’clock Saturday evening, the 22nd, was determined upon as the time and the jail yard as the place for the execution, and the prisoners were notified to prepare for death. At the appointed time an immense crowd of people assembled—both black and white—all eager to participate in the work of hanging. Captain James A. Hoskins, a republican in politics, was selected to act as executioner, and cheerfully performed the duty assigned him. The prisoners were led, placed in a wagon, the rope tied around their necks and the wagon pulled from under them. Everything was done quietly and orderly, and every man in the community acknowledges having participated in the hanging, and is willing to bear his share of the responsibility. We glory in the manhood displayed by the people of Brookhaven on this occasion, and especially the white and black republicans, who have shown that they will not attempt to screen such hell-deserving villains on account of their race and color. We are opposed to lynch law under most circumstance, but in this instance we believe it was just and right in the sight of both God and man, and especially when we consider the law’s delays, and the tact that we have a Governor who pardons almost every black villain who commits a crime. We believe these scoundrels should have been burned instead of hanged.”—emphasis added

From the 1/28 News, citing the Dallas Commercial, writes, “On Monday [probably the18th] some wagoners found the dead body of a negro man hanging to a limb on Mountain Creek, near the Goodsell crossing, in this county, some fourteen miles from Dallas. It proved to be the body of a mulatto named Rube, and suspicion attaches to a man by the name of Dill. The brother of Dill had been arrested for stealing. This negro was bribed by a brother of Dill’s to swear to an alibi, and attend the court regularly. During the pending of the trial Dill escaped from jail. After the escape, the negro wen tot he brother and demanded his promised five dollars a day for his attendance. This he refused to pay, and the negro then informed on him, when he was arrested for bribery, and released under bonds. The wife of the negro man says that Dill came to their house some two weeks ago and took him out, and nothing more was seen of him until his dead body was found. His throat was cut, which was evidently done before he was hung.” The Weekly Herald reports that Marion Dill has been charged with “... being one of the party who hung and afterward cut the throat of a negro boy, a few miles from this city, in January last.”—bond was set at $10,000 so Dill was remanded to jail. The Tri-Weekly Herald says “Dallas Commercial of the 3rd, says: Marion Dill, brother of William Dill, the notorious express robber, who was yesterday arrested in Jacksboro, has been lying in jail for several months, charged with the murder of a negro, named Reuben Johnson. The negro had give testimony before the grand jury, charging Marion Dill and others with robbery. After this, Dill and his crowd caught the negro, and after hanging him a to tree for some time, took him down and cut his throat. Dill was subsequently arrested, and now lies in jail. The friends of Dill, consisting principally of murderers, thieves, and robbers, swear that he shall never be hung or go to the penitentiary, and Sheriff Barclay has been aware that these ruffians have been congregating here [Dallas] for several days, intent upon releasing him from jail.” The 7/3 Daily Herald reports the testimony of George W. Nelly, who states that he found Johnson hanging “about 20th of January 1875”; a Calm Read testified that “In Christmas in 1874” Reuben Johnson was staying at his house, when, around midnight, three men came to Read’s and took Reuben Johnson away on a Sunday night, which could have been on the 20th or 27th of December, but Mrs. Bell testified that Dill and Rice took her husband out the Sunday night after Christmas—the 27th—and her husband returned a couple of hours later; her husband, William Bell, stated that that the incident happened on January 27, 1874—that’s not possible, likely December 27, 1874, and that night Johnson was hanged and had his throat cut by Dill; the date of 27 December is also verified by the testimony of a Charles Deitz. According to the 2/21/1878 News, the facts in the Marion Dill murder case: “The facts of the case, an old one, are: In 1874, William Dill, brother of the deceased, was indicted for theft of wheat from Henry Taylor. Reuben Johnson, colored, living on Dill’s place, was the only witness for the State. Marion Dill tried to get him to swear to certain fictitious circumstances to prove an alibi. Johnson refused, and Marion Dill was indicted for subornation and released on bond. To get Johnson out of the way, it was determined to kill him. Marion Dill, Elijah Rice and one Bell went to his house, ten miles distant, secured him, hung and and cut his throat.”—on the stand, Bell testified that Dill and Rice hung Johnson, and then to make sure he was dead, Dill cut Johnson’s throat. 

Note: at Dill’s trial, 10 voted for conviction and 1 for not guilty.

notes:
The Sentinel reports that about six miles from Colfax, a Mrs. Lacour lived with her 17 year-old daughter and her two sons. On then night of the 28th, some black men fired shots into her house; Lacour and her children fled and sought refuge in the home of a black woman, and later fled toward the woods. “They had not, however, gone but a short distance before they were overtaken by one of the negroes ... whom both recognized as Hampton Henderson, a colored man of a notoriously bad character, who three or four years ago outraged and murdered a colored woman.” Henderson then raped the daughter in the presence of her mother, and fled. A Mr. Wells went to the home of Henderson and exchanged gun fire but Henderson escaped and is now being hunted. The Democrat states that Hamp Henderson [22] and four other unnamed negroes were killed by the citizens of Grant parish. From the Gazette, citing the Picayune of the 11th, “Last evening we learned the sad intelligence of the death of Miss Lacour, the unfortunate victim of the Grant parish outrage.” And then, “A New Orleans dispatch of the 14th says: The Times’ special reports the killing by citizens of seven of the nine negroes recently implicated in the Grant parish outrage [the rape of Miss Lacour].” The Argus states that Miss Lacour died from injuries resulting from an outrage in Grant Parish but the 11/16 Times-Picayune, however, states that Miss Lacour is not dead and that rumor had been started by a deranged uncle, and “Miss Lacour recognized Henderson as one of the party who committed the outrage, and he, Henderson, having confessed to the guilt of the others, was in turn accused by them of equal complicity. Four of the negro perpetrators of this appalling crime have been shot, but not before the positive identity had been had of each one’s guilt.” From the Express, citing the New Orleans Republican, “Additional particulars have been received which fasten the Lacour outrage in Grant parish, upon one ‘Hamp’ Henderson, a former slave ....” The American reports, dateline Bayou Sara, 13 November, that Hampton Henderson and two unnamed black men were arrested and brought to Colfax on Sunday, the 9th, and turned over to the sheriff, “... but citizens took charge of them, conveying them in the direction of C. C. Nash’s residence. They were shot after confessing that nine others were concerned in the attack on Madame Lacour’s residence. Mumford Wells shot two more the day following, near Mr. Loushard’s house .... On Tuesday [11th] fifteen citizens from Alexandria surprised three more hiding from arrest. Another one was hung in Rapides parish the same day. 

While reporting on a case of alleged embezzlement, the 5/22 Times-Picayune writes, “After the difficulty at Colfax, in 1873, the tax collector of that district declined to serve, and Mumford Wells, a large planter in the section, was appointed as such. He, it appears, went quietly to work collecting, and had gather some two thousand dollars in money when the outrage on Miss Lacour occurred. She being some relative of Wells, he very properly got together a few friends and lynched the negro who perpetrated the outrage. Fearing arrest under the Ku-Klux act, and knowing the horrors of imprisonment to which he would be here subjected, he gathered up his books and papers and fled to Texas, leaving his deputy, M. S. Peeler [who would later be charged with embezzlement] behind, with a copy of  the books and rolls.”

Note: it is clear that Hampton Henderson and likely three others were lynched on the 9th near Colfax.

From the Chronicle, “Lexington, Ky., Nov. 4, 1872.—The ku-klux took from their home in East Hickman precinct, in Fayette county, near Lexington, night before last, a Republican negro named Samuel Hawkins, his wife, and daughter, and carried them to the Kentucky river, where it is supposed they were drowned. Their bodies were found yesterday. ... No special charge was made against him. The supposed object was the intimidation of republican voters. No steps have been taken to discover the murderers.” From the Patriot, “Lexington, Ky., April 10.—Last Fall a negro family of three persons—a husband, wife and daughter—were taken from their home in Jessamine county, and was supposed to have been drowned in Marble Head [Marble Creek in USGS] by the Ku-Klux. On Sunday last a negro, while fishing, drew up a half decomposed body which was recognized by the clothing as Mahala Harokins, the murdered wife of the family mentioned. Her arms and legs were pinioned, and a fifteen pound rock tied to her feet.” Essentially the same report appears in the Advertiser, and other newspapers, with the name Mahala Hawkins. The Gazette prints a letter: “A little more than one year ago, in Jessamine County, about seven miles from Nicholasville, the county seat, and about twenty miles from Lexington, a colored man, his wife and daughter, were taken from their home in the night by a gang of mounted men, and have not since been heard of. It was rumored a few months ago, that the body of the woman had been found in a neighboring creek, and hands and feet still severally bound together with cords. This man was of more than ordinary promise. He was industrious, and was getting on in the world. He was the father of a numerous family, had purchased a piece of land, got a house built, and was in excellent repute. ... No arrests in this case, although it was reported that 25 mounted men were engaged in the abduction and murder of the three negroes. One would suppose that the girl would have been spared, but the party probably found that some of them were recognized, and the girl was old enough to be a witness. [signed] L. L. Pinkerton, Late Professor of Belles Lettres and Political Science in Kentucky University, Lexington, Sept. 11.” From the Times, “Lawless Kentucky. The Louisville Courier-Journal commends to the attention of the Kentucky Legislature, which recently refused to pass a bill for the repression of lawlessness, the provisions of which were commended by the Governor of Kentucky in a carefully prepared message, the facts of a murder committed in Montgomery Count, the other day, by a band of masked gentry by courtesy called outlaws, and in reality scoundrels and cowards, whose mates, belike are not to be found in any community in the civilized world, outside of Kentucky. The Journal continues: ... In Jessamine County, ... a family of three or four negroes, two of them, as we recollect it, were children, after being foully murdered were dumped into sacks and sunk in the Kentucky River.

Note: according to the 1870 census, there’s no George (of appropriate age) or Samuel Hawkins in Fayette Co. there’s a Samuel Hawkins, 40, living with his wife Mahala Hawkins, 28, and children: Francis Hawkins, 15, and five other children in District 3, Jessamine Co. Jessamine County borders Fayette County on the south—apparently the Hawkins family lived in Jessamine Co., right on the Fayette Co. border.

The negroes are flying in terror to Frankfort.” According to the Herald, on the 11th, sixteen Ku klux rode into Stamping Ground where they shot at a black man but he ran away. Next “They then rode down the Frankfort turnpike. Pretty soon they came to where an old colored man named Cupid, who was a shoemaker, lived. He threw up his hand to beg their mercy, but they fired, and one shot striking the hand shattered it, and passing through him, he fell dead. They rode on to what is know as the Watkins place, where four or five parties of well-doing blacks resided, and at once being firing on them. They shot one black man in the bowels, and he will certainly die. ... By this fire of the blacks, one of the Ku-Klux, who seemed second in command, was shot through the breast and died soon afterward. 
According to the Republican, the ku klux attacked the blacks then “The blacks seized their arms and returned their fire killing one kuklux dead, and shooting another through the body. A general fire was then opened on both sides, but it soon became too hot for the mask murderers, and they rode off, leaving one dead man and two dead horses on the field. Four of the negroes were wounded, but none dangerously. An inquest was held over the dead kuklux yesterday, and he turns out to be a man from Henry county named Force.” From the 3/20/1873 Gazette, “1871.—January 11—[ku klux] Visit Stamping Ground, just over the Scott line, and kill one or two old negroes. Same night attack negroes at Lee Watkins’ near Forks of Elkhorn, Foree, of Henry County, killed in the attack, and possibly one of the negroes shot.” From the 4/3/1871 Gazette’s list of murders and outrages in Kentucky: “Ku-Klux attack negro cabins at Stamping Ground, in Scott. Forse [one of the ku klux] and two negroes killed.” From the Memorial, “No. 108. Ku-Klux visited negro cabin at Stamping Ground, in Scott County; forces (white) and Ku-Klux killed two negroes; negroes killed in self-defense.” According to the Tribune, the 15-20 ku-klux were from Henry County.

Note #1: it seems likely that at a minimum two blacks were killed by ku klux in Scott county, Cupid near Stamping Ground and an unnamed black man near Fork Elkhorn. Going to consider the deaths of the two black men and the coincidental death of the white ku klux, Force/Forse/Foree, as one incident.

From the Index, “Charleston, Feb. 14—Much excitement prevails in Columbia owing to the outrages of the Ku-Klux in the upper counties. notes: From the Herald-Tribune, “Raleigh, May 2.—The Sentinel publishes to-day an account of a terrible outrage said to have been committed near Rutherford Court House. Silas Weston, a free negro before the war, has been for many years been living with Polly Steadman, a white woman of loose character, who has or had four white children, the oldest about 14, the youngest nearly 2 years of age. ... The sworn deposition of the woman, Polly Steadman, states that on Wednesday evening, April 26, shortly after nightfall ... the dog began to bark violently; looking through the chinks between the logs, she received a pistol bullets in the eye. The [three] men mentioned above then rushed in, shot Silas dead, and struck down the children. The bed-clothes were piled on the floor and fired, and the men departed. The woman managed to drag herself and one child, less injured than the rest, out doors. The others were burned as they lay. The assassins have been arrested.” The Telegram gives the location is 11 miles north of Rutherfordton and “A party of three men entered the house of Silas Weston, a negro, shot and stabbed to death himself and three of his children, and leaving for dead his wife and an infant. They then set fire to house saying ‘now lets leave as fast as hell will let us.’”—the wife escaped and testified that Govan Adair, Columbus Adair and Martin Bayner were the perpetrators who have been captured and jailed at Rutherfordton.” According to a long story in the Patriot, this happened at night on the 25th. From the Herald, “A family, consisting of the husband, wife and four children, residing in Rutherford county, North Carolina, were at their evening repast one evening, when an armed band of masked men broke into their cottage ... murdered the Elias [Silas later in the article] and three children, horribly mutilated Elias’s wife, Polly [she survived]. They then burned down the house. The murdered children were: David Weston, age 8; Theodosia Weston, age 6; William Herbert Steadman, age 10-12—he was the son of Polly from a previous marriage. Two of the lynchers, Columbus Adair and Govan Adair, were legally executed on 12 July 1872 in Hendersonville; a third one was convicted as well Martin Baynard. The report in the Jeffersonian gives the location of the lynching as Morgan Township, and specifies that Polly Steadman was white while Silas was a “free negro” before the war.

He was soon afterwards lodged in the County jail at Madison. ... Accordingly, a few nights after his incarceration a body of disguised mounted men visited Madison for the purpose of administering summary punishment to the culprit, but owing to the absence of the jailer and being unable to force the doors of the jail, they failed to carry out their designs. The next day, when the news of the Ku Klux raid became known, the negroes, who are nearly in the majority there, became fearfully excited and riotous in their demeanor. They assembled in large numbers, armed themselves, and avowed their determination to protect the prisoner at the hazard of their lives, and even threatened to release him. ... On yesterday morning, however, between twelve and one o’clock, a huge force of men entered the town and reparted towards the jail. notes:
According to the American, ... “On last Wednesday [26th] night near 11 o’clock the house of Mr. Francis J. Knight, who owns a mill, and who resides a mile from Decatur, Ala., was surrounded by a party of men supposed to number thirty or forty, a part of whom were armed with shot guns and other arms. Mr. Knight, who is sixty years of age, was called out, and, suspecting no mischief, obeyed the summons. As soon as he appeared they commenced firing upon him. ... His right arm was shattered with buckshot, and he received several wounds in other parts. They declared it to be their intention to take his life. But it being night-time, the old man eluded them. They left and in his wounded and bleeding condition he returned to his house .... While still prostrate, the armed men returned to his house on last Sunday [30th] night. Unceremoniously entering, they commenced firing in indiscriminately though the bedding. Quivering under their fire, and received some of the shot,the old man feigned to be dead, and really he was not far from it. Supposing their work complete, the party left. ... [some friends carried Knight, in his bullet riddled bed, to Nashville for care and “it is thought he will recover] ... Mr. Knight says that he did not know that he had an enemy in the world, and assigns no special cause for this deliberate attempt upon his life, though he says he has his ideas about it, which he prefers not divulging at the present.” According to the Enquirer, citing the Nashville Union, “T. J. Knight, the old gentleman who was riddled with buckshot near Decatur, Alabama, and brought to Nashville a few days ago, died of his wounds at St. Vincent Hospital Sunday morning. Coroner P. W. Brien held an inquest over his remains, and the jury rendered a verdict that he ‘came to this death from gun-shot wounds from the hands of Alexander Tarver and Polk Mackner.’ ... [Tarver wanted Knights home and property] ... In order to carry out his [Tarver’s] sanguinary designs he collected together, one night, two weeks ago, a band of ruffians, twenty in number, went to Knight’s house, forced an entrance, and with muskets riddled Knight’s bed and body with buckshot. They left Knight for dead, but the shot had inflicted only a few slight wounds. Subsequently discovering that they had failed in their bloody purpose, the assassins returned, poured another volley into Knight and again left him for dead. ... To prevent further attempts upon his life he was brought to Nashville, but only to die in the midst of strangers. The murdered man was sixty-five years of age.” After reporting testimony on ku klux violence in Alabama, the Journal notes: “In 1869, Jesse Knight, a local preacher, was shot in his own house in Morgan county, and died in a few days. He had lived all his live [sic] in the county where he was shot. He was a steady, sober, and intelligent man, almost universally respected.” The Critic-Record notes that the “troubles” in Morgan county continue, but no details.

notes: The 2/4 Sun states “Wyche Drumgoole, a colored man, has confessed the murder of Mrs. Basset Rawlings, in Brunswick co., Va., reported several days ago. From the Standard, citing the Petersburg Courier, “Wyche Drumgoole, a colored man, and the brother to [illegible] who had been discharged by Mrs. Rawlings, on Sunday night confessed that he committed the murder, and that he was hired to do so by cook’s husband. He says he approached Mrs. Rawlings’ window, aimed his gun at her and pulled the trigger, but it missed fire. He then took his gun down and cleared away [illegible]. In this way and taking deliberate aim, his gun was discharged. The rumor that Drumgoole and Hammock had been treated to a bit of lynch law was unfounded—they are no in jail awaiting that punishment which we trust the law will award them. So, says the Roanoke News.” From the 3/7 Sun, citing the Petersburg Index, “Toward the end of last January Mrs. Bassett Rawlings, of the county of Brunswick, was murdered while sitting in her chamber, being shot dead from the outside of the house. Suspicion fell upon two negro men by name Wyche and Harrison Hammock, who had some difficulty with the husband of the murdered woman. They were arrested and held in jail for trial. Since their arrest it is said that one or both of them confessed the deed. On Monday [28th] last a party of men broke into the jail of Brunswick county and put to death one of the men, leaving the other also for dead.” From the Advertiser, citing the Petersburg Index, “The negroes were lodged in the jail at Lawrenceville for trial, where they remained until Monday last, court day. At a late hour of that night, we are informed, the jail was forced by unknown persons—all disguised—and the negroes were shot in their cells. They were left for dead, though on the following day both were found to be still alive. The murderer (Wyche) has since died, and the probability is that Hammock will die also. There is no the least suspicion, we hear, who the attacking parties were, nor is it known whether they were white or colored.” The Times reports that Harrison Hammock survives.

name: Henry Miller
accusation: Murdering a white man
chicago_tribune: Chicago Tribune inventory covers the years 1882-1918
