notes:
The Times-Argus reports, “Sam Colvin, jr., and Henry Miller (negroes) are in the Greene county jail for killing Samuel A. Snoddy a few weeks ago.” The 2/23 Alabamian states, citing the Eutaw Whig, “We understand that Henry Miller, a freedman committed to jail, on a preliminary trial, for the murder of the late Samuel Snoddy, has made a full and free confession that he and he alone committed the murder.” From the 4/6 Alabamian, “We learn, through private sources, that the negroes charged with the murder of Samuel Snoddy, who made their escape from the Eutaw jail, were recently captured and hung.” The Republican reports, “Ku Klux in Greene County. On, or about the 7th of March, an industrious and peaceful colored man named Sam. Colvin, was found hung to a tree near Union, Greene county, with sixteen bullets holes in his body. No arrests have been made, and no notice of the murder has been given by the Ku Klux organ of that county.” According to the Advertiser, “The facts of the case demonstrate that the disorders in the county [Greene] commenced with the robbery and cruel murder of a respectable and aged citizen (white) Mr. Sam’l Snoddy, by a number of negroes. Some of these negroes were arrested and confined in prison, but subsequently escaped, as was suspected by the criminal connivance of outside parties. They were, however, subsequently again caught and together with an old colored man, who had harbored them, after their escape from prison, were killed by parties unknown, but supposed to be the friends of the murdered citizen, Mr. Snoddy. After reporting testimony on ku klux violence in Alabama, the Journal notes: “Hon. William Miller, Collector of the port at Mobile (a resident of Green county, Alabama, since 1836...) ... In December, 1869, Sam. Colvin, Sam. Caldwell, and Henry Miller (the latter having once been the property of witness) were arrested on suspicion of having murdered one Sam. Snoddy, (white). Henry Miller and Sam. Caldwell escaped from jail, after which Henry Miller was found dead a few days after, and Caldwell has never been seen since, although a skeleton was found afterwards supposed to be his. About the same time Sam. Colvin was taken from jail by a band of men, supposed to be the same who murdered the other two, and was found hung, with sixteen bullet holes in him.”

Note: since no other reports mention an old man, going to ignore. Eutaw is the county seat. The date is not clear but in late February or early March. Going to count as one incident with two victims although they may have been killed on different dates.

name: Jack Burton
accusation: Altercation with ku klux
chicago_tribune: Chicago Tribune inventory covers the years 1882-1918
daniel_williams_tuskegee: Williams inventory covers the years 1882-1964
eji: EJI inventory covers the years 1877-1950
naacp: NAACP Thirty Years of Lynching covers the years 1889-1918, with 1919 in appendix
notes:
From the Gazette, reporting on testimony on ku klux violence, “Jack Burton, killed at Lauderdale in the spring of 1870, by disguised men. —Kaizer, shot, and lost an arm at the same time.”—in the 10/25 Gazette his name is spelled Krizer”. From the Herald, citing the Meriden [sic] Mercury of 5 March, “Some time recently a party of white men pursued a negro from Alabama, who had committed some aggravated crime and taken to flight, and captured him at Lauderdale [station?]. They proceeded to bind him with cords to secure him to take him back. Two negroes, somewhat distinguished as prominent Loyal Leaguers and leaders of their race in that neighborhood interposed serious objection to the proceeding—namely, Jack Burton, a member of the Board of County Police, late slave of one of the Burtons, of Sumter county, Ala., and Wesley Kiser, late slave of R. J. Mosley, our present sheriff. Burton confined his objections to a protest, but Kiser raised a crowd of negroes and pursued the party with the prisoner, starting with a threat to rescue him [the unnamed black man] or die in the attempt. These facts probably have some connection with the mysterious homicides at Lauderdale last night [4th]. Burton and Kiser had lately built a hut a little beyond the far end of the switch, and were sleeping there last night, when a few minutes before the arrival of the down mail train a party of white men entered their cabin, and by the light of a single match which they struck fired upon them in the bed. They were both wounded, but both sprang out of bed and dashed by the men who had come with such deadly intent. It was a vain effort at escape—they were both quickly shot down in front of the cabin. ... Jack Burton, the member of the Board of County Police was killed. Wesley Kiser was not dead at latest accounts, and it is barely possible may recover. One of his arms has been amputated, and it is said the surgeons are of opinion that the other arm may have to be amputated. This morning a negro woman, Eliza Smith, arrived from Lauderdale, went before E. L. Bramlette, and made affidavit that J. T. Jamison and four other persons to her unknown were the parties to the killing.” Essentially the same report appears in the Enquirer, which says that Kiser is dying.

Note: couldn’t find a Wesley Kiser/Kaizer/Krizer/Kaiser in 1870 or 1880 Mississippi census—going to assume he died of his wounds. Couldn’t find a J. T. Jamison in either Mississippi or Alabama in 1870 census. The 1870 census lists John Burton, 40, black, living with his family in Lauderdale Co.

Two of the persons hanged were brothers, by name, Lunn, and the third was one John Smith, whose numerous namesake will, no doubt, no insist on claiming kin with him. The hanging of these men, though an extreme measure ... to have been an act of simple justice.” After reporting on the murder of Joe Grimes by, apparently, the same men who hung the Lunns, the Bulletin has this to say: The Lunns were all ardent Confederates hated a Yankee like a viper, and thought it no moral wrong to kill a nigger; and all of the known members and sympathizers of the gang (excepting a few weak ones,) were at all time violent Confederates.”

Note: going to assume a date of 19 June. 1870 Matagorda census lists a Benjamin Lunn, 25; William Lunn, 23, (and his 22 year-old wife, Annie E. Lunn) and Edwin Lunn, 21—all born in Mississippi and all living together on Nelson’s Creek and Tres Palacios. The 1880 Fayette Co., Texas census lists Edwin D. Lunn, 9, living with his parents W. W. Lunn, 33, born in Mississippi and A. E. Lunn, 33, born in Texas. Based on these census data, going to assume that the two brothers who were hung were Benjamin and Edwin. There were two possible John Smith’s in 1870 Matagorda census: John B. Smith, 38; John R. Smith, 16; John M. Smith, 34—John B. and John R. both were living Nelson’s Creek and Tres Palacios, whereas John M. Smith was living in the “Colorado Valley East and West of River”. John B. Smith appears in the 1880 Matagorda census.

The News reports, dateline Bernard, 29 June, “After the execution of the outlaws [the two Lunn brothers and John Smith], a part of the other assembly [the lynchers] came upon a cabin near Elliott’s old ferry, on the Colorado, in which a negro, a desperate villain and one of the gang of freebooters, was found. With a view of making him disclose the hiding places of others, they called on him to come out and surrender. He advanced to the door and fired, killing young Edward Anderson, of Wharton, and was himself thereupon shot down. It is unfortunate that the negro was killed ....” From the Bulletin, “Trespalacios Creek, June 24. On Thursday, the 23d, a squad of citizens, who are laudably engaged in ridding the country of brigands and murderers, surrounded house on Jenning’s Creek, belonging to a freedman named Joe Grimes, thinking that they had entrapped one or more of the rascals (Wilburn Lunn was thought to be inside). One of the squad (Mr. Edward Anderson, son of James Anderson, of Wharton), approached very near to the house, and called to the inmates to open the door. Joe Grimes, who was in the house answered that he was in bed, but would open the door as soon as he could dress himself; in the next moment he fired a double-barreled shot gun at Anderson, though the window killing him instantly. The life of Joe Grimes, the freedman, quit its earthly tenement by fourteen bullet holes, which penetrated his vile carcass. No other members of the fraternity were found in the house. ... Jenning’s Creek run into the Colorado river in Matagorda county, on the west side, a short distance above [upstream] the ‘Old Geo. Elliott Ferry.’ ... The Lunns were all ardent Confederates hated a Yankee like a viper, and thought it no moral wrong to kill a nigger; and all of the known members and sympathizers of the gang (excepting a few weak ones,) were at all time violent Confederates.” The same story appears in the Weekly Bulletin.

After reporting testimony on the lynchings at Cross Plains, the Journal notes “On the same night [as the lynchings in Cross Plains, 11 July 1870], and by the same band of disguised men that perpetrated the above [Cross Plains, Calhoun Co.] outrage, Essex Hendricks, an old colored man, was put to death by hanging and shooting. Some eight persons were arrested charged with having been concerning in these murders, but the grand jury declined to find any bill against them.” From the Telegraph, “The Rome Courier, of Sunday [24th], says the parties who were indicted as accessories to the murder of the negro who was shot by disguised men near Griffth’s Mill, at the time of the Cross Plains [Calhoun Co.] riot, about a year since, were tried at Center [Centre, Cherokee Co.] last Wednesday, and acquitted. Johnson, of Floyd county [Georgia], was one of the party.”—it is not clear, however, if this report is referring to the lynching of Essex Hendricks/Hendrick or Green Little. Johnson, of Floyd county [Georgia], was one of the party.”—it is not clear, however, if this report is referring to the lynching of Essex Hendricks/Hendrick or Green Little. From the 7/17 Appeal, Information was received in the city on Friday ... that a young man named Schofield, aged between eighteen and twenty years old, had been brutally and inhumanly murdered by a band of armed and disguised men, at or near Cuba station, on Thursday [14th] night. ... Later he hinted to them that he knew something [a particularly unwise decision]. He was then arrested on the charge of stealing and place under a ice-house by the constable. There he was strung up by his thumbs and tortured. Later he was removed and hanged. The Enquirer story retells the events leading to Schofield’s lynching but doesn’t give a date. From the Herald, “Memphis, April 1. ... An application for a new trial of the case of Poston and Graes, convicted of K Kluxing young Scofield, near Cuba, this county, was overruled by Judge Flippin to-day, and they were sentenced to be hung on the 20th of May.”

From the Herald, “Beck, the murderer of the Good family on favorite [illegible] who was brought through here last week from Indiana by the sheriff was taken from jail at Austin [Tunica Co.], Miss., yesterday morning by forty citizens, taken to l_wor_e [Favorite] Island and hung to a tree over the sport where he had buried Mrs. Good. He it said, acknowledged the murder.” From the Inquirer, “Memphis, Aug. 11.—Beck, the murderer of the Good family on Favorite Island, who was brought through here last week from Indiana by the Sheriff of Tunica county, Miss., was taken  from the jail at Austin, Miss., yesterday, by a party of citizens, and hanged to a tree over the spot where he had buried Mrs. Good.” The same story appears in the Critic-Record. The Gazette reports that Charles Beck, 18, was accused of murdering a family named Goode on Favorite Island, Tunica county, Miss.; “On the 10th inst. he was taken out of Tunica County Jail by a masked mob, put on board one of a fleet of twenty-five or thirty skiffs and carried to Favorite Island to a tree beneath which one of his victims, old Mrs. Goode, was buried.” Beck was from Indiana and, apparently, changed his name when he came to Mississippi to William Saunders; he also said reportedly, he had been “idle and had followed about a menagerie and circus.” The Patriot, citing the Memphis Avalanche of the 12th, reports that “On Wednesday morning a large number of men gathered around the jail in Austin, took the prisoner out by force, brought hi down to the river’s edge, placed him in a skiff and rowed up the river to Favorite Island, and hung him to a tree over the sport where the aged Goodes fell beneath a murderer’s axe some two months ago. Another account, from what appears to be a reliable source, says that ... twenty men took Beck out of jail, manned a fleet of skiffs as a sort of guard, and the prisoner was rowed across the river by the waning light of the moon on Wednesday morning, about 8 o’clock, to a sand-bar on the Arkansas shore, and there, under the long shadows of the trees, the crowd fathered round their victim, and feasted their drunken eyes upon his pallid face and trembling lips and tottering limbs, while curses and blasphemies disturbed the quietude of the morning air. ... A grave was scooped out of the sand .... [Beck was thrown into the grave.] Two or three of the stoutest stood upon his body while the hole was being filled up, lifting their feet every now and then to keep on a level with the rising sand. As the sand went in these men actually danced upon the smothering victim beneath, and the whole crowd broke out in an unearthly song. At length, when the hole was filled up and heaped over, a ‘stag dance’ was improvised, and twenty vigilantes carried on the revel till the sun rose above the horizon ....” According to the Times-Democrat, — Beck “... acknowledged to having outraged old Mrs. Goode before murdering her.”

Note: its possible that the location of Beck’s murder could be in Lee Co., Arkansas—that’s across the Mississippi river from Austin.

notes:
The 11/11 Banner reports, “From the Lebanon Herald of yesterday [10th], we obtain the following details of the cowardly assassination of a poor old negro, by miscreants in masks, a short distance from the town of Lebanon. ... [he was shot on the 4th] ... The victim was a negro man named Nathan Shorter, who lived on what is known as ‘the Fred. Golladay place,’ about two miles and a half north-east of Lebanon, between the Hartsville and the Hunter’s Point pikes. About twelve o’clock on the night above mentioned, a party of from five to ten, completely disguised and armed, entered the yard in front of Shorter’s residence, and called to him to come out. As soon as he appeared on the portch, he was asked if he had a gun. Before he had time to reply, one of the party cried, ‘Kill the d__d scoundrel!’ and another, who carried a shot-gun, immediately fired at Shorter. The charge, which consisted of seven buckshot, took effect in his breast, and he fell and died almost instantly. The men then went off together. ... Nathan Shorter was well known by many of our citizens. He was an old man, and had the reputation, among the white people and his own race, of an honest, reliable, industrious and inoffensive negro, who took no part in politics. ... His murderers were disguised with high conical hats of paste-board, and otherwise arrayed in the paraphernalia supposed to be peculiar to the ghostly brotherhood.” According to the Chronicle, “The friends of reconstruction seem to be at work in Middle Tennessee. On Friday night, a body of masked men called Nathan Shorter, a colored man, from his residence near Lebanon and killed him. The presumption is that he voted the Republican ticket, and foreited his life therefor.” The 12/13 Banner offers the theory that Shorter was killed by blacks because “Shorter was the friend of the white.”

Note: interestingly the only reasons offered for his murder was political: he voted conservative (i.e., Democrat) and was killed by blacks, or he voted Republican and he was killed by whites.

According to the Southerner, citing the Goldsboro Messenger, a gang of robbed the tomb of one John Williams, a wealthy and highly respected citizen of Kingston; on the 21st the sheriff and posse got involved with the allege grave robbers in which one black man was killed; “Several negroes, and the one white man were arrested and brought in. In the 9/10 Journal, while reporting on the trial of some of the lynchers notes that the victims were Richard Nobles (white), Robert Grady, Cater Grady, Jno. Miller, and Daniel /Dan Smith. According to the Commerce, the mob numbered seventy-five men took, on 24 January, Richard Nobles (white), Bob Grady, Cater Grady, and Daniel Smith from the Kinston jail where they were accused of “murder, rape, and arson. They were imprisoned ... for violating the person of Mrs. Frank Miller ... ; burning of several dwelling-houses; and for the murder of Mr. John Miller and wife.” The 9/10 Watchman states that the prisoners were accused of murdering Col. Nethercutt, the “Foscue’s whole family slain; John Miller and wife were brutally murdered, and the person of a respectable lady was violated.” 

Note: the 9/10 Journal states, page 1, citing the Raleigh Standard, that “A. Monroe, a young lawyer of Kinston, has been arrested, charged with complicity in the bridge murders last winter, in which several persons were taken fro Kinston jail, brutally murdered and their bodies thrown off the bridge into Neuse river.” The Pioneer has more on the many persons arrested in this lynching.

notes: From the Mobile Register, “Augusta, March 13. Dr. G. W. From the Dealer, “An Atlanta Georgia special to the Tribune gives details of the murder of Dr. Darden by the Ku Klux. It appears that in a personal difficulty with Wallace, editor of the Ku Klux paper at Warrenton, Darden shot Wallace; he immediately surrendered to the civil authorities and was placed in jail. On Friday, Sheriff Norris fearing that Darden would be unsafe there, called on the better class of citizens to act as a posse to guard the jail over night, but the citizens declined to act, being overawed by a band of Ku Klux numbering about one hundred who had taken possession of the town. This band demanded the keys of the jail from the Sheriff. On his refusal to deliver them up their demonstrations became so violent that he was compelled to seek safety in flight, taking the keys with him. The band at midnight returned to the jail and broke in, but fearing that Darden had a pistol, the cowardly assassins built a fire at the door way and smoked him out. Dr. Darden asked of them time to make a will, which was granted. He was then taken out in presence of his wife and children and barbarously murdered by these savages, not less than 150 pistol balls piercing his body.” The Columbia Register mentions the lynching of a Dr. Darden by the kuklux for killing a man named Wallace.

From the South-Western, citing the Texas Republican of the 9th, “A young man by the name of Col. Green, who is said to have been a new settler in the county, left Henderson on Saturday evening last [3rd], in a state of intoxication, for home. When he got about seven miles from town, on the Marshall road, he stopped at the widow Griffin place, where a body of negroes were making a crop, and ordered his supper. While eating it he was seized by five negroes, who tired his hands behind him, dragged him about a half mile and hung him. They treated him very brutally, throwing him over the fences as they reached them, bruising his face and otherwise maltreating him. While he was hanging they rolled back a log, dug a trench, threw him in it before life was extinct, and then rolled the log back to its former place. Two of the negroes were preachers. The principal one engaged in the murder, Julius Jones, stood by with a gun, directing the others, and telling them he would kill the first one that flinched. ... Five negroes were arrested, who confessed the crime, and were taken to Henderson and placed in jail. This was on Monday [5th]. On Tuesday [6th] night, about 11 o’clock, a mob went to the jail, and hung every one of them on the public square, fronting each side of the court house, the two preachers together.” Essentially the same account appears in the Times-Picayune, and other out-of-state newspapers. The 4/14 News, citing the Henderson Times of the 7th, states that the white man was Col. Peter Green and that he stopped at the negro cabins on the “plantation of Mrs. Griffin”, and he ordered some negroes to feed him, which led to an altercation: “Whilst he was eating he laid his pistol down. This was taken by a negro man, Isaac, the occupant of the cabin. By this time two other negro men, Jordan Jones, Sam, Henry Brown and Julius __, were in the room—Jordan Jones armed with his gun, and Julius with an axe. Jordan Jones gave orders to tie the hands of Col. Green behind him, which order was carried out by Sam and Isaac. Immediately after he was tired, the negroes carried him across the plantation. Sam and Henry leading him. At the back of the plantation, about three-quarters of a mile from the cabins, they hung him to a hickory tree until dead.”—no mention of Green being beaten or dragged or dumped into a trench. From the 4/23 News, “Speaking of the lynching of the negroes who murdered Col. Green, the last Henderson Times says: On Friday a squad of U. S. soldiers arrived from Necogdoches [sic] to look into the matter and ascertain the facts in reference to the hanging of the negroes. On Saturday Mr. Green, a brother of Col. Green, proclaimed that he was the leader of the party who hung the negroes. He was immediately arrested and placed under guard.” According to the Bulletin, citing the Henderson Times, a mob of 50 disguised men attacked the jail “about midnight” and hanged three in front of the Baptist church and two near the court house, also that Jordan was a preacher.

The Times reports, citing the Tuskaloosa [Independent] Monitor of the 27th, that on the 20th, a young white man named Murchison Findley, was shot and killed on the Cochrane plantation, four miles from Northport, when he and three of his friends approached the cabin of a family of “bad negroes”—it was believed that a man named Levi, “son of old Aaron”, fired the fatal shot. “In a subsequent article the Monitor states that three of the negroes who were engaged in the murder were pursued and overtaken by a party of men, and, upon refusing to surrender and showing fight, were instantly shot.” The Republican writes, “The Tuskaloosa Riot. For two weeks past our city has been filled with rumors of a riot near Tuskaloosa, the particulars of which we have not yet been able to learn. It was once reported that fourteen colored and three white men had been killed, but the number of deaths has dwindled to one. It appears that one night, about three weeks ago [April], four young men visited the residence of a negro near Northport, and tried to break into his house, using threatening language against a colored man who was harbored there. After they had been warned to leave and refused to do so, the colored man shot into the crowd, killing of the young men, who is represented to have been the leader of the movement. The rest of the party returned to Northport for reinforcement, and during their absence, the family left for parts unknown. There is still much excitement in Tuskaloosa over the affair, and ... the Governor has been petitioned to send militia there to keep the peace.” According to the 5/15 Journal, two drunk white men, “desperadoes of ‘Sipsey Swamp’” hassled a black boy and told his father; the father and “another freedman” found the men and exchanged hot words. Later additional “Sipseyites” went to the cabin of the father and were fired on; “Up to this time, therefore, the deaths arising from this particular difficulty were two white men and two negroes. In the meantime, a freedman had been arrested and put in jail. He was regularly apprehended under a warrant which charged participation in some of the riotous proceedings to which we are referring. It may be mentioned, however, that this prisoner knew many of the Sipsey men engaged in this mob, and might be an important witness to identity them. ... On the first night after the Sipsey roughs learned of the imprisonment they went to the jail, broke it open, took the negro out, carried him a few yards from the building, directly in front of the old State House and murdered him in cold blood.” The 5/29 Journal publishes a letter which refers to a black man being taken from the jail in Tuskaloosa [Tuscaloosa] and shot by a mob sometime within the recent past. From the Monitor, “Citizens of other counties, around Tuskaloosa, are earnestly solicited to be on the watch for the negro man Levi Cochrane—one of the murderers of young Findley. ... If apprehended, we would be glad to be informed in what county jail he is lodged.”

notes:
The 5/5 Dispatch reports that Joe Holmes, a black member of the Virginia Constitutional Convention, was shot and killed at Charlotte Court House in the afternoon of Monday [3rd] by a white man named John Marshall Jr. or by one of his two friends (— Boyd and — Morris) following an altercation. The Express, dateline Richmond, 4 May, that Joseph Holmes was killed at Charlotte courthouse on the 3rd: “A personal difficulty occurred between him and John Marshall, son of Judge Marshall, of whose family Holmes was formerly a body servant. Both parties drew pistols and commenced firing, which was participated in my Marshall’s friends. After being shot, Holmes walked into the courthouse and fell dead.” In the Herald’s account, there was a confrontation between John Marshall, accompanied by friends, and Joseph Holmes followed by a fire fight in which Holmes was shot by Marshall and/or his friends. The Messenger reprints a story from the Richmond [Daily State] Journal which reports the murder of Joseph R. Holmes; “In the morning of the day, on which Holmes met his death, Marshall and his party had pursued and shot at a colored man, and boasted that they had killed him. Marshall was heard to several witnesses to say. ‘I’ve killed one negro, and I’ll have Joe Holmes’ blood before night.’— ... Holmes was in the Court House, endeavoring to get a warrant for the arrest of Marshall for shooting the colored man .... [apparent Marshall confronted Holmes, accompanied by his brother Griffin, a cousin named Boyd, and a Mackey Morris; Marshall hit Holmes on the head and then shot him in the chest] ... Holmes started for the Court House, and the whole party commenced firing upon him as he had. ... just as he entered the Court-House he fell dead. ... Holmes was murdered because he was a Republican, and obnoxious to the young Rebel Democracy of whom Marshall is a leader in that section.” The Virginian account adds nothing but characterizes the convention as the “Black Crook Convention.” According to the 5/11 Dispatch, a black man named Jack Watkins was charged with complicity in the murder of Holmes: apparently after escaping Charlotte courthouse after killing Holmes, John Marshall and another young man named Richardson stayed at the home of Jack Watkins before moving on—guess Watkins would have been charged with adding and abetting.

Note: the Richmond Daily State Journal is not available online in any resource. This is not a classic lynching and it appears that Holmes was killed by the bullet fired by one person, yet the circumstances suggest that it was more than a straightforward racially motivated murder.

The next morning she, in company with her sister, went in search of her husband, and found him hung a short distance from the house, on the public road, dead. She also found hung, the body of her brother, near that of her husband. ... On the breast of her husband’s body was pinned a piece of paper, ‘All barn-burners, and women-offenders, we Ku klux hang until dead, dead, dead.’”—these were the barns of “Messrs. Jones, Minor and Morrow. The 3/8 Herald reports the testimony of Lucinda Morrow that the lynching took place in Orange County but by “Ku Klux from Alamance [County].” According to the 3/16 Herald, citing ku klux murders in Alamance county, “Thomas J. Morrow and his brother-in-law, both colored, were taken some time in the fall of 1869 from their homes and families, and hanged by the neck, for alleged barn burning.”

The citizens on repairing to the place where they heard the shots, found the dead bodies of Avant and Thompson. Where the Ku-Klux came from was a conjecture. From the internet: “Cyrus Guy was born circa 1845, in Alamance County, North Carolina. He is listed in the 1860 census as "Si Guye" and as a "mulatto," living in the household of William Guye (a laborer, and likely Cy's father), along with five other members of the Guy family. The Guy fa mily also appears in the 1850 (without Cyrus) and 1870 censuses.
   According to a 1937 WPA interview with Ben Johnson, a former slave of Gilbert Craig, Cyrus Guy was hanged "for a scandalous insult to a white woman" by a group of Ku Kluxers "a hundert strong." They tried him in the woods, and scratched Guy's arm to draw blood in order to write a proclomation or "sentence" that Guy was to be hung "'tween the heavens and earth till he [is] dead, dead, dead" (which seems to have been a standard Klan hanging oath). The next morning, they hanged Guy on the road, with his sentence over his head. For at least four days, Guy's body hung from the tree, and the sheriff finally took his body down. This period of Orange County history was a time when the Klan harrassed and murdered several black residents of the county; Robert Fitzgerald, a bi-racial teacher who was living in Hillsborough at the time, reported numerous outrages against Orange County's citizens in his diary.
   In a 1871 letter/official statement to the U.S. Office of the Adjutant General from North Carolina Governor William Holden, he documents a story where "A colored boy in Orange County taken at midnight from his father, while they were burning charcoal, and hanged. The charge was that he had made some improper and foolish remark about the white ladies. His body hung ten days until the vultures partly consumed it, and no one during that time dared to take him down."
   A series of receipts, recently scanned by Stewart Dunaway from the North Carolina State Archives, shed some light on the incident and what eventually happened to Guy's remains. A December 2, 1869 appointment from Superior Court Judge George Clarke to John Turner to act as coroner and remove Guy's body states that Guy was hanged on the High Rock Road "above the Poore House," and that Turner was to assemble a jury of twelve men and hold "an inquest over the body" of the then "dead man unknown."
   James McCracken, who lived near where Guy was lynched, was paid by the sheriff to make a coffin and transport Guy's body to the Poor House cemetery; James Bain was paid for digging the grave and for burying Guy. Someone named Fowler was also paid for his part in the burying process. Guy was buried in the Orange County Poor House cemetery, in a grave that is currently unmarked.”

notes:
From the News, “Texas Ranger says D. McKinney, lately of Austin, shot Clay Searcy, Esq., of Anderson, in Navasota [Grimes Co.], on the 13th. McKenney, is reported to be a desperado, and the Ranger say he behaved in an outrageous manner towards Searcy before shooting him.  ... Searcy was not killed, but we presume he cannot recover. McKinney was sent to jail in Anderson [Grimes Co.]. The Ranger tells the sequel: Mayor Jones sent a party to Anderson to bring down McKinney for trial [to Navasota]. On the way back with the prisoner, in a strip of woods, the guard was halted by a crowd of sixty armed men. There were ordered to lay down their airs and give up the prisoner. When the guard protested and remonstrated, they were ordered peremptorily to hush up. The men were all disguised and blackened, and all spoke in broken English and Dutch. McKinney was hung to a limb, and the rope or limb broke and he fell down. He was then tied securely and hung over ten feet high, and left hanging.” The same story appears in the Herald. The Bulletin’s account reprints a story from the Navasota Ranger, in which Clay Searcy, of Anderson, was shot by Dan McKinney, from Goliad Co., during an altercation in a barber shop; McKinney was jailed in Anderson; when being transported from Anderson to Navasota, McKinney was taken by sixty men and hung. According to the Express, citing the Houston Journal, there was an altercation between Captain H. Clay Sarcy, a lawyer, and a man named McKinney, a “horse drover”, from Goliad county, which happened in a barber shop in Navasota [believe this should be Anderson] on Tuesday, the 11th.; “On Wednesday evening, the jailor of Anderson, with six men, started with McKinney to Navasota, where he was to be tried the next day. About half way between Anderson and Navasota, the guard was met by an armed force of about fifty men, and the prisoner was rescued, since which nothing has been heard of him. Sercy, when last heard from, was in a critical condition ....”

According to the Picayune, “There has been lynch law violence in the back portion of Rapides parish, of which Dorinda Huffman and her son Moses, and Henry Cornies, all colored, were victims. They were hung persons who were Union men during the war. Nathan Green, another negro, was shot and killed. Warrants are out for the men accused of these outrages.” From the Republican, “Rapides Parish. ... Nathan Green, Henry Corwin, Moses Huffman, and Marinda Huffman were murdered on the twenty-first of March on Holloway prairie. ... Green, Corwin and the Huffmans were taken from houses while attending prayer meetings, and one of them shot and the others hung.” From the “Report of the Joint Committee. ... Parish of Rapides. In the parish of Rapids it is in evidence that on the 21st day of March, 1868, Henry Cornice, Nathan Green, Marinda Hoffman and Moses Hoffman (all colored), were murdered while attending a prayer meeting at Hollowell’s Prairie, by a party of men, among whom were Larken D. Carby, Willard Carby, Lewis Folly, and A. C. Bell, who were the actual murderers, and Wm. Cartin and Spencer Davenport, who were witnesses. The two Carbys and Folly were arrested by the United States authorities. The parties above mentioned as having been murdered, had met and were having a prayer meeting in one of their houses, when about 9 o’clock P. M., two men cam e and guarded the door, while two others went inside and tied the hands of Henry Cornice, Marinda Hoffman and Nathan Green, and took them out and hung them; during the time they were guarding the door, one of the parties named Moses Hoffman, undertook to make his escape, and was shot down dead on the spot.” In the “Use of the Army” account, page 341, the victims are: Henry Cornie, Nathan Green, Marinda Hoffman, and Moses Hoffman and the place was Hollaway’s Prairie.

Note: according to advertisements in the Alexandria Louisiana Democrat, Rapides Nursery is located one mile from Alexandria on the Hollowell’s Prairie road.

notes:
The Tri-Weekly Republican prints a letter from Bastrop, dated 28 March, reporting “This week as been one of excitement to Bastrop county. Two freedman have been killed, one white man by the name of Taylor (a stranger) was shot to pieces in the street by a party of men of De Witt county, and two other white men who were accidentally passing at the time were severely wounded.” The 4/2 Bulletin states, citing the Bastrop Advertiser of 28 March, “On Wednesday evening last, 25th instant, our town was the scene of considerable excitement and confusion by the sudden and unexpected advent of a posse of citizens, eight in number, from Clinton, DeWitt county, in search of a party of desperadoes charged with horse stealing and murder. Two men, named Charley Taylor and James Sharpe, said to be connected with a clan of 14 men, charged with horse stealing, left DeWitt county a few days since .... they arrived in Bastrop on Monday [23rd] last. On the afternoon of Wednesday the posse of citizens ... arrived in our town and discovered Taylor and Sharp walking up Main street ... demanded their surrender—but they seemed to not to regard this order ... [Taylor tried to enter a store but was shot by the DeWitt men; Sharp escaped temporarily but was soon captured] ... He [Sharp] was taken into custody by Mr. Sutton, in charge of the posse in search, and the same evening started with the prisoner to DeWitt county. ... Two Germans from the country, named Longee, father and son, were accidentally wounded during the firing—the father slightly, but the son severely, though not dangerously.” From the 4/7 News, citing the Bastrop Advertiser of 4 April, “We have learned from reliable authority that the squad of eight citizens from DeWitt county, under command of Mr. Sutton, who killed Charley Taylor in this place on Wednesday, 25th inst., and captured his associate James Sharpe, and started with him to DeWitt county, after passing Lockhart [Caldwell Co.], riddled their prisoner with bullets, a short distance from that place, and left the body on the roadside.” The same report appears in the Texas Republican. According to the 4/14 Bulletin, citing the Bastrop Advertiser, that “The young German Longe, who was accidentally wounded in this place on the 24th ult., in the firing by the party under Sutton, from DeWitt county, who killed Charles Taylor, on that occasion, died of the wound on Tuesday night last.”

The Tri-Weekly Republican prints a letter from Bastrop, dated 28 March, reporting “This week as been one of excitement to Bastrop county. Two freedman have been killed, one white man by the name of Taylor (a stranger) was shot to pieces in the street by a party of men of De Witt county, and two other white men who were accidentally passing at the time were severely wounded.”

Note: 1860 Bastrop census lists a Frank Lang, 40, born in Germany, along with his wife, Frannia Lang, 47, and male son, Frank, 10, who was along born in Germany. Couldn’t find this family in 1870 Texas census.

Two men, named Charley Taylor and James Sharpe, said to be connected with a clan of 14 men, charged with horse stealing, left DeWitt county a few days since .... they arrived in Bastrop on Monday [23rd] last. On the afternoon of Wednesday the posse of citizens ... arrived in our town and discovered Taylor and Sharp walking up Main street ... demanded their surrender—but they seemed to not to regard this order ... [Taylor tried to enter a store but was shot by the DeWitt men; Sharp escaped temporarily but was soon captured] ... He [Sharp] was taken into custody by Mr. Sutton, in charge of the posse in search, and the same evening started with the prisoner to DeWitt county. ... One report is, that the parties killed were horse thieves; another is that the killing grew out of an old neighborhood feud. Perryville is near where the corners of McLennan, Coryell and Bell counties join.” The 5/7 Tri-Weekly Republican, citing the Waco Examiner of 28 April, states “Just as we go to press a report reaches us, for the authenticity of which we do not vouch, as we have no time to inquire into it, that one night last week a number of men visited the neighborhood of Perry, in this county [McLennan], and going to the house of a man by the name of Shackelford, called him out, and, without a moment’s warning, fired upon and killed him. A brother of Shackelford’s fired upon the party, killing one of them, said to be a man by the name of Jackson.” According to the 5/28 Tri-Weekly Republican, on 23 April “... a party of men led by two rebel captains and numbering about sixteen men, went to the house of Benjamin s. Schoonover, near Perry in the county of McLennan, and waking up the family, ordered the men, composed of the father and two sons, to take their stand in the yard, when they opened fire upon them with the six-shooters, killing the old man and one of his sons, George, the other escaping. ... On the Tuesday [21st] previously the same party had killed a man named Shackleford, who was a member of one of the companies raised by John Hancock for the U. S. service during the war. A brother of Shackleford avenged his death by killing one of the attacking party, an assassin named Jackson.” From the South-Western, “We learn that there were seven persons in all killed in the Perryville affair last week. Only two Shoonovers were killed, the father and son, George. The other son, Pete, escaped. A man named Jackson, not mention in our last, was Ed Jackson, of the attacking party, and is reported as having been a man highly respected.” The Republican publishes a letter demanding “… bring to justice the assassins of the following men, all assassinated in Bell county, or by assassins from Bell county, and of their dates given: 1868. ... Ed Jackson.” Also, same page, “… bring to justice the assassins of the following men, all assassinated in Bell county, or by assassins from Bell county, and of their dates given:  1868 ... Shackleford.”

Note: there’s a Perryville in Bastrop Co. and another in Wood county but neither are near “corner of McLennan, Coryell, and Bell counties” According to The Handbook of Texas Online, “Perry was a small community two miles north of Moody in southwestern McLennan County.” The 1860 Walker Co. census lists a John C. Shackelford, 19, living with his mother, Mary, 51, and male siblings: Thomas G. Shackelford, 22, and George W. Shackelford, 16, and female sibs. Neither John C. nor George appear in the 1870 Texas census. Don’t know if this George W. Shackelford is the same as the lynching victim.

Jasper confessed the crime after it was conclusively proven against him, and he was committed to jail [presumably in Livingston, the county seat]. The citizens in the neighborhood, where the murder was committed, came disguised at night, broke in the jail, and took Jasper out and hung him, between the Wooden place and Mr. Sam’l Hale’s, where he was found the next morning. Waller was arrested, because he was the jailor, or rather the assistant to the jailor.” From the Enquirer, citing the Livingston Journal of 16 May, reports that the lynching of Jasper happened about “two weeks ago”.

Bowles said he was twenty-four years old, and had a mother, two brothers and three sisters living in Austin. Miller died defiantly, Bowles died calmly, and Lee coolly proposed climbing the tree and fixing the rope to hang himself. He was Bradley county, Tennessee, and had a permit form Brownlow to carry arms for his protection.” The Bulletin has a very long report on this incident noting that Miller, Bowles and Lee were captured in Panola county and states that Bowles and Lee were hung  “at the town of Douglas”—this is probably Douglass in Nacogdoches Co., which is about ten miles from the southern border of Panola Co., and a few miles east of the Cherokee Co. border, and Miller was riddled with bullets when he tried to escape, presumably at the same place; apparently Masters said that he was from Anderson Co.

He was also a leader in the insurrectionary movement above referred to. ... on the nights of the 26th and 27th of last month, a large number of colored persons, about forty or fifty in number, marched into the town of Cornersville in military order, carrying army guns, congregating and about a school house on the public ....” The Gazette reports the testimony of a Wells Scott, of Cornersville: “Further says that on the night of the 5th of July a party of the Ku-Klux Klan went to the house of Mint Burks, on Samuel Marshall’s farm, and took him from his bed and killed him.” From the American, citing testimony of the Secretary of State of Tennessee reported in the New York Tribune of 9 April, “In the Fall of 1868 I remember hearing of the killing of a colored man by the name of Burch, or Burk, near Cornersville, in Maury county. I think he was accused of attending a debating society and justifying emancipation.”

notes:
According to the 7/17 Republican, reporting a letter dated 8 July, “On Monday [6th] night, about two o’clock, a party of rowdies in disguise—generally believed to be a squad of the Ku Klux Klan called at the house of a freemen, in Coulee Croche, twelve miles south of Opelousas, and aroused the inmates. The man of the house lying ill on his bed, suspicious of foul play, called for his gun. A volley was immediately fired upon the cabin and its inmates by the Klan. Three women and one man were dangerously wounded; two are not expected to recover. The 7/18 Republican, headline “The Coulee Croche Massacre. Three Killed and Two Wounded,” prints a letter dated 12 July, “Yesterday I obtained from eye-witnesses the following particulars of the midnight raid which culminated in the massacre of Coulee Croche, twelve miles south of Opelousas, on Monday, July 6. A party of men, about fifteen in number, armed and disguised, near twelve o’clock rode up to the house of John B. Francois, a freeman, on or near the plantation of Marcell Richard, ... [put a notice on his door saying that he must leave within twenty days, and signed K.K.K. They then rode to other houses and made threats]. ...  A house in the vicinity was next surrounded. Man, alarmed, stepped to the door, and seeing the crowd cried out, ‘Pass here.’ He was immediately fired upon. Firing lasted some five minutes. Several buckshot lodged in his arm. His wife was mortally wounded in the head, and died next day. In a room adjoining a woman with child was shot in left breast. A miscarriage immediately followed, and mother and child are both dead. Another [woman] was severely wounded in the thigh. Affidavits have been made against the following parties who have been recognized among the raiders: Andrew Meche, G. Meche, Cyprien Meche, Edward C. Gardnier, and Thomas Moore. From the Report of the Joint Committee, page 16, “Parish of St. Landry ... On the 7th day of July, 1868, two colored men [women?] and one child were murdered and two colored men wounded by a party of men in disguise. No clue to the guilty parties has been obtained.” A second entry on same page, “On the 7th of July, 1868, a party of twelve or fifteen men, masked, among which Andre Mèche, Geracis Mèche, Cyprian Mèche, Edward C. Gardner, Thomas Moore, Alexander Smith and Pat Louney were recognized, came about 10 o’clock at night to the house of Spencer Stewart, colored, killed his wife and mortally wounded his grand-daughter, and also wounded himself in the arm and shoulder, and his daughter-in-law in the thigh.” On page 17, it’s reported that “... about fifteen of them surrounded a cabin on Mr. M. Richard’s plantation [on the 6th], and fired into the same, and wounded a man named Stewart, his wife, and three others of his friends. His wife and two others have since died.” Testimony in “Use of the Army”, page 188, says that at one or two o’clock in the morning of 7 July, 12-15 persons attacked the home of Spencer Stewart, who was living in a house belonging to Marcel Richard, containing Spencer, his wife, his step-son, John Bapteste, and his wife, and the step-son’s daughter who was pregnant; Spencer’s wife and daughter of his step-son were killed and her child; a list of those participating is essentially the same as the list above. But on page 159, “Affidavit of Spencer Stewart, of Saint Landry, shows that his house was beset by a party of twelve or fifteen men, on the 7th of July, who murdered his wife, mortally wounded the daughter of his step-son, who died two days after; wounded deponent in arms and sholder, and the wife of his step-son in the thigh, and riddled the house with bullets.”—no mention of a child.

Note: there is a discrepancy on how many died: (1) Stewart’s wife, his granddaughter—daughter of his step-son, and her unborn child; or (2) Stewart’s wife and his granddaughter. Going to out the two adult women as lynch victims and the child as a coincidental death. There is also discrepancy as to whether the attack was on the 6th or 7th. Coulee Croche is a stream in St. Landry Parish.

One of the negroes supposed to have been concerned in the murder of young Freeland is still at large.” According to the Ledger, citing the Columbia Herald of 18 July, the murderer of Tink Freeland, who was killed on Sunday [11th], was Alfred Rainey, 14, and that he was being taken to Columbia to jail when another party “... took the prisoner forcibly from them and immediately hung and shot him. In his confession he implicated several other negroes, who were immediately arrested. No convicting evidence could be brought against one of them, a woman, and she was released. Another one, a young man, arrested as an accomplice, was brought to town and lodged in jail. On Tuesday [13th] he was ordered to be tried in his own district, by Esquire Harris, but before the trial came off he was taken from his guard by a party of men, unknown, and has not since been heard from.” This also appeared in the Herald. The white people would not permit it to be done. ... [from al letter] ... Great excitement at Millican. The negroes in mass demanded one William Holliday to hang him. The white people turned out to protect him. A line of battle was formed and skirmishing for about an hour. Five of the negroes were killed. Number of wounded not known.” From the 8/1 Bulletin, “The riot at Millican [Brazos Co.] on the 15th and 16th inst., is yet unexplained, but all accounts agree in stating that 25 or 30 freedmen were killed, whilst not a single white man was slain.” From the Herald, citing the Galveston News, writes “... the incipient riot [at Millican] was quelled ... the number killed, as ear as he [Lt. Green U. S. Army] could learn, was seven blacks; no white man killed or wounded. The first reports of the killing were greatly exagerted [sic].” The 8/4 Bulletin reports, page 4, that “That the whites were in no danger is evidenced by the fact that none were hurt, although five blacks were killed. The killing of the first freedman for entering the town was murder, as was also that of Parson Brooks.” On page 5 is the “Official Report on the Millican Riot ... On the following day (the 18th) I learned from a freedman that Brooks had been hung, which was subsequently found true, his body having been found on the 25th by a freedman while hunting stock. His body was decomposed to such an extent as to render identification impossible except by articles of clothing, pencil, knife, and the loss of a portion of his forth finger on the right hand. .... The number killed and wounded are as follows: Harry Thomas, c. m. [colored man], the leader of the freedmen, Moses Hardy, c. m., King Holiday, c. m., wounded and the 17th; Dan Zepher, c. m., killed on Thursday, the 16th; Geo. E. Brooks, c. m., preacher, supposed to have been killed on the 18th; wounded, Mae [Mac] Moore, c. m., short though right shoulder, slight wound, and Robert —, c. m., wounded and missing. The Courier publishes a letter from Crab Orchard [Lincoln Co.], dated 20 September, that states that “last night” two members of the Adams family and three-four of their friends attacked the home of Cummins, near the Lincoln-Pulaski border; Rodney Adams broke down the door and was immediately killed—the rest of the mob shot and killed Cummins’ daughter and Cummins himself. From the Whig, “On last Saturday night, the 19th, instant, some eight or ten Ku-Klux visited the house of a citizen of Pulaski county, Kentucky, by the name of Stephen Cummins, and in an engagement with him killed him and his daughter. He killed one of them dead on the ground and wounded another, who I have learned has since died. The one killed dead on the ground was Rodney Adams, of Lincoln county, Kentucky. The crowd of Ku-Klux were from Crab Orchard [Lincoln Co.], Kentucky, and vicinity. After they had killed Cummins, his daughter was lamenting over her dying father, and they shot her, putting the pistol almost against her person. ... His wife was lamenting over her dead husband, and they ordered her with an oath to dry up or they would shoot her, and then turned to Cummins, where he lay dead on the floor, and shot him again, remarking that there was one d-d Abolitionist out of the way.” According to the Herald, on the night of the 19th Adams, of Garrard County, was one of four or five men who attacked the house of a man named Cummins who lived “on the line between Rocastle [Rockcastle Co.] and Pulaski [county]; Cummins shot Adams and then Adams shot Cummins—both men died; the shooting continued with the result that Cummins’ daughter was killed and his son “dangerously wounded”. This was part of an ongoing feud between the two families. Apparently Cummins had killed Adams’ father in a fight sometime past. From the 4/3/1871 Gazette’s list of anarchy in Kentucky: “Mob attacks Cummins’ house, in Pulaski. Cummins, his daughter and a man named Adams killed in the attack, September 18, 1868.” From the Memorial, No. 22. Mob attacked Cumin’s house in Pulaski County; Cumins, his daughter, and a man named Adams killed in the attack, September 18, 1868.”

Note: going to assume that the mob was from Lincoln Co., that it wasn’t ku-klux, and the incident happened either in the late hours of the 18th or early hours of the 19th. Lincoln Co. is adjacent to Garrard Co., and both are just north of Pulaski county. Rodney Adams was a member of the lynch mob and his was a coincidental death.

One the same morning (Wednesday,) a number of negroes from adjoining plantations posted themselves along the road near Mr. Brownlee’s, and when the latter left the residence of Mr. Saggus, his father-in-law, in company with Mr. Francis Ogden, they surrounded them, and then deliberately shot them down. notes: From the Gazette, “Huntsville, Ala., Nov. 1—Three hundred Ku Klux were parading about last night, while a Republican mass meeting was in progress, 50 or sixty shots were fired. Judge Horton, a marked man, was mortally wounded. Three negroes were killed and many wounded—all Republicans.” The Press gives his name as Gustavus Horton and that he was a probate judge. The 11/6 Herald states: “Judge Horton, a marked man, was mortally wounded. Two negroes were killed, and many wounded, all Republicans.” The 11/4 Avalanche, citing the Huntsville Independent of 1 November, reports that a large body of ku klux rode into Huntsville and paraded around the public square and then retired some distance; concurrently there was a mass meeting of “Radicals”, mostly black, on the square. The black started a general firefight that resulted in two blacks killed (one outright and one fatally wounded) and Judge Thurlow, white, being fatally wounded. In this account, the Radical blacks were the instigators of the violence; “The negro killed was named Alexander Reid; shot through the heart at the foot of the steps leading to the Mayor’s office. George Roper, negro, mortally wounded, shot through the body, in the arm, and beat over the head. He was known, certainly, to be one of the attacking party, being seen with a shot gun in his hands. The third negro, named Milton Martin, had a flesh wound in the side.” The 11/7 Avalanche reports that Judge Thurlow died of his wounds.

Note Simpson Mason was assassinated by the ku klux on 19 September in Fulton Co. Based on these report it seems reasonable to believe that Bryant was lynched by the ku klux in early November, most likely in Fulton Co.

Matthews ordered four negroes to take Perry into the cane, interrogated him, after which they stood him against a tree and shot his ear off. He broke from them. They then interrogated Jackson, and shot him in the face, wounding him mortally. He lived to tell who did it, and said the force then went to the house of Thomas Hooper—aged sixty—mounted him, passed Lewisburg in the night took him to a bottom eight miles below [south] town, and kept him there all night. The next morning they tied him on a mule, with a rope around his neck, fastened to the horn of a negro’s saddle, in which condition he was met half way between Portland [Ashley Co.] and Springfield [Conway Co.], on a by-road, and near there was afterward found shot dead with a load of buck shot. ... The detail of negroes went to Springfield, and reported that he had been killed in attempting to escape. the Sheriff, (Radical), on seeing him, pronounced him murdered, and he deemed the entire proceedings as illegal.”

newkirk: Unnamed White, 12/1866, Greene Co., White Male, Rape
notes:
From the Leader, “A respectable married lady was violated in Greene county last week, in the absence of her husband. Five negro men and three low white men are implicated. The five negroes and one white man are in jail. There is great excitement among the people.” From the Herald, “Five negroes were taken from the Green county jail, North Carolina, on Tuesday [8th] last, by a body of armed men and lynched. There were charged with outraging the person of Mrs. Miller.” Essentially the same story appears in the Dealer and the Herald-Tribune. From the Times-Picayune, citing the New Bern (NC) Commercial of the 12th, “A white man and three negroes, a few days ago, violated the person of Mrs. F. N. Miller, of Green county, during the absence of her husband. [They were arrested.] ... on Tuesday night last, a large number of them [citizens of Green county] took the prisoners out of jail and [illegible] subjected them to a horrible, but well-merited death.” Citing the Raleigh Standard, the Gazette reports, “The jail in Greene county broken open and five men taken out; their throats cut and their bodies thrown in Contenina [?] creek.” No date given. The 1/15 Standard, citing the Newbern Journal of Commerce, says one white man and five black men have been arrested and changed with outraging Mrs. F. X. Miller; “Last Tuesday night an armed band of men visited the jail, arrested the jailor, took the keys form him, removed the prisoners and inflicted upon them a punishment which the brutal crime charged upon them richly deserved, although the mode of punishment cannot be approved by a law abiding people. Lynch law cannot obtain the sanction of the good citizen, though he may believe the criminal richly deserved the punishment.” According to the Journal, citing the Newbern Journal of Commerce, “Bodies Found.— ... We understand two or more of the party recently lynched in Greene County, for the outrage committed on Mrs. Miller, have been found in the Neuse [river].”

Note: Snow Hill is the county seat of Greene Co. Going to assume that  five black men and one white man lynched.

Trowbridge was under indictment in our Court for having killed a negro in Perryville some two years previously.”—later in the story his name is Jerry Trowbridge.

notes:
From the Whig, “The Charleston Courier of Thursday says: ‘A private letter from Pendleton states that a serious outbreak had just occurred at Pickens Court House, South Carolina. In the melee a resident of Pickens, a Mr. Hunnicutt, was killed. A military force from Anderson had been ordered up to the scene of disturbance.” From the Telegraph, citing the Columbia Chronicle, “We are informed that on Saturday night last, in Pickens district, near Perryville, on the Blue Ridge Railroad, a white man named Bryce was engaged in opening a Union League. It is not known whether there were any other whites present than Bryce. The number of colored men was about two hundred. During the exercises, a white youth named Smith, who was intoxicated, forced his way into the Lague and exhibited his pistol, but is not certainly known that the weapon was discharged. The appearance of young Smith exasperated the negroes, and they sallied out to overtake him. He thereupn ran a quarter or half a mile, and took refuge in a building where a debating society, composed of the young [white] people of the neighborhood, was peacefully holding a meeting. Smith was in nowise connected with this society. The negroes surrounded the house, a large proportion being armed, it is said, with pistols and muskets, and commenced an indiscriminate attack upon the members, who were unarmed .... One of the shots fired by the negroes took effect upon the person of a young man named Hunnicutt, which proved fatal in less than five minutes.” From the Constitutionalist, citing the Anderson [SC] Intelligencer, “The Pickens Riot.—We have no ascertained any further important particulars concerning the disgraceful riot near Hunnicutt’s Crossing, on Saturday night, 12 inst. ... we learn that Alex. Bryce, Jr., of Wallhalla, and several negroes in that vicinity, were arrested by the military and lodged in Pickens jail. Upon affidavits, the civil authorities arrested Rev. Elias Cannady (colored), of this place [Anderson], and he has been sent to Pickens for trial, as one of the leading spirits of this horrible outrage. He is a Baptist preacher, and well known throughout this section. A gentleman who left Pickens on Monday afternoon informs us that the grand jury had found true bills against seven of the number arrested.” The Democrat reports that “Nine colored persons and a white man named Alexander Bryce, all members of a Union League, at Walhalla, were indicted for the murder of Miles M. N. Hunnicut, a white youth, fourteen years of age, on the evening of the 12 ultimo, while the latter was present at a debating society near Hunnicutt’s Crossing in Pickens District. ... on the evening of the 12th of October, these youths [young men of Oak Grove academy], their parents and friends, had thus assembled, and that while engaged in their usual exercises, without a suspicion of trouble or difficulty, they were rudely disturbed by curses and denunciations, which brought every inmate of the house to his feet in amazement and alarm. Note: until 1868, Walhalla was in Pickens Co.; in 1868 Oconee Co. was created which encompassed Walhalla.

The Appeal reports, “About half a mile north of Shelby Depot, and about four miles from Hickory Withe [Fayette Co.], the bodies of two men were discovered in the Loosahatchie river .... It is thought that they were victims of the prowling band who have been committing outrages in that vicinity, and as yet have eluded the vigilance of the people of the neighborhood, who have been successful only in capturing and executing one [Frank Jones] of the most daring among them.” From the Dispatch, “Judge Lynch. Prath. Going to assume the location as Shelby Co. but could have been either Tipton or Fayette counties. Date uncertain. Unknown number of killers.

notes:
The News publishes a letter from Brownsville dated 5 December, “... I learn this evening by the mail from the upper country that the rancheros, exasperated at being left without protection against the cattle thieves, which are doing such business on this frontier, have formed themselves into a vigilance committee. A few days ago they captured three thieves as they were on the point of crossing a large drove of stolen cattle into Mexico and hung them on the spot.” The Bulletin writes, “We have a file of the Rio Grande Courier to December 28th, from which we glean the following information. ... In the neighborhood of Fort Laredo, some cattle thieves stole three hundred head from the Mexicans and crossed with them into Texas leaving one beef that had given out, a few miles from the river. According to the Times, “about six weeks ago” an “outrage” was committed by a black man named Kit on two children of a Mr. Hudgins, near Eldorado; Kit was recently captured and was taken and lynched while being transported back to Eldorado. The Republican states, citing the Monroe (La.) Intelligencer, that two children of John G. Hudgins were murdered on the morning of the 7th [apparently in November, 12 year-old girl and 8 year-old boy]—there was an attempted rape of the girl and her body was mutilated. From the Champion, “Cairo, Dec. 15.—The negro who committed [sic] the outrage on two children, near lEdorado [sic], Ark., a short time since, an account of which was telegraphed, has since been arrested, and admitted the crime. He was immediately lynched by the citizens of Eldorado.” From the Advertiser, “The Arkansas Outrage—The outrage which was committed by a negro named Kit on two children of Mr. Hudgins, near Eldorado, Ark., has been promptly avenged. Short after the outrage was committed, four colored men, stimulated by the reward of $1,000, started after Kit, and found him working on a farm abut fifty miles from Eldorado. He admitted to them that he had one the fiendish deed, but stated as an excuse that he did it in revenge. On being brought back Judge Lynch took charge of him and executed him in short order.” From the Union, “A negro in Arkansas was lynched as soon as caught for an outrage upon two children.”

Note: the Civil War diary of George W. Lewis reports that the unnamed black man was burned to death on 22 November for a 8 November murder of two children.
